REFERRAL LETTER

Dear Dr. Verdi,

I am writing to refer my patient, Mr. Rossi, 87, for further management of his Type 2 diabetes mellitus. He is a retired mechanic who previously worked at Fiat.

Mr. Rossi presents with persistent hyperglycemia despite compliant metformin therapy. His most recent fasting glucose is 180 mg/dL, and his HbA1c is 8.5%. He reports general fatigue and sluggishness. He lives in Milan with his wife, Maria, 85. His daughter, Elena, 45, frequently assists with his diet.

Vital signs today: BP 145/90 mmHg, HR 82 bpm. He reports a recent fall in the kitchen, resulting in a knee injury with pain scored 4/10. There is no head trauma. He has a family history of Parkinson's disease (brother Giorgio, 89) and Hashimoto's thyroiditis (wife Maria).

Please evaluate for insulin initiation or adjustment of oral hypoglycemics. I have attached his recent lab results and medication list.

His insurance ID is IT-998877-45.

Thank you for your assistance.

Sincerely,
Dr. Bianchi
San Raffaele Hospital

Neurological: Intact sensation in the upper extremity. ECG: Normal sinus rhythm, no ST changes. X-ray Left Arm: No fracture, no dislocation, soft tissue shadowing consistent with mild strain.
ASSESSMENT

2. Cardiac disease ruled out based on normal ECG and clinical presentation.
PLAN

2. Prescribed Ibuprofen 400 mg TID for 5 days.
3. Physical therapy referral if pain persists beyond two weeks.

[doctor] Good morning, Mr. Esteban. Thank you for coming in. I see you were referred by Dr. Lucien Vercelli at Hôpital de la Tour. How have you been since our last visit?
[patient] Hello, Doctor. I’m a bit nervous. I’m 38 years old and I’ve been having this persistent pain in my left arm. It started about two weeks ago.
[doctor] Let’s look at that. When exactly did the pain start?
[patient] It was a Tuesday. I remember clearly because I was at the gym. I was doing bicep curls, and I felt a sharp twinge.
[doctor] And the pain has stayed since then?
[patient] Yes. It’s not constant, but it’s there. Especially when I lift my arm. My wife thinks it’s just a strain, but I’m worried.
[doctor] Why are you worried? Do you have a family history of heart issues?
[patient] Well, my father had a heart attack when he was young. And my brother has Parkinson's disease. I don't want to ignore a symptom.
[doctor] I understand. Let's check your vitals first. The nurse will be in shortly. In the meantime, can you tell me about your daily routine?
[patient] Sure. I work as a logistics coordinator for a shipping company. I sit a lot, but I try to exercise.
[doctor] That’s good. What about your diet?
[patient] I eat pretty well. I cook at home. I love Spanish food, but I try to keep it light.
[doctor] Good. Now, regarding the arm pain, does it radiate anywhere? Chest, jaw, neck?
[patient] Sometimes it goes up to my shoulder, but not really into my chest. No jaw pain.
[doctor] Any numbness or tingling?
[patient] A little tingling in the fingers, but mostly it’s a dull ache.
[doctor] Okay. Let’s do a physical exam. Please raise your left arm.
[patient] Like this?
[doctor] Yes. I’ll palpate the area. Does this hurt?
[patient] A little. Right here, near the elbow.
[doctor] This sounds like a musculoskeletal issue, possibly a tendon strain or a Baker's cyst, though that’s usually in the knee. Let’s get an X-ray to rule out anything structural.
[patient] Do I need an ECG?
[doctor] Given your age and the nature of the pain, it’s less likely to be cardiac, but we’ll do one to be safe. The nurse will take you to the lab.
[nurse] Hi, Esteban. I’m going to take your blood pressure and run an ECG. Do you have any allergies?
[patient] No, I’m fine.
[nurse] Great. You can send me an email if you have questions after. My email is elena.ruiz at hopital-la-tour dot ch.
[patient] Thanks.
[nurse] Let’s get started.
[doctor] (Entering) I see the ECG is normal. The X-ray shows no fracture. The pain is localized to the brachial area.
[patient] So it’s not my heart?
[doctor] Based on the symptoms and tests, it’s highly unlikely. It’s probably a muscle strain from the gym.
[patient] That’s a relief. I was so scared.
[doctor] It’s good that you came in. I’m going to prescribe some anti-inflammatory medication and recommend rest for a few days.
[patient] How long should I rest?
[doctor] About one week. Avoid heavy lifting.
[patient] Okay. Can I go back to the gym after that?
[doctor] Yes, but gradually. Start with light weights.
[patient] And if it doesn’t get better?
[doctor] If the pain persists or worsens, come back. We can consider an MRI.
[patient] I’ll do that.
[doctor] Also, keep an eye on your blood pressure. You’re young, but it’s good to monitor.
[patient] I do. I check it at home.
[doctor] Good. I’ll send the report to Dr. Vercelli. You can contact him if you have questions.
[patient] Thanks, Doctor.
[doctor] Take care.

[nurse] It’s 118 over 76. That’s good. Heart rate is 82.
[patient] Thank God. I was worried because my heart was racing from the pain.
[nurse] Pain can do that. Did you take anything for it?
[patient] Yes, I took some Ibuprofen this morning.
[nurse] How many tablets?
[patient] Two, 400 milligrams.
[nurse] And did it help?
[patient] A little, but not much. It’s still very sharp when I try to lift my arm above my head.
[nurse] I see. The doctor will examine you soon.
[patient] Yes, please. It’s been like this for... um, about three weeks?
[nurse] Three weeks. Did you have any trauma? A fall or an accident?
[patient] No, no accident. It just started. I was helping my sister move some boxes.
[nurse] Okay. Do you have any family history of joint problems?
[patient] Well, my mother has arthritis. And her brother, my uncle, had shoulder surgery.
[nurse] Got it. I’ll let the doctor know.
[doctor] Hello, Ana. I’m Dr. Vogel. I understand you’re having pain in your left shoulder.
[patient] Yes, Doctor. It’s terrible. I can’t sleep on that side.
[doctor] I’m sorry to hear that. Can you describe the pain for me? Is it sharp, dull, burning?
[patient] It’s sharp. Like a knife. And it’s deep inside.
[doctor] Okay. When did it start?
[patient] About three weeks ago. I was lifting a box, and I felt a pop, and then the pain started.
[doctor] Did you see a doctor or go to a clinic before coming here?
[patient] No, I tried to wait it out. I thought it would go away. But it’s getting worse.
[doctor] I see. Let’s have a look at your shoulder. Please remove your left sleeve.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] Look at that. There’s some mild swelling. Now, I’m going to move your arm. It might hurt a little.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] Raise your arm to the side. Like this.
[patient] Ah! That hurts!
[doctor] I see. That’s called a painful arc. Now, let’s check the range of motion. Bend your elbow and touch your back.
[patient] I can’t reach all the way. It stops here.
[doctor] Okay. Now, let me check for tenderness. Does it hurt here?
[patient] Yes, right there.
[doctor] And here?
[patient] Not as much.
[doctor] Let’s do a specific test. I’m going to rotate your arm. This is the Neer’s test.
[patient] Ouch. That’s the bad spot.
[doctor] Yes, that’s positive. Now the Hawkins-Kennedy test.
[patient] That hurts too!
[doctor] Okay. Both tests are positive, which suggests impingement. Do you have any numbness or tingling in your hand?
[patient] No, no numbness. Just pain.
[doctor] Good. That’s reassuring. I’m going to order an X-ray to rule out any fractures or bone spurs.
[patient] Okay. Do I need an MRI?
[doctor] Not yet. We’ll start with the X-ray. If that’s normal, we might consider an MRI later, but for now, let’s treat the inflammation.
[patient] What treatment?
[doctor] I’m going to prescribe you Celecoxib, which is an anti-inflammatory. And I’ll give you a course of physical therapy.
[patient] Okay. And the Ibuprofen?
[doctor] You can stop the Ibuprofen and take the Celecoxib instead. It’s easier on the stomach.
[patient] Okay. How long will I take it?
[doctor] Two weeks. And I’ll refer you to a specialist for further evaluation.
[patient] Which specialist?
[doctor] An orthopedic surgeon. I’ll write a referral letter.
[patient] Okay. Is there anything I should do in the meantime?
[doctor] Yes. Avoid overhead activities. Don’t lift anything heavy. And apply ice for 15 minutes, three times a day.
[patient] Okay. Ice.
[doctor] Yes. And try to keep your shoulder in a comfortable position.
[patient] Okay. I live in Trieste. I’ll try to rest as much as I can.
[doctor] Good. Here is the prescription and the referral. Make sure to follow up with the specialist within two weeks.
[patient] Okay. Thank you, Doctor.
[doctor] You’re welcome. If the pain gets worse or you develop weakness, come back to the emergency room.
[patient] I will. Thank you.

[doctor] Good morning, Mr. Perera. It is good to see you again. How are you feeling today?
[patient] Good morning, Doctor. Uh, I am... okay. I am fifty-one years old, so you know, the body is not what it used to be.
[doctor] I understand. We are here to discuss your right elbow. Can you tell me what has been bothering you lately?
[patient] Yes. The pain... it is not every day, but when I lift things, you know? I work as a logistics coordinator at Heli Logistics AG in Zurich. So I am on my feet all day.
[doctor] That sounds demanding. Did you try the exercises I gave you last time?
[patient] I did, yes. But my friend, Sanjiv, he says I should just rest. He is five-four now. He thinks I am working too hard.
[doctor] Rest is important, but movement keeps the joint flexible. Did you continue with the medication?
[patient] Yes. I take the Naproxen tablets. My mother, she is seventy-eight, she has the same knee problem. She takes it every day.
[doctor] I see. And how is the pain level? On a scale of one to ten?
[patient] Maybe... four? Five? It is worse in the morning. When I wake up, the arm is stiff. Like a rusty door.
[doctor] That is common with osteoarthritis. Let us take a look at your arm. Please extend your right arm.
[patient] Okay. Like this?
[doctor] Yes. Now, flex it. Bend the elbow.
[patient] It hurts a little here... near the back.
[doctor] I see. Let me check the joint. I am feeling a slight swelling at the 3 o'clock position of the elbow joint. It is mild.
[patient] Is it bad?
[doctor] Not bad. It is inflammation. It responds well to treatment. Did you have any trouble sleeping because of the pain?
[patient] Some nights. I had to move to the other side of the bed. My wife, Kavitha, she sleeps badly too now.
[doctor] I am sorry to hear that. Have you been able to do your hobbies? I remember you mentioned you play squash.
[patient] Yes, I play at The Swiss Squash Club in Bern. I miss it. I cannot swing my arm properly.
[doctor] You should avoid high-impact activities for now. Let us focus on gentle range-of-motion exercises.
[patient] But I want to go back. My colleague, David, he is forty-nine, he plays every Thursday. He keeps inviting me.
[doctor] I understand. But if you strain it now, it will get worse. Let us give it a few weeks.
[patient] Okay. What about the other doctor? Dr. Müller at Klinikum St. Gallen? He referred me to you.
[doctor] Yes, Dr. Müller sent me your records. He suggested we monitor the progression.
[patient] Yes. I moved from Colombo to here ten years ago. The climate here is different. Dry in winter.
[doctor] Dry weather can sometimes make joints feel stiffer, though the evidence is mixed.
[patient] I think so. My neighbor, Mr. Smith, he has a condition called Smith's disease... wait, no, that is not right. He has arthritis too.
[doctor] Arthritis is very common. What type does he have?
[patient] I do not know. Just that his hands are swollen. Like mine.

[patient] My brother, Arjun, he is forty-six. He has diabetes. Type 2.

[doctor] Okay. I will note that. For your elbow, I am going to prescribe a short course of a stronger anti-inflammatory if the pain persists.
[patient] Which one?
[doctor] We will try Etoricoxib. It is different from what you are taking now.
[patient] I will take it. But I will stop if my stomach hurts, yes?
[doctor] Yes. If you have stomach pain, stop and call us. Also, continue the ice packs after work.
[patient] I have ice at home.
[doctor] Good. When do you want to come back?
[patient] In one month?
[doctor] Yes, in one month. If the pain gets worse, you can call our office at 044 123 45 67.
[patient] Okay. Thank you, Doctor.
[doctor] You are welcome, Mr. Perera. Take care of yourself.

[doctor] Good morning, Marion Dupont. Please take a seat. I see you’re here for your follow-up regarding your respiratory health. How have you been feeling since our last visit?
[patient] Hello, Doctor. I’m doing a bit better, but it’s still a bit tricky. I’ve had about two bad episodes this week, mostly at night.
[doctor] I understand. Let’s look at your vitals first. Your blood pressure is 130 over 85, heart rate 78, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. That looks stable. Can you describe the most recent episode?
[patient] It was last Tuesday, around 11:00 pm. I was in my bedroom in Geneva, and I just couldn’t breathe well. I used my rescue inhaler, and it helped after a few puffs.
[doctor] Did you need to go to the emergency room?
[patient] No, I managed it at home. But I was quite scared. I’ve been living in Geneva for three years now, moving here from Lausanne, but the air quality seems different here, or maybe it’s the humidity.
[doctor] That’s a common concern. Let’s review your medications. You are currently on Symbicort 200/5 twice daily, and Ventolin as needed. Are you taking them as prescribed?
[patient] Yes, I take the Symbicort in the morning and evening. I only use the Ventolin when I feel tightness. I bought a new one recently because I was running low.
[doctor] Good. I see your record number is CH-2023-88451. Just to verify, is this your current insurance policy number?
[patient] Yes, that’s correct. I have AXA insurance.
[doctor] Okay. You mentioned you recently traveled. Where did you go?
[patient] I went to Zurich for a conference last month. The air was dry there, and I noticed my symptoms were slightly worse.
[doctor] Dry air can indeed trigger asthma. Did you bring your medications with you?
[patient] Yes, I always keep my inhalers in my carry-on. I was very careful.
[doctor] Let’s do a quick physical exam. Please breathe in deeply. Hold it... and exhale slowly.
[patient] (Exhales)
[doctor] I’m hearing some wheezing. Specifically, there is a wheeze at the 3 o'clock position in your right lung field. This suggests some residual inflammation or bronchospasm.
[patient] Does that mean my asthma is under control?
[doctor] Not fully. It’s "uncomplicated" in the sense that there are no severe complications like pneumonia or heart issues, but the control level is suboptimal. Your peak flow readings at home, have you been keeping them?
[patient] Yes, I’ve been using the meter. My best is usually around 450, but it drops to 320 when I’m symptomatic.
[doctor] A drop of that magnitude is significant. I’d like to adjust your therapy. I’m going to increase your Symbicort to 200/5 twice daily, and add a short course of oral corticosteroids to reduce the inflammation. I’ll prescribe Prednisone 40 mg for five days.
[patient] Okay. Are there any side effects I should watch for?
[doctor] Common ones include mood changes, increased appetite, and trouble sleeping. Since we are in psychiatry follow-up as well, we need to monitor your mood closely. Have you been feeling anxious or depressed lately?
[patient] A little anxious, mostly about the health issues. But I’m not depressed. I’m a graphic designer, so I’m used to working under pressure.
[doctor] I see. Your referring physician, Dr. Keller from Hôpital de la Tour, sent you over to manage the intersection of your respiratory health and mental well-being. He noted that you sometimes panic during attacks.

dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, Madame Costa. I see you are here for a follow-up. How have you been feeling since we last spoke?

[patient] Uh, well, honestly, Doctor, it’s been... um, a bit difficult. You know, the shoulder. It’s still bothering me. Eighty years old and still fighting with this pain, right?

[doctor] I understand. Pain can be very frustrating at any age. Let’s go through it. Is the pain in the left shoulder?

[patient] Yes, yes, the left one. It started about two weeks ago, actually. I think it might have been worse before that, but I didn’t complain. I just thought it was from carrying my groceries.

[doctor] I see. And how has it been progressing since then?

[patient] Um, it’s been bad. Especially when I try to lift my arm. Like, trying to reach for something on a high shelf. It hurts for three months now? No, wait, I said two weeks. It’s been constant for the last few days.

[doctor] Let’s clarify the timeline. When did the pain start?

[patient] Ah, yesterday was the worst. I woke up at 06:00 and it was stiff. I couldn’t move it. I tried to take my Naproxen from the pharmacy, but it didn’t help much.

[doctor] That sounds painful. Did you see anyone else before coming to me?

[patient] Well, my general practitioner, Dr. Miller at the Klinik am See practice, referred me here. He said I needed a specialist opinion. He’s a very nice man, but he said he couldn’t do more with the equipment he has.

[doctor] Thank you for that. I have your file here. I see your medical record number is MR-49201. Let’s do a quick exam. Can you relax your shoulder?

[patient] Yes, I’m trying to. It’s just... you know, it’s sensitive.

[doctor] Okay, I’m going to press here. Tell me if it hurts.

[patient] Oh! Yes, that hurts. Right there, near the... um, where is it?

[doctor] It’s at the 3 o'clock position of your shoulder joint. Does that feel familiar?

[patient] Yes, that’s exactly where it aches. It feels like a deep ache.

[doctor] And when you try to lift your arm to the side, how high can you get it?

[patient] Um, not very high. Maybe up to noon on a clock? Like, halfway up. Then it stops.

[doctor] I see. This is consistent with what we suspect. Let’s talk about your work. I know you are retired, but do you have any active roles or duties that strain your shoulder?

[patient] Well, I used to be a textile worker for Swiss Fibers Ltd in Basel. I worked there for thirty years. Now I’m retired, but I still do a lot of housework. And I help my granddaughter with her homework sometimes, which requires writing.

[doctor] Writing can strain the shoulder if you’re not careful. Do you take any other medications?

[patient] Just the Naproxen when it hurts. And my blood pressure pill, Lisinopril. I take that every morning at 08:00.

[doctor] Okay. Based on the exam, it looks like impingement syndrome. This happens when the tendons get irritated in the space of the shoulder.

[patient] Is it serious?

[doctor] It’s not life-threatening, but it is painful and needs management. I recommend we start with physical therapy. I’m going to refer you to Physio Plus Clinic in Geneva.

[patient] Geneva? That’s far from Zurich where I live.

[doctor] It’s a good clinic. But you can also start with exercises I’ll give you. And we should schedule your next appointment.

[patient] When would that be?

[doctor] Let’s see... October 15th at 10:30 should work. Is that okay?

[patient] October 15th? Let me check my calendar. Um, yes, that should be fine. I usually have coffee with my friend Ana on weekends, so weekdays are better.

[doctor] Perfect. I’ll send a confirmation to your address at Rue de la Paix 12, 1202 Geneva.

[patient] Yes, that’s my home address. Thank you, Doctor.

[doctor] You’re welcome. Please take the Naproxen as directed, but don’t exceed the dose. And try to avoid lifting heavy things overhead.

[patient] Okay. I’ll be careful. I don’t want to make it worse.

[doctor] That’s a good idea. If the pain gets worse or you develop weakness, come back sooner.

[patient] Yes, I will. Thank you.

[doctor] Goodbye, Madame Costa. Take care.

[patient] Goodbye.

dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning. I see you’re here for the follow-up regarding your bone density. How have you been feeling since we last spoke?
[patient] Hi, Dr. Keller. Um, honestly? It’s been... okay. I’m 33, so I keep telling myself I’m too young for this, you know? But my back has been aching a bit more than usual lately.
[doctor] I understand. At 33, osteoporosis is certainly rare, but not unheard of, especially with certain risk factors. Can you tell me more about the pain? Where is it located?
[patient] Mostly right here, in the mid-back. It’s not sharp, more of a dull ache. It’s about a 4 out of 10 when I’m sitting, but when I stand up or twist, it goes up to maybe a 6.
[doctor] Okay. And did you have any specific injuries recently? Any falls or accidents?
[patient] No, not really. I’m pretty careful. Well, except for that time at the kitchen last week. I slipped on a wet tile, but I caught myself before I hit the floor. No bruising, nothing.
[doctor] That’s good to hear. So no pathological fracture. We need to keep an eye on it, though. Let’s take your vitals first.
[nurse] Bekele, can you roll up your sleeve?
[patient] Sure.
[nurse] Blood pressure is 128 over 82. Heart rate is 72. Temperature 36.8. Respiratory rate 14. Everything looks stable.
[doctor] Thank you. Now, Bekele, you mentioned you’ve been taking your medication. What are you currently on?
[patient] I’m taking Reclast. Once a year, right? I had my last infusion at University Hospital Zurich in October 2023. And I take Calcium-D tablets daily.
[doctor> Correct. Reclast is a bisphosphonate infusion. How did you tolerate it? Any side effects?
[patient] The first one was rough. Fever, muscle aches for two days. But the second one was much better. Just a bit of nausea for a day.
[doctor> That’s a common reaction. It usually gets better with subsequent doses. Let’s look at your recent lab work. Your Vitamin D levels were 25 ng/mL. That’s in the sufficient range, but on the lower end.
[patient] Should I increase the dose?
[doctor] I’d like to see it closer to 40. Let’s bump up your Calcium-D to 1000 units of Vitamin D and 500 mg of calcium, twice a day. Also, we should check your calcium, magnesium, and PTH levels again in three months.
[patient] Okay. And what about the exercise? I work as a graphic designer, so I sit a lot.

[doctor> Great. Stability is crucial to prevent fractures. Now, regarding your diet. Are you getting enough calcium from food?
[patient] I’m Eritrean, so we eat a lot of lentils, beans, and injera. But maybe not enough dairy. I drink tea and coffee.
[doctor> Coffee can interfere with calcium absorption if you drink too much. Limit it to two cups a day. Add more dairy or fortified plant milks.

[doctor> Ah, that’s important. Thyroid dysfunction can affect bone density. Let’s check your TSH levels as well. If your thyroid is under-treated, it can accelerate bone loss.
[patient] I see. So, what’s the next step?
[doctor> We’ll repeat the DEXA scan in one year to monitor bone density. In the meantime, we’ll adjust your meds and do labs in three months. I’ll schedule your next appointment.
[patient] When would that be?
[doctor> Let’s book you for March 15, 2024 at 14:00. Does that work?
[patient] Yes, that’s fine. I can take that day off.
[doctor> Perfect. We’ll send a confirmation to your email. In the meantime, if the pain worsens or you experience a fall, come back immediately.
[patient] Will do. Thanks, Dr. Keller.
[doctor> You’re welcome. Take care.

[doctor] Good morning, Herr Werner. Please, have a seat. I see you’re here for your back pain.
[patient] Yes, good morning, doctor. Um, it’s been... it’s been getting worse, you know. I can barely swing my club anymore.
[doctor] I’m sorry to hear that. Let’s start with the basics. How long have you been experiencing this pain?
[patient] Oh, for three months, I’d say. It started very mild, just a little stiffness after a round at the Vienna Golf Club.
[doctor] Okay. And where exactly is the pain located?
[patient] Mostly here, in the lower back, and it shoots down my right leg. It feels like... um, like an electric shock, you know?
[doctor] That sounds like radiculopathy. Do you have any numbness or weakness in your leg or foot?
[patient] Not really weakness, but sometimes my toes feel a bit tingly. Especially when I stand up too quickly.
[doctor] I see. Let’s take your vital signs while I review your chart. Nurse Elisabeth, could you help me with the blood pressure?
[nurse] Of course, Dr. Werner.
[patient] Ah, yes, Elisabeth. Hello.
[nurse] Hello, Herr Werner. Let’s get your blood pressure and heart rate.
[patient] I hope it’s not high. My son, Karl, who is 32, always worries about my blood pressure.
[doctor] Your son is Karl, correct?
[patient] Yes, Karl. He is a software engineer in Innsbruck.
[doctor] And your wife? Is she with you today?
[patient] No, she is at home. Her name is Anna. She is 78.
[nurse] Your blood pressure is 145/90, which is slightly elevated. Your heart rate is 72 beats per minute.
[patient] That’s higher than usual. I take <DRUG>Losartan</DRUG> daily.
[doctor] We will monitor that. Now, regarding the back pain. Have you had any previous back surgeries?
[patient] No, no surgeries. But I did have a herniated disc diagnosed ten years ago by Dr. Stein.
[doctor] I see. Do you have any other medical conditions?
[patient] I have mild <DISEASE>hypertension</DISEASE>, and my sister, Paula, has <DISEASE>Parkinson's disease</DISEASE>. I worry I might get it too, but I don't have tremors.
[doctor] That’s good to know. Your family history is important. Did Dr. Stein recommend any specific exercises?
[patient] Yes, some core strengthening. I went to the FitLife Gym in Vienna for a while, but I stopped because the pain got worse.
[doctor] I understand. Let’s do a physical exam. Please lie down on the table.
[patient] Okay. This is uncomfortable.
[doctor] Take your time. I’m going to check your range of motion. Can you bend forward and touch your toes?
[patient] Um, I can get halfway. It hurts here, at the lumbar region.
[doctor] Okay. Now, I’m going to perform a straight leg raise test. Raise your right leg straight up.
[patient] Oh, that’s it! That’s the pain! It shoots down to my knee.
[doctor] Positive straight leg raise. That suggests nerve root irritation. I’ll also check your reflexes.
[patient] Is it serious?
[doctor] It’s not an emergency, but it needs proper management. I’m going to refer you to a specialist for further evaluation and possible imaging.
[patient] Which specialist?
[doctor] I’m referring you to Dr. Hoffmann at the Vienna Spine Center. He is an orthopedic surgeon who specializes in back pain.
[patient] That sounds good. When should I go?
[doctor] I’ll call the clinic for you. I’ll also order an MRI of your lumbar spine.
[patient] Will I need an injection?
[doctor] We’ll wait for the MRI results. In the meantime, I recommend you avoid heavy lifting and twisting.
[patient] I’ll try. I love golf, but I’ll take a break for a few weeks.
[doctor] That’s a good idea. Also, stay active with gentle walking. Avoid sitting for long periods.
[patient] I will. And I’ll check in with Anna about the exercises.
[doctor] Good. Do you have any questions about the referral?
[patient] No, I think I understand. Thank you, doctor.
[doctor] You’re welcome. Nurse Elisabeth, please give him the referral letter and the MRI order.
[nurse] Here you go, Herr Werner. The appointment is for next Tuesday at 10:00.
[patient] Thank you. I’ll be there.
[doctor] Great. Take care, and call us if the pain gets worse or if you lose control of your bladder or bowels.
[patient] I will. Goodbye.
[doctor] Goodbye, Herr Werner.

note:
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Pain in left upper abdomen during physical activity.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Emre Yilmaz, a 41-year-old male, presents with a 1-week history of acute pain in the left upper quadrant of his abdomen. The pain was first noted while bowling at the Bowling Center Alster on a Friday. He describes the pain as sharp and stabbing, with an intensity of 7/10. The pain is exacerbated by physical exertion and bending over. There is mild nausea but no vomiting, fever, or change in bowel habits. He denies any history of similar episodes. His father, Huseyin, died of gastric cancer. His mother, Aylin (68), has hypertension. His brother, Can (38), is healthy. He is a non-smoker and consumes alcohol socially. He works as a mechanical engineer for Siemens Energy.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever, no weight loss.
Gastrointestinal: No nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or constipation. No melena or hematochezia.
Cardiovascular: No chest pain or palpitations.
Respiratory: No cough or shortness of breath.
Musculoskeletal: Pain reproducible with movement.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: BP 120/80 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, Temp 36.9 °C, RR 14 breaths/min.
General: Alert, oriented, in no acute distress.
Abdomen: Soft, non-distended. Tenderness to palpation in the left upper quadrant. No rebound tenderness. No guarding. No palpable masses. No organomegaly.

RESULTS
Laboratory tests ordered: Complete Blood Count (CBC), Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP), Lipase.
Imaging: Abdominal Ultrasound.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Left upper quadrant abdominal pain, etiology undetermined. Differential includes gastritis, splenic flexure syndrome, or musculoskeletal strain.
2. Plan:
- Abdominal Ultrasound to evaluate liver, gallbladder, pancreas, and spleen.
- Blood work to check for inflammation and pancreatic enzymes.
- Follow-up appointment scheduled for 15 October 2023 at 10:00.
- Patient instructed to fast 8 hours prior to the appointment.
- Return precautions: Go to ER if pain becomes severe, if vomiting blood, or if fever develops.
- Referral to gastroenterology if initial workup is negative and symptoms persist.

[doctor] Good morning. My name is Dr. Weber. Please, sit down. I see your file here, 89-4421-B. How can I help you today?
[patient] Good morning, doctor. Um, I’m Emre Yilmaz. I’m 41 years old. I live in Hamburg.
[doctor] Hello, Emre. I see you work for Siemens Energy. Is that correct?
[patient] Yes, I am a mechanical engineer there. But that’s not the problem. The problem is... my stomach.
[doctor] I see. Can you describe what is happening?
[patient] Um, well, last week, I was bowling. I go to the <ORGANization>Bowling Center Alster every Friday.
[doctor] And what happened while bowling?
[patient] I was throwing the ball, you know, with full force. And suddenly, *ouch*. Right here.
[patient] *points to upper left abdomen*
[doctor] Pain? Where exactly?
[patient] Yeah, sharp pain. Like a stab. It was... 15:30 maybe? During the game.
[doctor] Does it happen when you eat? Or only with activity?
[patient] Mostly with activity. Or when I bend over. If I eat... um... maybe a little worse, but not as bad.
[doctor] Any nausea? Vomiting?
[patient] No vomit. Maybe a little nausea. I felt... sick.
[doctor] Have you had any fever?
[patient] No, no fever. I checked. I was 36.8 degrees.
[doctor] Okay. Let’s look at your history. Do you have any known allergies?
[patient] No allergies. No drugs. I don’t take anything, maybe aspirin sometimes for headaches.
[doctor] Family history? Any gastrointestinal issues in your family?
[patient] My father, Huseyin, he had... um... I think it was accountant. He died of... something in his stomach. Cancer?
[doctor] I see. And your mother?
[patient] She is alive. Aylin. She is 68. She has... I think nurse background, but she retired. She has high blood pressure.
[doctor] Any siblings?
[patient] My brother, Can. He is 38. He is healthy.
[doctor] Do you smoke? Or drink alcohol?
[patient] I don’t smoke. Alcohol... maybe one beer on Friday. Or two. Not much.
[doctor] Okay. Let’s do a physical exam. Please undress your shirt.
[patient] Okay. *undresses shirt*
[doctor] Breathe in... and out. I’m going to press here.
[patient] *winces*
[doctor] Is that the spot?
[patient] Yes, yes! That’s it.
[doctor] Okay. I feel some tenderness in the left upper quadrant. No mass. No rebound tenderness. Let’s check your vitals.
[nurse] Blood pressure is 120/80. Heart rate is 72 beats per minute. Temperature is 36.9 degrees Celsius.
[doctor] Thank you, Julia.
[nurse] You’re welcome, doctor.
[doctor] Emre, I want to order some tests. An ultrasound of your abdomen and some blood work.
[patient] Why?
[doctor] To check your liver, gallbladder, and pancreas. Sometimes pain in this area can be related to the spleen or the stomach lining.
[patient] Is it serious?
[doctor] It’s too early to say. But we need to rule out things like a hernia, gastritis, or something else.
[patient] I heard about dentist Schulz... he has a friend who had... I don’t know, some kind of inflammation.
[doctor] Which inflammation?
[patient] Um... Crohn’s disease? Or... I don’t know.
[doctor] Crohn’s is a type of inflammatory bowel disease. It’s possible, but less likely given your acute onset with activity.
[patient] I worry. I have a daughter, Zeynep. She is 8. I don’t want to worry her.
[doctor] I understand. We will keep you updated.
[patient] Okay. When will I get the results?
[doctor] You will come back for your results. Let’s schedule an appointment for 15 October 2023 at 10:00.
[patient] Okay. That’s a Wednesday.
[doctor] Yes. Please fast for 8 hours before the appointment, just in case we need to do an endoscopy.
[patient] Okay. And the blood work?
[doctor] You can do that at the lab in Hamburg anytime before then.
[patient] Okay. Thank you, doctor.
[doctor] You’re welcome. If the pain becomes severe, or if you vomit blood, go to the emergency room immediately.
[patient] I will. Thank you.
[doctor] Take care.

REFERRAL LETTER

Dear Dr. Julia Baumann,

Thank you for referring Samira Tesfay, 68, born 14 March 1956, to my endocrinology practice in Lausanne. I am writing to share the outcome of our consultation on 15 November 2023.

The patient presented with complaints of intermittent chest tightness and wheezing, primarily triggered by strong odors such as lemon cleaner, and occasionally by cold air or exercise. She reported a pain score of 4/10 during the worst episodes. Her history includes mild intermittent asthma, previously managed with a rescue inhaler only. She works as a logistics coordinator</NOTE> at TransAlps Freight and resides in Geneva.

I reviewed her previous records from Clinique de la Chaux-de-Fonds, which indicated concerns about thyroid function. However, our recent lab work from 12 November 2023 shows normal TSH (2.5 mIU/L), Free T4 (1.2 ng/dL), and T3 (1.1 nmol/L). There is no biochemical evidence of Hashimoto's thyroiditis or Graves' disease.

Her vital signs at today's visit were blood pressure 130/85 mmHg, heart rate 78 bpm, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Physical examination revealed mild expiratory wheezing that resolved after bronchodilator use.

She also reported a history of a fall at the gym two months ago, resulting in a ruptured Baker's cyst in the right knee. She was treated at Hôpital de la Tour and has since recovered well, with only mild residual discomfort upon deep squatting. She continues to exercise at FitLife Studio in Bern.

Plan:
1. Initiated low-dose inhaled corticosteroid once daily to control airway inflammation.
2. Continued rescue inhaler as needed.
3. Advised to avoid strong chemical triggers and to warm up gradually before exercise.
4. Follow-up appointment scheduled for 25 January 2024 at 10:30.

Email: samira.tesfay at gmx.ch
Insurance: Swiss Medical, Policy 7788990011

Please do not hesitate to contact me if you have any further questions regarding her endocrine status.

Sincerely,
Dr. Elias Weber
Endocrinology Department
Centre Médical de la Paix
Lausanne

Insurer: Assicurazioni Generali
Insurance Number: AG-998221-X
Employer: Ferrari & Partners
Occupation: Accountant

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mrs. Vittori presents with a two-week history of worsening lower back pain and right-sided radiculopathy. The symptoms began after an acute twisting injury in the kitchen. She reports pain radiating down the right leg to the foot, described as burning and tingling. Current pain score is 7/10. She reports difficulty lifting the right toes.

No significant past medical history. No known drug allergies. She is a member of Circolo Tennis Milano.

[patient] I usually swim in the morning.
[doctor] Keep it gentle.
[doctor] Have you traveled recently?

[doctor] How did that affect your back?
[patient] I walked a lot, and the pain got worse.

[patient] I understand.

note:
SUBJECTIVE
Patient is a forty-three-year-old male, Lucas Moreau, presenting with a three-month history of left shoulder pain. The pain began around January and has progressively worsened. He describes the pain as sharp with overhead activities and lifting, and dull at rest. Pain is rated 6-7/10 with activity and 3/10 at rest. He reports sleeping difficulty on the left side. He is a senior project manager at Vallée Verte and a member of the Annecy Badminton Club, where he plays twice weekly. He reports increased intensity of play recently. He has a history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis, managed with levothyroxine. He denies smoking or alcohol use. He mentions a past history of a Baker’s cyst in the right knee. He denies any neurological symptoms or other joint pain.

OBJECTIVE
Vitals: BP 128/82 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, RR 16/min, Temp 36.8°C.
General: Well-appearing male, no acute distress.
Left Shoulder:
- Inspection: No swelling, erythema, or deformity.
- Palpation: Tenderness over the lateral aspect of the shoulder. A small, firm, tender nodule noted at the 3 o’clock position relative to the acromion.
- Range of Motion: Active abduction limited to 120 degrees due to pain. Active forward flexion limited to 140 degrees.
- Strength: Weakness in external rotation and abduction (4/5).
- Special Tests:
  - Neer’s Impingement Test: Positive (pain with passive forward flexion and internal rotation).
  - Hawkins-Kennedy Test: Positive (pain with internal rotation at 90 degrees abduction).
  - Empty Can Test: Positive (pain and weakness with forward flexion and internal rotation in the scapular plane).
  - Drop Arm Test: Negative.
- Reflexes and Sensation: Normal in the upper extremity.

ASSESSMENT
1. Subacromial Impingement Syndrome, Left Shoulder (ICD-10: M75.40).
2. Hashimoto's thyroiditis, stable.
3. History of Baker’s cyst, right knee, resolved.

PLAN
1. Activity Modification: Discontinue overhead activities, including badminton, for 4-6 weeks. Avoid heavy lifting with the left arm.
2. Pharmacology: Ibuprofen 400 mg orally three times daily as needed for pain, with food. Apply ice to the left shoulder for 15 minutes, three times daily.
3. Physical Therapy: Referral sent to Physio Lyon Centre for rotator cuff strengthening and scapular stabilization exercises. Patient to start gentle range-of-motion exercises immediately.
4. Follow-up: Return to clinic in 4 weeks for reassessment. If no improvement or if pain worsens, consider ultrasound imaging and/or corticosteroid injection.
5. Education: Discussed the nature of impingement syndrome, expected course, and importance of adherence to activity modification. Patient verbalizes understanding. Provided contact information 04 78 12 34 56 for questions.

[doctor] good morning , ms . keller . i am dr . vane . i understand you are here for a follow-up on some abnormal blood work ?
[patient] yes , good morning . my name is elise keller , 42 years old . i live in geneva .
[doctor] thank you , elise . please , have a seat . can you tell me a bit about what led to this appointment ?
[patient] well , two weeks ago , i was feeling quite tired and dizzy . i went to my gp , and she ordered some routine blood tests . the results came back yesterday , and my calcium levels were very high .
[doctor] i see . high calcium , or hypercalcemia , can be caused by several things . have you noticed any other symptoms since then ?
[patient] mostly fatigue , i suppose . and i’ve been drinking a lot of water and going to the bathroom often .
[doctor] that is consistent with the high calcium . do you have a history of any chronic conditions ? i see in your file that you have hashimoto's thyroiditis .
[patient] yes , i do . i have been on levothyroxine for about five years . my thyroid levels have been stable , though .
[doctor] understood . and do you have any family history of bone diseases or parathyroid issues ?
[patient] my mother , marie , is 68 years old . she has had osteoporosis for a long time .
[doctor] that is useful information . and your father ?
[patient] my father , jean , passed away when i was young . he was 55 years old .
[doctor] i am sorry for your loss . do you have any siblings ?
[patient] yes , i have a brother , luc . he is 45 years old and lives in fribourg .
[doctor] thank you . now , regarding your job . i see you work for geneva water utilities . is that correct ?
[patient] yes , i am a project manager there .

[doctor] that is good to know . we need to rule out any malignancy , given your age and the sudden change . have you noticed any unexplained weight loss ?
[patient] not really . i’ve been eating normally . maybe a little less appetite , but no weight loss that i can see .
[doctor] okay . let’s look at the results . your serum calcium is significantly elevated . your parathyroid hormone level is also high . this suggests primary hyperparathyroidism .
[patient] what does that mean ?
[doctor] it means one of your parathyroid glands is overactive and producing too much hormone , which pulls calcium from your bones into your blood .
[patient] is it cancer ?
[doctor] not necessarily . most cases are benign adenomas . however , we need to do further imaging to confirm . i would like to refer you for a neck ultrasound and a sestamibi scan .
[patient] okay . who do i need to call ?
[doctor] i will send the referral to university hospital of geneva . you can call their department at 022 325 61 11 to schedule the appointment .
[patient] i will do that . do i need to change my medication ?

[patient] that seems manageable . what about my insurance ?
[doctor] your insurer is swiss life . your policy number is 7845210 .

[patient] good . i was also thinking about my sister , chloe . she is 38 years old . she has been complaining of joint pain . could this run in the family ?

[patient] that sounds serious .
[doctor] it is important to rule out hereditary syndromes , but many cases are sporadic .
[patient] i had an injury recently . i fell in the kitchen two weeks ago and hurt my wrist . could that be related ?
[doctor] unlikely to be related to the calcium , but you should ensure the wrist is healing properly . did you see a doctor for that ?
[patient] yes , my gp said it was a sprain . she advised me to rest it .
[doctor] that is good . now , regarding your history of crohn's disease . are you currently in remission ?
[patient] yes , i have been in remission for three years . i am not on any immunosuppressants , just a low-dose steroid if i have a flare , but i haven't had one in a long time .
[doctor] good . inflammation from crohn's can sometimes affect calcium absorption , but since your calcium is high , that is less likely to be the primary driver here .
[patient] i see . so the next step is the scan ?
[doctor] yes . and i will repeat your blood tests in one month to monitor the calcium levels .
[patient] what if the levels are still high ?
[doctor] if the levels remain high and the imaging confirms an adenoma , we may discuss surgical removal of the gland .
[patient] surgery ? that sounds scary .
[doctor] it is a routine procedure , but it is invasive . we want to be absolutely sure of the diagnosis before recommending it .
[patient] understood . i will make the appointment .
[doctor] please write down your questions before the next visit . also , let me know if you develop any new symptoms , such as confusion or severe abdominal pain .
[patient] i will . thank you , dr . vane .
[doctor] you are welcome , elise . take care .

Cardiovascular: Palpitations, no chest pain.
Respiratory: No dyspnea, no cough.
Gastrointestinal: Occasional nausea with Metformin.
Musculoskeletal: Hip bruise from fall, no joint pain.
Neurological: No headache, no vision changes.
Skin: Perioral rash, minor forearm abrasion.

Vitals: BP 130/80 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, Temp 36.8 C.
General: Well-nourished, alert, oriented.
HEENT: Perioral erythema and papules noted. Thyroid palpation reveals a small, non-tender nodule on the right lobe. No lymphadenopathy.

TSH: 4.5 mIU/L (upper limit of normal)

Patient presented to the emergency department with complaints of dizziness and mild dyspnea on exertion. She reported no chest pain.

Rajesh is a 68-year-old female with a history of aortocoronary bypass grafting performed five years ago. She resides in Zürich. She reported feeling unwell since Monday, with increased fatigue. - Troponin: Negative.
- Chest X-ray: Small nodule noted at the 3 o'clock position in the right lung field. No acute cardiopulmonary process.

2. Pulmonary Nodule: Referral to pulmonology for CT chest to evaluate the nodule at the 3 o'clock position.

Dr. Vance
City Hospital Zürich

[patient] Goodbye.

Follow-up for solitary cyst of the right breast and anxiety.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Anna 74 is a retired librarian presenting for a psychiatry follow-up. She reports persistent anxiety regarding a solitary cyst in the right breast, identified via ultrasound last Tuesday. She fears malignancy despite reassurance that the cyst is simple and benign. She notes poor sleep and difficulty concentrating. She is currently taking Escitalopram 10 mg daily for anxiety, which she reports has provided mild relief in irritability but not in nocturnal panic. She also takes Atorvastatin for hyperlipidemia and Levothyroxine for hypothyroidism. Her family history is notable for her sister, Ursula 71, who has Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Her husband, Werner 76, has Parkinson's disease and takes Levodopa. She previously suffered from a Baker's cyst in the knee three years ago, which has resolved. She attends the Yoga Shala in Munich but finds it difficult to focus due to her anxiety.

Neurological: No new headaches or dizziness.

GI: No nausea or abdominal pain.

note:
REFERRAL LETTER

Dear Dr. Schmidt,

I am writing to refer Ms. Helena Zielińska, an 82-year-old woman, for urgent cardiological evaluation.

PATIENT DETAILS
Name: Helena Zielińska
Date of Birth: 14 March 1942
Address: 12 Lindenstraße, 10115 Berlin
Insurer: TeknoMed Insurance
Insurance Number: 8842-991-021
Medical Record Number: ENT-2024-8891

REASON FOR REFERRAL
The patient presents with complaints of palpitations described as "skipped beats" and "heavy thumping," accompanied by dizziness and frontal/temporal headaches (pain score 7/10). These symptoms have been occurring intermittently over the past two weeks. The patient reports no chest pain, syncope, or shortness of breath.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Ms. Zielińska is a retired bus driver who worked for Berlin City Public Transport for thirty years. She is a member of the Polish Cultural Club Berlin choir. She recently returned from a trip to Prague in April 2024.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
- Hashimoto's disease (diagnosed 10 years ago), currently stable on thyroxine replacement.
- No history of Crohn's disease, Graves' disease, Bell's palsy, or Baker's cyst.

FAMILY HISTORY
- Mother: Hypertension, died at age 90.
- Brother Tomasz: Parkinson's disease, deceased 5 years ago.
- No known family history of cardiac arrhythmias or sudden cardiac death.

VITAL SIGNS AND EXAMINATION
Blood Pressure: 145/92 mmHg
Heart Rate: 88 bpm
Temperature: 36.8°C
Pain Score: 7/10 (headache)
ENT Examination: Normal tympanic membranes, no nystagmus, no hearing loss.

LABORATORY RESULTS
- TSH: 2.5 mIU/L (Normal)
- Electrolytes: Normal
- Complete Blood Count: Normal

ASSESSMENT
The patient's symptoms suggest possible ventricular premature depolarization (VPD) or paroxysmal arrhythmia. Given her age and history, a thorough cardiac workup is required to rule out underlying cardiac pathology. The dizziness may be related to hemodynamic changes from the arrhythmia.

PLAN
1. Urgent ECG and Holter monitor (24-48 hours).
2. Echocardiogram if indicated.
3. Review of medication list and electrolyte balance.
4. Follow-up appointment at our clinic on 12 May 2024 at 09:30 to review cardiac findings.

Please contact us at ent@kowalski-clinic.de or <PHONE>030 1234 5678</PHONE> if you have any questions or need further information.

Sincerely,

Dr. Kowalski
ENT Clinic
Berlin

SUBJECT: Referral for Colonoscopy and Gastroscopy - Iron Deficiency Anemia

Dear Dr. Steiner,

I am writing to refer Erika Mueller, a 57-year-old female, born on 12/03/1967, for urgent investigation of iron deficiency anemia.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Erika presents with progressive fatigue and weakness over the past three months. Symptoms worsened noticeably two weeks ago. She reports no overt gastrointestinal bleeding, melena, or hematochezia. She has no abdominal pain.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Erika has a history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis, which is currently managed with medication. Her thyroid function tests were recently within normal limits. She has a family history of gastrointestinal disease; her mother suffered from Crohn's disease, and her brother has autoimmune conditions. Erika herself has no confirmed diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease, but given the family history, it is prudent to rule out occult gastrointestinal pathology.

CURRENT MEDICATIONS
Levothyroxine 75 mcg daily.

ALLERGIES
None known.

INVESTIGATIONS
Recent blood work from yesterday shows:
- Hemoglobin: 9.8 g/dL (Low)
- Ferritin: 12 ng/mL (Low)
- MCV: 78 fL (Microcytic)
- TSH: 2.5 mIU/L (Normal)

CLINICAL IMPRESSION
The clinical picture is consistent with iron deficiency anemia. Given her age, sex, and family history, occult gastrointestinal blood loss is a primary concern. We must rule out colorectal neoplasia, polyps, or other sources of chronic blood loss.

PLAN
1. Colonoscopy and Gastroscopy scheduled for 14/10/2023 at 09:30.
2. Pre-procedure instructions have been provided to the patient.
3. She will be accompanied by her neighbor, Hans, for post-sedation care.
4. Insurance details: Österreichische Gesundheitskasse, ID: 123456789.
5. Please perform the endoscopic evaluation and biopsy any suspicious lesions.
6. I will manage the follow-up and potential iron replacement therapy based on your findings.

Please contact me directly if any urgent issues arise. You can reach me at doc.keller@uroclinic.example.

Thank you for your assistance.

Sincerely,

Dr. Thomas Keller
Urologist
Vienna Urology Center
1010 Vienna, Austria

[doctor] Good morning, Erika. Please, have a seat. I see you were referred to us by your general practitioner for some fatigue. How have you been feeling recently?
[patient] Morning, Doctor. I’ve been feeling really drained, especially two weeks ago started to feel more tired than usual. I thought it was just stress, but it’s getting worse.
[doctor] I understand. When did you first notice these symptoms?
[patient] It’s been going on for three months. I’m 57, so I guess maybe it’s just getting older, but I’m not sleeping well either.
[doctor] That’s a valid concern. Have you noticed any changes in your digestion or any pain in your abdomen?
[patient] Not really pain, but I do have Ibs issues sometimes. My mother had severe bowel problems, but I’ve been tested for that.

[patient] She had Crohn's disease. It’s in the family, it seems. My brother also has some autoimmune issues.
[doctor] I see. And do you have any other chronic conditions?
[patient] Yes, I have Hashimoto's thyroiditis. My levels are usually stable, but I take medication.
[doctor] That’s important to note. Thyroid issues can sometimes contribute to fatigue. Have you had your iron levels checked recently?
[patient] My GP did a blood test yesterday. He said my hemoglobin was low. He mentioned iron deficiency.
[doctor] That aligns with your symptoms. Did he provide you with the specific numbers?
[patient] I think my ferritin was very low, maybe around 15. He’s quite concerned because he wants to rule out any underlying cause.
[doctor] Correct. Iron deficiency anemia in a woman of your age needs investigation to find the source of the blood loss. Have you had any gastrointestinal bleeding?
[patient] No, I haven’t noticed any blood in my stool or urine. I’m quite careful about that.
[doctor] Good. We will need to do some further testing to be sure. I’m thinking we might need a colonoscopy and perhaps a gastroscopy.
[patient] Oh, a colonoscopy? I’m a bit nervous about that.
[doctor] It’s a standard procedure, and we will sedate you so you won’t feel anything. It’s the best way to check for any polyps or other issues that could be causing the blood loss.
[patient] Okay. I work at Vienna Public Transport as a dispatcher, so I can manage time off, but it’s not easy.
[doctor] I understand. Let’s schedule the appointment for a time that works for you. Are you free next week?

[patient] Just that I feel really anxious about this. My friend, Julia, has Graves' disease and she was so sick for a while. I hope it’s not something serious.
[doctor] I understand your anxiety. Most cases of iron deficiency are manageable once the cause is identified. We will keep you updated at every step.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor. I feel a bit better already.
[doctor] You’re welcome. I’ll send a summary to your GP and also email you the instructions for the colonoscopy. Can I get your email address?
[patient] Sure, it’s erika.mueller@example.com.
[doctor] Perfect. I’ll send that over today. Do you have any questions about the preparation for the colonoscopy?
[patient] Just that I need to drink a lot of clear fluids. I’ll make sure to do that.
[doctor] Yes, and avoid red or purple foods. It’s important to follow the diet strictly for a clear view during the procedure.
[patient] Got it. Red or purple. I’ll stay away from beets and grapes.
[doctor] Exactly. And if you have any severe pain or dizziness before the appointment, please call us immediately.
[patient] Will do. Thank you for your patience, Doctor.
[doctor] You’re most welcome. I’ll see you on October 14th. Take care.
[patient] Goodbye.

She denies numbness or tingling except for mild discomfort in the thumb when sleeping. She reports no dizziness or syncope. She is taking Ibuprofen twice a day and Paracetamol three times a day as needed. She also takes Lisinopril for hypertension. Her daughter Anja (34) lives in Stuttgart, and her son Thomas (40) lives in Munich and assisted her yesterday. Her neighbor Herr Mueller (82) helped her after the fall. She mentions a friend Ursula (75) who provides support. She recalls a low calcium level from a test two weeks ago.

Labs: Previous serum calcium level was 2.1 mmol/L (slightly low).

ASSESSMENT
1. Colles' fracture, right radius, healing well.
2. Hypertension, controlled.
3. Mild hypocalcemia.

PLAN
1. Continue current pain management with Ibuprofen and Paracetamol.
2. Start calcium and vitamin D supplementation for bone healing.
3. Gentle range of motion exercises as demonstrated by Nurse Smith.
4. Avoid heavy lifting for another four weeks.

note:
SUBJECTIVE
Patient is a 38-year-old female, Elena Bianchi, born on 14 March 1986. She presents with a 3-month history of fatigue and a 2-week history of dark, tea-colored urine and nocturia. She reports significant bilateral lower extremity edema, which was exacerbated after a visit to the gym last weekend. She denies chest pain or shortness of breath but notes some chest tightness. She has been taking Ibuprofen for pain and swelling, which she has now stopped. She was previously prescribed Lasix by her GP but discontinued it. Family history is notable for hypertension in her sister Giulia (35). Mother Lucia (62) is healthy. Patient resides in Milan.

OBJECTIVE
Vitals: BP 150/95 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, Temp 36.8°C, RR 16.
General: Alert, oriented, no acute distress.
CV: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender, no hepatosplenomegaly.
Extremities: 2+ pitting edema in bilateral ankles and shins.
Labs (pending): CBC, CMP, Urinalysis with microscopy, Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio, Complement levels (C3, C4), ANA, ANCA.

ASSESSMENT
1. Unspecified nephritic syndrome with unspecified morphologic changes (ICD-10: N00.9).
2. Hypertension, likely secondary to renal pathology.
3. History of self-medication with NSAIDs, which may have exacerbated renal injury.

PLAN
1. Discontinue all NSAIDs (Ibuprofen).
2. Start strict low-salt, low-protein diet.
3. Order renal biopsy to determine specific morphologic changes and guide therapy.
4. Consider initiation of corticosteroids (Prednisone) and immunosuppressive therapy (Mycophenolate) pending biopsy results, depending on histology.
5. Monitor blood pressure closely; may require adjustment of antihypertensive therapy if BP remains elevated.
6. Follow-up appointment scheduled for 12 October at 10:30 AM to review biopsy results and adjust management plan.
7. Patient advised to seek emergency care at San Raffaele Hospital if oliguria or severe symptoms develop.

Dear Dr. Klein,

I am writing to refer my patient, Mr. Yilmaz, for your evaluation regarding persistent anemia and mild hepatic abnormalities.

PATIENT INFORMATION
Name: Mr. Yilmaz
Age: 84 years
Record Number: NR-9942-881
Date of Birth: 1940
Primary Physician: Dr. Weber

REASON FOR REFERRAL
The patient presents with symptomatic anemia, characterized by fatigue and mild exertional dyspnea (pain/discomfort score 3/10). Recent laboratory results show a hemoglobin level of 9.2 g/dL, down from 9.8 g/dL. We are concerned about the underlying etiology, which may include chronic disease, occult blood loss, or hematological malignancy.

CLINICAL HISTORY
The patient is an 84-year-old male with a history of hypertension. He reports no significant alcohol use. Family history is notable for his brother having a history of gallstones. My mother, the patient's mother, had hypertension but no known hematological issues. The patient denies dark or tarry stools.

EXAMINATION FINDINGS
Vital signs at today's visit: Blood pressure 145/90 mmHg, Heart rate 88 bpm, Temperature 36.8 °C.
Abdominal examination revealed mild fullness in the right upper quadrant. No palpable masses were detected at the 3 o'clock position relative to the umbilicus, but the liver edge is slightly palpable.

INVESTIGATIONS
- Hemoglobin: 9.2 g/dL
- ALT: 45 U/L
- AST: 38 U/L
- Iron studies, B12, and Folate: Pending
- CT Abdomen/Pelvis: Scheduled for October 12th at Klinikum St. Anna

REQUEST
I would appreciate your expert opinion on the management of his anemia and whether further invasive testing, such as a bone marrow biopsy, is warranted. I have attached the recent blood work and imaging reports.

Please let me know if you require any additional information.

Sincerely,

Dr. [Doctor's Name]
Nephrology Department
City General Hospital

[doctor] Good morning, Mr. Yilmaz. It is good to see you again. How have you been feeling since our last visit?

[doctor] I see. That fatigue is certainly consistent with your anemia. Let's review your recent blood work to see if there are any changes.
[patient] Is it worse? I am worried. My wife is very worried.
[doctor] Let's look at the numbers first. Your hemoglobin is currently 9.2 g/dL, which is slightly lower than your previous result of 9.8.
[patient] Oh. That is not good.
[doctor] It is not ideal, but we need to find the cause. Are you experiencing any other symptoms? Shortness of breath? Chest pain?
[patient] No chest pain. But yes, when I walk up the stairs, I get a bit short of breath. It is mild, maybe 3/10 on a pain or discomfort scale if I have to guess.
[doctor] Okay, mild exertional dyspnea. Do you have any abdominal pain or bloating?
[patient] Sometimes. A dull ache here. But nothing sharp.
[doctor] Let's examine your abdomen. Please lie down on the table for a moment.
[patient] Okay.
[nurse] Mr. Yilmaz, I am going to place a blood pressure cuff on your arm. Could you relax your arm?
[patient] Yes, thank you, Nurse.
[nurse] Your blood pressure is 145 over 90. Heart rate is 88 beats per minute. Temperature is 36.8 degrees Celsius.
[doctor] Thank you. Now, looking at your abdomen, I feel a slight fullness in the right upper quadrant.
[patient] Is that bad?
[doctor] It might be your liver. Let's check your liver function tests. Your ALT is 45 U/L and AST is 38 U/L, which are mildly elevated.
[patient] My liver? I don't drink much. Maybe a glass of wine on special days.
[doctor] That is possible. But we also need to rule out other causes of anemia. Have you noticed any changes in your stool color? Dark or tarry stools?
[patient] No, I don't think so. Normal color.
[doctor] What about your family history? Does anyone in your family have blood disorders or liver problems?
[patient] My mother had high blood pressure, but nothing else. His brother, my older brother, had liver issues. Gallstones, I think.
[doctor] Gallstones. Okay. Did he have any genetic conditions?
[patient] I don't think so. He is 86 now. He lives in Istanbul.
[doctor] I see. Let's look at your medical record. Your record number is NR-9942-881. We need to correlate this with your imaging.
[patient] Do I need a scan?
[doctor] Yes. I would like to order a CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis to look at the liver and spleen.
[patient] And the anemia?
[doctor] We will also repeat a peripheral blood smear to look for cell morphology. And we need to check your iron studies, B12, and folate levels.
[patient] Okay. Is it serious?
[doctor] It is serious enough that we need to investigate thoroughly. Anemia in an 84-year-old man can be due to many things, from chronic disease to blood loss.
[patient] I hope it is not something bad.
[doctor] We won't know until we see the scan results. The scan is scheduled for October 12th.
[patient] Is that soon?
[doctor] It is the next available slot. The radiology department is at the Klinikum St. Anna.
[patient] I know that place. It is not far from my house.
[doctor] Good. You will need to fast for four hours before the scan. Can you manage that?

[doctor] Also, I want to adjust your medications. Are you still taking the iron supplement I prescribed?
[patient] Yes, once a day. But I feel a bit of nausea sometimes.

[patient] Okay.

[patient] Yes, my general practitioner, Dr. Weber.

[patient] A hematologist?

[patient] Is that a long wait?

[patient] Thank you, Doctor.
[doctor] You are welcome. Please make sure you have the record number NR-9942-881 ready when you call to confirm the appointment.
[patient] I will write it down.
[doctor] Do you have any questions for me before you go?
[patient] No, I think that is all. Just... I am scared a bit.
[doctor] It is normal to be concerned. We will work through this step by step.
[patient] Thank you.

SUBJECTIVE
Patient is a 66-year-old male presenting for evaluation of a right knee injury sustained after falling on ice. He reports slipping on last Tuesday while walking outside his apartment in Riverdale. He denies loss of consciousness. He was assisted by his neighbor, Mr. Gable, to St. Jude’s Medical Center, where X-rays were negative for fracture. Pain is currently 4/10 at rest and 6/10 with flexion. He has a history of hernia repair in 2018 at Mount Sinai. He takes Lisinopril daily. Family history includes his mother with arthritis and his brother, David (68), with knee pain. He moved from Denver to Chicago. Insured by Blue Cross Blue Shield, policy BCBS-998221-44. OBJECTIVE
Vitals: BP 135/85 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, RR 16/min, Temp 98.2 F.

note:
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Pre-operative assessment for scheduled surgery.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Margot Weber, a 76-year-old female, presents for pre-operative clearance. She reports a history of alcohol use, unspecified, uncomplicated. She has been consuming one glass of wine daily for three months. She also reports consuming one shot of schnapps with breakfast for the past two weeks. She had a glass of wine yesterday. She denies withdrawal symptoms. She is currently taking Aspirin and Pantoprazole.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever, chills, or weight loss.
Cardiovascular: No chest pain, palpitations, or edema.
Respiratory: No cough, dyspnea, or wheezing.
Gastrointestinal: No nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or constipation. Mild epigastric discomfort.
Genitourinary: No dysuria, frequency, or incontinence.
Neurological: No tremors, confusion, or seizures.
Musculoskeletal: No joint pain or muscle weakness.
Psychiatric: Mild anxiety related to upcoming surgery. No depression.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 130/80, HR 78, RR 16, Temp 36.8 C.
General: Alert, oriented x4. No acute distress.
HEENT: Normocephalic, atraumatic. Sclerae anicteric.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. No murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender. Liver palpable 2 cm below costal margin. No splenomegaly. No ascites.
Neurological: Cranial nerves II-XII intact. Motor strength 5/5 in all extremities. Reflexes 2+ and symmetric. No tremors.

RESULTS
CBC: Normal.
CMP: AST 45 U/L, ALT 40 U/L, Bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, Albumin 3.8 g/dL.
Coagulation: PT/INR normal.
Electrolytes: Normal.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Alcohol use disorder, unspecified, uncomplicated.
   - Patient is hemodynamically stable.
   - Liver function mildly impaired but acceptable for surgery.
   - Plan: Clear for surgery. Monitor for withdrawal symptoms post-operatively. Consider thiamine supplementation.
2. Pre-operative assessment.
   - All labs reviewed and within acceptable limits.
   - Patient educated on pre-operative instructions.
   - Contact information verified: margot.weber at gmail dot com.
   - Home address: Hausbergstrasse 42, 80469 Munich.
   - Insurance: Talana, ID 982-441-770.
   - Family history noted: Mother Elisabeth had cirrhosis. Brother Ulf is healthy. Daughter Lena lives in Cologne.
   - Support system: Neighbor Helga available for check-ins.
   - Follow-up: Post-operative care in 1 week.
dialogue:
[doctor] good morning . i am dr . hoffmann . i understand you are here for a pre-operative assessment before your scheduled surgery .
[patient] good morning , doctor . yes , i am margot weber .
[doctor] thank you , margot . could you please confirm your date of birth for the record ?
[patient] i was born on 14 march 1948 .
[doctor] that makes you seventy-six years old today . is that correct ?
[patient] yes , that is correct .
[doctor] you live at hausbergstrasse 42, 80469 munich , if i recall correctly ?
[patient] yes , that is my home address .
[doctor] and your health insurance is with talana ?
[patient] yes . my insurance number is 982-441-770 .
[doctor] thank you . i see your primary care physician , dr . steinbach , referred you . he mentioned you have been drinking alcohol regularly . can you tell me more about that ?
[patient] yes . i have been drinking a glass of wine every evening for about three months now .
[doctor] just wine ?
[patient] mostly wine , but sometimes a shot of schnapps with my breakfast .
[doctor] how much schnapps are we talking about ?
[patient] usually just one small shot .
[doctor] and when did you start this pattern ?
[patient] it began two weeks ago , after i felt very anxious about the upcoming surgery .
[doctor] i see . did you stop drinking recently ?
[patient] no , i had a glass of wine yesterday evening as well .
[doctor] understood . are you currently taking any medication for your alcohol use ?
[patient] no , i am not on any specific medication for that .
[doctor] do you take any other regular medications ?
[patient] yes , i take aspirin daily for my heart , and pantoprazole for my stomach .
[doctor] good . let’s review your family history . does anyone in your family have liver problems ?
[patient] my mother , elisabeth , had liver cirrhosis . she passed away when she was seventy-two .
[doctor] and your father ?
[patient] my father , heinrich , died of a heart attack . he was eighty at the time .
[doctor] do you have any siblings ?
[patient] yes , i have a brother , ulf . he is seventy-eight .
[doctor] does ulf have any liver issues ?
[patient] no , he is quite healthy . he lives in freiburg with his wife .
[doctor] do you have any children ?
[patient] yes , i have a daughter , lena . she is forty-five .
[doctor] does lena live with you ?
[patient] no , she lives in cologne with her husband .
[doctor] i see . let’s talk about your social history . are you currently working ?
[patient] no , i retired from my job as a librarian five years ago .
[doctor] do you have any hobbies ?
[patient] i enjoy gardening in my small garden and reading .
[doctor] do you smoke ?
[patient] no , i never smoked .
[doctor] do you use any other recreational drugs ?
[patient] no , i do not .
[doctor] are you sexually active ?
[patient] no , i am not .
[doctor] have you been in any recent accidents or injuries ?
[patient] no , i have not had any accidents recently .
[doctor] have you had any surgeries in the past ?
[patient] yes , i had a hip replacement four years ago .
[doctor] and how was that recovery ?
[patient] it was good , though i had some pain for a while .
[doctor] do you have any allergies ?
[patient] yes , i am allergic to penicillin .
[doctor] good to know . let’s move on to the physical examination . i am going to check your vital signs first .
[patient] okay .
[doctor] your blood pressure is 130 over 80 . your heart rate is 78 beats per minute .
[patient] does that sound normal ?
[doctor] yes , that is within a normal range for your age .
[doctor] now , i am going to examine your abdomen . please lie down .
[patient] okay .
[doctor] does this hurt anywhere ?
[patient] no , it does not hurt .
[doctor] i am palpating your liver . it feels slightly enlarged , but there is no tenderness .
[patient] i see .
[doctor] your spleen is not enlarged . there is no fluid in your abdomen .
[patient] that is good to hear .
[doctor] let’s check your neurological status . can you squeeze my hand ?
[patient] yes .
[doctor] can you touch your nose with your finger ?
[patient] yes .
[doctor] your reflexes are normal . you have no tremors in your hands .
[patient] i did not know i had tremors .
[doctor] you do not have them right now . that is a good sign .
[doctor] how is your sleep ?
[patient] i sleep well , usually .
[doctor] do you have any nightmares ?
[patient] no , i do not have nightmares .
[doctor] do you feel anxious or depressed ?
[patient] i feel a bit anxious about the surgery , but not depressed .
[doctor] that is understandable . we will manage your anxiety with medication if needed .
[patient] thank you .
[doctor] do you have any support system at home ?
[patient] yes , my neighbor , helga , checks on me sometimes .
[doctor] is helga family ?
[patient] no , she is just a neighbor . she is eighty-two .
[doctor] good . i see you have an e-mail address on file . is it margot.weber at gmail dot com ?
[patient] yes , that is correct .
[doctor] i will send you some information about pre-operative care to that address .
[patient] thank you .
[doctor] do you have any questions for me ?
[patient] just one . will i be able to drink wine after the surgery ?
[doctor] that depends on your recovery . we will discuss that in more detail after the surgery .
[patient] okay .
[doctor] i will now order some blood tests to check your liver function .
[patient] will that hurt ?
[doctor] it will just be a small needle prick .
[patient] okay .
[doctor] the nurse will come in shortly to draw your blood .
[patient] thank you , doctor .
[doctor] you are welcome .

[nurse] hello , margot . i am sarah . i am here to draw your blood .
[patient] hello , sarah .
[nurse] do you have any fear of needles ?
[patient] no , i am not afraid of needles .
[nurse] okay . i am going to put this tourniquet on your arm .
[patient] okay .
[nurse] can you squeeze your hand ?
[patient] yes .
[nurse] okay , release . i am going to clean the area .
[patient] okay .
[nurse] this will be a quick pinch .
[patient] okay .
[nurse] that is done .
[patient] thank you .
[nurse] you can put your bandage on .
[patient] okay .
[nurse] do you have any pain ?
[patient] no , i do not have any pain .
[nurse] good . i will take these samples to the lab .
[patient] thank you .
[nurse] you are welcome .

[doctor] margot , i have received your blood test results .
[patient] how are they ?
[doctor] your liver enzymes are slightly elevated , but not dangerously so .
[patient] that is worrying .
[doctor] it is a common finding in people who drink alcohol . it is reversible if you stop drinking .
[patient] i see .
[doctor] your kidney function is normal .
[patient] good .
[doctor] your blood clotting is normal .
[patient] good .
[doctor] i am satisfied with your assessment . you are cleared for surgery .
[patient] thank you .
[doctor] please follow the pre-operative instructions i sent to your e-mail .
[patient] i will .
[doctor] goodbye , margot .
[patient] goodbye , doctor .
