note:
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Pain in the right foot for two weeks.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Keller is an 86-year-old male presenting with right foot pain. He reports the onset of pain occurred two weeks ago while walking on a playground. He describes the pain as sharp and localized to the lateral aspect of the foot. The pain is exacerbated by weight-bearing and movement. He has been applying ice packs and taking paracetamol for pain relief. He denies any history of trauma such as a fall or direct impact. He mentions a recent trip to Interlaken is planned for next month, which may be affected by his current condition. He is a retired engineer and currently consults for TechFlow Solutions. He works from home most days but occasionally visits the office. His colleague Anna Schmidt has been informed of his reduced mobility. His medical record number is ZH-2024-99821. He was born on 14 March 1938.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever, chills, or fatigue.
Musculoskeletal: Pain in right foot. No other joint pain.
Neurological: No numbness or tingling in the foot or leg.
Cardiovascular: No chest pain or palpitations.
Respiratory: No shortness of breath or cough.
Gastrointestinal: No nausea or vomiting.
Genitourinary: No urinary symptoms.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: Blood pressure 135/85 mmHg, Heart rate 72 bpm, Respiratory rate 14/min, Temperature 36.8°C.
General: Alert and oriented. No acute distress.
Right Foot: Mild swelling observed on the lateral aspect. Tenderness palpated at the 3 o'clock position relative to the lateral malleolus. No erythema or warmth. Full range of motion in the ankle joint, though limited by pain on dorsiflexion. Pulses are 2+ and symmetric. Sensation to light touch is intact.

RESULTS
Previous bone density scan from January 2024 showed normal bone mineral density. No new laboratory tests ordered at this visit.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right foot lateral strain/sprain.
- Plan:
  - Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation (RICE) for 3-5 days.
  - Continue paracetamol for pain as needed. Avoid NSAIDs due to age and gastrointestinal history.
  - Wear supportive footwear with arch support.
  - Limit standing time at work. Work from home recommended for one week.
  - Follow up in clinic in 2 weeks if pain persists or worsens.
  - If pain does not improve in 2 weeks, refer to podiatrist for further evaluation.
  - Patient advised to contact clinic if swelling increases or if foot becomes hot/red.
  - Note sent to employer TechFlow Solutions regarding light duty restrictions.
  - Patient to email blood work from City Hospital Zurich to this office.
dialogue:
[doctor] good morning , mr . keller . my name is dr . weber . you are here for your annual occupational health check-up , correct ?
[patient] good morning , doctor . yes , i am . i’m a little early , but i wanted to make sure i didn't miss my slot .
[doctor] you are punctual , as always . let's begin with the standard questions . how have you been feeling generally ?
[patient] generally well , but i’ve had some trouble with my right foot lately . it’s been bothering me quite a bit .
[doctor] i see . can you tell me more about that pain ? when did it start ?
[patient] it started about two weeks ago . i was walking on the playground near my house , trying to keep up with my grandchildren , and i felt a sharp twinge .
[doctor] a playground . that’s a common place for uneven surfaces . where exactly is the pain located ?
[patient] it’s on the outer side of the foot , near the arch . if i press here , it hurts .
[doctor] let me take a look . please remove your right shoe and sock .
[patient] there we go .
[doctor] thank you . i see some mild swelling around the lateral aspect of the foot . i’m going to palpate a few spots . does this hurt ?
[patient] yes , right there . that’s the spot .
[doctor] i feel a tender point at the 3 o'clock position relative to the lateral malleolus . this is consistent with a strain of the peroneal tendons or a minor ligament sprain .
[patient] is it serious ? i have to work next week .
[doctor] it doesn’t appear to be a fracture , but we should be cautious . since you are 86 years old , we need to rule out any underlying bone density issues . have you had any recent blood work ?
[patient] i had a general check-up at city hospital zurich last month . my bone density was normal , though slightly on the lower side for my age .
[doctor] good to know . do you have the report with you ?
[patient] no , but i can email it to you . my medical record number is zh-2024-99821 .
[doctor] that will be helpful . how is your mobility ? can you walk without a cane ?
[patient] i can walk , but i favor the left foot now . my neighbor , hans meier , told me to use an ice pack . i’ve been doing that .
[doctor] ice is a good start . are you taking any medication for the pain ?
[patient] just some paracetamol . i try to avoid strong painkillers because of my stomach .
[doctor] that is wise . given your age , we should be careful with nsaids . let’s check your reflexes and sensation .
[patient] of course .
[doctor] does the foot feel numb or tingly ?
[patient] no , not really . just the pain when i put weight on it .
[doctor] i see . your sensation is intact . your pulses are strong . this looks like a soft tissue injury , likely exacerbated by the activity on the playground .
[patient] i shouldn’t have been walking so fast . the kids were running around , and i wanted to keep up .
[doctor] i understand . it’s important to stay active , but we must respect the limits of our joints . for the next few days , i recommend rest , ice , compression , and elevation .
[patient] and what about work ? i am a retired engineer , but i still consult for techflow solutions a few days a week .
[doctor] since you are consulting , you are likely on your feet for long periods . i would advise you to limit standing time . can you work from home this week ?
[patient] yes , that would be best . i will speak to my colleague , anna schmidt , and adjust the schedule .
[doctor] good . i will write a note to your employer confirming that you are fit for light desk duties but should avoid prolonged standing .
[patient] that would be very helpful . how long should i expect this to last ?
[doctor] with proper rest , the acute pain should subside in about 5 to 7 days . however , full recovery might take up to three weeks .
[patient] three weeks is a long time . i have a trip planned for next month .
[doctor] where are you going ?
[patient] i am going to interlaken to visit my son .
[doctor> interlaken has a lot of walking paths . you must be very careful . if the pain persists after two weeks , you should return for a follow-up .
[patient] understood . is there anything else i should watch out for ?
[doctor] watch for any increase in swelling or redness . if the foot becomes hot to the touch , see me immediately . also , ensure you are wearing supportive shoes .
[patient] i usually wear comfortable sneakers .
[doctor] make sure they have good arch support . i will refer you to a podiatrist if the pain doesn't improve .
[patient] thank you , doctor . i feel a bit better knowing it’s not a fracture .
[doctor] you’re welcome . i will send the summary to your general practitioner as well . do you have any questions for me ?
[patient] no , that covers everything .
[doctor] excellent . i will prepare the documentation . you are free to go .
[patient] thank you .
[doctor] goodbye , mr . keller .
[patient] goodbye .

note:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY

PATIENT INFORMATION
Name: Haluk Demir
Date of Birth: 14 March 1951
Age: 73
Record Number: UC-99204
Date of Visit: 17 October 2024
Time of Visit: 09:15

CLINICAL HISTORY
The patient presented to the urgent care clinic with a two-week history of worsening respiratory symptoms, including chest tightness and nocturnal dyspnea. The patient reported a preceding upper respiratory infection two weeks prior. He is a lifelong non-smoker. His past medical history includes hypertension, managed with Amlodipine, and a history of Prostatectomy performed three years ago. Family history is notable for Parkinson's disease in his brother, Mehmet. The patient moved from Istanbul to Berlin approximately five years ago. He is an active member of TSV Berlin 90, where he participates in table tennis.

EXAMINATION
Vital signs were stable. Physical examination revealed bilateral wheezing on auscultation. Cardiac examination was unremarkable. No acute joint deformities were noted, though the patient reported mild hip pain from a fall in the kitchen two weeks ago.

DIAGNOSIS
1. Acute exacerbation of mild intermittent asthma.
2. Hypertension (stable).

PLAN
1. Prescribed a five-day course of oral corticosteroids for the acute exacerbation.
2. Initiated daily controller therapy with Fluticasone inhaler to prevent future exacerbations.
3. Continued Amlodipine for blood pressure management.
4. Advised the patient to continue using his rescue inhaler as needed for symptoms.
5. Instructed the patient to monitor for hip pain and seek immediate medical attention if symptoms worsen or if there is severe respiratory distress.
6. Follow-up appointment scheduled for 24 October 2024 at 10:30 with Dr. Halloway.

PATIENT EDUCATION
The patient was educated on the proper use of inhalers and the importance of adherence to controller medication. He understood the risks of uncontrolled asthma and the need to complete the full course of steroids. He was advised to avoid triggers such as cold air and dust.
dialogue:
[nurse] Good morning. I see you have an appointment with Dr. Halloway. Please take a seat in the waiting area. Your name is...
[patient] Demir. My full name is Haluk Demir.
[nurse] Thank you, Mr. Demir. You were born on 14 March 1951, correct?
[patient] Yes, that is correct.
[nurse] Your record number is UC-99204. Do you have any immediate concerns?
[patient] Yes, I have been having trouble breathing for the last few days. It feels like my asthma is acting up again.
[nurse] I will let the doctor know. Please fill out these forms while you wait.
[doctor] Hello, Mr. Demir. I am Dr. Halloway. I see you are here for respiratory issues. How are you feeling today?
[patient] Not very well, Doctor. I am seventy-three years old, and I have had asthma for many years, but it is usually under control.
[doctor] I see. When did this current episode start?
[patient] It started about two weeks ago. I had a mild cold, and since then, my breathing has been worse.
[doctor] And how is it now? Are you having difficulty walking or talking?
[patient] A little. I feel tight in the chest. It is worse at night. I woke up last night gasping for air.
[doctor] I understand. Let us listen to your lungs. Please take a deep breath in... and out.
[doctor] I can hear some wheezing. This suggests an acute exacerbation of your mild intermittent asthma. Do you have your inhaler with you?
[patient] Yes, here. I use it when I feel tight, but it does not seem to work as well as before.
[doctor] That is concerning. Do you use a controller medication?
[patient] No, I only use the rescue inhaler. My doctor in Istanbul, where I lived before moving to Berlin, said I only needed it for emergencies.
[doctor] I see. Since you moved to Germany, have you seen a specialist here?
[patient] I saw a general practitioner in St. Clara Clinic six months ago. He gave me a new prescription, but I have not been using it regularly.
[doctor] Which medication was that?
[patient] I think it was Fluticasone. It is a powder inhaler.
[doctor] That is a corticosteroid. It is important for long-term control. You should not rely only on the rescue inhaler.
[patient] But I do not want to take too many drugs. I am worried about side effects.
[doctor] I understand. However, uncontrolled asthma can lead to serious complications. Let us check your lung function first.
[nurse] Mr. Demir, please come to the spirometry room.
[patient] Yes, coming.
[nurse] Please blow into this tube as hard as you can.
[patient] Okay.
[nurse] Good. One more time.
[nurse] Your FEV1 is 65% of predicted. This is lower than normal, confirming an exacerbation.
[doctor] Thank you. Mr. Demir, your lungs are currently inflamed. We need to treat this acute phase.
[patient] What will you do?
[doctor] I am going to prescribe a short course of oral corticosteroids to reduce the inflammation. You will also need to start using the controller inhaler daily.
[patient] Oral steroids? I heard they are dangerous.
[doctor] A short course, like five days, is generally safe and effective for an acute attack. It will help you breathe better quickly.
[patient] Okay. What about the inhaler?
[doctor] You will continue to use your rescue inhaler as needed, but you must start the Fluticasone daily. This will prevent future attacks.
[patient] And my other medications? I take Amlodipine for blood pressure.
[doctor] That is fine. No interactions with the asthma medication. Do you have any allergies?
[patient] No, I do not.
[doctor] Do you have any other medical conditions?
[patient] I had Prostatectomy three years ago. And my brother, Mehmet, has Parkinson's disease.
[doctor] I see. Family history is noted. Did you have any recent injuries?
[patient] Yes, I fell in the kitchen two weeks ago. I hit my hip.
[doctor] Did you go to the emergency room?
[patient] No, I just put ice on it. It hurts when I walk, but I can manage.
[doctor] We should be careful. Falls can be serious in older adults. If the hip pain gets worse, please see a doctor immediately.
[patient] I will.
[doctor] Let us also review your lifestyle. Do you smoke?
[patient] No, I quit ten years ago.
[doctor] Good. Do you exercise?
[patient] I am a member of TSV Berlin 90. I play table tennis there twice a week.
[doctor] That is great. Light exercise is good for lung health, but you should stop if you feel short of breath.
[patient] I will.
[doctor] Here is your prescription. You need to pick it up at the pharmacy.
[patient] Thank you.
[doctor] When should you follow up?
[patient] When?
[doctor] Please come back in one week to check your lung function again. I have an appointment for you on Friday, 24 October at 10:30.
[patient] Okay, Friday, 24 October at 10:30.
[doctor] Do you have any questions?
[patient] Just one. If I feel better, can I stop the steroid?
[doctor] No, you must finish the five-day course. Stopping early can make the inflammation come back.
[patient] Understood.
[doctor] Please rest and avoid cold air or dust. If you have severe chest pain or cannot speak in full sentences, call emergency services.
[patient] I will. Thank you, Doctor.
[doctor] You are welcome. Take care.

note:
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Marcus, a 56-year-old male, presents with left-sided hearing loss and tinnitus for two weeks. He reports a history of minor head trauma occurring in the kitchen of his private residence in Bologna. He was chopping vegetables when he accidentally struck his head against the counter/doorframe. He experienced immediate dizziness and muffled hearing, which has persisted. He denies vertigo, nausea, or otorrhea. He works as a logistics coordinator for LogiTrans.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Hypertension, managed with <ORGANization>Amlodipine</ORGANization>. Allergy to penicillin. No other significant history.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Lives with wife Sofia (54). Brother Luca (52) is available for support.

EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 130/85 mmHg.
ENT Exam: Left tympanic membrane shows mild retraction at the 3 o'clock position. There is a small area of fluid behind the eardrum. No perforation. Right ear is normal. No otitis externa.

ASSESSMENT
Traumatic otitis media with effusion (left).

PLAN
1. Prescribe Mometasone nasal spray, 1 spray per nostril twice daily.
2. Prescribe Pseudoephedrine 60mg, 1 tablet twice daily. Monitor BP due to hypertension.
3. Advise to avoid loud noises, heavy lifting, and straining.
4. Instruct patient not to drive if experiencing dizziness. Suggested Luca as backup driver.
5. Follow up in 2 weeks if symptoms persist or worsen. Consider audiogram or MRI if no improvement.
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning. Please, come in and have a seat. I see you’ve been having some trouble with your hearing?
[patient] Yes, doctor. Hi. Um, I’m Marcus. I’m 56 years old. It’s... it’s been annoying for a few weeks.
[doctor] Marcus, nice to meet you. Can you tell me exactly what’s happening? Is it one ear or both?
[patient] Mostly the left one. It feels like... you know, like there’s cotton in there. And sometimes a ringing. Tinnitus, I think my wife calls it.
[doctor] I see. And when did this start? Do you recall any specific event or injury that might have triggered it?
[patient] Um, well, it was... maybe two weeks ago? I was at home. Just my house in Bologna. I was in the kitchen.
[doctor] In the kitchen. Did you have an accident?
[patient] No, not really. I was chopping vegetables. And suddenly, *bang*. I think I hit my head against the edge of the counter. Or maybe the doorframe? It was dark, I was rushing.
[doctor] So, a blow to the head, specifically near the ear?
[patient] I think so. I didn’t bleed or anything, but I felt dizzy. And then the hearing got muffled. I thought it would go away, but it didn’t.
[doctor] Understood. Do you have any other symptoms? Dizziness, vertigo, nausea?

REASON FOR VISIT:
Follow-up for dyspnea and chest pressure. Patient reports worsening shortness of breath on exertion, specifically when climbing stairs or during work shifts at Volkswagen in Wolfsburg.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
Marek Kowalski, a 36-year-old male, presents with progressive dyspnea and mild chest tightness over the past two months. He describes the pain as a pressure sensation, rated 4/10 on the numeric pain scale. He works as a welder and plays amateur football for FC Hagen on Tuesdays and Thursdays. He reports that his stamina has decreased significantly compared to previous years.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
- Right upper lobectomy performed two years ago for a benign tumor, resulting in acquired absence of part of the lung.
- No history of diabetes or hypertension prior to this visit.

FAMILY HISTORY:
Father deceased of myocardial infarction. Sister Kasia is healthy.

SOCIAL HISTORY:
Works in manufacturing. Smoker (quit 5 years ago). Alcohol intake limited to Friday evenings.

VITAL SIGNS:
BP: 138/86 mmHg
HR: 92 bpm
SpO2: 94% on room air
Temperature: 36.8°C

EXAMINATION:
Cardiac auscultation reveals a soft systolic murmur, grade 2/6, best heard at the left sternal border, specifically at the 3 o'clock position. Lungs are clear to auscultation on the left side; decreased breath sounds on the right consistent with prior lobectomy. No peripheral edema.

INVESTIGATIONS:
- Troponin: Normal
- BNP: 350 pg/mL (Elevated)
- ECG: Sinus tachycardia, no acute ischemic changes.

ASSESSMENT:
Dyspnea secondary to reduced pulmonary reserve and early signs of cardiac strain. Likely pulmonary hypertension secondary to chronic hypoxia and reduced lung volume. The murmur suggests functional valve turbulence due to increased cardiac output.

PLAN:
1. Start Losartan 50 mg daily.
2. Start Metoprolol 25 mg twice daily.
3. Echocardiogram scheduled for next week to assess right ventricular function and estimate pulmonary artery pressure.
4. Activity restriction: No high-intensity exercise (e.g., competitive football) until echo results are reviewed.
5. Follow-up in two weeks with echo results.
6. Patient advised to seek immediate care if chest pain increases to >7/10 or if syncope occurs.

[doctor] Good morning, Mr. Kowalski. Please have a seat. I see you’re here for your cardiology follow-up. How have you been feeling since we last spoke?
[patient] Hi, Dr. Miller. Um, honestly? I’m still a bit out of breath, you know? Like, I can walk to the shop, but if I climb two flights of stairs, my heart just... pumps too hard.
[doctor] I understand. Let’s take your vitals first. Nurse, could you step in?
[nurse] Sure thing. Mr. Kowalski, let’s get your blood pressure and oxygen levels.
[patient] Okay. Thanks.
[nurse] Blood pressure is 138 over 86. Heart rate is 92 beats per minute. Oxygen saturation is 94 percent.
[doctor] Thank you. 94 percent is a bit low. Let’s talk about that. You mentioned the breathing issues. When did this start?
[patient] It started, uh, maybe two months ago? I was working at Volkswagen in Wolfsburg, and I noticed I couldn’t keep up with my colleagues on the assembly line.
[doctor] You work in automotive manufacturing?
[patient] Yeah, I’m a welder there. It’s heavy work. And I play football too, for SV Werder Bremen... wait, no, I play for a local amateur team, FC Hagen. I play every Tuesday and Thursday.
[doctor] I see. And how is your chest pain? On a scale of zero to ten, where ten is the worst pain imaginable?
[patient] Uh, maybe a four? It’s not sharp, more like pressure. Like a heavy blanket on my chest.
[doctor] Okay. Let’s listen to your heart. Take a deep breath in... and out.
[patient] [breathes deeply]
[doctor] I hear a soft systolic murmur. It’s most prominent at the left sternal border, specifically at the 3 o'clock position.
[patient] At the three o'clock? What does that mean?
[doctor] It means the sound is loudest when I place the stethoscope there. It suggests some valve turbulence. We need to investigate further. Do you have any family history of heart conditions?
[patient] My father died young, but I think it was just a heart attack. My sister, Kasia, she has Aetna insurance, but she’s in Poland. She’s fine.
[doctor] I see. Let’s look at your recent labs. Your troponin levels were normal, which is good. But your BNP is slightly elevated at 350 pg/mL. This indicates some strain on the heart.
[patient] Strain? Is that because of the lung?
[doctor] You mentioned you had a part of your lung removed?
[patient] Yes. Two years ago. I had a tumor. They took out the right upper lobe.
[doctor] Ah, I see. So you have an acquired absence of part of the lung. That changes the dynamics of your breathing and circulation.
[patient] Exactly. I feel like I can’t get enough air, so my heart works harder.
[doctor] That makes sense. The reduced lung volume means less gas exchange, so the heart has to pump faster and harder to compensate. This can lead to pulmonary hypertension.
[patient] Pulmonary hypertension? That sounds scary.
[doctor] It can be, but it’s manageable. We need to do an echocardiogram to see how your heart is handling the pressure.
[patient] When can we do that?
[doctor] I’ll schedule it for next week. In the meantime, we’re going to start you on Losartan 50 mg daily to help lower the blood pressure and reduce the strain on your heart.
[patient] Just a pill?
[doctor] Yes. And Metoprolol 25 mg twice a day to control your heart rate.
[patient] Okay. I’ll take them. What about the exercise? Can I still play for FC Hagen?
[doctor] I’d recommend you hold off on high-intensity sports for now. Light walking is fine, but no heavy lifting or sprinting until we see the echo results.
[patient] That’s a shame. I really enjoy the team.
[doctor] I understand. Your health comes first. We want to prevent any complications.
[patient] Okay. I’ll rest.
[doctor] Also, keep an eye on your symptoms. If the chest pain increases to a seven or eight, or if you feel dizzy, call us immediately.
[patient] Understood. And my insurance? Do I need to send anything to Aetna?
[doctor] You have Barmer insurance, correct? Your number is A123456789.
[patient] Yes, that’s right.
[doctor] I’ll send the referral and the prescription directly to them. You should receive the approval in a few days.
[patient] Thank you. I was worried I’d have to go back and forth.
[doctor] No problem. We’ll handle it. Do you have any questions about the medication?
[patient] Just... do I take them with food?
[doctor] Losartan can be taken with or without food. Metoprolol is best taken with food to avoid stomach upset.
[patient] Okay. With food. Got it.
[doctor] And remember, no alcohol with these medications.
[patient] I’ll be careful. I usually only have a beer on Fridays, but I’ll skip it.
[doctor] That’s a good idea. Let’s get you back on track.
[patient] Thanks, Dr. Miller. I feel a bit better knowing what’s going on.
[doctor] You’re welcome. We’ll see you in two weeks for the echo results.
[patient] See you then.

SUBJECTIVE
Elisabeth Wagner, a 47-year-old female, presents with complaints of fatigue and dizziness for the past two weeks. She is a project manager at NovaTech Solutions in Vienna. The patient reports that her general practitioner, Dr. Steiner, referred her due to abnormal liver function studies. She denies significant alcohol use, consuming only occasional wine. She recently started taking an herbal supplement, Cardo-Mix, for digestive issues. She has a history of using Ultracold for headaches. Family history is notable for her mother’s gallbladder issues and her uncle’s late-onset liver cirrhosis. She reports no other significant medical history. She is insured by Swarcovski Health Insurance, policy 7845-2910-44.

OBJECTIVE
Vital signs: BP 130/85, HR 72 bpm, Temp 36.8°C.
Physical Exam:
General: Alert, oriented, no jaundice.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender, no hepatosplenomegaly.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs.
Labs (from Dr. Steiner):
ALT: 85 U/L (elevated)
AST: 92 U/L (elevated)
GPT: 65 U/L (elevated)
Bilirubin: Normal
Ultrasound: Scheduled for tomorrow.
Past Visits: Routine check-up on October 12th with Dr. Steiner. Previous normal liver panel five years ago.

ASSESSMENT
1. Abnormal liver function tests (Elevated ALT, AST, GPT).
2. Fatigue.
3. Possible medication or supplement-induced liver injury (suspect Cardo-Mix).
4. Rule out other hepatic pathologies.

PLAN
1. Discontinue Cardo-Mix immediately.
2. Continue Ultracold as needed, but monitor for side effects.
3. Order comprehensive metabolic panel and viral hepatitis serology.
4. Abdominal ultrasound scheduled for tomorrow at 09:30 at MedPlus Imaging. Fasting required for eight hours.

[doctor] Good morning, Elisabeth Wagner. Please have a seat. I see you’re here regarding some abnormal lab results we received from your general practitioner.
[patient] Good morning, Doctor Hauer. Yes, Dr. Steiner referred me here because my liver enzymes were elevated. I’ve been feeling quite fatigued lately, but I didn’t think it was serious.
[doctor] I understand. Fatigue can be a symptom of many things. Can you tell me when you first started noticing this tiredness?
[patient] It began about two weeks ago. I work as a project manager at NovaTech Solutions in Vienna, so I have a lot of stress. I thought it was just overwork.
[doctor] I see. You are 47 years old, correct?
[patient] Yes, that is correct.
[doctor] Let’s look at the numbers. Your ALT and AST were significantly higher than normal. Have you been taking any new medications or supplements?
[patient] I have been taking Ultracold for occasional headaches, but I’ve been on that for years. Recently, I started taking a herbal supplement called Cardo-Mix for digestion.
[doctor] I would like you to stop taking that supplement immediately. Herbal products can sometimes affect liver function. Do you drink alcohol?
[patient] Only occasionally. Maybe a glass of wine on weekends. Nothing excessive.
[doctor] That is reasonable. Do you have a history of liver disease in your family?
[patient] My mother had issues with her gallbladder, and her brother, my uncle, had liver cirrhosis, but that was very late in life.
[doctor] Noted. I want to order a more comprehensive blood panel and an ultrasound of your abdomen to rule out any structural issues.
[patient] When would that be?
[doctor] We will schedule the ultrasound for tomorrow at 09:30 at our clinic’s imaging center. You will need to fast for eight hours before the appointment.
[patient] I can do that. Do I need a new referral?
[doctor] No, I will send the orders directly to MedPlus Imaging. Here is your insurance card. I see you are with Swarcovski Health Insurance. Your policy number is 7845-2910-44.
[patient] Thank you. By the way, my neighbor, Karl, had a similar issue with his liver a few years ago. He said it was related to a medication he was taking for blood pressure.
[doctor] It is possible. Medication-induced liver injury is a common cause. We need to look at your full medication list. Are you on any other drugs?
[patient] Just the Ultracold and the supplement. I don’t take anything else regularly.
[doctor] Okay. Let’s check your vital signs. Your blood pressure is 130/85, which is slightly elevated but not critical. Your heart rate is normal.
[patient] I feel a bit dizzy when I stand up quickly. Is that related?
[doctor] It could be dehydration or related to the fatigue. Make sure you are drinking enough water.
[doctor] Let’s review your past medical history. You had a routine check-up with Dr. Steiner on October 12th, correct?
[patient] Yes, that was when I felt the fatigue start.
[doctor] And before that, did you have any other liver tests?
[patient] I think I had one about five years ago when I was 42. The results were normal then.
[doctor] Good. That helps establish a baseline. I want to keep a close eye on this. We will see you again in three weeks to review the ultrasound results and the new blood work.
[patient] When exactly is the next appointment?
[doctor] It is scheduled for November 24th at 10:15. I will send a confirmation to your email, elisa.wagner at vienna-net dot at.
[patient] Thank you. I will stop the supplement today.
[doctor] That is a good step. If you experience severe abdominal pain, yellowing of the eyes or skin, or extreme weakness, please go to the emergency room immediately.
[patient] Understood. I will be careful.
[doctor] You have my direct line if you have urgent questions, but for non-urgent matters, please call the clinic switchboard at +43 1 555 0199.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor Hauer.
[doctor] You’re welcome, Elisabeth. Take care of yourself.

note:
SUBJECTIVE
Patient is a sixty-one-year-old male presenting with right shoulder pain for three months. Pain started gradually in February due to repetitive overhead work at Alfa Romeo. Acute exacerbation occurred yesterday while lifting a box. Pain is localized to the lateral shoulder, radiating to the elbow. Pain is worse at night and with overhead activities. Patient reports using Ibuprofen with partial relief. Family history is notable for Parkinson's disease in father and Hashimoto's thyroiditis in sister Lucia (twenty-eight years old). Patient works for Giuseppe, his supervisor.

OBJECTIVE
Vitals within normal limits. Right shoulder inspection shows mild atrophy of the supraspinatus muscle. Range of motion is limited in external and internal rotation. Positive Neer impingement test and Hawkins-Kennedy test. No tenderness over the acromioclavicular joint. No neurological deficits in the upper extremity.

ASSESSMENT
1. Right shoulder subacromial impingement syndrome, likely secondary to repetitive overhead occupational activity.
2. No evidence of rotator cuff tear on clinical exam, but further imaging may be required if conservative management fails.

PLAN
1. Rest from overhead activities.
2. NSAIDs: Ibuprofen 400mg PO TID with food for 7 days; Diclofenac gel to right shoulder QID.
3. Ice application 15 minutes TID for pain and inflammation.
4. Referral to physical therapy for rotator cuff strengthening and stretching. Referral sent to Mario's clinic in Como.
5. Occupational health clearance: Temporary restriction from overhead lifting and reaching.
6. Follow-up in 2 weeks. If no improvement, consider ultrasound or MRI.

REFERRAL LETTER

Dear Dr. Elena Ross,

I am writing to refer Eleanor Vane, 48 years old, DOB 14 March 1976, for urgent assessment of acquired bilateral breast and nipple atrophy.

The patient is a Warehouse Supervisor at Northgate Logistics. She resides at 14 Oakwood Avenue, LS6 3AB, Leeds and moved from Bristol to Leeds in 2021.

**Presenting Complaint:**
Ms. Vane presents with progressive bilateral loss of breast tissue and nipples over the past six months. She first noticed the changes during a trip to Edinburgh in September. She reports significant weight loss (approx. 5 stone) and fatigue.

**History:**
- **Medical History:** Diagnosed with thyroid dysfunction, managed with Levothyroxine. Previous concerns raised regarding Hashimoto's thyroiditis, though recent bloods show elevated thyroid levels, possibly suggesting a shift towards Graves' disease-like symptoms, though definitive diagnosis is pending.
- **Family History:** Mother has Graves' disease; Brother has Crohn's disease.
- **Social History:** Member of FitLife Gym, though activity has ceased recently due to fatigue. No smoking or alcohol excess.

**Examination Findings:**
- General: Cachectic appearance.
- Breast Exam: Bilateral absence of breast parenchyma and nipple-areola complexes. Skin intact, no masses, no lymphadenopathy.
- Thyroid: No palpable goiter.

**Investigations:**
- Recent thyroid function tests: Elevated TSH, Low Free T4.
- Mammography/Scan: Clear, no structural masses.
- General Bloods: Normal except for mild anemia.

**Reason for Referral:**
To investigate the cause of acquired lipodystrophy/breast atrophy. Differential diagnosis may include genetic lipodystrophies, autoimmune conditions, or rare endocrine disorders. I would appreciate your advice on further testing (e.g., genetic panel, detailed metabolic profile) and management plan.

Yours sincerely,

Dr. Aris Thorne
Occupational Health Physician

[doctor] Good morning. I see you’re here for your occupational health review. I’m Dr. Aris Thorne. Can I just confirm your details for the file?

[doctor] Thank you, Eleanor. And your date of birth is 14 March 1976?
[patient] Yes, that’s correct.
[doctor] Perfect. You’re currently employed by Northgate Logistics as a Warehouse Supervisor, correct?
[patient] Yes, I am. It’s been a bit stressful lately, to be honest.
[doctor] I can imagine. What brings you in today? Is there a specific concern on your mind?
[patient] Well, it’s... it’s quite hard to talk about, you know? But my breasts are just... gone. Or rather, they’ve disappeared.
[doctor] I’m sorry to hear that. Can you describe what you mean by "gone"? Is this a sudden change or gradual?
[patient] It’s been gradual, I think. Over the last few months. They’ve just... deflated. And my nipples are gone too. I’m talking about bilateral absence.
[doctor] Bilateral absence of the breasts and nipples. That is a significant physical change. When did you first notice this?
[patient] I noticed it about six months ago. I was getting ready for a trip to Edinburgh with a friend.
[doctor] Edinburgh. That sounds lovely.
[patient] It was, actually. We went in September. But I was self-conscious. I couldn’t wear my usual clothes. I felt like people were staring.
[doctor] I understand. Did you see your GP about this?
[patient] Yes, I did. I saw Dr. Sarah Jenkins at my local practice.
[doctor] And what did she do?
[patient] She examined me. She said it looked like severe atrophy. She ordered some blood tests and a scan.
[doctor] Did the tests show anything specific?
[patient] The scan was clear. No masses. The blood tests... well, my thyroid levels were a bit high. She mentioned Hashimoto's thyroiditis, but said it wasn't the cause of the breast loss.
[doctor] I see. High thyroid levels can be associated with various conditions, but direct breast atrophy is rare. Have you had any other symptoms?
[patient] I’ve been really tired. And I’ve lost weight. About five stone in the last year.
[doctor] Significant weight loss. Have you had any appetite changes?
[patient] Not really. I just eat less. I feel full quickly.
[doctor] Do you have any family history of endocrine disorders?
[patient] My mother had Graves' disease. And my brother has Crohn's disease.
[doctor] I understand. Let’s check your current medications. Are you taking anything for your thyroid or any other conditions?
[patient] I’m on Levothyroxine for the thyroid. And I take Paracetamol if I have a headache.
[doctor] Okay. Let’s do a quick physical exam. Can you please remove your top?
[patient] Of course.
[doctor] Thank you. I can see the skin is intact, but the tissue is indeed absent. The areola and nipple structures are not visible. This is consistent with severe lipodystrophy or perhaps a specific genetic condition, though acquired cases are rarer.
[patient] Acquired? But I didn’t have this before.
[doctor] Correct. We need to investigate why this is happening now. I’m going to refer you to a specialist for further evaluation.
[patient] A specialist? Like a surgeon?
[doctor] No, not a surgeon initially. I’m referring you to the Endocrine and Metabolic Unit at Manchester Royal Infirmary. They deal with complex hormonal issues.
[patient] Oh, good. I live in Leeds now.
[doctor] You mentioned earlier you moved. Where did you live before?
[patient] I was in Bristol for ten years. I moved to Leeds in 2021.
[doctor] I see. And where in Leeds do you live?
[patient] I live at 14 Oakwood Avenue, LS6 3AB, Leeds.
[doctor] Noted. Do you have any hobbies or activities that might be relevant? Sometimes physical activity can be a clue.
[patient] I used to go to the gym a lot. I’m a member of FitLife Gym in Leeds.
[doctor] Do you still go?
[patient] Not really. I just don’t have the energy.
[doctor] Okay. I will send the referral today. You should receive an appointment within six weeks. In the meantime, keep taking your Levothyroxine as prescribed.
[patient] Thank you, Dr. Thorne. I just want to get to the bottom of this.
[doctor] We will. Do you have any other questions before I finish?
[patient] No, I think that’s all.
[doctor] Good. My secretary will call you to confirm the appointment details.

Right Upper Extremity:
Inspection: No erythema, swelling, or deformity of the right elbow.

Range of Motion: Active flexion 0-120 degrees, extension 0-10 degrees (limited by pain).

[doctor] Bonjour, Madame. I understand you’re here for a follow-up regarding some heart palpitations we saw on your recent ECG. How are you feeling today?
[patient] Bonjour, Dr. Honegger. Honestly? I’m still a bit nervous. You know, when I read that report, my heart just... skipped. I don't know how to explain it. It’s just there, *thump*, and then a pause.
[doctor] That is exactly what we are looking at. The ECG showed some ventricular premature depolarizations. Do you feel them often now?
[patient] Not constantly. Maybe a few times a day? But yesterday, while I was walking near the lake, it happened several times in a row. I had to stop and catch my breath.
[doctor] Did you feel dizzy or faint?
[patient] No, no fainting. Just a bit of shortness of breath. And maybe a little chest tightness, like a 3/10 on the pain scale. Nothing severe, but annoying.
[doctor] Understood. Let’s take some vitals today. Nurse, could you check her blood pressure and heart rate?
[nurse] Yes, Doctor. Madame, please roll up your sleeve. ...Okay, your blood pressure is 135/85. Heart rate is 72 beats per minute. Rhythm is irregular, but regularizing.
[doctor] Thank you. Your blood pressure is slightly elevated, but not dangerously so. Now, let’s talk about your history. You mentioned in the intake form that you work as a librarian?
[patient] Yes, at the public library in Geneva. It’s quiet, so I notice every little beat of my heart.
[doctor] I see. And do you have a family history of heart conditions?
[patient] Yes. My mother had high blood pressure, but she died of something else. However, my brother Thomas had a serious arrhythmia diagnosed when he was young. I’m worried it’s genetic.
[doctor] That is a valid concern. We need to rule out any structural issues or electrolyte imbalances. I’ve ordered some blood work. Your potassium and magnesium levels were normal last time, but we will check again.
[patient] And the medication? I’m taking Metoprolol 50 mg twice a day, as you prescribed.
[doctor] Yes, that’s correct. It’s a beta-blocker. Have you been taking it consistently?
[patient] Mostly. I forgot one dose last week because I was traveling to Lausanne for a conference.
[doctor] Consistency is key. Missing doses can sometimes trigger those extra beats. How has your sleep been?
[patient] Poor, unfortunately. I wake up around 3 am and can’t fall back asleep. I worry about the next day.
[doctor] Stress and lack of sleep can definitely exacerbate palpitations. Have you tried any over-the-counter sleep aids?
[patient] I used some melatonin, but it didn’t help much. I also drink tea with honey, but I’ve cut down on caffeine. I used to have three coffees a day, now it’s just one in the morning.
[doctor] Good move. Caffeine is a known trigger for ventricular ectopy. Let’s look at your ECG trace again. These premature beats are isolated, meaning they don’t come in clusters or runs of three or more. That is reassuring.
[patient] But what if they change? What if it becomes more frequent?
[doctor] That is why we are monitoring you closely. If you start feeling lightheaded, or if the episodes become very frequent—more than 10 in a minute—you should come in immediately or go to the emergency room.
[patient] Understood. And the stress test?
[doctor] We need to see how your heart responds to exertion. I’m referring you to Dr. Lacroix at the Clinique de la Colline. He specializes in arrhythmias.
[patient] Is he good?
[doctor] He is an excellent cardiologist. I’ve worked with him before. I will write a referral letter today.

[doctor] Good morning, Mr. Hoxha. I see you’re here for a follow-up. How have you been since we last spoke?
[patient] Good morning, Doctor. Honestly? It’s been a nightmare. I’ve been in so much pain, you know? My side, the right side, it hurts like hell.
[doctor] I’m sorry to hear that. Let’s take a look at the file. I see you were referred by Dr. Keller from Hospital Zurzach. She mentioned you had some acute issues. Can you tell me when this started?
[patient] It started, um... maybe two weeks ago? I was in Prishtina for a family wedding. My cousin Besnik was getting married. We ate a lot of meat, you know, traditional food. And then the pain started.
[doctor] And you were in Prishtina at that time?
[patient] Yes, I flew back to Switzerland on Tuesday. But the pain didn’t stop. It’s been here, uh, off and on, but mostly on.
[doctor] Okay. And where exactly is the pain?
[patient] Right here. Right upper quadrant. Under the ribs. It’s like a burning, but also a sharp pain. Like a knife, sometimes.
[doctor] And does it radiate anywhere? To your back, your shoulder?
[patient] Yes, to my right shoulder. And sometimes to the middle of my back. It’s very uncomfortable.
[doctor] On a scale of zero to ten, how bad is the pain right now?
[patient] Uh... maybe a seven? Or an eight? It’s been worse at night.
[doctor] I see. Have you had any fever or chills?
[patient] Yes, I had a fever. Maybe three days ago? I felt hot and shivering. I took some Ibuprofen, but it didn’t help much.
[doctor] Did you go to the emergency room when you were in Prishtina?
[patient] No, I thought it would pass. I was worried about the cost, you know? And I wanted to come back to Switzerland to see my regular doctor. But then it got worse.
[doctor] I understand. Did Dr. Keller do any tests before referring you to me?
[patient] Yes. She did a blood test and an ultrasound. The ultrasound showed something in my gallbladder. She said it was a stone, but she wasn’t sure if it was blocked.
[doctor] Right. Let’s check those results. I have the lab work from last week. Your white blood cell count was elevated. And your liver enzymes were slightly high.
[patient] Is that dangerous?
[doctor] It indicates inflammation. Let’s do a physical exam. Please lie down on the table.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] Breathe in deeply... hold it... and out.
[patient] Ouch!
[doctor] I see. There’s tenderness in the right upper quadrant. And when I press here and you breathe in, it hurts, right? That’s a positive Murphy’s sign.
[patient] Yes, yes, that’s it.
[doctor] I also noticed a small, firm lump in your left breast, at the 3 o’clock position. It’s probably benign, but I’ll want to follow up on that separately. It’s not related to your abdominal pain.
[patient] Oh, I didn’t notice that. Is it cancer?
[doctor] No, don’t worry. It’s likely a fibroadenoma or a cyst. I’ll refer you for a breast ultrasound. But first, let’s focus on the gallbladder.
[patient] Okay. What do you think is wrong?
[doctor] Based on your symptoms, the physical exam, and the previous ultrasound, it looks like acute cholecystitis caused by a gallstone. The stone is likely stuck in the cystic duct, causing inflammation.
[patient] So, what do I need to do? Do I need surgery?
[doctor] Probably. But first, we need to control the inflammation. I’m going to start you on Amoxicillin-Clavulanate to prevent infection. And Omeprazole to protect your stomach.
[patient] Okay. And the surgery?
[doctor] I’ll contact the surgical team at Hospital Zurzach. They might want to see you for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. That’s the standard treatment.
[patient] When?
[doctor] As soon as possible. Once the inflammation goes down a bit. I’ll call you within 24 hours to schedule it.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor. I’m so glad I came.
[doctor] You did the right thing. Make sure you take the antibiotics as prescribed. And avoid fatty foods for now.
[patient] I’ll do that. No more meat for a while.
[doctor] That’s a good idea. And if the pain gets worse, or if you get a high fever, go to the emergency room.
[patient] Okay. I will.
[doctor] Let’s get your insurance details sorted. What is your insurer?
[patient] It’s Swiss Life.
[doctor] And your policy number?
[patient] It’s SL-482910-KH.
[doctor] And your medical record number here?
[patient] I think it’s MR-2023-8845.
[doctor] Perfect. I’ll make sure all the documents are sent to the surgeon. Do you have any questions?
[patient] No, I think that’s all. Thank you.
[doctor] You’re welcome. Goodbye.

[doctor] then we’ll see it clearly on the ct . for now , the x-ray is reassuring . the finding is small and stable .
[patient] stable ? it’s been there for three months .
[doctor] yes , and it hasn't grown significantly . that’s a good sign . malignancies tend to grow .
[patient] i see . so , no medication needed ?

[patient] understood . he’s also allergic to penicillin .
[doctor] noted . does he have any other conditions ? like parkinson's or bell's palsy ?
[patient] no . he’s quite robust . just the knee issue .
[doctor] alright . let’s wrap up . the plan is a ct scan on 25 may 2024 . we will review the results in two weeks .
[patient] thank you . i really appreciate your calmness . it’s easy to panic when you see abnormal on a report .
[doctor] that’s my job . keep him hydrated , and maybe reduce the brufen if it’s not needed for pain .
[patient] will do . he’s got a game on saturday with fc buechser . i’ll tell him to rest .
[doctor] good idea . if you have any questions , call our office .

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Marcelo Rossi is an 85-year-old man with a history of multiple sclerosis, presenting for a routine nephrology follow-up. He reported a recent fall at the gym, resulting in left knee pain. He denied any head trauma. He reported increased leg tremor, which he was concerned might be indicative of Parkinson's disease. He also reported dry eyes and redness, leading to a thyroid evaluation. - Multiple sclerosis (diagnosed 1990)
- Hypertension
- Hyperlipidemia
- No history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis or Baker's cyst.
- No history of Graves' disease confirmed yet, but suspected.

MEDICATIONS
- Furosemide 40 mg daily
- Gabapentin 300 mg at night
- Multivitamin

ALLERGIES
- No known drug allergies

EXAMINATION
General: Alert and oriented.
Neurological:
- Cranial nerves: II-XII intact. No facial asymmetry (ruling out Bell's palsy).
- Motor: 4/5 strength in lower extremities. Resting tremor noted in left leg.
- Sensory: Decreased sensation in left leg.
- Reflexes: Hyperreflexia in lower extremities.
- Lhermitte's sign: Positive upon neck flexion.

- Slit lamp examination revealed mild anterior uveitis.

note:
SUBJECTIVE
The patient is a 35-year-old woman with a chief complaint of a perioral rash for 3 weeks. She describes it as small red bumps that itch, particularly when sweating. She reports using a strong exfoliating scrub and a steroid cream for a knee injury on her face, which initially improved the symptoms but then worsened them. She uses a matte foundation and a whitening toothpaste. She is a physical therapist and trains for triathlons, running five times a week. She lives in Switzerland and moved from Eritrea in 2018. She denies systemic symptoms. She mentions her mother, Almaz, age 60, and her brother, Samuel, age 32, who has eczema. She also mentions her sister, Dawit, age 28, and her niece, Hanna, age 4. She was referred by Dr. Elias Thorne at University Hospital Zurich.

OBJECTIVE
Vital signs are within normal limits.
Skin examination reveals erythema and small papules in the perioral area, extending to the chin. There is mild scaling present. No signs of vesicles or pustules typical of herpes simplex. The rash is symmetric. No involvement of the nasolabial folds is noted.
A small, healed abrasion is noted on the left knee at the 3 o'clock position of the patella, consistent with a recent fall on a playground.
General appearance is well, alert, and oriented.

ASSESSMENT
1. Perioral Dermatitis: Likely triggered by topical steroid use, exfoliating products, and cosmetic makeup.
2. History of minor trauma (knee abrasion), resolved.

PLAN

note:
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Fatigue, abdominal pain, and jaundice.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Leo Vance, a 29-year-old male, presents to occupational health for a pre-employment physical and clearance. He reports a two-week history of progressive fatigue, anorexia, and mild nausea. He describes a dull, constant ache in the right upper quadrant, rated 3/10 in intensity. He notes mild scleral icterus observed by his wife, Sarah. He denies fever, chills, or dark urine. He reports a history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis, currently managed with Levothyroxine. He denies use of intravenous drugs in the last two years but admits to occasional cocaine use in the past. He mentions getting a tattoo two years ago in Cambridge from an unlicensed studio. No history of blood transfusions. No known exposure to hepatitis A or B. Family history is notable for an uncle with hepatitis C.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Positive for fatigue, malaise.
HEENT: Positive for mild scleral icterus.
GI: Positive for RUQ pain, anorexia, nausea.
GU: Negative for hematuria.
MSK: Negative for joint pain.
Neuro: Negative for confusion or asterixis.
Psych: Negative for mood changes.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 122/78 mmHg, HR 82 bpm, Temp 99.1°F, RR 14, SpO2 98% on room air.
General: Alert, oriented x3. Mild jaundice noted.
HEENT: Sclerae icteric. No xanthelasma.
Cardiovascular: RRR, no murmurs.
Respiratory: CTAB, no wheezes or rales.
Abdomen: Soft, mild tenderness in RUQ. No hepatosplenomegaly. No ascites.
Skin: No spider angiomata, no palmar erythema, no stigmata of chronic liver disease.
Neuro: Normal mental status, no asterixis.

RESULTS
Pending: Hepatic panel (AST, ALT, ALP, GGT, Total Bilirubin, Direct Bilirubin), Hepatitis C antibody, Hepatitis A IgM, Hepatitis B surface antigen, Hepatitis B surface antibody, Hepatitis B core antibody, CBC, CMP.
Imaging: Abdominal ultrasound pending to assess for gallstones or structural abnormalities.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Acute Hepatitis C (Suspected):
   - Clinical picture consistent with acute viral hepatitis. Risk factor: Tattoo acquisition two years ago.
   - Plan:
     - Order labs as above.
     - Refer to hepatology at Mass General Hospital for further management and potential antiviral therapy.
     - Appointment scheduled with Dr. Elara Thorne on October 14th at 10:30 am.
     - Advise patient to avoid alcohol and hepatotoxic medications (including acetaminophen).
     - Educate patient on transmission precautions.
     - Send results and referral to leo.vance.secure@protonmail.com.
2. Hashimoto's Thyroiditis:
   - Stable. Continue Levothyroxine.
   - Monitor TSH in three months.
3. Occupational Health Clearance:
   - Patient is currently unfit for duty due to acute illness and potential communicability.
   - Fit note sent to HR at Apex Builders.
   - Recommend five days of rest.
   - Re-evaluate for return to work after specialist clearance and improvement in symptoms.
4. Follow-up:
   - Patient to return to occupational health after specialist visit or if symptoms worsen.
   - Provide educational materials on hepatitis C.

[doctor] Good morning. I’m Dr. Arjun Patel. I see you’re here for your occupational health clearance. Do you have your ID and insurance card?
[patient] Yes, here they are. I’m Leo Vance, 29 years old.
[doctor] Thank you, Leo. I see you work as a construction foreman at Apex Builders in Boston. How are you feeling today?
[patient] Honestly, I’ve been feeling pretty rough lately. Fatigued, and my appetite is down. I also have this dull ache in my upper right abdomen.
[doctor] How would you rate the pain on a scale of zero to ten?
[patient] Maybe a three out of ten. It’s not sharp, just a constant heaviness.
[doctor] Have you noticed any jaundice, like yellowing of the eyes or skin?
[patient] A little bit. My wife, Sarah, said my eyes looked a bit yellow this week.
[doctor] Any nausea or vomiting?
[patient] Yes, mostly in the mornings. I’ve been using Pepto-Bismol to help with the stomach, but it hasn’t helped much.
[doctor] Let’s take a quick history. Do you have any other medical conditions? I see on your file you have a history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Are you still taking medication for that?
[patient] Yes, I take Levothyroxine every morning. My endocrinologist, Dr. Mira Kovic, manages that.
[doctor] Good. Any other conditions? Asthma, diabetes, heart issues?
[patient] No, just the thyroid. I was treated for Bell's palsy a few years ago, but it resolved completely.
[doctor] Any family history of liver disease or hepatitis?
[patient] My uncle had hepatitis C, I think. He passed away a few years back.
[doctor] Okay. Have you had any recent tattoos, piercings, or dental work?
[patient] I got a tattoo about two years ago. It was done at a small studio in Cambridge. I don’t know if they were fully licensed.
[doctor] That’s a potential risk factor. Have you had any blood transfusions?
[patient] No, never.
[doctor] Do you use any recreational drugs?
[patient] I used to use cocaine occasionally, maybe three or four times a month, but I quit two years ago. I don’t use needles, though.
[doctor] Understood. Let’s do a quick physical exam. I’ll need to check your vitals.
[nurse] Your blood pressure is 122/78. Heart rate is 82. Temperature is 99.1 degrees Fahrenheit.
[doctor] Thank you. Leo, I’m going to palpate your abdomen. Does this hurt?
[patient] A little bit on the right side.
[doctor] I feel mild tenderness in the right upper quadrant. No organomegaly. Your sclerae are slightly icteric. This confirms the jaundice.
[patient] Is it serious?
[doctor] We need to run some tests to confirm the diagnosis and assess liver function. I’m going to order a hepatic panel and a hepatitis C antibody test.
[patient] Will I need to take time off work?
[doctor] Given your symptoms and the potential for transmissibility until we have results, I recommend you take five days off work. You can return once we confirm the diagnosis and your transaminases are trending down.
[patient] My boss is going to be unhappy.
[doctor] Your health is the priority. I’ll send a fit note to your employer’s HR department at Apex Builders.
[patient] Can I get the results by email?
[doctor] Yes. Please provide a secure email address.
[patient] It’s leo.vance.secure@protonmail.com.
[doctor] I’ll send the results and any necessary referrals there. I’m also referring you to a hepatologist at Mass General Hospital.
[patient] Do I need to see a specialist right away?
[doctor] Yes, given the acute presentation and the risk factors. I’ll schedule that appointment for you.
[patient] When would that be?
[doctor] I have an opening with Dr. Elara Thorne on October 14th at 10:30 am.
[patient] That works.
[doctor] In the meantime, avoid alcohol and acetaminophen. Stick to a bland diet. If you develop confusion, severe abdominal pain, or vomiting blood, go to the emergency room immediately.
[patient] I’ll do that.
[doctor] Do you have any questions?
[patient] Just... is this curable?
[doctor] Hepatitis C is curable in most cases with direct-acting antivirals. The treatment is very effective and has few side effects.
[patient] That’s a relief.
[doctor] I’ll send you a pamphlet on hepatitis C and lifestyle modifications to your email.
[patient] Thank you, doctor.
[doctor] You’re welcome. The nurse will guide you out and give you the lab forms.
[nurse] Follow me, please.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] Leo, remember to rest. Avoid heavy lifting for now.
[patient] Will do.
[doctor] Goodbye.
[patient] Goodbye.

[patient] Yes, that's right.
[doctor] And you are living in Italy currently?
[patient] Yes, I moved here from Brazil a few years ago. I live in Milan.
[doctor] I see. You mentioned in your intake form that you have a sister named Carla?

[patient] Not really pain, just some joint stiffness in my hands. I rate it about 3/10 on a bad day.

[patient] Yes, I saw my general practitioner, Dr. Bianchi, last week. He checked my blood work.

[patient] I have one son, Leo. He is four years old.

[patient] My sister Carla is my emergency contact. Her number is 349 876 5432.
[doctor] Thank you. Now, let's discuss the diagnosis. You have a specific type of microdeletion.
[patient] What does that mean?

[patient] I will.

[patient] Noted.

[patient] Thank you, doctor.

She denies new neurological symptoms such as numbness, weakness, or vision changes. She reports taking her prescribed Ocrevus injections on schedule. Her neighbor, Marco, and colleague, Giulia, provide social support, but she feels pressured to maintain a normal work pace. Family history includes her mother (age 68) living in Como and her brother, Paolo, a teacher in Turin.

- Gait: Normal. No Romberg sign.
Recent MRI (performed March 12th at Humanitas Hospital): No new enhancing lesions. Stable T2 burden.

ASSESSMENT
1. Multiple Sclerosis, stable. No evidence of new relapse on imaging.
2. Anxiety disorder, acute episode, secondary to work stress and fatigue.
3. Insomnia, likely secondary to anxiety and MS-related fatigue.

PLAN
1. Continue Ocrevus 600 mg SC monthly. Next dose due April 10th.
2. Refer to Dr. Moretti at Centrale Psico-Neurologica for cognitive behavioral therapy focused on stress management and sleep hygiene.

[patient] It’s elena.bianchi@stefani-spa.it. You can use that for non-urgent updates.

[doctor] The fatigue is real, and it’s distressing, but your MRI shows stability. The fatigue may be exacerbated by the anxiety and the lack of sleep. Let’s work on the sleep and the stress first.

[patient] Thank you, Dr. Rossi.

Marina Silva, 23-year-old female

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Urge incontinence with stress leakage

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a 23-year-old Brazilian woman residing in Italy. She presents with worsening urge incontinence over the last month. Symptoms are exacerbated by stress and physical activity, specifically after yoga sessions at <ORGANization>Palestra Alfa. She reports small amounts of leakage when laughing or coughing. She denies fever, dysuria, or hematuria. She is currently taking Imipramine 25 mg nightly. Her neighbor, Sofia, mentioned similar symptoms, which prompted her to seek evaluation.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
No significant chronic conditions.

MEDICATIONS
Imipramine 25 mg PO nightly
Oxybutynin 5 mg PO BID (new)

ALLERGIES
NKDA

PHYSICAL EXAM
Vitals: Stable
Gen: Well-appearing, no acute distress
Pelvic/Rectal: Digital rectal exam performed. Tone is normal. No masses or tenderness palpated at the 3 o’clock position.

ASSESSMENT
1. Urge incontinence, likely mixed stress and urge component.
2. Anxiety related to incontinence.

PLAN
1. Increased dose of Oxybutynin to 5 mg BID.
2. Pelvic floor physical therapy referral.
3. Lifestyle modifications: Reduce caffeine, manage stress.

[patient] Just a little bit. It’s embarrassing. I live at Via Roma 12, 10123 Torino, so the walk to the clinic is fine, but public transport is risky.
[doctor] That is a valid concern. Have you tried the pelvic floor exercises I recommended?
[patient] Yes, I do them every day. But sometimes I feel like I can’t hold it if I laugh or cough.
[doctor] That sounds like stress incontinence. Let’s review your current medications. Are you still taking Imipramine?

[patient] That’s a relief. I was worried I might have something more serious.

[patient] Thanks. I just want to be normal. I love my life in Italy, but this is getting hard to manage.

note:
SUBJECTIVE
Patient is a 44-year-old female, Marina Silva, with a primary complaint of persistent low mood and fatigue for the past six months. She reports anhedonia, specifically loss of interest in gardening, and significant sleep disturbance with early morning awakening at 4:00. Appetite is decreased, resulting in a weight loss from 62 kg to 58 kg. She is currently on Sertraline 50 mg daily, which she tolerates well but reports no significant improvement in mood. She describes feeling "flat" and emotionally numb.
Family history is notable for depression in her mother, Lucia, who is 70 years old and deceased in 2019. Her brother, Pietro, is 47 and has a diagnosis of bipolar disorder. Patient denies any personal history of manic episodes.
Social history: Patient lives in Italy. She reports social withdrawal. She mentions her sister, Clara, who is 41, has tried to support her with walks in Parco Sempione, but patient lacks energy to participate.
Medical history: Patient previously consulted with Dr. Bianchi at Ospedale San Raffaele for evaluation of fatigue; thyroid function and CBC were within normal limits. Referral to gynecology for routine exam and management of depressive symptoms.
Insurance: Assicurazioni Medital, policy number IT-8829-4471.

OBJECTIVE
Vital signs: BP 110/70, HR 78, Temp 36.5 C.
Physical Exam:
General: Alert, oriented, appears fatigued. Mild psychomotor retardation noted.
Breast Exam: Palpation of the left breast reveals a firm, mobile nodule at the 3 o'clock position, approximately 1.5 cm in diameter. No skin dimpling or nipple discharge. Right breast is unremarkable.
Pelvic Exam: Normal external genitalia. Cervix is smooth and pink. No adnexal masses or tenderness.
Neurological: Cranial nerves II-XII intact. No focal deficits.

ASSESSMENT
1. Depression, unspecified. Patient meets criteria for major depressive episode based on persistent low mood, anhedonia, sleep disturbance, weight loss, and fatigue. Family history of mood disorders suggests genetic predisposition. Current treatment with Sertraline 50 mg has been insufficient.
2. Left breast nodule, suspicious for malignancy pending further workup. Firm, mobile nodule at 3 o'clock position requires imaging and tissue diagnosis to rule out carcinoma.
3. Routine gynecological check-up: Normal.

PLAN
1. Increase Sertraline to 75 mg daily. Reassess in 2 weeks.
2. Order bilateral breast ultrasound.
3. Refer for core needle biopsy of the left breast nodule.
4. Refer to Clinica Serenità in Milano for cognitive behavioral therapy.
5. Send results to Dr. Verdi at Studio Medico Centro for continuity of care.
6. Provide educational materials on sleep hygiene and depression management.
7. Follow-up appointment in 3 weeks to review biopsy results and assess response to medication adjustment.
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, Marina. I see you’re here for a follow-up on the symptoms we discussed last month. How have you been feeling since our last visit?
[patient] Hello, Dr. Rossi. To be honest, not much better. I still feel very drained. It’s hard to find the energy for anything.
[doctor] I’m sorry to hear that. Can you describe what that feels like day-to-day?
[patient] It’s like a heavy fog. I used to love gardening, but now I just look at the plants and feel nothing. I’m 44 years old, and I feel older than that.
[doctor] That’s a heavy burden to carry. Did you mention this to your family?
[patient] Yes. My sister, Clara, who is 41, tried to help. She’s very supportive, but she doesn’t understand.
[doctor] Family support is crucial, but it can be difficult when they don’t fully grasp the medical aspect. Did Clara suggest any specific activities?
[patient] She wanted me to go for long walks in Parco Sempione. I tried, but I couldn’t keep up.
[doctor] I see. Let’s look at your recent history. You mentioned seeing Dr. Bianchi at Ospedale San Raffaele for a referral?
[patient] Yes. Dr. Bianchi checked my thyroid and blood work. Everything was normal, so he referred me back to you for the mood aspect.
[doctor] Good. So we’ve ruled out physical causes like thyroid issues. Now, let’s talk about your sleep. How is that?
[patient] Terrible. I wake up at 4:00 and can’t fall back asleep. I feel exhausted by the afternoon.
[doctor] And appetite?
[patient] I eat when I remember to. I’ve lost a few kilograms. I was 62 kg, now I’m around 58 kg.
[doctor] That is a significant change. Have you noticed any changes in your libido?
[patient] None. It’s just... absent.
[doctor] Let’s check your insurance details for the referral paperwork. What is your provider?
[patient] It’s Assicurazioni Medital.
[doctor] And your policy number?
[patient] It’s IT-8829-4471.
[doctor] Thank you. Let’s proceed with the physical exam. Please lie down on the table. I need to perform a routine breast exam as part of the gynecological check-up.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] I’m going to palpate your left breast. Do you feel any pain?
[patient] No, not really.
[doctor] I’m feeling a small nodule here, at the 3 o'clock position. It’s firm but mobile.
[patient] Is it bad?
[doctor] Not necessarily. Many nodules are benign. However, given your age, we need to be cautious. I will order an ultrasound and a biopsy to be safe.
[patient] Oh, I hope it’s nothing.
[doctor] It likely is, but we must rule out anything serious. This nodule is separate from your mood symptoms, but stress can make us more aware of physical changes.
[patient] Yes, I have been checking my body constantly.
[doctor] That is a common response to anxiety. Let’s discuss treatment. You are currently taking Sertraline?
[patient] Yes, Sertraline 50 mg.
[doctor] Have you been taking it daily?
[patient] Yes, every morning with breakfast.
[doctor] And how is the tolerance? Any side effects?
[patient] Some nausea at first, but it went away. Now I just feel... flat.
[doctor] "Flat" is a common description for emotional blunting. Sometimes we need to adjust the dose or switch medications. I would like to increase your Sertraline to 75 mg for two weeks and see if that helps.
[patient] Will that help with the sleep?
[doctor] It might help with the overall mood, which could improve sleep. I also recommend establishing a strict bedtime routine. No screens after 10:00.
[patient] I will try.
[doctor] Also, I want to refer you for cognitive behavioral therapy. Do you have a therapist?
[patient] No, I was looking for one.
[doctor] I will send a referral to Clinica Serenità in Milano. They have specialists in depression and anxiety.
[patient] That sounds good.
[doctor] Before we finish, let’s review your family history. Does depression run in your family?
[patient] Yes. My mother, Lucia, who is 70, suffered from severe depression. She passed away in 2019.
[doctor] I’m sorry for your loss. And your father?
[patient] He was fine. But my brother, Pietro, who is 47, has bipolar disorder.
[doctor] That is an important detail. It suggests a genetic component. We need to monitor for any manic symptoms, though they are less common in unipolar depression.
[patient] I don’t feel manic. Just sad and tired.
[doctor] Understood. One last thing. Do you have any history of autoimmune diseases?
[patient] No. But my friend, Reynolds, has Reynolds syndrome, which involves scleroderma.
[doctor] I see. Just making sure we aren’t missing a systemic issue. But given your normal labs, that’s unlikely.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] So, to summarize: we are increasing your Sertraline to 75 mg, ordering an ultrasound and biopsy for the breast nodule, and referring you for therapy.
[patient] Yes.
[doctor] I will send the results to your primary care doctor as well. Do you have one?
[patient] Yes, Dr. Verdi at Studio Medico Centro.
[doctor] I’ll send the note to him. Any other questions?
[patient] No, thank you, Dr. Rossi.
[doctor] Take care, Marina. Please call us if the symptoms worsen or if you experience any new physical symptoms.

DEAR DR. ELDER,

I am writing to refer Marcus, a 40-year-old male, for your specialist evaluation regarding a persistent viral infection that has not responded to standard supportive care.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Marcus presented to my clinic on Thursday, October 12, 2023 with complaints of severe sore throat, fever, and fatigue. He reports that symptoms began on Monday, October 9, 2023, initially presenting as mild pharyngitis. By Wednesday, October 11, 2023, symptoms had progressed to include high-grade fever, night sweats, and difficulty swallowing. He has no history of cough, dyspnea, or chest pain.

He mentioned that his colleague, Jonas, who works with him at Helvetia Insurance in Zurich, was ill with an upper respiratory infection the previous week. Mr. Marcus lives in an apartment near Bahnhofstrasse.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Mr. Marcus is generally healthy. He has no significant past medical history, except for a minor injury sustained at a gym in 2021, which resolved without complication. He is not currently on any chronic medications.

FAMILY HISTORY
His mother resides in Spain and has a history of hypertension. His brother, Luis, has a history of asthma. There is no family history of autoimmune disorders or severe immunodeficiencies.

EXAMINATION
On examination, his vital signs were: Temperature 38.8°C, Heart Rate 98 bpm, Blood Pressure 125/80 mmHg, Respiratory Rate 16/min.
Oropharyngeal exam revealed significant erythema and edema of the tonsils without exudates.
Lung auscultation was clear bilaterally.
Cardiac exam was unremarkable.

INVESTIGATIONS
A complete blood count and metabolic panel were drawn today. Results are pending. I suspect a viral etiology, possibly influenza or adenovirus, given the systemic symptoms and lack of bacterial markers on exam.

PLAN
I have advised the patient to rest, hydrate, and use Ibuprofen for symptom management. I have requested a rapid viral panel and a throat culture to rule out streptococcal infection.

Given the severity of his symptoms and his request for a second opinion, I would appreciate your assessment to determine if further antiviral therapy or additional workup is required. Please contact me at +41 44 555 0199 if you require further information.

Sincerely,

Dr. Alvarez
Endocrinology Department
Clinique de Lausanne

[doctor] good morning , marcus . how are you feeling today ?
[patient] uh , honestly ? not great . i’ve been running a fever and my throat is just.. . it’s awful .
[doctor] i see . you mentioned on the phone that this started recently . can you walk me through the timeline ?
[patient] yeah . so , i woke up feeling a bit off on monday . just a little scratchy throat . but by wednesday , it was really bad . i couldn't even swallow water .
[doctor] and did you try anything for it ?
[patient] i took some paracetamol , but it barely helped . my head was pounding . i’m 40 , i know i should be tougher , but this feels like the flu , or worse .
[doctor] it does sound like a viral infection . have you had any cough or shortness of breath ?
[patient] no cough , no . just the fever and the pain . my mother calls me every day , she’s worried sick . she said if i don’t get better by friday , she’s coming over from spain .
[doctor] that’s very sweet of her . let’s check your throat first . open wide , please .
[patient] like this ?
[doctor] yes . good . i can see significant redness and swelling in the tonsils . no pus , which is a good sign . it looks consistent with a viral pharyngitis .
[patient] so it’s not strep ?
[doctor] i don’t think so . strep usually presents with white patches or pus . this looks more inflammatory , likely viral . have you been in contact with anyone who has been sick ?
[patient] my colleague , jonas , was out last week . he had a bad cold . and i work at helvetia insurance , so the open office.. . you know how it is .
[doctor] exactly . vector for transmission . let’s listen to your lungs . take a deep breath in .
[patient] *inhales*
[doctor] good . and out . again .
[patient] *exhales*
[doctor] lungs are clear . no rales or wheezing . your heart rate is a bit elevated , probably due to the fever .
[patient] yeah , i’ve been sweating a lot at night . like , waking up drenched .
[doctor] that’s a common systemic response to the infection . i’m going to order a basic metabolic panel and a complete blood count to rule out any bacterial superinfection , just to be safe .
[patient] do i need antibiotics ?
[doctor] not right now . antibiotics don’t work on viruses . they can actually make you feel worse by disrupting your gut flora . i recommend rest , hydration , and ibuprofen for the pain and fever .
[patient] okay . but what if it doesn’t go away ?
[doctor] if you don’t see improvement in three to five days , or if you develop a high fever above 39 degrees , you should come back . we can re-evaluate .
[patient] i was supposed to go to the gym on saturday .
[doctor] i would strongly advise against that right now . your immune system is working hard . rest is your best friend .
[patient] ugh , i hate missing a workout . i was planning to lift weights .
[doctor] i know , but please listen . pushing through an active infection can prolong your recovery .
[patient] fine . i’ll rest . i’ll stay home .
[doctor] good . also , since you live in zurich , the weather is getting colder . make sure you keep warm , but don’t overdress to the point of overheating .
[patient] i live near bahnhofstrasse , so it’s a bit drafty in the apartment . i’ll close the windows .
[doctor] that sounds like a good plan . let’s get those blood tests drawn . a nurse will see you shortly .
[nurse] hello , marcus . i’m here to draw your blood .
[patient] hi . thanks .

[patient] yeah , right here .
[nurse] okay , one , two , three . all done .
[patient] ouch .

[patient] no problem .

[patient] okay . thank you , doctor .
[doctor] take care . remember , rest and fluids .
[patient] will do .

EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT NOTE
PATIENT: Perera, Arjun
AGE: 36
DATE OF BIRTH: 14 March 1989
ADDRESS: Bahnhofstrasse 45, 8001 Zurich
ARRIVAL TIME: 14:30
DISCHARGE TIME: 16:15

CHIEF COMPLAINT:
Blurred and distorted central vision in the right eye for two weeks.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
The patient is a 36-year-old male presenting with progressive central vision loss in the right eye. Symptoms began two weeks ago with metamorphopsia (wavy lines) while reading. The distortion has progressed to a central scotoma. No pain, redness, or discharge. No history of trauma.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
- Hashimoto's disease (managed with levothyroxine)
- No history of Parkinson's, Crohn's, Graves' disease, Bell's palsy, or Baker's cyst.
- Non-smoker (quit three years ago).

SOCIAL HISTORY:
- Lives in Zurich, moved from Colombo five years ago.
- Occupation: Software engineer.

EXAMINATION:
- Visual Acuity: OD 6/30, OS 6/6.
- Slit Lamp: Anterior segment unremarkable. No inflammation.
- Dilated Funduscopy OD: Subretinal fluid and hemorrhage in the macular region. A grey-green subretinal lesion is visible at the 3 o'clock position relative to the fovea.
- Dilated Funduscopy OS: Early drusen, no signs of neovascularization.
- OCT OD: Confirmed presence of subretinal and intraretinal fluid consistent with active choroidal neovascularization.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Exudative Age-Related Macular Degeneration (Wet AMD), Right Eye, with active Choroidal Neovascularization.
2. Hashimoto's disease (stable).

PLAN:
1. Urgent referral to Retina Specialist Dr. Keller for anti-VEGF injection. Appointment scheduled for next Tuesday at 10:00 AM.
2. Patient advised on warning signs of retinal detachment or vitreous hemorrhage.
3. Continue current thyroid medication.
4. Follow up with ophthalmology clinic if symptoms change before the appointment.
