Stable. Patient understood the diagnosis and plan. Referral printed and provided.

PHYSICIAN: Dr. Vane
dialogue:
[doctor] good afternoon . i am dr . vane , the ophthalmologist on duty . i see your sister , meera , is with you . could you tell me your name and date of birth ?
[patient] my name is arjun perera . i was born on 14 march 1989 .
[doctor] thank you , arjun . i see you are 36 years old . you are here because of vision problems in your right eye ?
[patient] yes , doctor . it started two weeks ago . i was reading a document on my laptop and the lines in the middle looked wavy . i thought it was just screen glare , so i ignored it .
[doctor] and how is it now ?
[patient] it has gotten worse . the center of my vision is dark and blurry . i can see the edges , but the middle is gone . it feels like there is a black spot right in the middle .
[patient_guest] he is very stressed about this , doctor . he works as a software engineer for helvetia tech solutions , and he relies entirely on his eyes for coding .
[doctor] i understand . that must be very worrying . did you have any pain , redness , or discharge from the eye ?
[patient] no pain at all . it is just the vision loss . it happened very gradually over the last two weeks .
[doctor] have you had any other health issues recently ? any new medications ?
[patient] no , i am generally healthy . i do have a history of hashimoto's disease thyroiditis , but that is under control with levothyroxine . i take it every morning .
[doctor] understood . and do you have any family history of eye problems ?
[patient_guest] my mother had cataracts , but that was in her late sixties . i don't know of anyone in the family with macular degeneration .
[doctor] let us look at your medical history . you listed your address as bahnhofstrasse 45, 8001 zurich . is that correct ?
[patient] yes , that is my home . i moved to zurich from colombo about five years ago .
[doctor] thank you . i will now perform a dilated eye exam . i will put some drops in your eyes to widen your pupils . it may sting a little .
[nurse] i will put the drops in now , please keep your eyes open .
[patient] okay .
[nurse] all done . please wait here for a few minutes until the dilation takes effect .
[patient] does it hurt ?
[nurse] not really , just a bit of watering . the doctor will be with you in ten minutes .
[doctor] (returning) the dilation is complete . let us look at the back of your eye .
[patient] is it serious ?
[doctor] i can see some changes in the macula . there is a lesion in the center . i need to do a special test called optical coherence tomography , or oct , to see the layers of the retina .
[patient] what does that show ?
[doctor] it will show us if there is fluid or abnormal blood vessels . based on the initial look , i suspect you have wet age-related macular degeneration . this means there are new , fragile blood vessels growing under the retina , which are leaking fluid and blood .
[patient] but i am only 36 . isn't that for old people ?
[doctor] it is called age-related , but it can happen in younger people , especially if there is a genetic component or other risk factors like smoking . do you smoke ?
[patient] no , i quit three years ago . i never drank alcohol .
[doctor] good . let us look at the oct results .
[doctor] (after a pause) the scan confirms my suspicion . there is active choroidal neovascularization . this is the wet form of macular degeneration . the fluid is causing the distortion you are seeing .
[patient] can it be fixed ?
[doctor] we cannot reverse the damage that has already happened , but we can treat the active leak to stop it from getting worse and potentially improve your vision . the treatment involves injections into the eye .
[patient] injections ? into the eye ?
[doctor] yes , it is called anti-vegf therapy . it is a standard treatment . it is very common and effective .
[patient_guest] how often does he need these ?
[doctor] usually , we start with a series of injections , perhaps one a month for a few months , and then we monitor how he responds .
[patient] what if i don't treat it ?
[doctor] if left untreated , the bleeding and fluid can cause permanent scarring in the macula , which would lead to severe , irreversible central vision loss .
[patient] that is scary .
[doctor] it is serious , but very treatable . we need to act quickly . i am going to refer you to our retina specialist , dr . keller , for the first injection .
[patient] when can that be ?
[doctor] i can make an appointment for next tuesday at 10:00 am .
[patient] that works .
[doctor] in the meantime , please avoid straining your eyes too much . if you experience sudden flashes of light , a curtain over your vision , or a sudden increase in floaters , come back to the emergency department immediately .
[patient] i will do that .
[doctor] also , keep taking your thyroid medication as prescribed . there is no interaction with the eye treatment .
[patient] thank you , doctor .
[doctor] you are welcome . the nurse will give you the referral paperwork .
[nurse] here is the referral . you can book the appointment directly through the hospital portal or call us at 044 123 45 67 .
[patient] thank you .

She recently traveled to Paris with her daughter, Sarah, who is 55. The patient is a resident of Portland, having moved from Chicago decades ago. She is an avid bridge player at the Maplewood Senior Center but has recently had to suspend participation due to pain.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS

Neurologic: Positive for left leg radiculopathy.
Musculoskeletal: Positive for lumbosacral tenderness.

[doctor] Good morning, Margaret. I see you’ve been referred to me by Dr. Aris Thorne at St. Jude’s Medical Center. What brings you in today?

[patient] Hello, Doctor. Yes, Dr. Thorne suggested I come to see you because my back pain is getting worse. It’s been hurting for about three weeks now.

[doctor] I’m sorry to hear that. Can you describe the pain? Is it sharp, dull, or burning?

[patient] It’s mostly a deep ache, but sometimes it shoots down my left leg. It feels like a pinching sensation.

[doctor] And where exactly does the pain start?

[patient] Right here, in the lower back. Around my sacrum.

[doctor] Okay. Did anything specific trigger this? Did you lift something heavy or twist?

[patient] Not really. I was gardening, which I love, but I didn’t lift anything heavy. I just bent over to pull some weeds.

[doctor] Gardening can be tricky. Do you play any sports or go to a specific facility for exercise?

[patient] I used to play bridge every Thursday at the Maplewood Senior Center, but I’ve had to stop because of this pain.

[doctor] I understand. How old are you, Margaret?

[patient] I’m 89 years old.

[doctor] And your date of birth?

[patient] My birthday is March 12, 1935.

[patient] I live in Portland, Oregon.

[doctor] And where did you grow up?

[patient] I moved here from Chicago about forty years ago.

[doctor] That was quite the move. Did you travel recently?

[patient] Yes, I went to Paris last month with my daughter, Sarah.

[doctor] How old is Sarah?

[patient] She is 55. We had a wonderful time, but the walking did a number on my back.

[doctor] That makes sense. Do you have any other medical conditions? I see in the chart that you have Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

[patient] Yes, I’ve had that for years. I take my medication daily.

[doctor] And any other chronic conditions?

[patient] I had a cousin, Robert, who had Parkinson's disease, but I don’t think I have that. I just have this back issue.

[doctor] Got it. Let’s check your family history. Does anyone in your family have similar back problems?

[patient] My mother, Eleanor, had terrible arthritis, but not disc issues. My brother, James, is 86 and has some knee problems.

[doctor] Okay. Are you on any other medications?

[patient] Just my thyroid pill and some occasional ibuprofen for the pain.

[doctor] I see. Let’s take a look at your back. I’m going to ask you to lie down for a moment.

[nurse] I’ll help you up onto the table, Margaret.

[patient] Thank you, dear.

[doctor] Can you raise your left leg while I keep your knee straight?

[patient] It hurts when I lift it.

[doctor] That’s a positive straight leg raise, which suggests nerve irritation. Let me palpate the area.

[patient] That’s the sore spot.

[doctor] I feel some tenderness here. Let’s look at the imaging results from St. Jude’s.

[patient] Yes, Dr. Thorne sent them over.

[doctor] The MRI shows a displacement at the L5-S1 level. It’s pressing slightly on the nerve root.

[patient] Is that dangerous?

[doctor] Not immediately, but it explains your leg pain. We need to manage this carefully.

[patient] What are our options?

[doctor] We can start with conservative therapy. Physical therapy, anti-inflammatories, and maybe some heat.

[patient] I’d like to avoid surgery if possible.

[doctor] We will definitely try conservative measures first. I’m going to prescribe a short course of medication and refer you to physical therapy.

[patient] That sounds good.

[doctor] Also, I noticed you mentioned Robert. Did he have any other conditions?

[patient] He had Crohn's disease later in life, which was very difficult for him.

[doctor] I’m sorry to hear that. It’s good that we’re catching your back issue early.

[patient] Yes, I’d like to keep moving. I don’t want to stop my bridge game.

[doctor] With the right therapy, I’m confident you can return to your activities.

[patient] That’s a relief.

[doctor] I’ll write the prescription and send the referral to your physical therapist.

[patient] Thank you, Doctor.

[doctor] You’re welcome, Margaret. Do you have any questions?

[patient] No, I think I understand.

[doctor] Great. I’ll see you in two weeks to check on your progress.

[patient] Okay, goodbye.

dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, Rafael. Please, come in and have a seat. I see you are here for your follow-up regarding the headaches.
[patient] Good morning, Doctor. Yes, thank you. It has been... um, quite a bit.
[doctor] How have the headaches been for you since our last visit?
[patient] Well, they are still there. You know, not as bad as before, but... um... two weeks ago I had a really bad one.
[doctor] I see. Two weeks ago. Can you describe that episode?
[patient] Yes. I was at the gym, doing some lifting. And suddenly, the pain hit. It was sharp.
[doctor] Where exactly did you feel the pain?
[patient] Here, behind the eyes. And also on the left side of the head. It felt like a pressure.
[doctor] And did you take any medication?
[patient] I took my usual sumatriptan. But it didn't help much. I had to lie down.
[doctor] Did you have any nausea or vision changes?
[patient] A little nausea. Yes. My vision was a bit blurry for a few minutes.
[doctor] I see. That is concerning. Let us check your vitals first. Nurse, could you please take his blood pressure and heart rate?
[nurse] Of course, Doctor. Mr. Rafael, I am going to put this cuff on your arm now.
[patient] Okay.
[nurse] Your blood pressure is 135 over 85. Heart rate is 78.
[doctor] Thank you. 135 over 85 is a bit elevated. Let us sit down. How is your general health otherwise?
[patient] I am a software engineer, so I sit a lot. But I try to exercise.
[doctor] That is good. You mentioned an injury at the gym. Was it a specific accident?
[patient] Yes. I was doing deadlifts. I dropped the bar on my foot. It hurt a lot.
[doctor] Did you go to the emergency room for that?
[patient] No, I just iced it. It is okay now. But the headaches started around the same time.
[doctor] I see. A temporal relationship. Let us review your history. You are 37 years old, correct?
[patient] Yes, I am 37.
[doctor] And you are originally from Brazil, living here in Italy.
[patient] Yes, I moved here three years ago.
[doctor] Do you have any family history of headaches or hypertension?
[patient] My mother has high blood pressure. She is 62. And my sister, Lucia, has migraines. She is 34.
[doctor] And your father?
[patient] My father, João, passed away last year. He had diabetes.
[doctor] I am sorry to hear that. Do you have any children?
[patient] Yes, a son. Mateus. He is 8.
[doctor] And you are married?
[patient] Yes, to Camila. She is 35.
[doctor] Okay. Let us look at your labs. I ordered some blood tests last week.
[patient] Yes, I went to the lab yesterday.
[doctor] The results are back. Your blood count is normal. Your electrolytes are normal. But your cortisol level is slightly high.
[patient] High? Is that bad?
[doctor] It can be. Stress can elevate cortisol. But we need to rule out other causes. Your thyroid function is normal.
[patient] Good. I am worried it is something serious. Like a tumor or something.
[doctor] I understand your concern. But the most common cause of new headaches in men your age is tension or migraine. However, given the severity and the associated symptoms, we need to be thorough.
[patient] What do you mean?
[doctor] I would like to order an MRI of your brain. With and without contrast.
[patient] An MRI? Why?
[doctor] To check for any structural abnormalities. It is a standard precaution.
[patient] Okay. How long does it take?
[doctor] About 45 minutes. We will schedule it for next week.
[patient] Next week? Can I get it sooner?
[doctor] The earliest slot is next Tuesday.
[patient] Okay. I will try to take the day off.
[doctor] Good. In the meantime, please monitor your blood pressure at home.
[patient] I have a monitor. I check it every morning.
[doctor] Excellent. What are the readings usually?
[patient] Around 120 over 80. But yesterday it was 130 over 85.
[doctor] 130 over 85. That is borderline. Let us keep an eye on it. Have you changed your diet?
[patient] I eat a lot of pasta. And pizza. You know, Italian food.
[doctor] Yes, that can be high in sodium. Try to reduce salt intake.
[patient] I will try.
[doctor] Also, are you sleeping well?
[patient] Not really. I wake up at 3 am often.
[doctor] That can worsen headaches. Have you tried melatonin?
[patient] No.
[doctor] I will prescribe some. Take 5 mg at night.
[patient] Okay. Thank you.
[doctor] One more thing. You were referred by Dr. Silvio from San Raffaele Hospital.
[patient] Yes, he is my general practitioner.
[doctor] He mentioned you had a previous episode of syncope.
[patient] Yes, three months ago. I fainted in the kitchen.
[doctor] In the kitchen?
[patient] I was washing dishes. I felt dizzy and fell.
[doctor] Did you hit your head?
[patient] A little. On the counter. But I didn't lose consciousness for long. Maybe 10 seconds.
[doctor] Okay. That is important to note. Any other symptoms since then?
[patient] Just the headaches.
[doctor] I see. Let us finalize the plan. We will do the MRI, continue the sumatriptan as needed, and add melatonin.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] And please, keep a headache diary. Record the time, intensity, and triggers.
[patient] Yes, Doctor.
[doctor] If the pain becomes severe, or you have new symptoms like weakness or speech difficulty, go to the emergency room immediately.
[patient] Understood.
[doctor] Thank you, Rafael. The nurse will give you the appointment details.
[patient] Thank you.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

PATIENT INFORMATION
Name: Marco Rossi

Age: 22

Insurance Policy Number: 849201-B
Address: Via Roma 12, 24100 Bergamo, Italy

REASON FOR ADMISSION
Patient presented to the emergency department with acute right knee pain and swelling following a slip on a wet football pitch. Initial assessment suspected ligamentous injury.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a 22-year-old male logistics coordinator working for FastTrack Shipping in Milan. He reported injury occurred while playing football near Parco Sempione. He experienced immediate pain and swelling in the right knee, limiting his ability to bear weight. He has no prior history of knee surgery. He reports using Advil for pain management since admission. He has a known allergy to penicillin. He currently takes Omeprazole for acid reflux.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
No significant past medical history except for the mentioned allergy and acid reflux. No history of autoimmune diseases in the patient.

FAMILY HISTORY
Father, Luca, 58, history of knee replacements.
Mother, Sara, history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis.
Sister, Elena, 25, diagnosed with Rheumatoid Arthritis.
Brother, Paolo, 28, chef, lives with patient.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Right knee: Mild swelling, tenderness over the posterior aspect of the knee. No instability noted on initial exam. Range of motion limited due to pain. Neurovascular status intact.

IMAGING
MRI of the right knee revealed a Grade 1 sprain of the posterior cruciate ligament (PCL). No meniscal tears or other significant abnormalities.

DIAGNOSIS
1. Sprain of posterior cruciate ligament of right knee, initial encounter (Grade 1)

PLAN
1. Discharge with crutches and right knee brace.
2. Weight-bearing as tolerated with crutches for 2 weeks.
3. Ice, rest, compression, and elevation (RICE protocol).
4. Pain management with prescribed Advil. Avoid additional NSAIDs without consultation.
5. Physical therapy referral to Marco Bianchi in Como for range-of-motion exercises starting after 2 weeks.
6. Follow-up appointment scheduled for November 2, 2024 at 10:30.
7. Certificate of incapacity sent to FastTrack Shipping for Marco Rossi.
8. Patient educated on brace care and warning signs of complications.

PROGNOSIS
Good. Expected full recovery with appropriate rehabilitation. Return to work and sports activity to be determined based on progress in physical therapy.

CONTACT INFORMATION
Doctor: Dr. Rossi
Nurse: Giulia
Patient Email: m.rossi.22 at example dot com

[doctor] Good morning, Marco. I’m Dr. Rossi. We’ve been reviewing your MRI results from last night, and I’d like to discuss your discharge plan. Do you have any questions before we start?

[doctor] I understand. The MRI confirms a sprain of the posterior cruciate ligament, or PCL, in your right knee. It’s a Grade 1 sprain, which is good news. It’s not a full tear. How has the pain been since the injury?
[patient] Ouch, yeah. It started when I was playing football. I slipped on the wet pitch at the stadium near Parco Sempione. I think I hyperextended it a bit. The pain is manageable, but swelling is there.
[doctor] Okay. We’ve been giving you Advil for the pain and inflammation. Have you noticed any improvement?
[patient] Yes, a bit. But I’m worried about work. I’m a logistics coordinator for FastTrack Shipping in Milan. I have to stand a lot.
[doctor] That’s understandable. We are prescribing a knee brace and crutches. You’ll need to avoid weight-bearing on that leg for the first two weeks. Your insurance, Sanità Integrativa, should cover the brace. Did you bring your insurance card?
[patient] Yes, here it is. My policy number is 849201-B. I hope they don’t ask for too much paperwork. My boss, Giulia, is very strict about attendance.
[doctor] No problem. I’ll send a certificate of incapacity directly to FastTrack Shipping. Now, regarding your family history. You mentioned earlier that your father has some joint issues?
[patient] Yes, my father, Luca, is 58 years old. He has had knee replacements before. And my sister, Elena, is 25. She had Rheumatoid Arthritis diagnosed last year.

[patient] No, I don’t think so. But my mother, Sara, has Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Is that related?
[doctor] Not directly related to PCL injuries, but it’s good to document. We will note that in your chart. Now, let’s talk about the physical therapy. I’ve referred you to Marco Bianchi, a physiotherapist at the clinic in Como. He is very good with sports injuries.
[patient] Oh, Marco? I know him! He’s my neighbor. We live in the same building in Bergamo. I can probably get a slot with him easily.

[patient] Thanks, Doctor. I feel a bit better knowing it’s not a tear.
[doctor] That’s right. It’s a sprain. With proper rehab, you should make a full recovery. Just be patient.

[doctor] That’s a good sign. Alessandro is a good athlete. You should be too.

[nurse] Giulia here. I can show you how to use the crutches.

note:
SUBJECTIVE
Patient is an 80-year-old male presenting for a follow-up of moderate persistent asthma. He reports increased wheezing and tightness in the chest, particularly when walking to the market last week. He used his rescue inhaler (Ventolin) with partial relief but felt worried about passing out. He admits to missing maintenance medication (Symbicort) doses during a trip to Prague for his birthday on May 12th. He restarted the medication on May 15th. He denies fever, night sweats, or fainting. He mentions his brother, Ilir, has Parkinson’s. He recalls his mother, Shpresa, had asthma and possibly thyroid issues, but denies personal history of Hashimoto’s or Graves’ disease. He takes Lipitor and Aspirin. He consumes herbal tea prepared by his wife, Elira.

OBJECTIVE
Vital signs stable. Lungs: Mild wheezing heard in the right lower lobe. Peak flow: 320 L/min (personal best 380 L/min). Spirometry from April 20th showed moderate obstruction. No signs of Baker’s cyst exacerbation in the knee, though patient reports mild knee pain.

ASSESSMENT
1. Moderate persistent asthma, poorly controlled (GINA Step 3).
2. Medication non-adherence due to travel.
3. Risk factor: Herbal tea consumption.

PLAN
1. Increase Symbicort to 2 puffs twice daily.
2. Continue Ventolin as needed for rescue.
3. Discontinue herbal tea due to potential drug interactions.
4. Educate on proper inhaler technique and use of spacer.
5. Follow up in 3 months on August 10th.
6. Patient to monitor symptoms and contact clinic if worsening. E-mail summary sent to arben.krasniqi at gmail dot com.
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, Arben. It is nice to see you again. How have you been feeling since we last spoke?
[patient] Hello, Doctor. Uh, well, honestly? It’s been a bit of a rollercoaster, you know?
[doctor] A rollercoaster is not usually how we describe asthma. Can you be more specific?
[patient] Well, I mean, generally okay. But last week, when I was walking to the market, I felt that tightness again. The um, the wheeze.
[doctor] Did you use your rescue inhaler?
[patient] Yes, yes. Two puffs. And it helped, but slowly. Not like before. I was worried I was going to pass out.
[doctor] That is not good. You should not be feeling like you might pass out. Have you been taking your maintenance medication?
[patient] The... the blue one? Ventolin? No, that’s the rescue one. The other one, Symbicort? I forgot a few days.
[doctor] Forgot a few days? Which days?
[patient] Uh, I was on a trip. I went to Prague. It was for my birthday, you know? May 12th. I was so busy looking at the castles, I forgot the morning dose.
[doctor] May 12th was three weeks ago. Did you restart it when you got back?
[patient] Yes, yes. I restarted it on May 15th. But the air there... the smoke from the factories, I think. And the cold.
[doctor] Let’s check your lungs. Please breathe in deeply through your mouth.
[patient] Like this?
[doctor] Yes, hold it for a second, then blow out slowly.
[patient] *breathes*
[doctor] I’m hearing some mild wheezing in the right lower lobe. It’s not severe, but it tells me your airways are still a bit reactive.
[patient] Is it because of the age? I am eighty now. My lungs are old, like the rest of me.
[doctor] Age is a factor, but control is key. Let’s look at your chart. You had that spirometry test last month, on April 20th. The results showed moderate obstruction.
[patient] Yes, I remember that. The machine made a funny sound.
[doctor] It does. And your doctor, Dr. Weber, at Klinikum Zürich, sent over the report. It confirms moderate persistent asthma.
[patient] My brother, Ilir, has something similar. He has Swiss Re insurance, so he goes to a different clinic. He says his doctor gave him a different inhaler.
[doctor] Everyone’s asthma is unique. What about your family history? Did your mother have breathing issues?
[patient] Oh, my mother, Shpresa. She had terrible asthma. She used to sleep sitting up. But she also had... what is it... Swiss Health covers that? No, wait, she had a heart condition.
[doctor] Did she have a specific diagnosis?
[patient] I think it was related to her thyroid? Like Graves’ disease? I don’t know, it’s been so long. She passed away in 2015.
[doctor] I see. Let’s focus on you. You mentioned you’re worried about passing out. Have you had any dizziness or fainting episodes?
[patient] No, no fainting. Just the tightness. And maybe a bit of dizziness when I climbed the stairs in Prague.
[doctor] Okay. I want to adjust your treatment. We will increase your maintenance inhaler. Instead of one puff, you will take two puffs, twice a day.
[patient] Two puffs? That’s a lot.
[doctor] It is safe. And you must use your spacer. Are you using a spacer?
[patient] The plastic tube? Yes, I have one. It’s in my bag.
[doctor] Good. Make sure you rinse your mouth after using the steroid part. That prevents thrush, you know?
[patient] The white spots in the mouth? I had that once.
[doctor] Yes. Now, regarding your travel. You went to Prague recently. Did you carry your rescue inhaler?
[patient] Always. I keep it in my jacket pocket.
[doctor] Good. But you need to plan better. If you are traveling, bring extra medication. What if you lost it?
[patient] I would be in trouble. I will buy more next time.
[doctor] Also, you mentioned your brother Ilir. Does he have any other conditions?
[patient] He has... Parkinson’s. It started slowly. Tremors in his hands.
[doctor] That is a different condition. But it’s good to know your family history. Do you have any joint pain or stiffness?
[patient] My knee hurts sometimes. My doctor says it might be a Baker’s cyst. I don’t like that name.
[doctor] It’s just a fluid-filled sac behind the knee. It can cause swelling. But that’s separate from your asthma.
[patient] Yes, I know. I just want to breathe well.
[doctor] We will focus on that. Let’s review your current medications. You are on Symbicort and Ventolin. Are you taking any other drugs?
[patient] I take Lipitor for my cholesterol. And Aspirin for the heart.
[doctor] And any supplements?
[patient] No, no supplements. My wife, Elira, makes my tea. She puts in some herbs.
[doctor] Which herbs?
[patient] I don’t know. Just green leaves.
[doctor] Please stop the herbal tea. Some herbs can interact with your asthma medication or increase your heart rate.
[patient] Oh, I see. I will tell her.
[doctor] Also, check your e-mail. I sent you a summary of our last visit. Your address is arben.krasniqi at gmail dot com. Did you receive it?
[patient] Yes, I did. It was in my spam folder. I am not very good with computers.
[doctor] That is common. Let’s make sure it’s in your inbox next time. Now, let’s talk about your symptoms. When did the wheezing start this morning?
[patient] Around 8:00. I was getting dressed.
[doctor] Did you use your inhaler then?
[patient] No, I waited until I went outside.
[doctor] You should use it when you feel the symptom, not just when you go outside.
[patient] Okay. I will remember.
[doctor] How is your sleep?
[patient] I sleep okay. Maybe I wake up once, to go to the bathroom.
[doctor] Any night sweats or fever?
[patient] No, no fever.
[doctor] Good. Let’s do a peak flow check. Blow into this tube as hard as you can.
[patient] *blows*
[doctor] 320. That is lower than your personal best of 380. It suggests some obstruction.
[patient] Is that bad?
[doctor] It’s a sign we need to adjust your treatment. As I said, we are increasing the Symbicort.
[patient] Okay. And when do I come back?
[doctor] In three months. On August 10th.
[patient] August 10th. I will write that down.
[doctor] Also, call us if your symptoms worsen. Do you have my direct line?
[patient] Yes, I have it in my phone.

SUBJECTIVE
Patient is a 47-year-old woman presenting with complaint of bilateral breast heaviness and discomfort, predominantly on the left side. Symptoms have progressed gradually over the past six months. She reports no skin changes, nipple discharge, or distinct lumps upon self-examination, though she notes general density. Patient mentions a family history of breast hypertrophy; her mother underwent surgery for similar enlargement. Patient has a family history of hypertension and diabetes; her brother, Paul, manages both conditions. Patient currently takes oral contraceptives and uses Ibuprofen as needed for headaches. She recently sustained a fall in the kitchen, landing on her hip and back, but denies direct chest trauma. Patient is a graphic designer working in Geneva. She reports no alcohol or tobacco use. She has no known drug allergies.

OBJECTIVE
Vital signs: Blood pressure 135/85 mmHg, Heart rate 72 bpm, Respiratory rate 14/min, Temperature 36.8°C.
Physical Examination:
- General: Well-appearing, in no acute distress.
- Chest: Breast examination reveals bilateral hypertrophy of glandular tissue. Tissue is dense but elastic. No discrete masses, nodules, or areas of induration palpated. No skin dimpling, erythema, or retraction. Nipples are everted, no discharge.
- Lymph Nodes: No axillary or cervical lymphadenopathy.
- Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs.

ASSESSMENT
1. Breast hypertrophy (benign).
2. Essential hypertension (mild).

2. Prescription for high-support, non-underwire bra to alleviate mechanical discomfort.
3. Patient advised to discuss hormonal contraception options with her primary care physician, Dr. Moreau in Lausanne, as hormonal factors may contribute to tissue growth.

[doctor] Good morning, Mrs. Halloway? Please, have a seat. I see you’ve been referred by Dr. Sterling at the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh. Can you tell me a little about what brought you in today?
[patient] Yes, good morning. Um, it’s actually a bit embarrassing, isn't it? Dr. Sterling mentioned something about a heart murmur, but I keep thinking it’s just the plumbing in my house. You know, the pipes knocking?
[doctor] I understand. Let’s clarify. When did you first notice this? Was it yesterday, or has it been going on for a while?
[patient] Oh, it’s been there for three months, I think. Maybe longer. I’m not great with dates. I just feel this fluttering, or is it a thumping? It’s in my chest.
[doctor] Okay. And have you had any other symptoms? Shortness of breath, dizziness, or chest pain?
[patient] Not really. Just... um, sometimes I get a bit winded climbing the stairs. But I’m 72, so I guess that’s normal? I do my Pilates at the Lothian Pilates Collective on Tuesdays, and I’m fine there.
[doctor] That’s good to hear. You’re active. Now, regarding your medical history. I see on the chart that you have a history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Is that still being monitored?
[patient] Yes, yes. My GP checks it every six months. I take the tablets. But I’ve been reading about all sorts of things. Is this related to my thyroid? Or is it... you know, the heart?
[doctor] It’s unrelated to the thyroid, I’m glad to say. We need to look at the heart valves. Let’s do a quick physical exam. I’m going to listen to your heart with the stethoscope.
[patient] Oh, right. Do I need to undress?
[doctor] No, just loosen the top a bit. I’ll be gentle. I’m listening here, at the apex of the heart, which is roughly at the 5 o'clock position relative to your left side.
[patient] Ouch, that’s a bit tickly.
[doctor] I’m sorry. I’m listening for the murmur. I can hear a soft systolic murmur. It’s grade 2 out of 6. Not very loud. Do you feel anything right now?
[patient] No, just the stethoscope. It’s cold.
[doctor] No problem. Now, I need to order an echocardiogram to look at the valves. It’s a non-invasive test, just like an ultrasound. It will show us if the mitral valve is leaking, which is common at your age.
[patient] Is it dangerous?
[doctor] Not at all. It’s very safe. We also need to check your blood pressure and do an ECG to rule out any electrical issues.
[patient] Okay. So, what happens next? Do I need to see a specialist?
[doctor] We’ll send the results to Dr. Sterling. But I want to see you again to discuss the findings. How does 14th of November sound for a follow-up?
[patient] 14th of November? Let me check my diary. Oh, that’s a Tuesday. I have my Pilates class, but it ends at 10:00. Can I come at 11:00?
[doctor> Yes, 11:00 works perfectly. I’ll book you in. Is there anyone else you’d like to involve in this?
[patient] No, I’m managing fine. My daughter, Sarah, is in Manchester, so she can’t really come. But I’m okay.
[doctor] Understood. Just make sure to bring your medication list to the next appointment. And if you experience any severe chest pain or fainting, go to the emergency department immediately.
[patient] Right, right. Emergency. I’ll be careful.
[doctor] Also, keep an eye on your blood pressure. If it spikes, let me know. Do you have any questions before we wrap up?
[patient] No, I think I’ve got it. It’s just a murmur, not a... what’s the word... a heart attack?
[doctor] Exactly. It’s a structural issue, likely age-related. We’ll monitor it. It’s not an emergency, but it needs checking.
[patient] That’s a relief. I was worried it was something worse, like... I don’t know, some kind of cancer or something.
[doctor] The symptoms you described are classic for a valve issue, not cancer. But we will do the echo to be sure.
[patient] Okay. Thank you. You’re very reassuring.
[doctor] It’s my job. Let me write your prescription for the echo referral. You can get it done at the Edinburgh Imaging Centre on 2nd of November.
[patient] 2nd of November? Is that too soon?
[doctor] It’s good to get it done quickly. The sooner we have the images, the better. You’ll need to fast for four hours before the test.
[patient] Fasting? I can manage that. I usually skip breakfast anyway.
[doctor] Just ensure you have water. Do you have any allergies to contrast dye? We won’t use contrast for the echo, but it’s good to know for the future.
[patient] No, no allergies. I’m quite healthy, apart from the thyroid.
[doctor] Great. I’m noting your NHS Number 987-654-3210 in the system. If you can’t attend the appointment, please call the clinic on 0131 555 0123.
[patient] I will. I’m not great with phones, but I’ll try.
[doctor] We have a simple system. You just dial the number and follow the prompts.
[patient] Okay. Thank you, Doctor.
[doctor] You’re welcome, Mrs. Halloway. Take care.
[patient] Thank you. Goodbye.
[doctor] Goodbye.

note:
SUBJECTIVE
Patient is a 21-year-old male, Luca, residing in Italy. He presents with a 2-day history of sore throat, malaise, and fever. He reports a peak temperature of 38.5°C last night. He took Paracetamol with partial relief. He describes a bitter taste in his mouth. He denies cough, runny nose, or rash. He mentions a recent trip to São Paulo one month ago. He works as a barista and is a member of the FC Bologna United soccer team. He reports minor ankle discomfort from a recent practice session at the gym but denies current pain. Family history is notable for Hashimoto's thyroiditis in his mother, Elisa, aged 52. His sister is Giulia, aged 24. He has no known drug allergies. His insurance is with AXA, policy number AX-99204-B. He is followed by Dr. Ferreira at Clinica Santa Lucia.

OBJECTIVE
Vital signs: Temperature 37.8°C, Heart Rate 88 bpm, Blood Pressure 115/70 mmHg, Respiratory Rate 14 breaths/min.
General: Alert, oriented, in no acute distress.
HEENT: Sclerae anicteric. Oral mucosa dry. Tonsils are erythematous with mild exudates. No cervical lymphadenopathy.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs.
Respiratory: Clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender.
Neurologic: Non-focal.
Labs/Tests: Rapid strep test negative.

ASSESSMENT
1. Acute upper respiratory infection, unspecified.
2. Negative for Group A Streptococcus.
3. No evidence of bacterial superinfection at this time.

PLAN
1. Symptomatic management: Continue Paracetamol for fever and pain as needed.
2. Hydration: Encourage increased fluid intake (water, electrolyte solutions).
3. Rest: Recommend bed rest for the next 2-3 days.
4. Follow-up: Patient to follow up with Dr. Ferreira at Clinica Santa Lucia in 48 hours for re-evaluation.
5. Return precautions: Return to ED if fever persists > 3 days, if difficulty breathing develops, or if a rash appears.
6. Disposition: Discharged home with instructions.

[doctor] Good morning. I see you're here for a sore throat and some general malaise. My name is Dr. Alvarez. Can you tell me a bit more about what's been going on?
[patient] Yeah, hi. Um, it started about two days ago. I just felt weird, you know? Like my head was heavy. And then my throat started hurting.
[doctor] Two days is a typical timeframe for a viral illness. Do you have a fever? Have you checked your temperature?
[patient] Yeah, I did last night. It was pretty high. Like, around 38.5 degrees. I took some Paracetamol but it didn't really help much.
[doctor] I see. Any other symptoms? Cough, runny nose, perhaps?
[patient] Mostly just the throat. It’s really scratchy. And I have this weird taste in my mouth. Um, I’m Luca, by the way.
[doctor] Nice to meet you, Luca. You mentioned a taste issue. Is that metallic or bitter?
[patient] Bitter, I think. Like... old coins. Weird, right?
[doctor] Not uncommon with certain infections. Let’s look at your throat. Open wide and say "Ah."
[patient] Aaaah.
[doctor] Okay, close. I see some redness and a little bit of white coating on the tonsils. Let me check your ears. Hold still.
[patient] Okay. Um, do I need antibiotics?
[doctor] Not yet. This looks very much like an acute upper respiratory infection, likely viral. We usually don't prescribe antibiotics for viruses. Let's do a rapid strep test to rule that out.
[patient] Oh, okay. I was hoping for pills.
[doctor] A nurse will be in shortly to take a swab. In the meantime, can you tell me about your medical history? Any chronic conditions?
[patient] No, I'm pretty healthy. I'm 21. I work as a barista in Bologna.
[doctor] That’s a busy job. Do you have any allergies to medications?
[patient] No, I don't think so. I took Aspirin once and I felt fine.
[doctor] Good. Do you have any family history of autoimmune diseases? Like Hashimoto's or Graves' disease?
[patient] Um, my mom has Hashimoto's. She's 52. And my sister, Giulia, is 24. She’s fine, though.
[doctor] Thanks. Do you have any known contact with someone who has strep throat or a severe cold?
[patient] Maybe. I went to São Paulo last month for a trip. It was crazy there.
[doctor] São Paulo? That’s a long trip. Did you get sick on the plane or right after?
[patient] No, not right away. I felt fine until I got back to Italy and started working again. I was stressed, you know?
[doctor] Stress can lower your immune defenses. Let’s wait for the nurse to come in for the swab.
[nurse] Hi Luca, I'm Sarah. I need to do a throat swab.
[patient] Hi. Does it hurt?
[nurse] It might tickle a bit. Open your mouth.
[patient] Aaah.
[nurse] Okay, that’s good. I’ll run the test.
[patient] Thanks.
[nurse] You’re welcome. I’ll be out of your way.
[doctor] Thank you, Sarah. The test will take a few minutes. In the meantime, let’s review your medications. Are you taking anything else?
[patient] No, just that Paracetamol from yesterday.
[doctor] And do you have insurance? I need to process the visit.
[patient] Yeah, I have AXA. My number is AX-99204-B.
[doctor] Got it. Do you have a primary care physician who referred you here?
[patient] No, I just came in because I couldn't sleep. I thought I should see someone.
[doctor] That’s okay. We can refer you back to your GP if needed. Who is your GP?
[patient] It’s Dr. Ferreira at Clinica Santa Lucia.
[doctor] Noted. Do you have any hobbies? You mentioned being stressed.
[patient] I play soccer. I’m in a team, FC Bologna United. We practice every Tuesday and Thursday.
[doctor] That’s great. Staying active is good, but rest is important when you’re sick. Did you play last week?
[patient] Yeah, I played on Tuesday. I got a little hurt in the gym... wait, no, on the field. I twisted my ankle a bit.
[doctor] Is it still painful?
[patient] No, it’s fine now. Just the throat is bad.
[doctor] Okay. Let’s check your temperature again.
[nurse] Your temperature is 37.8 now.
[patient] It went down?
[doctor] Yes, the Paracetamol is working. Your heart rate is 88, which is normal for a fever.
[patient] I feel a bit dizzy.
[doctor] That’s common with fever. Drink plenty of fluids. Water, tea, broth.
[patient] Okay. Do I need to see Dr. Ferreira again?
[doctor] Yes, in two days. If you don’t improve, or if you get a high fever that doesn’t go down, come back to the emergency department.
[patient] Okay. And if I have a rash?
[doctor] If you develop a rash, it could be a sign of something else, like scarlet fever. Come back immediately.
[patient] Got it. Scarlet fever. I’ve heard of that.
[doctor] Yes. It’s caused by strep bacteria. Since the swab is negative, it’s less likely, but keep an eye out.
[patient] The swab?
[nurse] It’s negative. No strep.
[patient] Oh, good. So it’s just a virus.
[doctor] Exactly. An acute upper respiratory infection, unspecified. It will run its course.
[patient] How long does it take?
[doctor] Usually 5 to 7 days. You’ll feel better in a few days.
[patient] Thanks, Dr. Alvarez.
[doctor] You’re welcome, Luca. Take care.

PATIENT NAME: Marco Rossi
DATE OF BIRTH: 12/05/1981
RECORD NUMBER: MR-2024-88391

REASON FOR VISIT
Patient presents with acute onset right foot pain, specifically localized to the lateral ankle, following an inversion injury two weeks ago. Patient reports inability to bear full weight and significant pain during inversion.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Marco Rossi, a 43-year-old male, reports twisting his right ankle while running in a park two weeks ago. The injury occurred during a routine run, where he cut across the grass. He experienced immediate pain and swelling. He initially sought care from his primary physician, Dr. Huber at Mediclin Bern, who diagnosed a sprain and provided a brace. However, symptoms have persisted and worsened, with pain currently rated 7/10 on a numeric rating scale. Patient is a semi-professional footballer for FC Zurich and has missed recent training sessions. He reports no numbness or tingling. He recently traveled to Madrid one month ago, where he was asymptomatic.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
No significant past medical history. No known drug allergies.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Works as a logistics manager. Active lifestyle, plays football. Non-smoker. Occasional alcohol use.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs:
Blood Pressure: 120/80 mmHg
Heart Rate: 72 bpm
Temperature: 36.8°C
Respiratory Rate: 14/min

Right Foot/Ankle Exam:
- Significant swelling and erythema over the lateral malleolus.
- Tenderness to palpation over the anterior talofibular ligament.
- Pain with passive inversion (7/10).
- Pain with joint compression tests (squeezing 1st and 5th toes).
- No pain with eversion.
- No neurological deficits noted.

DIAGNOSIS
1. Right ankle sprain, suspected grade II or III (Anterior Talofibular Ligament injury).
2. Rule out occult fracture or syndesmotic injury.

PLAN
1. Imaging: X-ray of the right ankle (AP, lateral, mortise views) ordered today. MRI of the right ankle scheduled if X-ray is negative or if pain persists.
2. Laboratory Work: Complete Blood Count (CBC), C-Reactive Protein (CRP), and Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) ordered to rule out infection or systemic inflammation. Blood draw performed today.
3. Treatment:
   - Prescription for a rigid walking boot for six weeks.
   - RICE protocol (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation) instructed.
   - Ibuprofen 400 mg every 8 hours with food for pain and inflammation.
   - Non-weight-bearing on the right foot until further evaluation.
4. Follow-up: Appointment scheduled for March 15, 2024 at 14:30 with Dr. Alan Schmidt.
5. Referral: Copy of this note sent to Dr. Huber at Mediclin Bern.
6. Patient Education: Discussed the importance of rest to prevent chronic instability. Patient advised to contact clinic at +41 31 555 0192 if symptoms worsen, numbness occurs, or if he develops fever.

PROVIDER
Dr. Alan Schmidt
Clinic for Orthopedic Sports Medicine

RESIDENCE: Annecy

CHIEF COMPLAINT: Fatigue, dizziness, palpitations.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
Patient is a 58-year-old male presenting with two weeks of fatigue and dizziness. Symptoms started after a business trip to Strasbourg. He reports orthostatic dizziness and palpitations. No chest pain or shortness of breath. He has a history of Crohn's disease, currently managed with Humira. He also has a history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis, which is well-controlled. Recent blood work from his primary care physician showed a hemoglobin of 9.5 g/dL and low ferritin. He is concerned about his anemia.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
1. Anemia, unspecified (chronic)
2. Crohn's disease
3. Hashimoto's thyroiditis

MEDICATIONS:
- Humira 40 mg SC weekly
- Levothyroxine 75 mcg PO daily

ALLERGIES:
NKDA

BP: 110/70 mmHg
HR: 98 bpm
RR: 16 breaths/min
SpO2: 97% on room air

Her symptoms began while she was visiting her sister in Budapest for her birthday on May 12. She was referred by Dr. Stefan Keller at Klinikum Wien after an echocardiogram performed on June 1 revealed a reduced ejection fraction. She denies chest pain, palpitations, or syncope.

note:
SUBJECTIVE
Patient is a 22-year-old male, Emre Yilmaz, presenting with acute onset of lower back pain and left-sided radiculopathy. Symptoms began two weeks ago after lifting a heavy barbell at the gym. He describes the initial pain as sudden and sharp, followed by radiating pain from the left buttock down the posterior thigh to the calf and big toe. He reports paresthesia (tingling) in the left big toe. Denies fever, weight loss, or bowel/bladder incontinence. No prior history of back pain. Family history: my mother has chronic back stiffness, but no radiculopathy. Patient works as a logistics coordinator at TransGlobal Freight, involving prolonged sitting. No known drug allergies.

OBJECTIVE
Vitals: BP 120/80, HR 72, Temp 36.8°C.
General: Well-appearing, no acute distress at rest.
Musculoskeletal:
- Lumbar spine: Mild paraspinal muscle spasm on the left. Tenderness to palpation in the left paraspinal region. A small, tender swelling is noted at the 3 o’clock position relative to the lumbar spine (left side).
- Range of Motion: Limited forward flexion due to pain. Extension preserved.
- Neurological:
  - Straight Leg Raise (SLR): Positive on the left at 40 degrees with reproduction of radicular pain. Negative on the right.
  - Reflexes: Patellar reflex 2+ bilaterally. Ankle jerk 2+ on the right, 1+ on the left (slightly diminished).
  - Strength: 5/5 in bilateral hip flexion, knee extension, and ankle dorsiflexion. Slight weakness (4/5) in left ankle plantarflexion.
  - Sensation: Mild paresthesia in the left S1 dermatome (lateral foot and big toe).

ASSESSMENT
1. Lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy (L5-S1 level suspected based on symptoms).
2. Acute low back pain.

PLAN
1. Conservative management:
   - Activity modification: Avoid heavy lifting and prolonged sitting. Use ergonomic supports.
   - Cryotherapy: Ice pack to the lumbar region for 15 minutes, 3 times daily, for the first 3-4 days. Switch to heat if stiffness persists.
   - Physical Therapy: Referral sent to Spine Care Clinic Berlin via e-mail referral@spinecare-berlin.de.
2. Pharmacotherapy:
   - Ibuprofen 400 mg PO TID with food for 10 days.
   - Cyclobenzaprine 10 mg PO at bedtime for 7 days.
3. Follow-up:
   - Return to clinic on 12 May at 14:30.
   - Patient advised to contact office at 030 1234 5678 if pain worsens or new neurological deficits (weakness, incontinence) occur.
4. Medical Record Number: M-8842-9931.

note:
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Fatigue and decreased exercise tolerance.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Gertrud Müller, a 90-year-old female, presents for evaluation of progressive fatigue and reduced running capacity. She reports feeling tired for the past 3 months. She is an avid runner, typically running 5 times per week, but has had to reduce her duration to 20 minutes due to exhaustion. She also reports feeling cold, constipation, dry skin, and hair thinning. She had a minor fall in the kitchen recently, resulting in a shin contusion, which is healing. She was referred by Dr. Hans Weber from Universitätsklinikum München after routine blood work showed abnormal thyroid function.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Positive for fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain (2 kg).
Gastrointestinal: Positive for constipation.
Integumentary: Positive for dry skin and hair thinning.
Musculoskeletal: Positive for shin contusion (resolving), knee discomfort with running.
Neurological: Positive for insomnia (waking at 4 am).
Cardiovascular: Negative for palpitations, chest pain.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 135/85 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, Temp 36.8°C.
General: Alert, oriented x3. No acute distress.
Skin: Dry, cool to touch.
HEENT: No exophthalmos. Thyroid palpable, non-tender, no nodules.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender, bowel sounds present.

RESULTS
TSH: 12.5 mIU/L (High)
Free T4: 0.7 ng/dL (Low)
TPO Antibodies: Positive
CBC: Within normal limits
Electrolytes: Within normal limits

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Hypothyroidism, likely secondary to Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.
Plan:
- Start Levothyroxine 25 mcg PO daily on an empty stomach, 30 minutes before breakfast.
- Repeat TSH and Free T4 in 8 weeks.
- Educate patient on medication timing and potential side effects.

2. Contusion, left shin.

- Return if signs of infection develop.

Plan:
- Monitor. Likely related to hypothyroidism. Reassess after thyroid levels normalize.

4. Insurance and Administration.

- Insurance ID: TK-998877665
- Follow-up appointment scheduled for 8 weeks from today.
- Patient to contact office at 089-1234-5678 if questions arise.
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, Gertrud Müller. Please, have a seat. I see you have your daughter Katrin with you today. How are you both doing?
[patient] Oh, hello, Doctor. I am Gertrud. I am... uh, I am 90 years old, you know. Still standing on my own two feet, mostly.
[nurse] Just checking your blood pressure first, please.
[patient] Yes, yes. Here it is.
[nurse] Okay, 135 over 85. A bit high, but we know that. Let’s let the doctor take it from here.
[doctor] Thank you, Sarah. Gertrud, I reviewed your file. You were referred to me by Dr. Hans Weber from Universitätsklinikum München. Is that correct?
[patient] Yes, that is right. Dr. Weber said I need to see someone because my energy levels are... they are strange.
[doctor] Can you tell me a bit more about that? What has been changing?
[patient] Well, you know, I live in Munich, but I spent last June in Freiburg visiting my brother Werner. He is 88.
[doctor] And how did you get there?
[patient] By train. It is a lovely trip. But before that, in the spring, I started feeling very tired. Just... um... fatigue.
[doctor] Fatigue can be many things. Do you have any pain?
[patient] Not really pain. But my knees hurt when I run.
[doctor] Run? At your age?
[patient] Yes! I am a runner. I run five times a week. It keeps my mind sharp. But lately, I cannot run as far. Maybe only 20 minutes before I have to stop.
[doctor] That is quite active for 90. What do you run on?
[patient] Usually in the park near my home. But last week, I fell in the kitchen.
[doctor] In the kitchen?
[patient] Yes. I slipped on a wet floor. I hit my shin. It bruised badly. Katrin, my daughter, is 55, she helped me clean it.
[doctor] I see. And besides the fatigue and the knee pain, do you feel cold? Or have you gained weight?
[patient] Yes, I do feel cold. Even in October. And I have gained about two kilos. I don’t know why. I eat the same.
[doctor] How are your bowel movements?
[patient] Oh, that is a problem. I am constipated. Very constipated.
[doctor] And do you have any dry skin or hair loss?
[patient] My hair is thin, yes. And my skin is dry.
[doctor] I see. Let’s look at your lab results from October 12th.
[patient] Yes, Dr. Weber sent them.
[doctor] Your TSH is elevated at 12.5. And your Free T4 is low.
[patient] What does that mean?
[doctor] It suggests your thyroid gland is not producing enough hormone. This is called hypothyroidism.
[patient] Is it... is it that disease? Like my cousin?
[doctor] You mean Herbert?
[patient] Yes, Herbert. He has Hashimoto’s.
[doctor] Yes, Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is a common cause of hypothyroidism in women. It is an autoimmune condition.
[patient] Autoimmune? So my body attacks itself?
[doctor] In a way, yes. But it is treatable. We can give you medication to replace the hormone.
[patient] What kind of medication?
[doctor] Levothyroxine. It is a very standard treatment.
[patient] Will it help me run?
[doctor] Once your levels are normalized, your energy should improve. The fatigue is likely due to the low thyroid, not just age.
[patient] I hope so. I want to continue running. It is my life.
[doctor] Absolutely. We want you to stay active. But we need to monitor your levels.
[patient] How often?
[doctor] Every six to eight weeks at first, until we find the right dose.
[patient] Okay. And my insurance? I am with TK.
[doctor] Yes, I see your insurance card. Your number is TK-998877665.
[patient] Yes.
[doctor] I will write the prescription. You can pick it up at any pharmacy.
[patient] I go to the one on Schillerstraße.
[doctor] That works. And you should follow up with me in eight weeks.
[patient] I will book an appointment.
[doctor] Please make sure to include this visit in your records. Also, keep an eye on that shin injury.
[patient] It is healing. Katrin puts cream on it.
[doctor] Good. If it becomes red or hot, come back.
[patient] Yes, doctor.
[doctor] Do you have any other symptoms? Any heart palpitations?
[patient] No, no palpitations. But I sleep poorly.
[doctor] How many hours do you sleep?
[patient] Maybe six. I wake up at 4 am and cannot fall back asleep.
[doctor] That can also be related to the fatigue and general malaise.
[patient] Yes.

note:
SUBJECTIVE
João Silva, 18 years old, presents with a 3-week history of erythema, papules, and pustules around the mouth, nose, and chin. Patient reports burning and stinging, especially with acidic foods. Denies fever, chills, or systemic symptoms. History includes use of hydrocortisone cream and a heavy moisturizer. Patient works as a logistics coordinator at TransAlpina Logistics. Moved from Porto to Zurich six months ago. Recent trip to Lisbon. Referral from Dr. Weber at Hôpital de la Tour. No known drug allergies. Friend Carlos has Psoriasis.

OBJECTIVE
Vitals: BP 120/80, HR 72, Temp 36.8°C.
Skin Exam: Erythematous, scaly plaques with small papules and pustules on the perioral area, chin, and nasolabial folds. Central face spared. No comedones. No signs of secondary infection. No lymphadenopathy.

ASSESSMENT
1. Perioral dermatitis, likely exacerbated by topical steroid use and heavy moisturizers.
2. Rule out allergic contact dermatitis (patch test ordered).

PLAN
1. Discontinue hydrocortisone cream and heavy moisturizers.
2. Start Metronidazole gel 0.75% to affected areas BID.
3. Use gentle, non-comedogenic moisturizer.
4. Avoid spicy foods and heavy makeup.
5. Keep skin clean after sweating; use clean towel.
6. Patch test scheduled for November 12.
7. Follow-up in 4 weeks.
8. Notify referring physician Dr. Weber.
9. Contact number for clinic: 044 123 4567.
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning. I’m Dr. Vogel. I see you’re João Silva, 18 years old. What brings you in today?

[patient] Um, hi. Yeah, so... my face is really bothering me. It started getting red and itchy around my mouth. You know, like a rash.

[doctor] Okay. Can you describe where it is exactly?

[patient] It’s mostly around the lips, but also under the nose. And a bit on the chin. It’s not on the forehead, though.

[doctor] I see. How long has this been going on?

[patient] Uh, maybe three weeks? It came up slowly. At first, I thought it was just dry skin from the winter.

[doctor] Did you try any creams?

[patient] Yeah, I used some hydrocortisone cream I had left over. And then I started using that heavy moisturizer I bought from Swiss Pharmacy.

[doctor] And did that help?

[patient] No, actually, it got worse. It’s burning a bit now. And sometimes it stings when I eat acidic things.

[doctor] Okay. Let’s take a look. Please turn your head to the left. Now right. Good. I’m going to use a dermatoscope. It might feel cold.

[patient] Okay.

[doctor] I see small papules and pustules. There’s some scaling. The central part of your face looks a bit spared, which is typical. I don’t see any comedones, which is good. That helps rule out acne.

[patient] Acne? I don’t get acne. I’m clean, you know?

[doctor] Yes, and the pattern here is different. This looks like perioral dermatitis. It’s a specific type of eczema.

[patient] Why do I have it? Is it an infection?

[doctor] It’s not an infection in the bacterial sense. It’s often related to skin barrier disruption. Have you been using any new skincare products recently?

[patient] I started using a new cleanser. And I’ve been working out a lot at Club Helvetia. Maybe the sweat?

[doctor] Sweat can be an irritant, but the heavy moisturizer and the steroid cream are likely the main culprits. Steroids can actually make perioral dermatitis worse if used on the face.

[patient] Oh. I didn’t know that. I was using it for the inflammation.

[doctor] It’s a common mistake. I need you to stop using the steroid cream immediately. And we need to simplify your skincare routine.

[patient] So what do I use?

[doctor] I’m going to prescribe a gentle, non-comedogenic moisturizer. And we will use a topical antibiotic to calm the inflammation.

[patient] Like... Metronidazole?

[doctor] Yes, Metronidazole gel. And possibly a short course of oral doxycycline if it’s severe. But let’s start with the gel.

[patient] Okay. Do I need to see my GP?

[doctor] You can mention this to Dr. Weber at Hôpital de la Tour. He referred you here, so he will be aware of the diagnosis.

[patient] Right. Dr. Weber said to come here because it wasn’t responding to his treatment.

[doctor] Correct. Now, let’s talk about other factors. Have you been traveling recently?

[patient] Yeah, I went to Lisbon last month. For my birthday.

[doctor] Did you change your diet? Eat more spicy food?

[patient] Hmm, I ate a lot of pastéis de nata. And some spicy street food. But I think it started before I went.

[doctor] Okay. What about stress? You’re a student?

[patient] No, I work. I’m a logistics coordinator at TransAlpina Logistics.

[doctor] How is work?

[patient] It’s busy. I moved from Porto to Zurich only six months ago. Still adjusting.

[doctor] That can be stressful. Does stress affect your skin?

[patient] I don’t know. I have a friend, Carlos, who has Psoriasis. He says stress makes it flare up.

[doctor] That’s possible. Let’s look at your medical history. Any allergies?

[patient] No, no known allergies. I’m not on any other medications.

PATIENT NAME: Brunner, Hans
DATE OF BIRTH: 15 March 1948

CLINICIAN: Dr. Alice Weber

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient, a 76-year-old male residing in Zurich, presented for a follow-up evaluation of a left knee injury sustained during downhill skiing. The incident occurred on 20 October 2024 in St. Moritz. The patient reported initial pain and swelling, which has partially subsided but persists as stiffness during activity. He engages in various winter sports, including snowboarding, sledding, and snow tubing, typically with his brother Thomas (72) and nephew Lucas (45).

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
The patient is a retired engineer formerly employed by Swiss Federal Railways. He has no significant chronic medical conditions. Family history is notable for his mother Elena having arthritis, and his sister Anna (74) having undergone bilateral knee replacements. His brother Thomas has hip osteoarthritis.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Blood pressure 130/85 mmHg, heart rate 72 bpm, temperature 36.8°C, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min.
Left knee examination revealed mild effusion and tenderness at the 3 o'clock position on the lateral aspect. Range of motion was limited to 0-110 degrees due to pain. No ligamentous laxity was noted on Lachman or anterior drawer tests.

INVESTIGATIONS
MRI of the left knee performed at Kantonsspital Zürich on 28 October 2024 showed a small meniscal tear.
Laboratory results: Hemoglobin 14.5 g/dL, C-reactive protein 10 mg/L.

ASSESSMENT
1. Left knee meniscal tear, status post conservative management.
2. Chronic stiffness and mild inflammation.

PLAN
1. Continue physical therapy twice weekly, focusing on quadriceps strengthening.
2. Apply cryotherapy (ice packs) for 15 minutes post-activity.
3. Avoid high-impact activities and steep skiing slopes for 4-6 weeks.
4. Snow tubing and gentle sledding are permitted.

6. Follow-up in 6 weeks or sooner if symptoms worsen.

note:
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right elbow pain, medial aspect, for 2 months.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Arta is a 27-year-old female who presents with pain in the medial aspect of her right elbow. The pain began on March 15, 2024 and has been progressively worsening. She describes the pain as sharp and aggravated by gripping, shaking hands, and repetitive wrist flexion. She is a graphic designer and uses a computer mouse extensively. She also plays squash three times a week at the Zurich Squash Club. She reports increasing her training intensity after returning from a trip to Thailand on March 10, 2024. She previously visited the emergency room on April 2, 2024 and her primary care physician, Dr. Muller, on April 20, 2024, receiving advice for rest and ice, with minimal improvement.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever, chills, or weight loss.
Neurological: No numbness, tingling, or weakness in the right hand or fingers.
Musculoskeletal: Pain localized to the medial epicondyle. No swelling, redness, or warmth. No pain in the neck, shoulder, or wrist.
GI: No nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain.
Cardiovascular: No chest pain or palpitations.
Respiratory: No cough or shortness of breath.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 120/80, HR 72, Temp 36.8 C.
General: Alert and oriented, in no acute distress.
Right Elbow:
Inspection: No visible deformity, swelling, erythema, or warmth.
Palpation: Tenderness over the medial epicondyle.
Range of Motion: Full flexion and extension, limited by pain at end range.
Strength: 5/5 in shoulder and elbow. Wrist flexion against resistance reproduces pain (positive Cozen's test).
Neurovascular: Intact sensation in the median, ulnar, and radial nerve distributions. Capillary refill < 2 seconds.

RESULTS
Ultrasound of the right elbow (performed today): Shows thickening of the common flexor tendon origin at the medial epicondyle, consistent with tendinopathy. No fluid collection or tear identified. No signs of a Baker's cyst.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Medial Epicondylitis, right elbow.
- Education: Discussed the diagnosis and the importance of activity modification. Advised to stop playing squash and reduce computer use for 4-6 weeks.
- Medications: Prescribed Voltaren gel to apply to the medial elbow three times daily for 2 weeks. Ibuprofen 400 mg as needed for pain, not to exceed 1200 mg per day.
- Referral: Referred to physiotherapy at Physio Center Zurich for eccentric strengthening exercises.
- Follow-up: Return to clinic on May 20, 2024 at 14:00 to assess progress.
- Patient Address: Bahnhofstrasse 45, 8001 Zurich.
- Insurance: Swiss Life Health, ID 7845-293-110-44.
- Family History: Mother has Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Uncle Elbasan has diabetes.
- Patient DOB: May 12, 1997.

[nurse] Good morning. I see you have an appointment with Dr. Weber at 10:00. Can I have your name and date of birth?

[patient] I live at Bahnhofstrasse 45, 8001 Zurich.

[patient] Yes, here. It is with Swiss Life Health.
[nurse] I see. The number is 7845-293-110-44?
[patient] Yes, that is correct.
[nurse] Perfect. I will call you when Dr. Weber is ready.
[patient] Okay.
[nurse] (Two minutes later) Dr. Weber is ready for you now.
[patient] Thank you.
[doctor] Good morning, Arta. I am Dr. Weber. How are you today?
[patient] Hi, Doctor. I am okay, but my elbow hurts a lot.
[doctor] I see. What brings you in today?
[patient] It is my right elbow. The inside part hurts when I use my hand.
[doctor] How long has this been going on?
[patient] It started about March 15, 2024. I thought it would go away, but it is getting worse.
[doctor] And what makes it worse?
[patient] Lifting things, shaking hands, even opening a jar. I am a graphic designer, so I use my mouse and trackpad a lot.
[doctor] Do you do any sports or hobbies that might strain the elbow?
[patient] I play squash. I go to the Zurich Squash Club three times a week.
[doctor] I see. Did you increase your intensity recently?
[patient] Yes, I started training harder after my vacation in Thailand. I came back on March 10, 2024, and I wanted to get back in shape quickly.
[doctor] That makes sense. Sudden increases in activity can cause overuse injuries. Have you seen a doctor for this before?
[patient] I went to the emergency room on April 2, 2024, at 22:30. They gave me some painkillers and said it was a strain.
[doctor] Did they do any imaging?
[patient] No, just a check-up. I also saw my primary care physician, Dr. Muller, on April 20, 2024. He recommended rest and ice.
[doctor] Did that help?
[patient] A little, but not really. I still have pain when I grip things.
[doctor] Let’s take a look at your elbow. Please extend your arm.

[doctor] (Examining) I am going to press on the inner part of your elbow here. Does that hurt?
[patient] Yes, that is exactly where it hurts.
[doctor] Now, I am going to ask you to resist me while I push your wrist down. This tests the muscles that flex your wrist.
[patient] (Winces) Oh, that hurts.
[doctor] Okay, relax. That is a positive test for medial epicondylitis, also known as golfer's elbow.
[patient] Golfer's elbow? I don't play golf.
[doctor] The name is a bit misleading. It affects the muscles on the inside of the elbow, which are used in gripping and wrist flexion. It is common in people who do repetitive arm movements, like squash or computer work.
[doctor] Do you have any other health conditions?
[patient] No, I am generally healthy. I take no medications.
[doctor] Any allergies?
[patient] No.
[doctor] Family history?
[patient] My mother has Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Her brother, Elbasan, has diabetes.
[doctor] I see. Any history of autoimmune diseases or joint problems in your family?
[patient] No, just what I mentioned.
[doctor] Have you noticed any swelling, redness, or warmth in the elbow?
[patient] No, it just hurts.
[doctor] Any numbness or tingling in your hand or fingers?
[patient] No.
[doctor] Do you have pain in your neck or shoulder?
[patient] No, just the elbow.
[doctor] Have you had any recent infections or fevers?
[patient] No.
[doctor] Okay. I will order an ultrasound to confirm the diagnosis and rule out other issues like a tear or a Baker's cyst, though that is less likely in the elbow.
[patient] Will I need an MRI?
[doctor] Probably not at this stage. The ultrasound should be sufficient. If it doesn't improve with conservative treatment, we might consider an MRI.
[patient] What is the treatment?
[doctor] The mainstay of treatment is rest, activity modification, and physical therapy. You will need to stop playing squash for a while and reduce your computer use.
[patient] That is going to be hard. I really like squash.
[doctor] I understand. But pushing through the pain can make it worse. I will write you a prescription for a topical anti-inflammatory cream, like Voltaren gel, and oral pain relief if needed, such as Ibuprofen.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] I will also refer you to a physiotherapist at Physio Center Zurich for specific exercises to strengthen the forearm muscles.
[patient] Great. When should I come back?
[doctor] Let's schedule a follow-up in four weeks. I have an appointment available on May 20, 2024 at 14:00.
[patient] That works.
[doctor] Good. If the pain gets worse or you develop numbness, call us.
[patient] Understood. Thank you, Doctor.
[doctor] You are welcome. The nurse will take you to the ultrasound room.
[patient] Okay.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Shortness of breath and chest tightness for three months.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS

The symptoms are primarily experienced at rest, particularly in the morning or during periods of high mental stress. She reports that the shortness of breath is rated 8/10 in severity. The symptoms do not occur during physical exertion, such as her handball practice. She denies chest pain radiating to the jaw or arm, syncope, or palpitations that persist after the episode. She reports associated dizziness and a sensation of heart racing, with a self-reported heart rate of 110 bpm during episodes. She moved to Austria three months ago and is currently living with her brother, Ivan. She works as a logistics coordinator at Alpine Freight Solutions. She reports poor sleep quality, waking up at 3:00 am frequently.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Fatigue, poor sleep.
Cardiovascular: No chest pain, no palpitations at rest.
Respiratory: No cough, no wheezing, no hemoptysis.
Neurological: Dizziness during episodes, no focal deficits.
Psychiatric: Increased anxiety, worry about work and family.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 128/82 mmHg, HR 96 bpm, Temp 36.8°C, RR 14, SpO2 98% on room air.
General: Well-appearing female, in no acute distress.
HEENT: Normocephalic, atraumatic.

RESULTS
Pending: CBC, TSH, T3, T4, Electrolytes, BNP.

- Patient presents with classic symptoms of panic attacks (shortness of breath, tachycardia, dizziness) occurring at rest.
- Physical exam and history are negative for cardiac or pulmonary pathology.
- Plan:
    - Increase sertraline from 50 mg to 100 mg daily.
    - Refer to therapy for Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT).
    - Follow up in two weeks to assess response and side effects.
    - Patient advised to seek emergency care if symptoms become severe or unmanageable.
    - Limit caffeine and alcohol intake.
    - Continue handball activities as tolerated.

2. Rule out secondary causes (Thyroid, Anemia).
- Ordered labs: CBC, TSH, T3, T4, Electrolytes, BNP.

[doctor] I understand that is distressing. Can you describe the sensation? Is it sharp, dull, or just a feeling of tightness? And on a scale of zero to ten, how severe was the shortness of breath?

[doctor] That is helpful to know. Have you had any other symptoms? Any dizziness, fainting, or chest pain that radiates to your jaw or arm?

[doctor> Ah, that is a significant adjustment period. Have you been sleeping well?

[doctor] Yes, we will send you to the lab at Labor Innsbruck. You can go there tomorrow at 8:00.

[doctor> I would like to increase your sertraline to 100 mg per day. This should help with the anxiety over the next few weeks.
[patient] Will I have side effects?
[doctor> It is possible to feel a bit more jittery or nauseous for the first few days, but it should subside.
[patient] I will try it. I really want to feel normal again.
[doctor] I am confident we can manage this. Let’s schedule a follow-up in two weeks to see how you are feeling.
[patient] Thank you, Dr. Weber.
[doctor] You are welcome. Please make sure to rest and try to limit caffeine intake this week.
[patient] I will.
[doctor] If you have any severe chest pain or if the shortness of breath becomes unmanageable, please go to the emergency room immediately.
[patient] Understood.
[doctor] Here is the summary for your records. Please review it and sign.
[patient] *(Signs document)*
[doctor] Thank you. Goodbye, Milica.
[patient] Goodbye.

She has a family history of thyroid disease in her sister, Jane, but no personal history of thyroid disorders.

Musculoskeletal: Right elbow pain as above. No joint swelling or redness.
Neurologic: No numbness, tingling, or weakness in the upper extremities.

SUBJECTIVE
Anjali Perera, a 37-year-old female, presents with intermittent palpitations and dizziness for three weeks. She reports a "fluttering" sensation in her chest. She moved from Phnom Penh, Cambodia to Switzerland two years ago. She lives at Seestrasse 12, 6340 Baar. She reports a recent fall in the kitchen due to dizziness. She is a member of Studio Lotus for yoga. Referral from Dr. Keller at Clinique de la Colline. Family history: mother has diabetes; maternal uncle had a myocardial infarction. No known drug allergies.

OBJECTIVE
Vitals: BP <VITAL>130/85 mmHg</VITAL>, HR <VITAL>110 bpm</VITAL>, RR <VITAL>16/min</VITAL>, Temp <VITAL>36.8°C</VITAL>, SpO2 <VITAL>98%</VITAL>.
Physical Exam: Alert, oriented x3. Regularly irregular rhythm, no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally. No jugular venous distension. No peripheral edema. Neurological exam unremarkable, no focal deficits.

ASSESSMENT
1. New onset atrial fibrillation, paroxysmal.
2. Dizziness, likely secondary to arrhythmia.
3. Fall risk due to dizziness.

PLAN
1. Diagnostics: Order ECG, Echocardiogram, Complete Blood Count, Electrolytes, Thyroid Function Tests (TSH, Free T4).
2. Medications: Start Amiodarone <DOSE>200 mg</DOSE> PO once daily for rate/rhythm control.
3. Follow-up: Return to clinic on October 14th at 10:30 AM to review labs and ECG.
4. Lifestyle: Avoid heavy lifting and high-intensity exercise for one week. Continue yoga but modify as tolerated.
5. Safety: Educated on stroke prevention and signs of emergency. Contact Studio Lotus coach if dizziness occurs during class.

[doctor] Hello, I’m Dr. Weber. Thank you for letting me come to your home today. I see you are Anjali Perera.

[patient] Oh, maybe three weeks ago? It comes and goes. My brother says I’m just stressed, but it feels different.
[doctor] I understand. You mentioned in the form that you moved to Zurich from Cambodia a few years ago?
[patient] Yes, I lived in Phnom Penh before. The climate here is... Switzerland is very cold, you know?
[doctor] It certainly is. Let’s check your vitals. I’ll place the cuff on your arm. Does this hurt?
[patient] No, it’s okay. Just... squeeze.
[doctor] Your blood pressure is <VITAL>130 over 85</VITAL>. Your pulse is irregular. Let me listen to your heart with the stethoscope.
[patient] Is it bad?
[doctor] The rhythm is irregularly irregular. This is consistent with atrial fibrillation. I need to do a bit more testing to confirm and check your thyroid levels.
[patient] Atrial what?
[doctor] Atrial fibrillation. It’s a common heart rhythm disorder. It’s not usually life-threatening, but it needs management.
[patient] I do yoga at Studio Lotus every Tuesday. I thought that kept my heart strong.
[doctor] Yoga is excellent for stress, but sometimes the heart needs medication to keep the rhythm steady or to prevent clots.

[doctor] That is a family history we need to keep in mind. Diabetes and heart disease can be linked.
[patient] I’m scared. What if it’s serious?
[doctor] It’s manageable. Many people live full lives with atrial fibrillation. The key is monitoring and prevention of stroke.
[patient] Stroke?
[doctor] Yes, if the blood clots in the heart, it can travel to the brain. We use a score called CHA2DS2-VASc to assess risk.
[patient] That sounds complicated.
[doctor] It’s just a checklist. Age, hypertension, diabetes, heart failure, stroke history, vascular disease, and sex.
[patient] I’m 37. I don’t have diabetes.
[doctor] Correct. Your risk is currently low, but we will monitor it. I’m going to prescribe Amiodarone to help control the rate.
[patient] Amiodarone. I’ll take it.
[doctor] Yes. Once a day. And I want to see you in my office to review the results.

[patient] Thank you, Dr. Weber.
[doctor] You’re welcome. If you feel faint or have chest pain, call emergency services immediately.
[patient] I will.
[doctor] I’ll send the test orders to your lab.

note:
SUBJECTIVE
Patient is a 41-year-old female with a chief complaint of progressive dyspnea and dry cough. She reports the cough has been present for three months but has worsened significantly over the last two weeks. She experienced a fever yesterday and general malaise. She reports losing approximately five pounds recently due to poor appetite. She works as a composting facility manager at GreenLeaf Farms in Portland, where she is exposed to organic dust daily. She reports significant shortness of breath with minimal exertion, such as walking to the mailbox. She tripped and bruised her knee in the kitchen yesterday but denies other significant trauma. Family history is notable for asthma in her mother, Sarah (68), and severe allergies in her brother, David (38). Patient’s date of birth is May 12, 1983.

OBJECTIVE
Vitals: BP 118/76, HR 92, RR 20, Temp 37.8°C, SpO2 94% on room air.
General: Alert, oriented, appearing mildly distressed.
Lungs: Diffuse fine crackles (velcro-like) heard bilaterally in the lower lobes. No wheezes or rhonchi.
Heart: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender.
Extremities: Mild ecchymosis on the right knee, otherwise unremarkable.

ASSESSMENT
1. Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis (HP), likely due to organic dust exposure. The clinical presentation of subacute cough, dyspnea, fever, and weight loss, combined with occupational exposure and auscultatory findings of crackles, is highly suggestive of HP.
2. Right knee contusion, minor.

PLAN
1. Imaging: Ordered High-Resolution CT (HRCT) of the chest to evaluate for ground-glass opacities or mosaic attenuation typical of HP. Appointment scheduled for October 24 at 2:00 PM.
2. Referral: Referral sent to City Pulmonology Clinic for further evaluation and possible bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage.
3. Occupational Health: Patient advised to stop working at GreenLeaf Farms immediately to prevent further exposure. Note provided for employer, Mike.
4. Medications: Continue supportive care. Ibuprofen for knee pain. No steroids started until imaging results are reviewed with pulmonology.
5. Follow-up: Patient to return to clinic in two weeks to review CT results and discuss further management.
6. Education: Discussed signs of worsening respiratory status (increased dyspnea, chest pain, high fever) and advised to seek emergency care if these occur.

[doctor> Do you have any questions about the medication?

[patient> My mother had osteoporosis.
[doctor> Understood. And your brother?
[patient> He’s fine. He’s Stefan.

[patient> No. Just the fracture.
