[doctor] Thank you, Yonas. I see you are 45 years old. What brings you in today?
[patient] I have been feeling very short of breath, especially when I walk up stairs. It started about three weeks ago.
[doctor] I understand. Did you have any chest pain or palpitations?
[patient] No chest pain, but my heart feels like it is pounding fast. I went to the emergency room last Monday because I could not sleep at night.
[doctor] And what did they find there?
[patient] They said my heart was not pumping well. They gave me some pills and sent me home. But I am still tired.
[doctor] Okay. You mentioned you live in Switzerland. Do you work here?
[patient] Yes. I work as a logistics coordinator at Helvetia Freight Solutions. It is a busy job. I have to lift boxes sometimes.
[doctor] That can be difficult with your symptoms. When did you last feel this heavy?
[patient] Every day. I take a medication called Lasix that the doctor gave me. It makes me go to the toilet a lot, but I feel a little better.
[doctor] And do you have any other health conditions?
[patient] My father had heart problems. He died of a stroke. I think I might have Graves' disease too, my sister has it. I have had my thyroid checked before.
[doctor] I see. Did you take any other medications recently?
[patient] I take Levothyroxine for my thyroid. And sometimes Ibuprofen for back pain.
[doctor] Ibuprofen can sometimes affect the kidneys and fluid balance. Did you injure your back recently?
[patient] Yes. I fell at the gym last February. I landed on my back. It hurt for a while, but it is okay now.
[doctor] I am sorry to hear that. We need to be careful with those painkillers. Did you have any swelling in your legs?
[patient] Yes, my ankles are swollen in the evening. I have to wear tight socks to sleep.
[doctor] That is consistent with what we suspect. I have ordered an echocardiogram to look at your heart valves and pumping strength.
[patient] Is it serious, Doctor?
[doctor] It is a condition called left ventricular failure. It means the left side of your heart is weak. It is not your fault, but we need to manage it carefully.
[patient] Can I still work? I have a big project at Helvetia Freight Solutions coming up in June.
[doctor] We will see after the tests. For now, you should avoid lifting heavy boxes. Your doctor at the clinic, Dr. Keller, will review the results with us.
[patient] I am worried. I have an appointment with my physiotherapist on Thursday at 10:00 am.
[doctor] Please bring your medication list. By the way, do you smoke or drink alcohol?
[patient] No, I do not smoke. I drink beer sometimes on weekends. Maybe one or two.
[doctor] We will discuss that later. I am going to start you on a new medication, Carvedilol, to help your heart pump better.
[patient] Is that safe?
[doctor] Yes, it is standard care. You might feel tired at first. If you feel dizzy, sit down immediately.
[patient] Okay. I will write down my questions. I have a cousin, Daniel, who lives in Asmara. He has Parkinson's disease. I want to know if this is similar.
[doctor] It is different. Parkinson's affects movement and the brain, while this affects your heart muscle.
[patient] I see. My insurance number is 756.890.123.456. I hope you can send the report to my GP, Dr. Burns.
[doctor] Certainly. We will send the report to Medical Center Zurich where Dr. Burns practices.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor. I feel a bit better knowing we have a plan.
[doctor] That is good. The nurse will bring you your discharge papers and the prescription for Carvedilol.

note:
SUBJECTIVE
The patient is a 49-year-old female, Elisabeth Wagner, born on 14 March 1975. She resides in Vienna but previously lived in Salzburg. She is employed as a graphic designer. She presents with a three-month history of pain, tingling, and numbness in the left hand, primarily affecting the thumb, index, and middle fingers. The symptoms are worse at night, often waking her around 2 am, and are exacerbated by repetitive hand movements such as typing. She has a positive response to shaking the hand. She has tried ibuprofen with limited relief and used a wrist brace at night for two weeks, which provided some improvement. She reports dropping objects due to weakness. No other significant medical history. No current medications. Family history is notable for arthritis in her mother. She was referred by Dr. Huber.

OBJECTIVE
Vital signs: Blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, pulse 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98%.
Physical examination:
- Left hand: Positive Tinel's sign at the carpal tunnel. Positive Phalen's test with reproduction of symptoms within 30 seconds. Mild weakness in grip strength noted. No atrophy of the thenar eminence. Sensation to light touch is slightly diminished in the median nerve distribution. Right hand is unremarkable.
- Upper extremity: No swelling, erythema, or deformity. Range of motion is full and painless except for the provocative maneuvers.

ASSESSMENT
Carpal tunnel syndrome, left upper limb. Likely etiology related to repetitive strain from occupational activities. Conservative management is indicated as the initial step.

PLAN
1. Initiate night-time wrist splinting. Prescribed a neutral-position wrist splint to be worn during sleep for the next 4-6 weeks.
2. Ergonomic evaluation of workstation. Advised to use an ergonomic mouse and keyboard, and to take frequent breaks.
3. Avoidance of aggravating activities. Minimize repetitive wrist movements.
4. Follow-up appointment scheduled for 12 May 2024 at 10:30 am to reassess symptoms and function.
5. Patient education on carpal tunnel syndrome and signs of worsening condition.
6. Contact information provided for urgent inquiries: dr.muller@pulmonologyclinic.at.

[patient] yes , that is right . i moved from salzburg to vienna about three years ago . i still have many friends back there .

[patient] well , i have been experiencing pain and tingling in my hands , mostly on the left side , for three months . it started subtly , but now it is quite annoying .
[doctor] can you describe the pain ? is it sharp , dull , or burning ?
[patient] it feels like a burning sensation , mostly in my thumb , index finger , and middle finger . sometimes my ring finger is involved , but the little finger is usually fine .
[doctor] when does it typically occur ? is it worse at night or during the day ?
[patient] it is definitely worse at night . i often wake up around 2 am because my hand feels numb and painful . i have to shake it out or hold it under cold water to get relief .

[doctor] i see . have you noticed any weakness in your grip strength ?

[doctor] did you try any over-the-counter medications or remedies ?
[patient] i took ibuprofen for a few days , but it didn't really help the numbness . i also tried wearing a wrist brace at night , which i bought from a pharmacy in wien .
[doctor] did that provide any relief ?
[patient] it helped a little . i woke up less often when i wore it . but i stopped wearing it because it felt restrictive during the day , and i only wore it at night for about two weeks .
[doctor] that is good to know . let's check your vital signs before i examine your hand . i will measure your blood pressure and pulse .
[patient] sure .

[patient] thank you .

[patient] yes .
[doctor] i will press on the palm of your hand just below the base of your thumb . does that reproduce the tingling ?

[doctor] this is a positive tinel's sign . now , i will ask you to extend your wrists back . hold that position for a few seconds .

[patient] yes , it starts to tingle after a few seconds .
[doctor] this is a positive phalen's test . it suggests that the median nerve is being compressed in the carpal tunnel .
[patient] so , what is the diagnosis ?
[doctor] based on your symptoms , your history , and the physical examination , it is highly likely that you have carpal tunnel syndrome . this is a condition where the median nerve is squeezed as it passes through the wrist .
[patient] is it serious ? will i need surgery ?
[doctor] not necessarily . most cases can be managed with conservative treatment first . we will start with a night splint to keep your wrist in a neutral position while you sleep . this helps to reduce swelling and pressure on the nerve .

[doctor] if the symptoms persist or worsen despite conservative management , we may consider a corticosteroid injection . if that fails , then we would discuss surgical options , such as carpal tunnel release . but let's start with the conservative approach .
[patient] how long should i wear the splint ?

[patient] when should i come back for a follow-up ?

[doctor] yes . and try to avoid repetitive wrist movements as much as possible . if you must type , try to keep your wrist neutral and not bent .
[patient] i will be more careful .

[patient] no , i am generally healthy . i do not take any regular medications .
[doctor] good . any family history of hand or joint problems ?
[patient] my mother has arthritis , but i don't think it is related to this .
[doctor] that is possible , but carpal tunnel syndrome is often related to repetitive strain or anatomical factors . let's see how you respond to the treatment .
[patient] i hope it works . it is really affecting my sleep .
[doctor] it is a common issue , and many people find relief with the splint . let's give it a try .
[patient] thank you , doctor .
[doctor] you are welcome . the nurse will give you the splint prescription and the appointment confirmation .
[patient] okay .
[doctor] if you have any questions , don't hesitate to call the clinic or e-mail me .
[patient] i will . thank you .

SUBJECTIVE
Miguel Santos, a 43-year-old male, presents to the emergency department with chief complaint of chest pain. He reports the pain started today at 10:00 AM while exercising at Studio 33 Fitness in Zurich West. He describes the pain as a tightness in the center of the chest, radiating to the left arm, rated 8/10 in intensity. The pain is exacerbated by exertion and relieved by rest and sublingual nitroglycerin. He took one 300 mg Aspirin tablet at home. He has no history of similar episodes. He denies dizziness, nausea, or diaphoresis. He has a family history of myocardial infarction in his father, Santos, at 55 five years ago. He is a software engineer and resides in Zurich. He moved from Lisbon, Portugal, ten years ago. He is insured by Helvetia with insurance number 88-4455-6677-11. He is allergic to Penicillin. He currently takes Lisinopril 10 mg daily. He denies smoking or recreational drug use. He plays football for FC Zurich’s amateur league. He reports a recent minor shoulder injury at the gym.

OBJECTIVE
Vital signs: BP 138/88 mmHg, HR 92 bpm, RR 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air.
Physical exam: Patient appears anxious but in no acute distress. Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. Cardiac exam reveals regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Chest wall is non-tender to palpation. No edema in extremities.
ECG: Normal sinus rhythm, no ST-segment elevation or depression, no T-wave inversions.
Labs: Troponin I level is 0.02 ng/mL (normal < 0.04 ng/mL). Complete blood count is within normal limits. Basic metabolic panel is unremarkable.

ASSESSMENT
1. Chest pain, rule out acute coronary syndrome (ACS).
2. Hypertension, well-controlled.
3. History of exercise-related chest pain.

PLAN
1. Admit for observation.
2. Repeat ECG in 2 hours.
3. Repeat Troponin I in 3 hours.
4. Continue Lisinopril 10 mg daily.
5. Administer Ibuprofen 400 mg PRN for pain, with Omeprazole 20 mg daily for gastric protection.
6. Administer sublingual Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg PRN for chest pain.
7. Maintain cardiac monitoring.
8. Discharge if Troponin remains negative and pain resolves.
9. Arrange follow-up with primary care physician within one week.
10. Provide patient education on warning signs of ACS.

REFERRING PHYSICIAN
Name: Dr. Lukas Keller
Practice: City Practice

REASON FOR VISIT
Patient presented with complaints of hematuria, unspecified. Symptoms started last Tuesday. Patient reports intermittent pinkish urine, no dysuria, no fever. History of nephrolithiasis. Recent use of NSAIDs.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Ms. Berisha, a 61-year-old woman, reports noticing blood in her urine for the past two weeks. Initial presentation was mild, described as "strawberry milk" color. No pain, no frequency, no urgency. She has a history of kidney stones. She moved from Pristina, Kosovo to Switzerland approximately 20 years ago. She is active and swims regularly at Aqua Club Bern. She mentions taking Ibuprofen for back pain for about 3-4 days last week. Her husband, Besnik, is present and confirms the timeline.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Hypertension
Nephrolithiasis (history of)
No known drug allergies

MEDICATIONS
Concor 5 mg daily
Ibuprofen PRN (discontinued during visit)
Multivitamins

SOCIAL HISTORY
Lives with husband Besnik.
Hobby: Swimming (Aqua Club Bern).
Non-smoker.
Occasional alcohol.

EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 130/80, HR 72, Temp 36.8 C.
General: Well-appearing, no acute distress.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender. No costovertebral angle tenderness noted on palpation, though patient reports dull ache on the right side.
Genitourinary: No external abnormalities.

DIAGNOSIS
1. Hematuria, unspecified (ICD-10: R31.9)
2. Hypertension (ICD-10: I10)

PLAN
1. Discontinue Ibuprofen. Use Paracetamol for pain if necessary.
2. Increase fluid intake to 2-3 liters per day.
3. Ultrasound of kidneys and bladder scheduled for tomorrow morning at 09:30 at University Hospital.
4. Follow-up visit in one week to review ultrasound results and urinalysis.
5. Return to emergency department if gross hematuria with clots, severe pain, or fever develops.

Phone: +41 79 123 45 67
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning. I see you are here for a follow-up regarding the blood in your urine. Can you tell me how you have been feeling since we last spoke?

[patient] Hello. Um, honestly? It's been... uh, quite stressful. I know I am 61, but I feel like my body is just giving up on me.

[doctor] I understand. Let's take it step by step. When exactly did you first notice the change in color?

[patient] It was last Tuesday. I was in the bathroom, you know, and I saw it was pink. Not bright red, just... pink. Like strawberry milk.

[doctor] And did it hurt?

[patient] Oh, no. No pain. Just the color. My husband, Besnik, he was worried, but I told him it was probably just from the exercise.

[doctor] Exercise? What kind of activity have you been doing recently?

[patient] I go swimming. I am a member of Aqua Club Bern. We have a group that meets in the morning. I have been going for years.

[doctor] That is good for your health. But did the hematuria stop?

[patient] It came and went. For about two weeks, it was mostly clear, but then yesterday, it was there again. Darker, actually.

[doctor] I see. Did you drink plenty of water?

[patient] Yes, I try. I live in Bern, near the Wyssstrasse, so I have the tap water. I drink maybe two liters a day.

[doctor] Okay. Now, let's talk about your history. Did you have any fever or chills?

[patient] No fever. Just a little back pain, on the right side. Like a dull ache.

[doctor] On the right side specifically?

[patient] Yes. I thought maybe my kidney was acting up again. I had a problem with stones when I was younger.

[doctor] That is a good point to consider. Have you been taking any new medications?

[patient] I am still on my blood pressure pills. Novartis makes them, I think. And I started taking some vitamins for my joints.

[doctor] Which vitamins?

[patient] Just the ones from the pharmacy. Nothing special. Oh, and I saw my GP, Dr. Keller, at the City Practice in Bern. He referred me to you because he was concerned about the persistence.

[doctor] I spoke with Dr. Keller. He mentioned your history of hypertension. Are you currently taking any other drugs?

[patient] I take Concor for the heart. And sometimes Ibuprofen for the back pain. I took it last week when the ache was bad.

[doctor] Ah, Ibuprofen. That can sometimes affect the kidneys if used frequently. Did you take it for more than a few days?

[patient] Maybe three days? Four days? I don't remember exactly. I just took it when it hurt.

[doctor] Let's have a look at your urine sample we collected earlier. The nurse has sent the results.

[patient] Yes, Miss Weber, the nurse, she was very kind.

[doctor] The test shows microscopic hematuria. We see red blood cells, but no bacteria. This rules out a simple infection for now.

[patient] Is it bad?

[doctor] Not necessarily. It could be from the kidney stones, or the medication, or even the intense swimming. But because you are 61, we need to be thorough.

[patient] I moved from Pristina to Switzerland twenty years ago. I am used to doctors, but... you know, it is scary when things change.

[doctor] I understand. Your address on file is Wyssstrasse 12, 3011 Bern. Is that still correct?

[patient] Yes, that is my home. I live there with Besnik.

[doctor] And your insurance? You are with SwissCare?

[patient] Yes, my insurance number is SC-998231-BN. I check it every month.

[doctor] Okay. I am going to order an ultrasound of your kidneys and bladder. It is painless and quick.

[patient] When?

[doctor] I have an appointment for tomorrow morning at 9:30. You will need to have a full bladder.

[patient] A full bladder?

[doctor] Yes, so we can see the bladder walls clearly. Try not to urinate for about two hours before the appointment.

[patient] Okay. I will do that. I have to wake up early.

[doctor] It is worth it. Also, stop taking Ibuprofen for now. Use Paracetamol if you need pain relief.

[patient] I will do that. I will call my friend Elena to drive me, if needed. She lives nearby.

[doctor] That is a good idea. Do you have any questions before I write the prescription?

[patient] Just... is it cancer? Everyone says that at my age, blood means cancer.

[doctor] That is a common fear, but in your case, with the history of stones and the recent Ibuprofen use, there are many benign explanations. The ultrasound will help us rule out serious issues.

[patient] I hope so. I really don't want to go through chemo or anything.

[doctor] Let's not jump to conclusions. We will look at the images first. If there is anything suspicious, we will discuss next steps. But for now, let's rule out the stones.

[patient] Thank you, Doctor. I feel a bit better hearing that.

[doctor] You are welcome. I will send the referral for the ultrasound to University Hospital. You will get a confirmation email.

[patient] My email is besniks.wife at mail dot ch. I check it in the morning.

[doctor] Noted. If you notice clots in the urine, or if the pain becomes severe, go to the emergency room. Otherwise, see you next week for the results.

[patient] Okay. I will go back to my swimming group, but I will be careful.

[doctor] Swimming is fine, just stay hydrated. Goodbye.

[patient] Goodbye.

[doctor] Okay, stop. That is positive. Now the Hawkins test. I’m going to rotate your shoulder forward and press down.

note:
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Pre-operative assessment for inguinal hernia repair; history of anaphylactic reaction to peanuts.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Marco Deluca, a 32-year-old male, presents for pre-operative evaluation prior to scheduled inguinal hernia repair. He was referred by Dr. Bianchi at the Swiss Medical Center. The patient reports a significant history of anaphylaxis triggered by peanut exposure two years ago. The initial event occurred in the kitchen when the patient accidentally crushed a peanut. Symptoms included rapid onset of dysphagia, angioedema of the face and lips, and hypotension leading to syncope. The patient’s partner, Giulia, administered an intramuscular epinephrine auto-injector. The patient was subsequently admitted to the Campus Lugano Hospital for observation. He has had no recurrent episodes since. The patient reports strict avoidance of peanuts and tree nuts and carries emergency medication at all times. He denies any current respiratory or cardiac symptoms. He reports a stable course of Hashimoto's thyroiditis managed with levothyroxine. He is allergic to penicillin.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever, chills, or weight changes.
Cardiovascular: No chest pain, palpitations, or dyspnea.
Respiratory: No cough, wheeze, or shortness of breath. History of childhood asthma, inactive for >10 years.
Gastrointestinal: No nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Abdominal pain limited to the hernia site.
Genitourinary: No dysuria or hematuria.
Musculoskeletal: No joint pain or swelling.
Neurologic: No tremors, weakness, or numbness.
Endocrine: Stable thyroid function.
Allergic/Immunologic: History of anaphylaxis to peanuts. Penicillin allergy (rash).

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Well-appearing male in no acute distress.
Vitals: BP 118/76 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, Temp 36.8°C.
HEENT: Normocephalic, atraumatic. No oral swelling.
Neck: Supple, no thyromegaly, no lymphadenopathy.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Respiratory: Clear to auscultation bilaterally, no wheezes or rales.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender, no organomegaly.
Groin: Right inguinal bulge, reducible, cough impulse present. Palpation reveals a small, non-tender, mobile nodule at the 3 o'clock position relative to the inguinal canal, likely a lipoma or benign lymph node.
Skin: No rashes, eczema, or signs of atopic dermatitis.
Neurologic: Intact cranial nerves, normal motor and sensory function.

RESULTS
Laboratory:
Complete Blood Count: Within normal limits.
Comprehensive Metabolic Panel: Within normal limits.
Thyroid Stimulating Hormone: 1.8 mIU/L (Normal).
Allergy Testing: Not performed today; history-based assessment.
Imaging: None new. Previous CT scan confirms right inguinal hernia.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right Inguinal Hernia:
- Cleared for surgery from the perspective of internal medicine.
- Communicate results to Dr. Bianchi at Swiss Medical Center and Dr. Keller, the surgeon.
- Patient to remain NPO after midnight.

2. History of Anaphylaxis (Peanut):
- High-risk patient for perioperative allergic reaction.
- Anesthesiology team notified of severe peanut allergy and history of anaphylaxis.
- Ensure availability of epinephrine, antihistamines, and steroids in the operating room.
- Use latex-free gloves and equipment.
- Patient to continue carrying personal epinephrine auto-injectors to the hospital.

3. Hashimoto's Thyroiditis:
- Stable.
- Continue levothyroxine with sips of water on the morning of surgery.

4. Penicillin Allergy:
- Documented.
- Avoid penicillin-class antibiotics for prophylaxis; use clindamycin or vancomycin if indicated per surgical protocol.

5. Nodule at 3 o'clock position in groin:
- Likely benign (lipoma/lymph node).
- No immediate intervention required.
- Monitor during physical therapy post-op; re-evaluate if it changes in size or becomes tender.
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, I am Dr. Rossi. I see here you have been referred by Dr. Bianchi at the Swiss Medical Center for a pre-operative assessment before your scheduled hernia repair. Can you please confirm your full name and date of birth?
[patient] Good morning. My name is Marco Deluca. I was born on 14 March 1992.
[doctor] Thank you, Marco. You are 32 years old. Before we begin, I need to document your contact information for the post-operative follow-up. Could you please provide your current e-mail address?
[patient] Sure, it is marco.deluca92 at gmail dot com.
[doctor] Noted. You currently live in Lugano, correct?
[patient] Yes, I reside in the Vernate district.
[doctor] Perfect. Now, the primary reason for today's visit is to assess your risk for severe allergic reactions during anesthesia. I understand you have a history of anaphylaxis. Can you tell me about the initial event?
[patient] Yes. It happened two years ago. I was in the kitchen preparing a salad. I accidentally crushed a peanut while chopping nuts for the dressing.
[doctor] And what happened immediately after the exposure?
[patient] Within minutes, I started feeling tightness in my throat. I could not breathe properly. My face and lips began to swell up rapidly.
[doctor] Did you lose consciousness?
[patient] I felt very dizzy and my vision blurred. I collapsed near the counter. My partner, Giulia, found me.
[doctor] Did she administer any medication?
[patient] She had an auto-injector in her bag. She gave me the injection in my thigh.
[doctor] What was the outcome?
[patient] I was rushed to the Campus Lugano Hospital. They kept me under observation for twelve hours. I recovered fully once the medication took effect.
[doctor] Have you had any similar reactions since that incident?
[patient] No, it has been a one-time event, but I am very cautious now. I strictly avoid all tree nuts and peanuts.
[doctor] That is important. Do you carry an emergency kit with you at all times?
[patient] Yes, I always carry two auto-injectors in my bag and keep a spare set in my car and at work.
[doctor] Excellent. Let’s move to your past medical history. Do you have any chronic conditions?
[patient] I was diagnosed with Hashimoto's thyroiditis about five years ago.
[doctor] Are you currently taking medication for that?
[patient] Yes, I take levothyroxine daily. My levels have been stable for the last year.
[doctor] Any other conditions? For example, skin issues like eczema or asthma?
[patient] I had mild asthma as a child, but I haven’t used an inhaler in over ten years. No eczema.
[doctor] How about any family history of allergies or anaphylaxis?
[patient] My mother has hay fever, but no severe reactions. My father is healthy.
[doctor] Do you have any known drug allergies?
[patient] I am allergic to penicillin. It causes a rash.
[doctor] And have you ever reacted to anesthetics or latex?
[patient] No. I had a minor dental procedure last year, and there were no issues with the local anesthetic.
[doctor] Let’s do a quick review of your systems. Do you have any current symptoms?
[patient] No, I feel well today. No shortness of breath, no chest pain, no abdominal pain other than the hernia site.
[doctor] Any issues with urination or bowel movements?
[patient] No, everything is normal.
[doctor] Do you have any neurological symptoms, such as tremors or weakness?
[patient] No. I am active and have no movement disorders.
[doctor] How about any swelling in your knees?
[patient] No, no joint pain or swelling.
[doctor] Let’s check your vital signs. I will take your blood pressure and heart rate now.
[nurse] His blood pressure is 118 over 76, heart rate is 72 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation is 99%.
[doctor] Thank you. Your vitals are within normal limits. Now, let’s examine the surgical site. I will look at your inguinal region.
[patient] Please.
[doctor] I can see the bulge on your right side. It is reducible. I am going to palpate the area. Does this hurt?
[patient] A little, but it’s manageable.
[doctor] I am checking the surrounding area. I notice a small, non-tender nodule at the 3 o'clock position relative to the inguinal canal.
[patient] Is that something to worry about?
[doctor] It is likely a benign lipoma or a small lymph node. It does not seem to be related to the hernia itself. I will document it, but it should not affect the surgery.
[patient] Okay, that’s a relief.
[doctor] Let’s review your medications again. Besides levothyroxine, are you taking anything else?
[patient] I take a multivitamin, but no other prescription drugs. I do not smoke and I drink alcohol socially, maybe once a week.
[doctor] When was your last meal?
[patient] I had breakfast at 07:30.
[doctor] Good. You are fasting from midnight, which is standard.
[doctor] Do you have any questions about the procedure?
[patient] Just one. Since I have this peanut allergy, what will you do if I have a reaction in the operating room?
[doctor] The anesthesiologist will have epinephrine and antihistamines ready. The operating room is equipped to handle anaphylaxis. We will also use latex-free gloves and equipment to minimize risk.
[patient] That’s good to hear.
[doctor] I will send your results to Dr. Bianchi at the Swiss Medical Center today.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor.
[doctor] You are cleared for surgery, provided the anesthesiologist agrees. I will contact your surgeon, Dr. Keller, with the assessment.
[patient] Great. I will wait for the call.
[doctor] Please stay hydrated but only with clear fluids until midnight tomorrow.
[patient] Understood. Thank you.

PATIENT: Marko Jovanović
DOB: 14.03.1979
AGE: 45
LOCATION: Vienna
OCCUPATION: Structural Engineer at BauTech Solutions
HOBBY: Plays football for Vienna United FC

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
Mr. Jovanović presents with right shoulder pain and limited range of motion. Symptoms began 3 weeks ago following a cable fly exercise at the gym. He describes a sharp pain at the anterior shoulder. Pain is worse with overhead activities and at night. He has stopped exercising at Iron Temple Gym since the injury.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
- Hypertension (controlled)
- Childhood asthma (resolved)

MEDICATIONS:
- Amlodipine 5 mg daily
- Multivitamins

ALLERGIES:
- NKDA

EXAMINATION:
- Right shoulder: Tenderness to palpation at the 3 o'clock position (anterior aspect).
- Range of motion: Reduced active elevation and internal rotation.
- Strength: Weakness in external rotation and abduction.
- No visible deformity (no "Popeye" sign).
- Neurovascular status intact.

ASSESSMENT:
Right shoulder tendinopathy / partial biceps tendon tear.

PLAN:
1. Rest from overhead activities and heavy lifting for 2 weeks.
2. Nurofen 400 mg PO TID with food for pain/inflammation.
3. Ultrasound of right shoulder scheduled in 48 hours.
4. Written note provided for employer BauTech Solutions regarding work restrictions (no climbing, no heavy lifting).
5. Follow-up in 2 weeks. If no improvement, consider corticosteroid injection.
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning. Please, come in and sit down. I see you’re here for the shoulder issue. How are you feeling today?
[patient] Hello. Uh, honestly, not great. It’s been... it’s been really painful these last few days. I can barely lift my arm.
[doctor] Okay, let’s start from the beginning. Can you tell me your full name for the file?
[patient] Yes, it’s Marko Jovanović.
[doctor] Thank you, Mr. Jovanović. And your date of birth?
[patient] 14th of March, 1979.
[doctor] So, you’re 45 years old. I see you’re based in Vienna. Do you work here?
[patient] Yes, I live here. I work as a structural engineer for BauTech Solutions. We handle a lot of bridge inspections.
[doctor] That sounds like a physically demanding job. When did this pain start?
[patient] About three weeks ago. I was at the gym, doing some cable flyes. I pulled a rep a bit too heavy, and I felt a sharp twinge right there, in the front of the shoulder.
[doctor] At the gym, I see. Did you continue exercising after that?
[patient] No, no. I stopped immediately. But it didn’t go away. I tried to ice it, but it got worse. Now it hurts even when I’m sleeping.
[doctor] I understand. Let’s take a look. Please remove your shirt on the right side.
[patient] Sure.
[doctor] Can you raise your arm above your head?
[patient] *groans* Yeah... it’s stiff. It’s like something is blocking it.
[doctor] Okay, try reaching behind your back to touch your spine.
[patient] No, I can’t. It’s too painful.
[doctor] I see. Let me palpate the area. I’m going to press here, near the front of your shoulder, at the 3 o’clock position.
[patient] Ouch! Yes, right there. That’s the worst spot.
[doctor] And here?
[patient] That’s okay. Just the front part is really tender.
[doctor] How is your range of motion? Can you open your mouth to eat?
[patient] Yes, eating is fine. It’s just the arm. I can’t do my overhead press anymore. I’m really missing my routine at Iron Temple Gym.
[doctor] I’m sorry to hear that. Let’s check the strength. Squeeze my hand with your right hand.
[patient] *squeezes*
[doctor] Okay, that’s decent. Now, resist me as I push your arm down.
[patient] *struggles* It’s weak. I can’t push back hard.
[doctor] Right. So we have some weakness and significant tenderness at the anterior shoulder. I suspect this is an injury to the biceps tendon, specifically a partial tear or significant inflammation.
[patient] Is it torn completely?
[doctor] Not completely, I don’t think. If it were completely torn, you’d have a visible "Popeye" deformity in your upper arm. I don’t see that. But it is a significant problem. I’ll order an ultrasound to confirm.
[patient] Okay. What can I do?
[doctor] First, we need to stop the irritation. I’m going to prescribe Nurofen 400 mg. You can take one every 8 hours with food for the pain and inflammation.
[patient] Got it.
[doctor] Also, I want you to rest the shoulder. No heavy lifting, no overhead activities. Avoid the gym for at least two weeks.
[patient] That’s going to be hard. I’ve been going there for five years.
[doctor] I know, but your health comes first. You can do some gentle range-of-motion exercises. I’ll give you a sheet.
[patient] What about the job? I have to climb ladders sometimes.
[doctor] For the next two weeks, you should avoid climbing ladders or lifting anything heavier than a cup of coffee. If you can’t do that, you might need a note from me for your employer at BauTech Solutions.
[patient] Yes, that would be helpful. My boss is understanding, but he needs proof.
[doctor] No problem. I’ll write that you are restricted from overhead work and heavy lifting for two weeks.
[patient] Thank you.
[doctor] Let’s also talk about your hobby. I see you mentioned the gym, but do you do anything else?
[patient] Oh, I’m a big fan of football. I play for a local team, Vienna United FC, on weekends.
[doctor] That’s great. But for now, you need to sit out the next few matches.
[patient] *sighs* I guess so. I was looking forward to the match this Saturday.
[doctor] I know it’s frustrating. But pushing it now could make the tendon tear worse, and then you’d be out for months.
[patient] You’re right. I don’t want surgery if I can help it.
[doctor] We’re aiming to avoid surgery. If the ultrasound shows it’s just inflammation and a partial tear, rest and anti-inflammatories should fix it.
[patient] What if it doesn’t get better?
[doctor] If there’s no improvement in two weeks, we might consider an injection. I’m thinking of a corticosteroid injection to calm the inflammation down.
[patient] Is that dangerous?
[doctor] It’s generally safe, but we don’t want to do it too often. It can weaken the tendon if used excessively. So, we’ll try oral meds and rest first.
[patient] Okay. Do I need to see a specialist?
[doctor] You are already in the rheumatology clinic, but this is more of an orthopedic issue. If it doesn’t improve, I’ll refer you to an orthopedic surgeon. But let’s give it time.
[patient] That sounds like a plan.
[doctor] Any other medical history I should know about? Allergies?
[patient] No allergies. I take multivitamins. I had high blood pressure a few years ago, but it’s under control now.
[doctor] What medication do you take for that?
[patient] Amlodipine 5 mg, once a day.
[doctor] Good. And any other conditions?
[patient] No, just a mild asthma when I was a kid, but I haven’t had an attack in ten years.
[doctor] Okay. Let’s wrap up. To summarize: you’re a 45-year-old man with right shoulder pain starting three weeks ago after a gym injury. You work as a structural engineer and play football for Vienna United FC.
[patient] Yes, that’s correct.
[doctor] Examination shows tenderness at the 3 o’clock position of the right shoulder, reduced active range of motion, and weakness in external rotation.
[patient] Yes.
[doctor] Plan: Rest, Nurofen 400 mg TID, ultrasound in 48 hours. If no improvement in 2 weeks, consider injection. I’ll write a note for your employer.
[patient] Thank you, doctor.
[doctor] You’re welcome. We’ll see you in two weeks for a follow-up.
[patient] See you then.

Routine occupational health follow-up for Hypertensive Heart Disease with Heart Failure. Patient reported worsening lower extremity edema and fatigue over the last three days.

The patient is a 54-year-old woman with a known history of Hypertensive Heart Disease and Heart Failure. She presented to the occupational health clinic for a scheduled follow-up. She reported increased swelling in her lower legs, particularly in the evenings, which correlates with her occupation as a warehouse supervisor involving prolonged standing. She denies chest pain but reports orthopnea when climbing stairs. She has been compliant with her medication regimen, including Betablockol and Cozaar. She admitted to taking Ibuprofen for a hand injury sustained in the kitchen last week, which was identified as a potential contributor to fluid retention and blood pressure elevation.

SOCIAL HISTORY:
- Occupation: Warehouse supervisor
- Non-smoker
- Limited alcohol intake

Guarded. Improvement expected with medication adherence and lifestyle changes.

Dr. Elena Vance
Occupational Health Physician
City Health Center Berlin

note:
SUBJECTIVE
Patient is a 21-year-old male, David Keller, born on March 12, 2003. He is a software engineer working in Winterthur. He presents with increased anxiety, headaches, and palpations. He reports feeling anxious in the evenings, worrying about his health, and having insomnia, waking up at 3:00 am. He denies chest pain, shortness of breath, or facial weakness. He has a history of essential hypertension, diagnosed June 2023. He is currently on Amlodipine 5 mg daily but admits to inconsistent adherence. He has a family history of hypertension (father) and Hashimoto's thyroiditis (mother). He mentions a past Baker's cyst in his right knee, resolved conservatively two years ago. He is referred by Dr. Müller from Kantonsspital Winterthur after an ER visit on October 14th for palpitations and arm pain, which were worked up as negative for cardiac causes. His medical record number is 2024-883910.

OBJECTIVE
Vital Signs:
Blood Pressure: 152/98 mmHg
Pulse: 92 bpm
Temperature: 36.8°C
Respiratory Rate: 16/min
Pain Score: 6/10 (headache)

Physical Exam:
General: Alert, oriented x3, anxious affect.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. Systolic murmur grade 2/6 heard at the apex, at the 5 o'clock position. No S3 or S4.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender, no masses.
Neurological: No focal deficits. No tremors. Facial symmetry intact.
Extremities: No edema.

Assessment
1. Essential Hypertension (ICD-10 I10): Uncontrolled, likely exacerbated by inconsistent medication adherence and high stress levels.
2. Health Anxiety: Patient expresses significant worry about having serious medical conditions such as Parkinson's, Crohn's, or Bell's palsy, despite negative workup.
3. Insomnia: Chronic sleep disturbance related to anxiety and caffeine intake.

Plan
1. Diagnostics:
   - Order blood tests: TSH, Free T4, Complete Metabolic Panel (including electrolytes and kidney function), Lipid Panel.
   - Recheck blood pressure in 2 weeks.
2. Medication:
   - Continue Amlodipine 5 mg daily. Emphasize importance of daily adherence.
   - Consider adding a beta-blocker (e.g., Bisoprolol) if blood pressure remains elevated or if palpitations persist, after reviewing lab results.
3. Lifestyle Modifications:
   - Reduce caffeine intake to max 1-2 cups of coffee per day.
   - Implement stress management techniques (e.g., meditation, yoga).
   - Aim for 7-8 hours of sleep per night.
4. Referrals:
   - Refer to a psychologist or psychiatrist for cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) for anxiety and insomnia.
   - Follow-up appointment in two weeks to review lab results and adjust treatment plan.
5. Education:
   - Discuss the nature of essential hypertension and the importance of consistent medication.
   - Reassure patient regarding the benign nature of the systolic murmur, but plan for periodic monitoring.
   - Discuss the differences between Hashimoto's, Graves' disease, and other conditions he fears, to alleviate health anxiety.

[doctor] good morning , david keller . please , take a seat . how have you been since we last spoke ?
[patient] hi , dr . weber . um , honestly ? not great . i’ve been feeling really anxious lately . and my head hurts .
[doctor] i’m sorry to hear that . let’s take it step by step . first , the anxiety . is it constant , or does it come in waves ?
[patient] it’s mostly in the evening . like , i’m at home in winterthur , and i just can’t stop thinking about everything . you know ? like , what if i’m sick ? what if i’m going to have a heart attack ? i’m only 21 years old , but my mind won’t let me relax .
[doctor] that sounds like health anxiety . have you had any specific symptoms that triggered this ?
[patient] yeah , last week i had this pain in my left arm . and my heart felt like it was beating really fast . i went to the emergency room at kantonsspital winterthur on october 14th .
[doctor] i see . what did they find ?
[patient] nothing , apparently . they did an ecg , blood tests , everything . the doctor there , dr . müller , said it was probably just stress . but i didn't believe him . i still feel weird .
[doctor] let’s look at your records . i see you were referred to me by dr . müller from kantonsspital winterthur . your medical record number is 2024-883910 , correct ?
[patient] yeah , that’s me .
[doctor] okay . i see that you were born on march 12, 2003 . that makes you 21 . you mentioned a headache . can you describe it ?
[patient] it’s in my temples . like a tight band . it’s a 6 out of 10 on the pain scale . and i get dizzy sometimes when i stand up too fast .
[doctor] that dizziness could be related to your blood pressure . we know you have essential hypertension . have you been taking your medication ?
[patient] um , i try . i’m on amlodipine . but sometimes i forget . or i skip it because i don’t want to get dependent . is that bad ?
[doctor] it’s important to be consistent . inconsistent dosing can lead to blood pressure spikes , which might explain the headaches and the dizziness . let’s check your current vitals .
[nurse] mr . keller , could you step up to the chair ? i need to take your blood pressure and pulse .
[patient] sure .
[nurse] right arm , please . roll up your sleeve . okay , inflating .
[patient] it’s tight .
[nurse] sorry about that . your blood pressure is 152 over 98 . pulse is 92 beats per minute .
[doctor] thank you . that’s higher than we’d like . 152 over 98 is elevated . let’s examine you quickly .
[patient] is something wrong ?
[doctor] no , just a routine check . i’m going to listen to your heart . please , breathe in and out normally .
[patient] okay .
[doctor] i hear a systolic murmur at the apex , at the 5 o'clock position . it’s grade 2/6 . this is often benign , but given your history , we’ll keep an eye on it .
[patient] a murmur ? like a defect ?
[doctor] not necessarily a defect . sometimes it’s just blood flowing through the valve . but combined with your high blood pressure , it’s something to monitor . do you have any history of heart disease in your family ?
[patient] my dad has high blood pressure . he’s on three pills . my mom had hashimoto's thyroiditis , i think ? that’s an autoimmune thing , right ?
[doctor] yes , hashimoto's is an autoimmune condition affecting the thyroid . it’s different from graves' disease , which also affects the thyroid but causes hyperthyroidism instead . why do you ask ?
[patient] because i’ve been feeling really tired all the time . and my hair is falling out . i was worried i had something like that . or maybe parkinson's ? i read about it online .
[doctor] parkinson's disease is a neurodegenerative disorder that typically affects older adults . it involves tremors and stiffness . do you have any tremors ?
[patient] no . just the anxiety shakes .
[doctor] okay . let’s rule out thyroid issues . i’ll order blood work . tsh , free t4 , and a complete metabolic panel to check your electrolytes and kidney function .
[patient] will that take long ?
[doctor] results usually come back in 48 hours . in the meantime , let’s talk about your anxiety . you mentioned being in winterthur . do you work there ?
[patient] yeah , i’m a software engineer at swisstech solutions . it’s a high-stress job . long hours .
[doctor] that can definitely contribute to hypertension and anxiety . have you been sleeping well ?
[patient] not really . i get up in the middle of the night . like , at 3:00 am i’m wide awake . thinking about work .
[doctor] insomnia can worsen both anxiety and blood pressure . have you tried any relaxation techniques ?
[patient] i try to meditate . but it’s hard . i have a friend , lisa , who suggests yoga . but i don’t have time .
[doctor] what about alcohol or caffeine ?
[patient] coffee , definitely . maybe three cups a day . alcohol ? once in a while . a beer with friends .
[doctor] three cups of coffee can raise your blood pressure and increase anxiety . i’d recommend cutting down to one or two .
[patient] i can try . but what about the medication ? should i increase my dose ?
[doctor] not yet . let’s see how you respond to the blood tests . if your thyroid is normal , we might adjust your amlodipine dose or add a beta-blocker to help with both the blood pressure and the heart rate .
[patient] a beta-blocker ? will that make me feel tired ?
[doctor] it can , initially . but it can also help with the palpitations and anxiety symptoms . we’ll monitor your heart rate closely .
[patient] okay . and the headache ?
[doctor] we’ll recheck your blood pressure in two weeks . if it’s still high , we’ll consider imaging of your head to rule out other causes . but for now , let’s focus on consistency with your meds and reducing stress .
[patient] what if it’s not stress ? what if i have crohn's disease ? i have some stomach issues sometimes .
[doctor] crohn's disease is an inflammatory bowel disease . it usually presents with diarrhea , abdominal pain , and weight loss . do you have those symptoms ?
[patient] just some bloating . but no blood in the stool .
[doctor] then it’s unlikely to be crohn's . but i’ll note it . if the symptoms persist , we can refer you to a gastroenterologist .
[patient] okay . and what about bell's palsy ? i had a friend who got that . his face drooped .
[doctor] bell's palsy is a condition that causes temporary weakness or paralysis of the muscles on one side of the face . it’s often caused by a viral infection . have you had any facial weakness ?
[patient] no . just the headaches .
[doctor] okay . let’s move on . do you have any other medical conditions ?
[patient] no . just the hypertension . and i had a baker's cyst in my knee two years ago . it popped .
[doctor] that sounds painful . did you need surgery ?
[patient] no , just rest and ice . it’s fine now .
[doctor] good . let’s summarize . you’re a 21-year-old male with a history of essential hypertension , currently on amlodipine . you’re presenting with increased anxiety , headaches , and palpitations . we’ll order blood work to check thyroid function and electrolytes . we’ll also monitor your blood pressure closely .
[patient] what should i do in the meantime ?
[doctor] take your medication daily . reduce caffeine intake . try to get at least 7 hours of sleep . if you experience chest pain , severe shortness of breath , or a sudden change in vision , go to the emergency room immediately .
[patient] okay . and the anxiety ? should i see a therapist ?
[doctor] i think it would be beneficial . i can refer you to a psychiatrist or a psychologist who specializes in anxiety disorders .
[patient] that’s good . i was hesitant to go .
[doctor] it’s a brave step . mental health is just as important as physical health .
[patient] thanks , dr . weber .
[doctor] you’re welcome , david . we’ll follow up in two weeks . the nurse will call you with the blood test results .
[patient] okay . see you then .
[doctor] goodbye .
[patient] bye .

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

PATIENT INFORMATION
Name: Almeida, João
Date of Birth: 14 March 1937
Record Number: ORTH-2024-88921

REFERRAL
Referring Physician: Dr. Keller
Institution: University Hospital Zurich
Date of Referral: 28 September 2024

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Almeida, an 87-year-old male, presented to the orthopedic clinic with complaints of dizziness and giddiness. He reported that symptoms began approximately three months ago. The dizziness is described as a spinning sensation, often triggered by rapid changes in position, particularly standing up quickly or turning the head. The patient denies any history of falls, though he reported needing to hold onto walls for stability. He mentioned that his wife, Beatriz, 85, resides in a care facility due to her own health issues, including Hashimoto's disease. His daughter, Sofia, 42, resides in Lausanne and is his primary support contact. His son, João, contacted the clinic yesterday regarding the patient's concerns. The patient previously consulted Dr. Keller at University Hospital Zurich two weeks ago for a general evaluation, who referred him to orthopedics to rule out musculoskeletal causes.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
- Hypertension
- Osteoarthritis (knees), managed with Mobic as needed.
- Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia, managed with Lasix.
- No history of Parkinson's disease, Crohn's disease, Graves' disease, Bell's palsy, or Baker's cyst.
- Previous MRI of the knee performed May 2023 showed mild degenerative changes, no acute pathology.

SOCIAL HISTORY
The patient lives independently in Lausanne. He is retired from his former textile engineer role. He is a native of Portugal and has lived in Switzerland for over 40 years. He reports limited alcohol consumption.

EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Blood pressure 145/85 mmHg, Heart rate 78 bpm.
Neurological: Cranial nerves intact. No focal deficits. No signs of ataxia.
Orthopedic: Knee joints stable. No effusion. Full range of motion.
Vestibular: Dix-Hallpike maneuver positive on the left side, inducing nystagmus and dizziness. This is consistent with Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV).

ASSESSMENT
1. Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV), left-sided.
2. Hypertension, stable.
3. Osteoarthritis, chronic.

PLAN
1. Prescribed Betahistine 24 mg, to be taken twice daily for two weeks to manage nausea and dizziness.
2. Referral to physical therapy at Clinique du Jura for vestibular rehabilitation and balance training.
3. Advised patient to avoid rapid head movements and to stand up slowly.
4. Discussed medication interactions; advised to limit alcohol while on Betahistine.
5. Follow-up appointment scheduled for 26 October 2024 to evaluate response to treatment.
6. Patient educated on red flags: if symptoms include chest pain, slurred speech, or sudden weakness, he should seek emergency care immediately.
7. Contact information provided for Sofia to update the family.

note:
SUBJECTIVE
Barbara Kowalski, 92-year-old female, presents for a cardiology follow-up. She reports a recent episode of dizziness and near-syncope occurring at her private residence in Heidelberg. The incident happened when she slipped on a wet floor in her kitchen. She denies loss of consciousness, chest pain, or palpitations, although she noted a brief sense of "heart skipping." She reports a pain score of 2/10 for mild chest tightness. She admits to missing her cardiac medications for two days during a recent trip to Prague. She lives alone but has support from her daughter, Anja (34). She moved from Warsaw, Poland, to Germany approximately ten years ago.

OBJECTIVE
Vital signs: BP 135/85 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, RR 16, SpO2 96% on room air.
Physical Exam: General: Alert, oriented x3. Cardiac: Regular rate and rhythm, S1/S2 heard, no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lungs: Clear to auscultation bilaterally. Extremities: Trace edema in bilateral lower extremities. Neurological: Mild hand tremor noted, consistent with known Parkinson's disease.
Labs (from 10 May 2023): Potassium 3.2 mmol/L (low), Creatinine 1.1 mg/dL, Troponin negative.
ECG (Today): Sinus rhythm with occasional premature ventricular contractions (PVCs).

ASSESSMENT
1. Unspecified place in unspecified non-institutional (private) residence as the place of occurrence of the external cause: Fall/dizziness episode.
2. Hypokalemia: Likely contributing to PVCs and dizziness, exacerbated by medication non-adherence during travel.
3. Parkinson's disease: Stable, mild tremor noted.
4. History of Hashimoto's thyroiditis in family (sister Ewa).

PLAN
1. Start Metoprolol 25 mg daily at 08:00 to control PVCs and rate.
2. Replete potassium. Recommend dietary changes or supplementation.
3. Follow-up appointment scheduled for 15 October 2023 at 14:00.
4. Patient advised to monitor blood pressure at home with daughter Anja.
5. Caution regarding balance due to Parkinson's disease and fall risk at home.

note:
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right upper quadrant abdominal pain and nausea.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Arben Krasniqi is a 39-year-old male who presented to the emergency department with acute onset of right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and vomiting. The pain was described as constant and rated 8/10 in severity. He reported no prior similar episodes. He mentioned that he had been traveling to Vienna recently for work and suspected he may have eaten foods that triggered the episode. He has no history of biliary disease. Family history is notable for his brother, Blerim, who underwent cholecystectomy for similar symptoms.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever at home, but developed fever in the ER.
Gastrointestinal: Nausea, vomiting (x2), anorexia, no diarrhea, no melena.
Respiratory: No cough, no dyspnea.
Cardiovascular: No chest pain, no palpitations.
Neurological: No headache, no weakness.
Musculoskeletal: No joint pain.
Skin: No rashes, no jaundice.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: Temperature 38.2°C, Heart Rate 110 bpm, Blood Pressure 120/80 mmHg, Respiratory Rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air.
General: Alert, oriented, in mild distress due to pain.
Abdomen: Soft, non-distended. Positive Murphy's sign. Tenderness in the right upper quadrant. No rebound tenderness. No organomegaly.
Other: Unremarkable.

RESULTS
Labs:
White Blood Cell Count: 18,500/µL (elevated)
C-Reactive Protein: 120 mg/L (elevated)
Liver Function Tests: ALT 45 U/L, AST 38 U/L, Bilirubin 0.9 mg/dL (normal)
Amylase/Lipase: Normal.
Imaging:
Abdominal Ultrasound: Multiple gallstones in the gallbladder. Gallbladder wall thickening (4mm). Pericholecystic fluid. No common bile duct dilation. No choledocholithiasis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Acute Cholecystitis
- Diagnosis confirmed by clinical presentation and ultrasound findings.
- Treated with IV fluids, antiemetics, and antibiotics (Ceftriaxone).
- Symptoms resolved with conservative management.
- Plan: Elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy recommended to prevent recurrence.
- Referral to Dr. Keller at Kantonsspital Aarau for surgical consultation.
- Appointment scheduled for March 14th at 09:30.

2. Pain Management
- Discharge on Ibuprofen 400 mg TID and Paracetamol 500 mg PRN.
- Instructions given to take with food.

3. Diet and Lifestyle
- Low-fat diet recommended.
- Avoid large meals and fatty/fried foods.
- Increase fluid intake and fiber.

4. Follow-up and Warning Signs
- Patient instructed to return to ED or call +41 62 835 1234 if fever >38.5°C, severe pain, persistent vomiting, or jaundice occurs.
- Discharge summary sent to GP Dr. Ymeri.
- Patient educated on post-operative expectations for future surgery.

[doctor] dissolving stones with medication is rarely successful and takes a very long time . given your age and the fact that this was your first episode of acute cholecystitis , surgery is the standard of care . it is a minor procedure , usually done under general anesthesia , and you go home the same day or the next .

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right shoulder pain after a fall.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Anna Gruber, a 50-year-old woman, presented to the emergency department on Monday, 10th of November at 14:15 with complaints of severe right shoulder pain and limited range of motion. She reports slipping on ice in a park in Gratz approximately four hours prior to arrival. She denies loss of consciousness or head injury. Vital signs within normal limits. Right shoulder is tender to palpation, particularly at the upper end of the humerus. There is visible swelling and bruising. X-ray of the right shoulder reveals a non-displaced fracture of the upper end of the right humerus. No other fractures or dislocations are seen. Blood work is unremarkable.

1. Unspecified fracture of upper end of right humerus, initial encounter for closed fracture.
2. Hashimoto's disease, stable.

1. Right arm placed in a sling for immobilization.

6. Patient to contact SVA for insurance authorization for physical therapy.
7. Return precautions discussed: increased pain, numbness, or tingling in the hand.

Patient discharged to home at 17:45 in stable condition. Accompanied by daughter, Sophie (22). Discharge instructions provided in written and verbal form. Patient verbalized understanding.

[doctor] Good morning. I am Dr. Weber, the emergency physician. Can you tell me your full name and date of birth?
[patient] My name is Selam Tesfay. I was born on 14 March 1934.
[doctor] Thank you, Ms. Tesfay. You are 90 years old. What brings you to the emergency department today?
[patient] I have a pain in my left breast. It started about three weeks ago. It is a dull ache, but it gets sharper when I move.
[doctor] On a scale of 1 to 10, how would you rate the pain right now?
[patient] It is a 6 out of 10.
[doctor] Okay. Do you have any other symptoms? Fever, weight loss, night sweats?
[patient] No fever. I have lost some weight, maybe 2 kilograms in the last month. But no sweating.
[doctor] I see. Do you have a family history of breast or ovarian cancer?
[patient] My sister, Hanna, had breast cancer when she was 65. My mother, Mariam, died of heart disease, not cancer.
[doctor] Understood. Who is your primary care physician?
[patient] Dr. Keller at the practice in Basel. I moved here from Asmara in Eritrea many years ago.
[doctor] And have you been working recently?
[patient] I retired from my job as a librarian at the Cantonal Library in Basel ten years ago.
[doctor] Did you travel recently?
[patient] Yes. I went to Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, last month to visit my brother, Abraham. He is 88.
[doctor] Did you have any symptoms while you were there?
[patient] No. The pain started after I returned.
[doctor] Let me examine your breast. May I touch your chest area?
[patient] Yes, please.
[doctor] I can feel a small, hard lump in the upper outer quadrant. It does not seem to be attached to the skin.
[patient] Is it bad?
[doctor] We need to do an ultrasound and possibly a biopsy to know for sure. A nurse will come in to set up the monitor.
[nurse] Hello, Ms. Tesfay. I am Jana. I am going to attach these leads to your chest to monitor your heart rate.
[patient] Thank you, Jana.
[nurse] Your blood pressure is 145 over 85. Your heart rate is 82. Your temperature is 36.8 degrees Celsius.
[doctor] Thank you. Ms. Tesfay, based on your age and the nature of the lump, we suspect a possibility of intraductal carcinoma in situ. We will arrange for a mammogram and ultrasound today.
[patient] Cancer?
[doctor] It is a possibility, but not a diagnosis yet. Intraductal carcinoma in situ is often caught early and is very treatable.
[patient] I am worried.
[doctor] I understand. We will refer you to the breast clinic at the University Hospital for further evaluation. I will write a referral letter for Dr. Keller.
[patient] My daughter, Leila, is coming to see me later. She is 62. Can she be there when the results come out?
[doctor] Yes, that is a good idea. You should not be alone during this process.
[patient] Thank you.
[doctor] We will call you with the preliminary results in a few days. In the meantime, take acetaminophen for the pain if needed.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] Do you have any questions for me?
[patient] Just one. Is it because of the trip?
[doctor] Unlikely. Cancer is not caused by travel. It is related to genetics, age, and other factors.
[patient] I see.
[doctor] I will discharge you now with instructions to follow up with your doctor.
[patient] Thank you, Dr. Weber.

He reports slipping on a wet floor and striking his right lower leg against a metal shelving unit. The injury occurred yesterday. He denies loss of consciousness, head trauma, or other injuries. [doctor] Good morning. Please, have a seat. I see you are here for an occupational health assessment. My name is Dr. Rossi. Can you state your full name for the record?
[patient] Yes, good morning. My name is Lucas Andrade.
[doctor] Thank you, Lucas. And your date of birth?
[patient] I was born on 14 March 2001.
[doctor] So you are 23 years old. Correct?
[patient] Yes, that is correct.
[doctor] Where are you currently living?
[patient] I live in Verona.
[doctor] And where did you come from to move here?
[patient] I moved from São Paulo, Brazil. I have been in Italy for about two years now.
[doctor] I see. What is your current occupation?
[patient] I am a warehouse manager at <ORGANization>LogiTech Solutions.
[doctor] Understood. What seems to be the problem today?
[patient] I injured my right leg yesterday at work. I fell when a pallet slipped.
[doctor] Can you describe the mechanism of injury in more detail?
[patient] I was moving a heavy crate. The floor was slightly wet. I slipped, and my right shin hit the metal edge of the shelving unit.
[doctor] Did you lose consciousness at any point?
[patient] No, I was conscious the whole time. But it hurts a lot when I try to stand.
[doctor] On a scale of 0 to 10, with 10 being the worst pain imaginable, how would you rate the pain right now?
[patient] I would say it is an 8. It throbs constantly.
[doctor] Let us look at your medical history. Any known allergies?
[patient] No, I have no drug allergies.
[doctor] Any chronic conditions?
[patient] No, I am generally healthy.
[doctor] Do you take any regular medications?
[patient] No, nothing currently.
[doctor] Have you had any previous surgeries or injuries?
[patient] I had a minor appendectomy when I was young, but nothing related to my legs.
[doctor] Let us check your vital signs first. The nurse will take your blood pressure and heart rate.
[nurse] Mr. Andrade, please sit back. Your blood pressure is 118 over 76, and your heart rate is 82 beats per minute. Your temperature is 36.8 degrees Celsius.
[doctor] Thank you, Nurse. Those are stable. Now, let us examine the leg. Please lift your trouser leg.
[patient] It is very tender.
[doctor] I see significant swelling and bruising around the shin. I will palpate the area gently. Tell me if this is too painful.
[patient] Okay, go ahead.
[doctor] There is a distinct area of tenderness. I notice a localized hematoma. When I press here, at the 3 o'clock position relative to the knee joint, do you feel a sharp pain?
[patient] Yes, exactly there. That is the worst spot.
[doctor] Can you actively dorsiflex your foot? That means pulling your toes up toward your shin.
[patient] I can do it, but it is stiff.
[doctor] And plantar flexion? Pointing your toes down?
[patient] That is easier.
[doctor] Let us test your reflexes. I will tap your knee.
[patient] My leg kicked out.
[doctor] The reflex is normal. Now, we need to rule out a fracture. We will order an X-ray of your right tibia and fibula.
[patient] Do I need a CT scan too?
[doctor] Not at this stage. The X-ray is sufficient for initial assessment. If the X-ray is negative but the pain persists, we may consider further imaging.
[doctor] In the meantime, we will manage your pain. I am going to prescribe <DRUG>Brufen 400 mg</DRUG>.
[patient] Is that okay for me?
[doctor] Yes, <DRUG>Brufen</DRUG> is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug. Take one tablet every eight hours with food for three days.
[patient] What if the pain is still bad?
[doctor] If the pain is not controlled, you can take <DRUG>Paracetamol 1000 mg</DRUG> alongside it, provided you do not exceed the daily limit.
[patient] Are there any side effects?
[doctor] <DRUG>Brufen</DRUG> can sometimes cause stomach upset. Taking it with food helps. If you experience black stools or severe stomach pain, stop taking it and see a doctor.
[patient] Understood.
[doctor] I also recommend the RICE protocol. Rest, Ice, Compression, and Elevation.
[patient] I have some ice packs at home.
[doctor] Excellent. Apply ice for 20 minutes every two hours. Use a compression bandage to reduce swelling, but not too tight. Elevate your leg above the level of your heart when resting.
[patient] Will I be able to work tomorrow?
[doctor] Given the severity of the swelling and pain, I do not recommend heavy lifting or standing for prolonged periods. I will write a medical certificate for you.
[patient] How many days?
[doctor] I will give you a certificate for 3 days. After that, you should return for a follow-up if the pain has not improved significantly.
[patient] That works. I have a lot of paperwork to catch up on, so I hope to be back soon.
[doctor] Safety first. Do not push yourself. If you notice numbness, tingling, or if your foot turns cold or pale, go to the emergency room immediately.
[patient] I will keep an eye on that.
[doctor] Let us review the X-ray results. The radiologist has sent the report.
[patient] Did they see a break?
[doctor] The X-ray shows no fracture. It confirms a soft tissue injury, consistent with a contusion. There is no evidence of a bone break.
[patient] That is a relief.
[doctor] Yes. The diagnosis is a contusion of the right lower leg.
[patient] What else should I do?
[doctor] Continue with the medication and RICE. You can walk around the house if it is comfortable, but avoid long distances.
[patient] Can I use a crutch?
[doctor] You do not need crutches if you can bear weight, but if walking is very painful, using a crutch for a few days to offload the leg is acceptable.
[patient] I will try to manage without them first.
[doctor] Good. Let us discuss your return to work.
[patient] I need to make sure I am clear for my supervisor.
[doctor] I will note that you are fit for light duties only, if any, for the next 3 days. After that, you should be able to resume normal duties if the pain allows, but avoid heavy lifting for one week.
[patient] Heavy lifting is part of my job.
[doctor] Then you must be careful. Use mechanical aids like pallet jacks. Do not lift heavy crates by hand for at least 7 days.
[patient] I will speak to my manager about that.
[doctor] Do you have any questions about the medication or the injury?
[patient] No, I think I am clear.
[doctor] Is there anything else I can help you with?
[patient] No, thank you.
[doctor] You are welcome. The prescription is ready. Please pick it up at the pharmacy on the ground floor.
[patient] Thank you, Dr. Rossi.
[doctor] Take care, Lucas.

Patient is a 29-year-old woman, Giulia Rossi, presenting with right index finger pain and swelling. She reports an injury occurring yesterday while cooking at home in Milan. A pan handle struck the middle joint of the right index finger. She describes the pain as 7/10 at rest and 8/10 with movement. She was referred by Dr. Elena Conti from Ospedale San Raffaele for initial evaluation. Patient states she lives in Bergamo and works as a graphic designer. She denies other injuries. No history of anticoagulant use. No known drug allergies. Family history is notable for hypertension in her father and diabetes in her uncle Paolo.

OBJECTIVE
General: Alert, oriented, in no acute distress.
Vitals: BP 110/70 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, Temp 36.8°C, SpO2 99%.
Right hand exam:
- Inspection: Visible swelling and ecchymosis at the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint of the right index finger.
- Palpation: Tenderness over the PIP joint. No crepitus.
- Range of Motion: Active flexion and extension limited by pain. Passive motion reveals instability with a positive stress test, suggesting ligamentous injury.
- Neurovascular: Intact sensation in the median and ulnar nerve distributions. Capillary refill < 2 seconds. Palpable radial and ulnar pulses.

ASSESSMENT
1. Sprain of the proximal interphalangeal joint of the right index finger.
2. Rule out fracture (pending X-ray).

PLAN
1. X-ray of the right hand (PA and oblique views) to rule out fracture.
2. Buddy taping of the right index finger to the middle finger for support. Patient instructed to keep the tape dry (use plastic bag during showering).
3. Ice application 15-20 minutes every 3-4 hours for the first 48 hours.
4. Avoid heavy gripping or lifting for two weeks.
5. Pain management: Ibuprofen 400 mg every 6-8 hours as needed with food, or Paracetamol 1g every 8 hours.

note:
REFERRAL LETTER

TO: Dr. Weber
Kliniken Hainburg
Innsbruck

FROM: Dr. Hofmann
Endocrine Practice Vienna
Vienna

DATE: October 24, 2023

RE: Patient: Almberger
DOB: 15.03.1955
AGE: 68

Dear Dr. Weber,

I am writing to refer my patient, Mrs. Almberger, to your care for evaluation and management of medial epicondylitis, right elbow.

Mrs. Almberger is a 68-year-old female who presents with chronic pain in the right medial elbow, lasting for three months. She is an avid tennis player, participating weekly at the Tennis Club Kahlenberg in Vienna. She reports that the pain has progressively worsened, affecting her sleep and daily activities.

Medical History:
- Hashimoto’s thyroiditis (managed with levothyroxine)
- Family history: Sister with Parkinson's disease, Mother with Graves' disease and Crohn's disease.
- No known drug allergies.

Physical Examination:
- Tenderness over the right medial epicondyle.
- Pain on resisted wrist flexion and pronation.
- Range of motion: Full extension, slight pain on flexion.
- No significant swelling or erythema.

Current Management:
- I have advised activity modification and rest.
- Prescribed NSAIDs for two weeks.
- Recommended ice therapy.

Given the chronic nature of the pain and the impact on her quality of life, I would appreciate your evaluation for physical therapy and further management. Please keep me informed of your findings and treatment plan.

Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Sincerely,
Dr. Hofmann
Endocrinologist
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, Mrs. Almberger. Please, come in and have a seat. I see you’re here for your follow-up. How have you been since we last spoke?
[patient] Oh, good morning, Dr. Hofmann. Um, honestly? It’s been... well, it’s been difficult. The arm, you know? The right one. It’s still hurting.
[doctor] I’m sorry to hear that. Let’s look at the chart. You mentioned pain around the elbow. Can you point to the exact spot that bothers you the most?
[patient] Yes, right here. On the inside. Near the... what is it called again? The bone that sticks out?
[doctor] That’s the medial epicondyle. Yes. And how long has this specific level of pain been bothering you?
[patient] Oh, it’s been going on for three months. It started slowly, just a twinge, but now it’s constant. Even when I’m resting.
[doctor] I see. And what are you doing in your daily life that might be aggravating this? Do you have any specific hobbies or work activities?
[patient] Well, I don’t work anymore, thank God. But I play tennis. I go to the Tennis Club Kahlenberg every Tuesday and Thursday. I’ve been playing since I was young.
[doctor] Tennis involves a lot of gripping and wrist movement. That could certainly contribute to medial epicondylitis. Have you tried any treatments so far?
[patient] I tried some creams, you know, the ones from the pharmacy. And I iced it. But it’s not getting better. Actually, it’s getting worse.
[doctor] Let’s take a closer look. Can you extend your arm and turn your palm up? Hold that for a second.
[patient] Oh! Yes, that’s it. That’s the spot. It’s sharp.
[doctor] Okay, relax. Now, let’s check your range of motion. Bend your elbow back. Any pain?
[patient] Just a dull ache. Not as sharp as before.
[doctor] Understood. Now, let’s talk about your medical history to make sure this isn’t related to something else. Do you have any other chronic conditions?
[patient] Well, I have Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. I take my medication daily. And my sister has Parkinson's disease, which is why I’m a bit anxious about any tremors or pain.
[doctor] I see. Hashimoto’s is an autoimmune condition, but it typically doesn’t cause focal elbow pain. Parkinson’s is also usually neurological. This sounds like a mechanical issue.
[patient] Yes, that’s what I hoped. But my mother had Crohn's disease, and I worry about inflammation in general.
[doctor] That’s a fair concern, but Crohn’s is gastrointestinal. Let’s focus on the elbow. Have you noticed any swelling or redness?
[patient] No, no redness. Just a little bit of swelling, maybe. It feels tender to the touch.
[doctor] Let’s check your blood pressure and vitals while we talk. Nurse Steiner, can you come in for a moment?
[nurse] Of course, Dr. Hofmann.
[doctor] Thank you, Nurse Steiner. Mrs. Almberger, can you please roll up your left sleeve?
[patient] Sure. Oh, it’s cold in here.
[doctor] Just a moment. How are you sleeping? Is the pain waking you up?
[patient] Yes, actually. I wake up around 3 am because the arm aches. I have to change positions.
[doctor] That’s significant. Pain at night often indicates inflammation is persistent. What about your diet? Any changes recently?
[patient] No, I eat quite healthily. Lots of vegetables. I try to avoid gluten because of my sister’s condition, though I don’t have it myself.
[doctor] I see. Let’s look at your recent lab results. Your thyroid levels are stable, which is good. But I want to check for any general inflammatory markers.
[patient] Do I need a blood test?
[doctor] Just a simple one. It will help us rule out any systemic inflammation. Also, I want to refer you to a specialist for a physical therapy program.
[patient] A specialist? Here in Vienna?
[doctor] Yes. I’m going to refer you to Dr. Weber at the Kliniken Hainburg. He is an orthopedic specialist who deals with sports injuries.
[patient] That sounds good. But I live in Innsbruck. I moved here from Salzburg ten years ago.
[doctor] I see. And you’re currently residing in Vienna?
[patient] No, I live in Innsbruck. I travel to Vienna for my endocrinology appointments because my endocrinologist is here.
[doctor] I apologize for the confusion. So you live in Innsbruck, but your primary care is in Vienna?
[patient] Yes, exactly. I’m 68 years old, so I’m trying to manage travel as best I can.
[doctor] Understood. I will write a referral letter to Dr. Weber in Innsbruck so you don’t have to travel to Vienna for the orthopedic care.
[patient] That would be wonderful. Thank you.
[doctor] You’re welcome. Let’s also discuss your thyroid medication. Are you taking it at the same time every day?
[patient] Yes, usually in the morning. Sometimes I forget, but I try to be consistent.
[doctor] Consistency is key. Did you have any issues with absorption?
[patient] No, I take it on an empty stomach, as instructed.
[doctor] Good. Now, let’s talk about your family history again. You mentioned your sister has Parkinson's. Does anyone else in your family have autoimmune conditions?
[patient] My mother had Graves' disease, actually. Not Hashimoto’s. I was confused.
[doctor] Ah, I see. Graves' disease is also autoimmune. That makes sense. Let’s correct your chart.
[patient] Thank you. It’s important to have the right history.
[doctor] Absolutely. Now, let’s plan your next steps. You will see Dr. Weber for a physical therapy evaluation. In the meantime, I want you to rest the elbow.
[patient] Rest? But I want to play tennis.
[doctor] I understand. But you need to let the inflammation subside. I’ll prescribe some anti-inflammatory medication for two weeks.
[patient] Okay. And I can ice it?
[doctor] Yes, ice it for 15 minutes at a time, several times a day. And avoid gripping heavy objects.
[patient] I’ll try. It’s hard, though. I carry my grocery bags with that hand.
[doctor] Try to use both hands or a cart. It’s important to give it time to heal.
[patient] I’ll do my best.
[doctor] Also, let’s schedule a follow-up with me in six weeks. We can check your progress then.
[patient] Six weeks? That’s a long time.
[doctor] It’s standard for this type of injury. We want to see if the physical therapy is working.
[patient] Okay. I’ll book the appointment.
[doctor] Nurse Steiner, can you schedule the follow-up?
[nurse] Yes, Doctor. I’ll call her office to set it up.
[patient] Thank you, Nurse Steiner.
[nurse] You’re welcome.
[doctor] Is there anything else you’d like to discuss today?
[patient] Just... I’m worried it’s something serious. Like a tumor or something.
[doctor] I understand your anxiety. But based on the history and exam, this is classic medial epicondylitis. It’s common in tennis players. We will monitor it, but it’s unlikely to be anything sinister.
[patient] That’s a relief. Thank you for reassuring me.
[doctor] You’re welcome. We’ll keep an eye on it. Remember, if the pain worsens or you develop fever or significant swelling, come in sooner.
[patient] I will. Thank you, Dr. Hofmann.
[doctor] Take care, Mrs. Almberger.
