[doctor] Ah, yes. Unilateral renal hypoplasia. That means one kidney is smaller than normal. Do you have any documentation from that visit?
[patient] I think so. It was a CT scan. I live in 12 Rue des Lilas, 1004 Lausanne, so I went to the Hôpital de la Tour.
[doctor] That’s close enough. Now, what brings you in today specifically? Is the pain worse?
[patient] Well, I was at the gym yesterday. I was doing squats, and I felt a sharp pull. Then I went home, and I took some ibuprofen... wait, no, I took Nurofen. And this morning, I noticed my urine was... darker?

[patient] I take Nurofen sometimes for headaches. Is that bad?
[doctor] NSAIDs like Nurofen can reduce blood flow to the kidneys. In someone with one smaller kidney, we need to be careful. I recommend avoiding them. Use paracetamol instead.
[patient] Okay. So, what is the plan?

[patient] Okay. No Nurofen. Just water and paracetamol.

note:
REFERRAL LETTER

14 May 2024

Zurich University Hospital
Department of Gastroenterology
8706 Zurich

To:
Dr. Anja Weber
General Practice
8001 Zurich

Dear Dr. Weber,

Thank you for referring Chithra Perera, a 39-year-old woman, to our clinic for evaluation of left arm pain.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Ms. Perera presents with a three-week history of dull pain in her left upper arm, radiating to the elbow. The onset was precipitated by reaching for a heavy object in the kitchen. She reports that the pain is aggravated by movement and sleep. She has tried ice packs with minimal relief. She denies chest pain, shortness of breath, or jaw pain. She reports recent fatigue and mild mood changes.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
The patient has a history of Hashimoto's disease, currently managed with levothyroxine. She denies a history of Crohn's disease, though she mentions occasional gastrointestinal discomfort. There is a family history of Parkinson's disease in her sister.

EXAMINATION
Vital signs were within normal limits. On physical examination of the left shoulder, there is tenderness over the lateral aspect. A palpable, non-tender bulge was noted at the 3 o'clock position of the shoulder joint. The drop arm test was positive, suggesting possible rotator cuff involvement or bursitis. No signs of neurological deficit were observed. The examination of the abdomen was unremarkable.

ASSESSMENT
The clinical picture is most consistent with a musculoskeletal injury, likely rotator cuff tendinopathy or subacromial bursitis, secondary to an acute strain. Given the patient's history of Hashimoto's disease and reported fatigue, it is important to monitor thyroid function and rule out other autoimmune manifestations, although the unilateral nature of the pain makes a systemic autoimmune flare less likely as the primary cause. The mention of Parkinson's disease in the family history was noted, but the clinical presentation does not support this diagnosis.

PLAN
1. Ultrasound and X-ray of the left shoulder have been ordered to evaluate the soft tissue structure at the 3 o'clock position and rule out bone pathology.
2. The patient has been prescribed a short course of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for pain management.
3. Referral to Physio Center Limmat for physiotherapy and rehabilitation exercises has been made.
4. We recommend that you check the patient's thyroid function tests (TSH, Free T4) given her recent complaints of fatigue and mood changes.
5. If the pain persists beyond two weeks or if there is any significant swelling or warmth, the patient should return for further evaluation, possibly including an MRI.

Please feel free to contact our office if you have any questions or require further information. We will send the imaging results to your office and a copy to the patient's email address: chithra.perera85 at gmx.ch.

Sincerely,

Dr. Sarah Miller
Consultant Gastroenterologist
Zurich University Hospital

[doctor] Good morning. My name is Dr. [NAME]. I see you are here today for a follow-up regarding your right leg. Can you tell me what brings you in specifically today?

[patient] It started about three months ago. I was walking to the [LOCATION] station every day, and I noticed a twinge in the back of my heel.
[doctor] Did it get worse gradually or suddenly?
[patient] Gradually, Doctor. At first, it was only in the morning. But now, it hurts all day. Especially when I climb stairs.
[doctor] On a scale of zero to ten, with zero being no pain and ten being the worst pain imaginable, how would you rate it today?
[patient] Today, it is probably a seven. It is quite sharp when I stand up on my toes.
[doctor] Have you been doing any specific activities recently that might have aggravated it?
[patient] Yes. I went to [LOCATION] for a conference last month. I walked a lot there. The streets are cobblestone, which is not good for my knees or my heel.
[doctor] I see. And have you tried any treatments since our last visit in March 2023?
[patient] Yes. I am taking [DRUG] cream twice a day. I also did some stretching exercises that the physiotherapist showed me.
[doctor] Did those help at all?
[patient] A little bit, but not enough. The swelling is still there. I have an X-ray result from May 12, 2024 that you might have in my file.
[doctor] I do. Let me pull that up. Ah, here we are. The X-ray shows some calcification near the tendon, which is consistent with chronic tendinitis. We do not see any fractures.
[patient] Thank you. My brother, [NAME], has the same problem. He is also eighty-six. He says it is a matter of age.
[doctor] It is certainly associated with age, but it is also related to activity levels. You mentioned you are very active. What do you do for work?
[patient] I am retired, but I was a  for [ORGANIZATION] for forty years. I am still active. I play tennis on Thursdays at the [ORGANIZATION] club.
[doctor] Tennis involves a lot of sudden stops and jumps. That can be hard on the Achilles tendon. How often do you play?
[patient] Once a week. But I am thinking of stopping. It is painful during the match.
[doctor] That is a wise consideration. Let’s examine the leg. Please lift your right foot. Good. I am going to press on the tendon here.
[patient] That is the spot.

[doctor] Good morning. I see you are here for a pre-operative assessment. Can you confirm your full name and date of birth?

[patient] Uh, actually, I didn't notice anything really. I was at the gym, you know, doing my usual routine, and I pulled a muscle in my shoulder. So I went to the ER, and they did a CT scan to rule out anything internal. That’s when they saw the liver was enlarged.
[doctor] And when was that injury at the gym?
[patient] That was, um, two weeks ago. Yeah, exactly two weeks ago.
[doctor] Okay. Since then, have you had any abdominal pain, nausea, or changes in your appetite?
[patient] No, not really. Maybe a little fullness in the upper right side, but it’s like, you know, very mild. I eat normal food. I don't drink alcohol, and I don't smoke.
[doctor] That is good. Let’s look at your family history. Does your mother, Sofia, have any liver problems?
[patient] My mother is 45. No, she doesn't have liver issues. But my brother, Pablo, who is 22, had a minor appendectomy when he was younger.
[doctor] And your father?

[doctor] Understood. Do you have any allergies to medications or foods?
[patient] No, no allergies. I take no regular medications. Maybe some ibuprofen for the shoulder pain, but that was a few days ago.
[doctor] Have you had any previous surgeries or hospitalizations?
[patient] No, just the one for the shoulder check-up, but they didn't operate. Just imaging.
[doctor] Okay. I need to perform a physical examination. Please lie down on the table. I will palpate your abdomen. This might be slightly uncomfortable.

[doctor] I am feeling your liver edge. It is palpable about 3 centimeters below the costal margin. It feels smooth and firm. Do you feel any pain when I press here?

[doctor] Thank you. Your heart and lung sounds are normal. Now, I need to order some blood work to check your liver function and rule out viral causes. I will also need an ultrasound to get a better view of the liver structure.

note:
SUBJECTIVE
36-year-old female, Ellison, presents with bilateral hand numbness and tingling, predominantly affecting the thumb, index, and middle fingers. Symptoms are worse at night and upon waking, lasting approximately 20 minutes. She reports shaking her hands provides temporary relief. She is a data analyst at Vertex Dynamics and spends significant time typing and using a mouse. She has been using a wrist splint at night with partial relief. Patient has a history of Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, managed with Levothyroxine, and a past history of Graves’ disease (resolved). She also has a history of a Baker’s cyst. Denies weakness or dropping objects. No history of Parkinson’s disease or Bell’s palsy.

OBJECTIVE
Vitals: BP 118/76, HR 72, RR 14, Temp 98.6 F.
General: Well-appearing, no acute distress.
Hands:
- Inspection: Mild thenar eminence wasting bilaterally, more pronounced on the left.
- Sensation: Diminished light touch in the median nerve distribution (thumb, index, middle, radial half of ring finger) bilaterally.
- Phalen’s test: Positive bilaterally, reproducing tingling in the median nerve distribution after 30 seconds.
- Tinel’s sign: Positive bilaterally, eliciting paresthesia upon tapping the carpal tunnel.
- Strength: Grip strength 4/5 bilaterally. Opposition of the thumb is intact but slightly slower on the left.
- No swelling or erythema of the wrists.

ASSESSMENT
1. Bilateral Carpal Tunnel Syndrome, moderate severity.
2. History of Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, stable.
3. History of Graves’ disease, resolved.
4. Baker’s cyst, right knee, stable.

PLAN
1. Order bilateral wrist ultrasound to assess for median nerve swelling and carpal tunnel dimensions.
2. Continue nocturnal wrist splinting.
3. Ergonomic evaluation at work: ensure keyboard and mouse are at elbow height; take 5-minute breaks every 30 minutes for wrist stretches.
4. If symptoms persist or worsen, consider corticosteroid injection.
5. Follow up in clinic on next Tuesday to review ultrasound results.
6. Patient instructed to call clinic at 503-555-0198 if she develops constant numbness, significant weakness, or difficulty gripping objects.
dialogue:
[doctor] good morning , ms . ellison . i’m dr . thorne , your oncologist . please , have a seat . i see you’re here for a follow-up regarding your hands .
[patient] yes , dr . thorne . hi . it’s getting really bad lately .
[doctor] thank you for coming in . i know we’ve been focusing on your cancer treatment , but it’s important to address quality of life issues . can you tell me more about what’s happening with your hands ?
[patient] it started a few months ago , maybe around last month . i started waking up with my fingers numb , especially the thumb and index finger . it feels like i slept on them , but it doesn't go away quickly .
[doctor] how long does the numbness last in the morning ?
[patient] usually about twenty minutes . if i shake my hands , it helps a bit . but during the day , it’s mostly just tingling .
[doctor] do you shake your hands at work ? i see you are employed by vertex dynamics .
[patient] yes , i do . i’m a data analyst . i spend most of the day typing on a keyboard and using a mouse .
[doctor] that makes sense . prolonged repetitive motions can exacerbate this condition . do you have any pain in your hands or wrists ?
[patient] not really sharp pain , just an ache in the palm . sometimes it radiates up the forearm , but only when i’m gripping things tightly .
[doctor] and is it both hands ?
[patient] yes , both . the left one is a bit worse because i’m left-handed .
[doctor] okay . i’ve reviewed your medical history . i note you have a history of hashimoto’s thyroiditis . have you had any recent changes in your thyroid levels ?
[patient] my endocrinologist , dr . miller , checked them a few weeks ago . they were stable . i’m still on levothyroxine .
[doctor] good . thyroid issues can sometimes mimic or worsen nerve compression symptoms . did he mention anything else ?
[patient] no , just to keep taking the medication . i also had a scare last year with a diagnosis of graves’ disease , but it turned out to be just a nodule .
[doctor] i see . and you mentioned you’ve been using a wrist brace ?
[patient] yes , my primary care physician recommended it . i wear it at night . it helps a little , but i still wake up numb .
[doctor] let’s examine your hands . i’m going to check your sensation . can you hold out your hands , palms up ?
[patient] sure .
[doctor] i’m going to tap here . do you feel that ?
[patient] yes .
[doctor] and here ?
[patient] a bit weaker .
[doctor] okay . now , i’m going to press on the inside of your wrist . this is called phalen’s test . please flex your wrists down like this and hold for 30 seconds .
[patient] oh , that’s uncomfortable .
[doctor] do you feel any tingling or numbness ?
[patient] yes , starting in my thumb and middle finger .
[doctor] okay , relax . now , i’m going to perform tinel’s sign . i’ll tap gently over the carpal tunnel .
[patient] that tickles .
[doctor] do you feel any electric shocks or tingling in the fingers ?
[patient] yes , a little .
[doctor] alright . i also want to check your strength . squeeze my hand .
[patient] like this ?
[doctor] yes . good . now spread your fingers wide .
[patient] there .
[doctor] i notice some mild wasting in the thenar eminence , the muscle at the base of your thumb . this can happen with chronic compression .
[patient] does that mean it’s permanent damage ?
[doctor] not necessarily . if we treat it early , it’s often reversible . given your history of cancer and the fact that this is affecting your ability to work and sleep , i recommend we proceed with an ultrasound of your wrists to confirm the diagnosis and see the degree of swelling .
[patient] will i need surgery ?
[doctor] surgery is a last resort . we usually try conservative management first . this includes wearing a splint at night , avoiding repetitive motions , and possibly corticosteroid injections if the symptoms persist .
[patient] i’ve heard about bell’s palsy . is that related ?
[doctor] no , bell’s palsy affects the facial nerve . this is the median nerve in your wrist . they are completely different conditions .
[patient] okay . i also have a baker’s cyst in my knee , so i’m a bit worried about injections .
[doctor] i understand . the injection for carpal tunnel is local and very safe . we can discuss the risks and benefits in detail .
[patient] i live in portland , so the weather is always damp . does that affect it ?
[doctor] damp weather doesn’t cause carpal tunnel , but some people find it uncomfortable . it’s more about the mechanics of the wrist .
[patient] i see . so , what are the next steps ?
[doctor] i’m going to order the ultrasound . the tech will call you to schedule it . in the meantime , keep wearing the splint at night . try to take breaks every 30 minutes at work to stretch your wrists .
[patient] i’ll do that . i use a standing desk , so i can switch positions .
[doctor] that’s a great idea . also , make sure your keyboard and mouse are at elbow height .
[patient] i’ll check that . do i need to see a neurologist ?
[doctor] not yet . if the ultrasound confirms significant swelling , or if you develop weakness in your grip , we might refer you to a hand surgeon . but for now , let’s monitor it .
[patient] what if it gets worse ?
[doctor] if you experience constant numbness , or if you drop things frequently , call our office . you can reach us at 503-555-0198 .
[patient] got it . thank you , dr . thorne .
[doctor] you’re welcome , ms . ellison . we’ll review the ultrasound results at your next appointment , which is scheduled for next tuesday .
[patient] okay . thanks .

note:
SUBJECTIVE
Patient is a 24-year-old male, Rafael Santos, presenting with acute lower back pain of 3 days duration. Pain is described as sharp and localized to the lumbar region. Onset occurred after a basketball game at Palestra Aurora in Milan where he landed awkwardly. He reports a "pop" sensation at onset. No radiation to legs, no numbness or tingling. He is a mechanical engineering student from Brazil living in Italy. He recently traveled to Lisbon prior to the injury. Family history is notable for chronic back pain in his mother and knee injuries in his brother, Diego. He is a non-smoker and social drinker. No current regular medications, no allergies. He works part-time as a barista. He has private insurance with Sanità Nuova, policy number SN-998877-2024. Contact details: +39 333 123 4567, rafael.santos@example.com.

OBJECTIVE
Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination reveals tenderness to palpation in the lumbar paraspinal muscles, specifically at the 3 o'clock position relative to the spinous processes. Range of motion is limited in flexion and lateral bending due to pain and guarding. Extension is less painful. Straight leg raise test is negative bilaterally, with no radiation of pain. Neurological examination shows normal strength, sensation, and reflexes in the lower extremities. No midline spinal tenderness.

ASSESSMENT
Acute lumbar sprain (lumbar ligament sprain). No signs of radiculopathy or cauda equina syndrome.

PLAN
1. Rest and activity modification: Avoid heavy lifting, twisting, and prolonged sitting. Stand and walk gently as tolerated.
2. Medication: Ibuprofen 400 mg orally three times daily for 5 days with food.
3. Cryotherapy: Apply ice packs to the lumbar region for 20 minutes every 3-4 hours for the next 48 hours.
4. Heat therapy: May use heat after 48 hours for muscle relaxation.
5. Follow-up: Return to clinic on May 20, 2024 at 10:00 for reassessment.
6. Return precautions: Go to emergency department if symptoms of cauda equina syndrome develop (bladder/bowel incontinence, saddle anesthesia) or if significant leg weakness or numbness occurs.
7. Work: Advise patient to discuss time off or modified duties with employer to avoid aggravating the injury.

[doctor] Good morning, I am Dr. Rossi. I am here for your home visit as requested. How are you feeling right now?
[patient] Good morning, Dr. Rossi. I am Rafael. I am twenty-four years old. I am in a lot of pain.

[patient] It is right here, in my lower back. It started three days ago.
[doctor] Can you describe the pain? Is it sharp, dull, or burning?
[patient] It feels like a sharp stabbing pain, especially when I try to move my torso.
[doctor] What were you doing when it started?
[patient] I was playing basketball at Palestra Aurora in Milan. I made a bad landing and twisted my waist.
[doctor] I see. Did you hear a pop or feel a sudden give at the time?
[patient] Yes, there was a slight pop, and then the pain came on immediately. I had to sit down.
[doctor] Has the pain radiated anywhere else, like down your legs?
[patient] No, it stays right here in the lower back. It does not go into my legs.
[doctor] Do you have any numbness or tingling in your feet or hands?
[patient] No, no numbness. I can feel my feet perfectly.
[doctor] Can you walk? How is your mobility today?
[patient] I can walk, but it is very difficult. I have to bend forward. My neighbor, Luca, helped me get to the bathroom this morning.
[doctor] That is good to know. Let me check your details for the record. What is your full name?
[patient] Rafael Santos.
[doctor] And your date of birth?
[patient] May 14, 2000.
[doctor] Thank you. What is your phone number in case we need to contact you?
[patient] It is +39 333 123 4567.
[doctor] And an email address?
[patient] Sure, it is rafael.santos@example.com.
[doctor] You mentioned you are living here in Italy. Where are you from originally?
[patient] I am from Brazil. I moved here to study mechanical engineering at the university.
[doctor] That is a long distance. Did you travel recently before this injury?
[patient] Yes, I went to Lisbon for a short trip last month. But the injury happened after I came back.
[doctor] I understand. Now, let us discuss your insurance. Do you have private insurance or are you with the national system?
[patient] I have private coverage through Sanità Nuova.
[doctor] Can you give me your insurance policy number?
[patient] Yes, my number is SN-998877-2024.
[doctor] Thank you. Let us look at your medical history. Do you have any previous injuries to your back or neck?
[patient] No, this is the first time. I am usually quite fit.
[doctor] What about your family history? Does anyone in your family have back problems?
[patient] My mother has had chronic back pain for years, but I think it was due to age. My brother, Diego, plays football and has had knee injuries, but his back is fine.
[doctor] I see. Any history of herniated discs or scoliosis in the family?
[patient] No, not that I know of.
[doctor] Do you smoke or drink alcohol?
[patient] I do not smoke. I drink beer occasionally with friends, maybe once a week.
[doctor] What medications are you currently taking?
[patient] None regularly. I only took some paracetamol yesterday.
[doctor] Do you have any allergies to medications?
[patient] No, no known allergies.
[doctor] Alright, I am going to examine your back now. Please lift your shirt up slightly.
[patient] Okay, here you go.
[doctor] Thank you. I am going to press gently on different parts of your spine. Tell me if you feel pain.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] How is this? Right here?
[patient] That is a bit sore.
[doctor] And here?
[patient] Yes, that is the worst spot. It hurts a lot.
[doctor] I am noting tenderness at the 3 o'clock position relative to your spinous process. Let me check your range of motion. Try to bend forward.
[patient] *groans* Ouch. It is hard to bend.
[doctor] I see. You are guarding your movement. Now, try to bend backward.
[patient] That is actually a bit easier, but still stiff.
[doctor] And bend to the left?
[patient] Painful.
[doctor] And to the right?
[patient] Also painful, maybe a little less than the left.
[doctor] Let me check your legs. Please lie down on your back.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] I am going to lift your leg. This is to check for nerve tension. Tell me if you feel pain shooting down your leg.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] I am lifting the left leg.
[patient] No pain in the leg. Just some tightness in the back.
[doctor] Now the right leg.
[patient] Same thing. No shooting pain.
[doctor] Good. This suggests the problem is local to the muscles and ligaments, not the nerves. Let me check your reflexes.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] Your reflexes are normal. Your strength in your legs is also normal.
[patient] That is good to hear.
[doctor] Based on your history and this exam, it looks like a sprain of the lumbar ligaments.
[patient] Is it serious? Will I be able to go back to basketball?
[doctor] It is not life-threatening, but it needs care. You should rest for a few days. I am going to prescribe some anti-inflammatory medication.
[patient] What kind?
[doctor] I will prescribe Ibuprofen 400 mg. Take it with food, three times a day for five days.
[patient] Okay. Do I need to go to the hospital?
[doctor] No, not unless the pain gets much worse or you lose control of your bladder or bowels.
[patient] What if I get numbness?
[doctor] If you get numbness or weakness in your legs, go to the emergency room immediately.
[patient] I will be careful. Can I use heat or ice?
[doctor] Use ice for the first 48 hours to reduce swelling. After that, heat might help relax the muscles.
[patient] Okay. Ice first, then heat.
[doctor] Yes. Also, try to avoid sitting for long periods. Stand up and walk around gently.
[patient] I have to study for exams, so I sit a lot.
[doctor] Take breaks every 30 minutes. Do some gentle stretching if it does not hurt.
[patient] What about my job? I work part-time as a barista at a café.
[doctor] You should avoid lifting heavy things or twisting your body. Can you take a break from work for a few days?
[patient] I will try to arrange it with my manager.
[doctor] Yes, that is important. When do you want to come back for a follow-up?
[patient] In one week?
[doctor] Yes, let us schedule a follow-up for May 20, 2024 at 10:00.
[patient] Okay. Do I need to call to book it?
[doctor] No, I will send you an email confirmation to rafael.santos@example.com.
[patient] Thank you, Dr. Rossi.
[doctor] You are welcome, Rafael. Rest well. If you have any questions, you can call the clinic at +39 02 555 1234.
[patient] Thanks. I feel a bit better knowing it is just a sprain.
[doctor] Take care.

PATIENT NAME: Eleanor Smith
DATE OF BIRTH: 12 March 1992
RECORD NUMBER: 994821-M
ADDRESS: 14 Oakwood Avenue, M14 5PL, Manchester

CLINICAL SUMMARY
The patient, a 32-year-old female, was seen for a home visit following a referral from Dr. Alistair Grant at St. Mary’s Hospital. The primary diagnosis is bilateral exudative age-related macular degeneration (wet AMD) with active choroidal neovascularization, predominantly in the left eye.

HISTORY
The patient reports progressive blurring of central vision and metamorphopsia over the past few months. She uses an Amsler grid daily and reports a central scotoma. She works as a graphic designer and spends significant time in front of screens. She has a history of quitting smoking three years ago. She has no history of hypertension or diabetes.

FAMILY HISTORY
The patient’s mother, Margaret, has dry AMD. Her brother, James (35), has Crohn’s disease. An aunt has Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.

EXAMINATION
Visual acuity: Right eye 6/12, Left eye 6/18.
Slit-lamp examination: Anterior segment unremarkable.
Fundoscopy: Bilateral drusen. Left eye shows subretinal fluid and pigment epithelial detachment consistent with active choroidal neovascularization. Right eye shows early signs of exudation.
Amsler grid: Positive in both eyes, worse in the left.

ASSESSMENT
Bilateral exudative AMD with active CNV in the left eye.
Risk factors include family history and previous smoking.
The patient is young for this diagnosis, requiring aggressive management to preserve vision.

PLAN
1. Referral for anti-VEGF injections with Dr. Alistair Grant at St. Mary’s Hospital.
   - Next appointment: 15 October 2023 at 09:30.
   - Treatment: Eylea injections.
2. Follow-up with GP on 18 October 2023 at 14:00 to review post-injection status and vision progress.
3. Continue current medication: Atorvastatin 20mg daily.
4. Lifestyle advice: Continue non-smoking status, maintain healthy diet rich in leafy greens.
5. Patient advised to use Amsler grid daily and to contact GP or ophthalmology team immediately if there is any sudden change in vision.
6. No immediate change to general health medications.

DOCTOR SIGNATURE: Dr. Alistair Thorne
DATE: 29 September 2023
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, Eleanor. Thank you for having me. I’ve been waiting to speak with you after the ophthalmology report from St. Mary’s Hospital came through.
[patient] Oh, hello Dr. Thorne. Yes, please, sit down. I’m so sorry, I’ve been such a mess since the appointment.
[doctor] I understand. It’s a lot to take in. Can you tell me what the specialist, Dr. Alistair Grant at St. Mary’s, told you?
[patient] Well, uh... he said I have this, um, wet AMD. Age-related macular degeneration, but the wet kind. He said there’s new blood vessels growing underneath the retina.
[doctor] Yes, that is what we call exudative age-related macular degeneration. It sounds scary, but it is treatable. Did he mention if it was in both eyes?
[patient] Yes, both. He said it was active in the left eye, but there are signs it’s starting in the right one too. I was so worried because my mother, Margaret, has terrible eyesight.
[doctor] I see. Does your mother have a specific diagnosis?
[patient] She has dry AMD, mostly. But my brother, James, who is 35, has Crohn’s disease, and my aunt has Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. So I guess it’s all genetic or something?
[doctor] Family history is a factor, but it doesn’t mean you will definitely get the same conditions. However, given your young age, 32, we need to be proactive. You are quite young for this, which is why I’m here to coordinate care.
[patient] I know, right? I just... I work as a graphic designer from home, so I stare at screens all day. I’m at PixelPerfect Studio in Manchester.
[doctor] Screen time is a risk factor, but it’s not the only one. You mentioned you’re in Manchester? Let me check your address. I see you live at 14 Oakwood Avenue, M14 5PL, Manchester.
[patient] That’s right. It’s a bit of a trek to get to St. Mary’s for the injections.
[doctor] That’s why I’m managing the referrals. You need anti-VEGF injections. Did they give you a brand name?
[patient] Yes, Eylea. The nurse gave me the leaflet, but I haven’t read it yet.
[doctor] Good. Eylea is a standard treatment. It works by stopping those new blood vessels from growing and leaking fluid.
[patient] Will it hurt?
[doctor] It’s a needle, so there’s a sting, but it’s quick. The main goal is to preserve your central vision. You know, I had a patient recently, a Mr. Graves, who had Graves’ disease and also had vision issues from thyroid eye disease. He did very well with early intervention.
[patient] Graves? That’s a common name. I have a friend, Graves, who is a dentist.
[doctor] Yes, coincidences happen. Anyway, back to you. How has your vision been day-to-day?
[patient] It’s fuzzy. Like, if I look at a straight line, it looks wavy. I use an Amsler grid, the one you gave me.
[doctor] That’s a good tool. Do you see any scotomas? Dark spots?
[patient] Sometimes. Like, a gray patch in the middle. It’s frustrating because I love painting. I go to The Waterhouse Gallery in Leeds to study art.
[doctor] Leeds is a nice city. Do you travel there often?
[patient] Yes, I went there last May for a workshop. It’s about two hours from Manchester.

[patient] Yes, that is my birthday. I was born in Ohio.

[patient] Yes, I moved here in 1980. I missed the cold winters up north.
[doctor] I understand. Now, back to the elbow. The emergency room doctor said the fracture is stable. I want to keep you out of the sling for a few days, then start some gentle range-of-motion exercises.

[patient] Okay. I’ll try to drink more water.
[doctor] Good. Do you have any questions for me today?
[patient] No, I think I’m clear. Thank you for checking on my elbow.
[doctor] You’re welcome. I’ll see you in three months for a follow-up.
[patient] Okay. See you then.
[doctor] Bye, Marjorie.

[patient] It’s mostly constant. I used to love my job as a librarian at the City Library of Cologne, but now I just can’t face it. I’ve been working there for twenty years.
[doctor] That must be difficult to step back from. Have you discussed this with your colleagues?
[patient] Well, my neighbor, Ulrich, he works there too. He tried to help, but I didn’t have the heart to tell him I was struggling so badly. He’s a sweet man, though.
[doctor] And how is your sleep? Are you sleeping too much, or too little?
[patient] Too much, I think. I sleep all day, um, and then at night I’m wide awake. I stare at the ceiling. My daughter, Klara, who is forty-five, lives in Freiburg. She called me last Tuesday to check in.
[doctor] Did she notice anything specific when she spoke to you?
[patient] She said I sounded... flat. Like I wasn’t really there. She’s very observant. She’s forty-five now, just like me? No, wait, she’s younger. She’s thirty-eight.
[doctor] Thank you for correcting me. Does this affect your daily activities? Like cooking or cleaning?
[patient] Oh, yes. Last week, I was in the kitchen, and I dropped a plate. It shattered everywhere. I just stood there and cried. I couldn’t pick up the pieces. It felt like such a small thing, but I couldn’t do it.
[doctor] That sounds incredibly frustrating. Are you experiencing any other symptoms? Like changes in appetite or interest in things you used to enjoy?
[patient] I don’t have an appetite. I barely eat. And I used to love gardening, but now I just look at the dead plants and feel... nothing. Just empty.
[doctor] Have you been taking any new medications? Or changed your dosage of anything?
[patient] I’m still on my Atorvastatin for my cholesterol. And I started taking some herbal tea for sleep, but it didn’t help.
[doctor] I see. Let’s do a quick review of your systems. Any headaches?
[patient] No, no headaches. Just this heaviness in the chest. Like a stone is sitting on it.
[doctor] Any changes in weight?
[patient] I think I’ve lost a little. Maybe two kilograms in the last month.
[doctor] Okay. I’m going to document this as an unspecified mood disorder for now. I think it would be beneficial to see a specialist who can focus solely on your mental health. Would you be open to a referral?
[patient] Yes, please. I don’t want to be a burden to Klara. She’s my only family here. My mother, who passed away ten years ago, had depression too. It runs in the family.
[doctor] I understand. I will write a referral for Dr. Weber at the Psychiatric Clinic of Munich. He is very experienced with older adults.
[patient] That sounds good. When would I need to go?
[doctor] I will schedule an appointment for you. How does next Thursday look?
[patient] Next Thursday is fine.
[doctor] Excellent. I will set it for 10:30 AM. Here is the information. Make sure to bring your medication list.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor. I just hope this helps. I feel so... stuck.
[doctor] You are taking the right steps. We will monitor this closely. Do you have any questions for me before we wrap up?
[patient] No, I think I’m clear. Just... um... is there anything I should do in the meantime?
[doctor] Try to stick to a routine, even if it’s small. Walk outside for ten minutes. Eat regular meals. And please call me if things get worse.
[patient] Okay. Thank you.
[doctor] You’re welcome, Frau Hoffmann. I will see you at the follow-up.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Slipping, tripping, and stumbling without falling for two months.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Elena Rossi, a 46-year-old woman from Bergamo, presents to the neurology clinic for evaluation of gait instability. She reports a progressive onset of tripping and stumbling over the past two months. The patient describes the sensation as her feet getting "stuck" or heavy, particularly the left foot, which causes her to drag it. She denies actual falls, loss of consciousness, or head trauma. She notes no tremors, rigidity, or bradykinesia. She mentions a recent flu in January. She is currently managed for Hashimoto's thyroiditis with Levothyroxine. She denies any family history of neurodegenerative diseases, although her mother, Giulia (74), has Parkinson's disease, and her brother, Marco (42), has Crohn's disease.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever, chills, or significant weight loss.
Neurological: Gait instability, tripping. Denies diplopia, dysarthria, or syncope.
Eyes: No vision changes reported by patient, but noted on exam.
Respiratory: Non-contributory.
Cardiovascular: Non-contributory.
Gastrointestinal: No abdominal pain or change in bowel habits.
Musculoskeletal: No joint pain or swelling.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 120/80 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, Temp 36.8°C.
General: Well-appearing, no acute distress.
Neurological:
- Mental Status: Alert, oriented x3, coherent speech.
- Cranial Nerves: CN II-XII intact, except for CN VI.
- Oculomotor: Slight abduction deficit noted at the 3 o’clock position (right eye).
- Motor: 5/5 strength in all extremities. No pronator drift.
- Sensory: Intact to light touch and pinprick.
- Reflexes: 2+ and symmetric in biceps, triceps, patellar, and Achilles. Plantar responses downgoing bilaterally.
- Coordination: Mild dysmetria on heel-to-shin test bilaterally.
- Gait: Steppage-like gait with mild foot drop on the left side. Requires slight assistance to maintain balance on tandem walk.

RESULTS
Pending: MRI Brain and Cervical Spine (referred to Ospedale Papa Giovanni XXIII).
Pending: Blood panel including TSH, Free T4, ESR, CRP, ANA, and B12 levels.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Gait instability of unknown etiology.
   - Differential includes early neurodegenerative disorder (less likely given age and lack of other signs), inner ear pathology, or structural lesion.
   - The finding of oculomotor deviation at the 3 o’clock position warrants further imaging to rule out posterior fossa pathology.
   - Family history of Parkinson's disease in mother is noted but does not confirm diagnosis.
   - Patient has Hashimoto's thyroiditis; ensure thyroid levels are stable to rule out hypothyroid myopathy.
2. Plan:
   - MRI Brain with and without contrast ordered.
   - Blood work drawn today.
   - Follow-up in three weeks (approx. 15th of May) to review results.
   - Patient advised to return to ER for acute changes such as double vision or slurred speech.

[doctor] Good morning. I see you’re here for an initial consultation regarding some balance issues. Please, have a seat. I’m Dr. Rossi.
[patient] Good morning, Dr. Rossi. I’m Elena. Um, it’s nice to meet you.
[doctor] Nice to meet you too, Elena. Let’s start with the basics. Can you confirm your date of birth and age for the chart?
[patient] Yes, I was born on 14th of March, 1978, so I’m 46 years old.
[doctor] Thank you. And where do you currently reside?
[patient] I live in Bergamo, specifically at Via Dante Alighieri 12, 24124 Bergamo.
[doctor] Got it. Who is your primary healthcare provider or insurer?
[patient] I’m with ASL Bergamo. My insurance number is ASL-2024-BG-99821.
[doctor] Thank you. Could you also provide an email address for sending test results?
[patient] Sure, it’s elena.rossi.bergamo at gmail dot com.
[doctor] Perfect. Now, let’s talk about why you’re here. You mentioned "slipping and tripping." Can you describe what that feels like?
[patient] Um, well, it’s not really slipping like on ice, you know? It’s more like my feet... they get stuck, or my legs feel heavy. I stumble, but I don’t actually fall. It’s just... awkward.
[doctor] How long has this been happening?
[patient] Maybe... two months ago? It started gradually. I was walking to the market and my left foot just... sort of dragged?
[doctor] Did you hit your head or have any recent illnesses?
[patient] No, no head injuries. I had a bit of a flu in January, but that’s it.
[doctor] Do you have any other medical conditions?
[patient] Well, I have Hashimoto's thyroiditis. My endocrinologist, Dr. Bianchi, keeps my TSH levels stable.
[doctor] I see. And do you have any family history of neurological problems?
[patient] My mother, Giulia, who is 74, has Parkinson’s disease. And my brother, Marco, who is 42, has Crohn’s disease. I worry it might be genetic.
[doctor] That’s good to know. Have you noticed any changes in your handwriting, tremors, or stiffness?
[patient] No tremors. Maybe a little stiffness in the mornings? But mostly it’s the feet.
[doctor] Do you use any medications?
[patient] Just the Levothyroxine for my thyroid. And sometimes paracetamol if I have a headache.
[doctor] Okay. I’m going to do a physical exam now. Please stand up. Let’s look at your gait.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] Walk to the door and back. Nice and slow.
[patient] (walking)
[doctor] Stop. Now, stand on your left leg for ten seconds.
[patient] (wobbling slightly)
[doctor] You’re losing balance a bit. Let’s check your eyes. Look at this pen. Follow it with your eyes only.
[patient] (moving eyes)
[doctor] I noticed a slight deviation in your eye movement at the 3 o’clock position. That can be a sign of inner ear or brainstem issues.
[patient] Oh no. Is it serious?
[doctor] It’s just one finding. We need more data. I see you have a relative named Graves?
[patient] Oh, you know my cousin, Clara Graves? She’s 50. She lives in Como.
[doctor] I see. No relation to Graves' disease, I assume?
[patient] No, no, just a funny coincidence with her surname. She’s a dentist.
[doctor] Right. Let’s do some reflex tests. Tap here.
[patient] (reflex kicks)
[doctor] Normal. Let’s check your coordination. Finger to nose.
[patient] (performing test)
[doctor] Good. Now, heel to shin.
[patient] (performing test)
[doctor] There’s a bit of inaccuracy there. Let’s schedule some blood tests and a referral for an MRI.
[patient] An MRI? That sounds expensive.
[doctor] It’s covered by ASL Bergamo. I’ll send the referral to Ospedale Papa Giovanni XXIII.
[patient] Thank you, Dr. Rossi. I was really worried it was Parkinson's like my mom.
[doctor] It’s too early to say. The eye finding and the gait issue could be many things. We’ll start with the MRI and blood work to rule out inflammation or other causes.
[patient] Okay. When should I come back?
[doctor] In three weeks, around 15th of May. I’ll send the results to your email.
[patient] elena.rossi.bergamo at gmail dot com, yes.
[doctor] And if you have any new symptoms, like double vision or slurred speech, go to the emergency room immediately.
[patient] Understood. Thank you.
[doctor] My nurse, Sofia, will help you with the paperwork.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

PATIENT NAME: Eva Brandt
DATE OF BIRTH: 12 March 1978
RECORD NUMBER: REC-99887766
INSURER: Barmer
INSURANCE NUMBER: A123456789
REVIEWING PHYSICIAN: Dr. Weber

DIAGNOSIS
Moderate persistent asthma, acute exacerbation.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Eva Brandt, a 46-year-old woman, presented to the clinic with a three-month history of worsening respiratory symptoms. The symptoms intensified two weeks ago, characterized by increased frequency of reliever inhaler use, nocturnal cough, and chest tightness. The patient reported that the symptoms worsened significantly on October 15 while in the kitchen. She has a known history of asthma and house dust mite allergy. She was referred by Dr. Hoffmann from the University Hospital Cologne for further management of her poorly controlled asthma.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
- Respiratory: Wheezing, cough, dyspnea on exertion.
- Cardiovascular: No chest pain, no palpitations.
- Gastrointestinal: No nausea or vomiting.
- Neurological: No headaches or dizziness.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
- General: Alert, oriented, in no acute distress.
- Vital Signs: Blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, Heart rate 78/min, Respiratory rate 16/min, Temperature 36.8°C, Oxygen saturation 96% on room air.
- Chest: Wheezing heard bilaterally. No crackles or rhonchi.
- Abdomen: Soft, non-tender.
- Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. A soft systolic murmur was noted at the 3 o'clock position of the heart, likely a flow murmur, to be monitored.

INVESTIGATIONS
- Peak Flow: 70% of personal best.
- Chest X-ray: Ordered, pending results.
- Pulmonary Function Test: Ordered, pending results.

TREATMENT PLAN
1. Step up inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) dose.
2. Add long-acting beta-agonist (LABA) to maintenance therapy.
3. Continue short-acting beta-agonist (SABA) as needed for relief.
4. Educate patient on proper inhaler technique and trigger avoidance.
5. Caution regarding non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) due to potential cross-reactivity in asthma patients.
6. Follow-up appointment in two weeks to review peak flow diary and assess response to therapy.

PROGNOSIS
Good with adherence to treatment and avoidance of triggers.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS
- Take medications as prescribed.
- Monitor peak flow daily.
- Seek immediate medical attention if peak flow drops below 50% of personal best or if reliever inhaler is needed more than every four hours.
- Avoid known triggers, including house dust mites and strong odors.

CONTENTS OF DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS
- Inhaled corticosteroid/LABA combination inhaler.
- Short-acting beta-agonist inhaler.

SIGNATURE
Dr. Weber
November 10, 2023
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, please have a seat. I see you are here with your daughter. May I have your name, please?
[patient] Yes, my name is Eva Brandt. And this is my daughter, Lisa.
[doctor] Welcome, Eva, and Lisa. I am Dr. Weber. I see you were referred to me by Dr. Hoffmann at the University Hospital Cologne. Can you tell me why you are here today?
[patient] Yes, my asthma has been getting worse. It has been quite difficult for three months. I have been using my reliever inhaler more often than before.
[doctor] I understand. When did this increase in symptoms start?
[patient] It started about two weeks ago. I woke up with chest tightness and a cough that wouldn't go away.
[doctor] Have you had any night-time symptoms?
[patient] Yes, almost every night. I have to wake up and take my inhaler to breathe properly.
[doctor] And how often are you using the reliever inhaler during the day?
[patient] About four or five times a day. Before, it was only once or twice a week.
[doctor] That is a significant increase. Are you still taking your maintenance medication?
[patient] Yes, I take my preventer inhaler twice a day, exactly as prescribed.
[doctor] Good. Let's check your lungs. Please take a deep breath in for me.
[patient] Like this?
[doctor] Yes, exactly. Now breathe out slowly.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] I can hear some wheezing. It is widespread, but not very severe. Let's look at your peak flow readings. Do you have your diary with you?
[patient] Yes, my daughter brought it. Here it is.
[doctor] Thank you. I see your readings have dropped significantly since October 15.
[patient] Yes, that was the day I felt the worst. I was in the kitchen preparing dinner, and the smell of the onions triggered an attack.
[doctor] Food smells can be triggers for some patients. How is your peak flow now compared to your personal best?
[patient] It is about 70% of my best.
[doctor] That indicates moderate obstruction. Lisa, do you have any questions for me?
[patient_guest] Yes, doctor. My mother is very worried. She thinks she might have developed something more serious, like Emphysema or another lung disease.
[doctor] I understand your concern. Based on her history and current exam, this looks like a moderate exacerbation of her known asthma. We will need to investigate why it has flared up. Did she change her environment or start any new medications?
[patient] No, I haven't changed anything. I live in Munich, and the air quality has been reported as good lately.
[doctor] I see. Let's check your oxygen saturation.
[nurse] The saturation is 96% on room air.
[doctor] That is stable. I would like to order a chest X-ray to rule out any other issues, and a pulmonary function test to assess the severity of the obstruction.
[patient] Will I need to be hospitalized?
[doctor] Not at this stage. We will adjust your medication to bring you under better control. I am going to increase your inhaled corticosteroid dose and add a long-acting beta-agonist.
[patient] Is that safe?
[doctor] Yes, it is the standard of care for moderate persistent asthma. We will monitor your response closely.
[patient] How often should I come back?
[doctor] I would like to see you in two weeks to review your peak flow diary and check if the new regimen is working.
[patient] Okay. What if I get worse before then?
[doctor] If your peak flow drops below 50% of your personal best, or if you are using your reliever inhaler more than every four hours, you should go to the emergency department or call me immediately.
[patient] Understood.
[doctor] Lisa, it is important that you support your mother in taking her medications as prescribed and keeping the diary accurate.
[patient_guest] We will do that.
[doctor] Also, ensure she avoids known triggers. Is she allergic to any specific substances?
[patient] I am allergic to house dust mites. I use anti-dust covers on my bedding.
[doctor] Good. Are you taking any other medications?
[patient] I take Atorvastatin for cholesterol, and sometimes Ibuprofen for headaches.
[doctor] Be careful with Ibuprofen. Some patients with asthma react to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. If you notice your breathing gets worse after taking it, stop and let me know.
[patient] I will be careful.
[doctor] Your health insurance is with Barmer, correct?
[patient] Yes. My number is A123456789.
[doctor] Thank you. I will send the prescription and the test orders to your GP, Dr. Hoffmann.
[patient] That is helpful.
[doctor] Do you have any other concerns?
[patient] I am a teacher. I am worried about my students if I have an attack in class.
[doctor] That is a valid concern. Having your reliever inhaler with you at all times is crucial. Most teachers can manage well with proper control. If you feel an attack coming on, you should step out of the classroom, sit down, and use your inhaler.
[patient] That is good to know.
[doctor] Let's summarize. You have moderate persistent asthma. We are stepping up your therapy. You will have a chest X-ray and pulmonary function test today. I will see you in two weeks.
[patient] Thank you, Dr. Weber. I feel a bit more confident now.
[doctor] You are welcome. Lisa, please ensure your mother takes her evening dose before leaving.
[patient_guest] Yes, I will remind her.
[doctor] Here is the information sheet about the new inhaler technique. Please read it carefully.
[patient] Thank you.
[doctor] Goodbye.

[doctor] Good morning, Mr. Costa. It is time to discuss your discharge. How are you feeling this morning?
[patient] I am much better, doctor. The pain in my chest is gone. I just feel tired, which is normal after being here for three days.
[doctor] That is expected. Your heart rhythm has stabilized since we started the new medication regimen. Do you have any questions about your medications before you leave?
[patient] I have a lot of pills, doctor. I used to take two different blood pressure medicines, but now you are telling me to stop one?
[doctor] Yes. We are simplifying your therapy. You will continue taking Amlodipine 5 mg once a day. However, we are stopping the Betablocker because your heart rate was too low. Can you tell me what time you usually take your morning medicines?
[patient] I wake up early, around 6:00. I take them with my coffee.
[doctor] That is fine, but please ensure you take them with a small amount of food, not just coffee, to avoid stomach upset. Your daughter, Lucia, will be driving you home to Milan, correct?
[patient] Yes, my daughter Lucia is here. She is 45 years old and very helpful.
[patient_guest] Hello, Doctor. My father is very careful, but he can get confused with the new schedule. He is 81 and lives alone in Como.
[doctor] I understand. I have written a clear schedule on the discharge paper. It lists the morning and evening doses. Since you are moving from Brazil to live permanently in Italy, it is crucial that your local general practitioner, Dr. Rossi, reviews this list within one week.
[patient] Dr. Rossi is my friend Marco’s cousin. He will see me on Tuesday.
[doctor] That is excellent. Dr. Rossi can also monitor your electrolytes. You were admitted with a slight drop in potassium, which was corrected. You will need a blood test in two weeks.
[patient] I remember that. I had a similar issue five years ago when I was still working as a chemical engineer for Basf in Leverkusen.
[doctor] Working in a high-pressure environment can sometimes affect stress hormones. Now, let us review the other long-term therapy. You are also on Atorvastatin 20 mg for cholesterol. Do you have any side effects from that?
[patient] No, just some muscle soreness in my legs sometimes. It is not bad.
[doctor] If it becomes severe, stop the medication and call the clinic. Do not stop it on your own without consulting us. You are also taking Aspirin 100 mg daily. This is for your previous stent procedure in 2019.
[patient] Yes, I had the stent at Sant'Andrea Hospital in March 2019. My brother, Paulo, who is 78, came to Italy to see me during that hospital stay.
[doctor] It is good that you had support then. Your brother Paulo still lives in Sao Paulo, correct?
[patient] Yes, he lives in Sao Paulo. He calls me every Sunday.
[doctor] That is a good routine. Now, regarding your lifestyle. I see you are a member of the Como Chess Club. Do you still play?
[patient] I do, doctor. I play every Thursday evening. It keeps my mind sharp.
[doctor] That is a wonderful hobby. Just be careful with sitting for long periods. Try to stand up and stretch every hour.
[patient] I will try. I also walk in the park near the lake, usually in the morning.
[doctor] Walking is excellent for your heart. Did you have any falls or injuries recently?
[patient] No, I am careful. I used to be an avid tennis player, but I stopped after a fall in 2020. I hit my knee on the court.
[doctor] I am glad you recovered well. Let us check your heart one last time before you leave. Please lie down.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] I am going to listen to your heart now. I hear a slight murmur at the 2 o'clock position. It is likely a benign flow murmur, but we will monitor it.
[patient] Is that serious?
[doctor] No, it is not serious. It is common in elderly patients. It does not require treatment right now.
[patient] Thank you, doctor. I feel much better.
[doctor] You are welcome. Here is your discharge summary. Please read it carefully. If you have any chest pain, shortness of breath, or dizziness, go to the emergency room immediately.
[patient] I will. My daughter Lucia will take me home.
[patient_guest] Thank you for taking care of my father. Can we get a copy of the medication list for his pharmacist?
[doctor] Yes, I will have the pharmacy fax it to your local pharmacy in Como. Your pharmacist is Gianni, right?
[patient_guest] Yes, Gianni at the pharmacy in Como.
[doctor] I will send it to him. Please ensure your father takes his medications exactly as prescribed. Do not double up doses if you miss one.
[patient] I understand. I will set a reminder on my phone.
[doctor] That is a good idea. Do you have any other questions?
[patient] No, I think I am ready to go.
[doctor] Then let us finalize the paperwork. Nurse, can you prepare the discharge documents?
[nurse] Yes, doctor. I have them ready.
[doctor] Great. Mr. Costa, your record number is 459201. Please keep this number for your future appointments.
[patient] Thank you, doctor.
[doctor] Goodbye, Mr. Costa. Drive safely.
[patient] Goodbye.

[doctor] family history is important . did your mother have any other conditions ?
[patient] she also had crohn's disease , but that was late in life . my brother jean is doing well , actually .
[doctor] thank you . let's check your vital signs . your blood pressure is 135 over 85 . let's do a quick neurological exam . can you touch your nose with your eyes closed ?

[doctor] yes , that looks steady . now , let's check your reflexes . i am going to tap here .
[patient] that was a bit surprising .
[doctor] your knee jerk is normal . now , let's look at your eyes . i am going to shine a light .
[patient] it's bright .
[doctor] your pupils are equal and reactive . i noticed a small bruise on your forehead . is it tender ?

[doctor] i can see a slight swelling there . did you have any nausea or vomiting after the fall ?
[patient] no , no vomiting . i felt a bit dizzy for a few minutes , but then it passed . i went to the emergency department first just to be safe .

[patient] they took a ct scan of my head . it was clear . they said i had a mild concussion . they gave me pain medication and told me to rest .

[doctor] i would recommend taking it easy for a few days . avoid heavy cognitive tasks if you feel tired . you can return to valeo when you feel comfortable , perhaps starting with half days .

[patient] thank you , marie .
[doctor] one last thing . did you mention where you fell specifically ?
[patient] yes , on the ice near the lake in annecy .
[doctor] be careful with the ice there . it can be very treacherous in winter .
[patient] i will wear better shoes .
[doctor] good idea . let's schedule your follow-up appointment for march 15, 2024 at 10:30 .
[patient] that works for me .
[doctor] perfect . i will see you then . take care .
[patient] thank you , doctor .

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Patient is a 30-year-old male presenting with right knee pain and instability following a soccer injury.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient, Stefan, reports twisting injury to the right knee while playing soccer last weekend. He describes a "pop" sensation followed by immediate swelling and pain. He is currently residing in Vienna. He states that pain is exacerbated by bending and varus stress. He denies loss of consciousness or other trauma. He is a logistics coordinator and reports pain limits his ability to stand for prolonged periods.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for fever, chills, or systemic symptoms. No recent weight loss. No other joint pain.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Alert, oriented, in no acute distress.
Right Knee: Mild swelling noted. Tenderness to palpation along the lateral joint line.
Lachman Test: Positive, indicating some anterior laxity but less than expected for ACL tear.
Varus Stress Test: Positive at 30 degrees of flexion. A distinct gap is palpable at the 3 o’clock position of the lateral joint line.
Valgus Stress Test: Negative.
Range of Motion: Flexion 120 degrees, Extension 0 degrees, with pain at end range.

RESULTS
X-ray of the right knee: No fracture or dislocation noted. Soft tissue swelling is present.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Sprain of the lateral collateral ligament (LCL) of the right knee, Grade 2.
Plan:
- Recommend RICE protocol (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation).
- Prescribed Voltaren gel topically twice daily.
- Prescribed Ibuprofen 400 mg orally every 8 hours as needed for pain, with food.
- Advised to use a hinged knee brace for stability during ambulation.
- Refer to physical therapy for guided rehabilitation.
- Follow-up appointment scheduled for June 14 at 10:30 am at Vienna Orthopedic Center.

dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning. Please have a seat. I see you are here for a knee injury. Can you tell me what happened?
[patient] Um, hi. Yeah, so, I was playing soccer last weekend. I’m not a pro, just a hobbyist, but I made a bad turn and my knee sort of... popped? And then it swelled up.
[doctor] I see. That sounds painful. When exactly did this happen?
[patient] It was Saturday, around 4:00 pm. I’m living in Vienna now, but I’m from Serbia.
[doctor] Okay. And how is it feeling today?
[patient] It’s still a bit stiff. I can walk, but it hurts when I bend it. I’m 30 years old, so I thought I’d recover faster.
[doctor] Let’s take a look. Please remove your trousers and socks on the right leg.
[nurse] I’ll help you with the exposure. Is there anything in the room you’re allergic to?
[patient] No, I’m fine. Just a bit nervous.
[doctor] Relax. I’m Dr. Kovacs. I’m going to check the stability of your knee. This is the Lachman test.
[patient] Does it hurt?
[doctor] It might be uncomfortable. Okay, I’m pushing the tibia forward. Do you feel a give?
[patient] Yeah, there’s a bit of slack. It feels loose.
[doctor] And now I’ll check the varus stress. This puts pressure on the lateral side.
[patient] Ah! That’s the spot. That’s where it hurts the most.
[doctor] I see. There is a gap at the 3 o’clock position of the joint line when I apply stress. This suggests a sprain of the lateral collateral ligament.
[patient] So it’s broken?
[doctor] No, not broken. It’s a sprain. A Grade 2 sprain likely. The ligament is stretched and partially torn, but not completely ruptured.
[patient] Oh, thank God. So what do I do? Do I need surgery?
[doctor] Not right now. We need to protect the knee. I’m prescribing IcePack compression wraps and Voltaren gel. You should use the RICE method: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation.
[patient] And painkillers?
[doctor] You can take Ibuprofen 400 mg every six to eight hours, with food. Avoid alcohol.
[patient] Got it. How long until I can play soccer again?
[doctor] That’s hard to say. It depends on your recovery. Usually, it’s four to six weeks for a full return to sport, but you must wait for physical therapy.
[patient] I have a job, I’m a logistics coordinator. I stand a lot.
[doctor] That might be difficult. Try to limit standing. Use a cane if needed.
[patient] Where do I live? I mean, where is the clinic for the follow-up?
[doctor] We are here, at Vienna Orthopedic Center. Your address is on the form, 1010 Vienna, Wipplingerstraße 5, correct?
[patient] Yes, that’s my home.
[doctor] Good. I want to see you again to check the healing. Let’s book an appointment.
[patient] When?
[doctor] Let’s say next Tuesday, June 14, at 10:30 am.
[patient] Okay, June 14 at 10:30 am. I’ll write that down.
[doctor] Also, if you have family history of ligament injuries, tell me.
[patient] Um, my mother has a bad knee, but I don’t think it’s related. And my brother Marko had a knee injury too, a few years ago.
[doctor] Noted. Any other medical issues?
[patient] No, just a mild asthma, but I’m not using inhalers right now.
[doctor] Okay. I’ll do a simple X-ray to rule out a fracture, just to be safe.
[patient] Is that painful?
[doctor] No, just lie down. The nurse will take you to the radiology room.
[nurse] Follow me, please.
[patient] Thank you, doctor.
[doctor] You’re welcome. Take care of that knee.

REFERRAL LETTER

Date: 15 October 2023

To: Dr. Wagner
Department of Orthopedic Surgery
University Hospital Salzburg
Paracelsusstraße 1, 5020 Salzburg

Re: Referral for right foot pain

Dear Dr. Wagner,

I am writing to refer my patient, Stefan Petrov, 62 years old, for your evaluation of persistent right foot pain.

History of Present Illness:
Mr. Petrov presents with a two-week history of pain in his right foot. The pain is located on the lateral aspect and is exacerbated by weight-bearing. He reports mild swelling but no redness or numbness. The pain started insidiously, and he suspects it may be related to wearing new hiking boots. He has been using topical Voltaren gel and oral ibuprofen with partial relief. He works as a warehouse supervisor at Hofmann Logistics, which involves prolonged standing.

Past Medical History:
No significant past medical history. No diabetes or peripheral vascular disease.

Family History:
His mother had arthritis in her hands. His brother, Petar, has a history of knee problems.

Social History:
Mr. Petrov lives at 12 Hauptstraße, 5020 Salzburg. He is a member of the Salzburg Hiking Club.

Examination Findings:
On physical examination, there is mild swelling on the lateral aspect of the right foot. Palpation of the lateral midfoot elicits tenderness. Range of motion is limited by pain, particularly during inversion. There are no signs of acute fracture or significant deformity. I noted a specific area of tenderness at the 3 o'clock position relative to the navicular bone.

Assessment:
Lateral foot pain, differential diagnosis includes soft tissue strain, early osteoarthritis, or stress reaction.

Plan:
1. Rest and activity modification.
2. Continue topical NSAIDs and oral ibuprofen as needed.
3. Supportive footwear.
4. Referral to orthopedic specialist for further evaluation, including imaging (X-ray, possible MRI).

Please do not hesitate to contact me if you require any further information. You can reach me at my clinic or by email at doc.keller@salzburg-med.at.

Sincerely,

Dr. Anna Keller
Gynecology and General Practice
Salzburg

[doctor] Good morning. I see you are here for a follow-up regarding your foot pain. Can you tell me a bit more about what is happening?
[patient] Um, yes, doctor. It is, uh, really bothering me. I have been having this pain in my right foot. It started, you know, about two weeks ago.
[doctor] Okay. Where exactly is the pain located?
[patient] Well, it is mostly on the outer side. Sometimes it feels like there is something pressing against the bone.
[doctor] I see. Do you have any swelling or redness?
[patient] A little bit of swelling, yes. But no redness, I think.
[doctor] Let us take a look. Please remove your shoe and sock.
[patient] Okay. Here.
[doctor] Thank you. I am going to examine the foot now. This might be slightly uncomfortable.
[patient] No problem.
[doctor] I can see some mild swelling on the lateral aspect. When I palpate this area, do you feel pain?
[patient] Yes, that is it. Right there.
[doctor] Okay. I am going to check the range of motion now. Please try to turn your foot inward.
[patient] Uh, that hurts a bit.
[doctor] And outward?
[patient] Less painful, but still there.
[doctor] I see. Do you have any other symptoms? Numbness or tingling?
[patient] No, not really. Just the pain and the swelling.
[doctor] Have you tried any medication for this?
[patient] I took some ibuprofen. And I used that spray my friend, Milan, gave me.
[doctor] What was the name of the spray?
[patient] Uh, Voltaren. I think that is what it was called.
[doctor] Okay. Voltaren is a topical non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug. Did it help?
[patient] A little bit, but the pain came back quickly.
[doctor] I see. Let us look at your medical history. You mentioned you work as a warehouse supervisor at Hofmann Logistics?
[patient] Yes, that is correct. I stand a lot on my feet all day.
[doctor] That could certainly contribute to the strain. Do you have any history of diabetes or peripheral vascular disease?
[patient] No, my blood sugar is normal. My doctor checked it last year.
[doctor] Good. What about family history? Does anyone in your family have similar foot or joint problems?
[patient] My mother had arthritis, but that was in her hands. And my brother, Petar, he has had knee problems.
[doctor] I see. Have you had any recent injuries to the foot?
[patient] No, not that I know of. I didn't twist it or anything. It just started to hurt one day.
[patient] Well, maybe I was wearing new shoes. I bought some hiking boots last month.
[doctor] That is possible. New shoes can sometimes cause pressure points. Where do you live?
[patient] I live in Salzburg, Austria. My address is 12 Hauptstraße, 5020 Salzburg.
[doctor] Okay. And how can we contact you if we need to discuss the results further?
[patient] You can email me at stefan.petrov@example.com. That is the best way, I think.
[doctor] Noted. Now, let me explain what I am seeing. You have some signs consistent with lateral foot pain, possibly related to soft tissue strain or early arthritis. However, given the persistence, I think it would be wise to have a specialist opinion.
[patient] A specialist? Like an orthopedist?
[doctor] Yes. I am going to refer you to Dr. Wagner at the University Hospital Salzburg. He is an expert in foot and ankle surgery.
[patient] Okay. Will he do an X-ray?
[doctor] Yes, he will likely order an X-ray to rule out any fractures or bone spurs. He may also consider an MRI if the X-ray is inconclusive.
[patient] And what should I do in the meantime?
[doctor] I recommend resting the foot as much as possible. Avoid prolonged standing. You can continue using the Voltaren gel, but do not exceed the recommended dose. Also, try to wear supportive footwear with good arch support.
[patient] Okay. And should I keep taking the ibuprofen?
[doctor] You can take ibuprofen as needed for pain, but be mindful of your stomach. Take it with food.
[patient] Yes, I know. I have had stomach issues before.
[doctor] Exactly. Now, I am going to write the referral letter. It will include your details, the history, and my findings.
[patient] That sounds good. When will the letter be ready?
[doctor] It will be ready today. I will send it electronically to Dr. Wagner's office. You will also receive a copy.
[patient] Thank you, doctor.
[doctor] You are welcome. Do you have any other questions?
[patient] Um, no, I think that is all.
[doctor] Okay. I will see you in the waiting room to collect your documents.
[patient] Thank you.

[doctor] Good morning. I am Dr. Lefebvre. I see you are here for a foot injury. Please, take a seat. Can you tell me what happened?
[patient] Good morning, doctor. I am Marie-Claire Durand. I am 54 years old. My social security number is 284567901234567.
[doctor] Thank you, Mrs. Durand. So, how did this injury occur?
[patient] I was at my workplace, Lyon Textile Mills, in Lyon. I am a quality control inspector. I slipped on a wet floor in the kitchen area of the break room.
[doctor] A kitchen slip. That can be very treacherous. Did you feel a specific sensation when you fell?
[patient] Yes, I felt a loud pop in the middle of my right foot. It was excruciating. I couldn't put any weight on it.
[doctor] When did this happen?
[patient] It was this morning, around 08:30.
[doctor] And how long has the pain been present since then?
[patient] Since the fall, so about three hours now.
[doctor] On a scale of one to ten, with ten being the worst pain imaginable, how would you rate it now?
[patient] It is an eight. It throbs constantly.
[doctor] Have you tried any ice or elevation?
[patient] My colleague, Pauline, who is 29, helped me apply an ice pack. I have been keeping my leg up.
[doctor] That is good. Have you taken any medication?
[patient] I took some paracetamol, but it barely helps.
[doctor] Do you have any known allergies to medications?
[patient] No, I am not allergic to anything. I do have a history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis, but that is unrelated.
[doctor] I see. I will note that. Let's look at your foot. Can you please remove your shoe and sock from the right foot?
[patient] Yes, doctor. It is a bit stiff.
[doctor] I am examining the area. I can see significant swelling over the midfoot. There is a visible deformity. I am checking the stability of the joint.
[patient] It hurts when you touch it there.
[doctor] I am performing a stress test. This might be uncomfortable.
[patient] Yes, that is sharp pain.
[doctor] There is instability in the tarsometatarsal joint. This looks like a Lisfranc injury. I need to take an X-ray to confirm the extent of the dislocation.
[patient] Is it broken?
[doctor] It is likely dislocated, and there may be fractures. We need imaging. The nurse will take you to the radiology department.
[nurse] Hello, I am Nurse Stefan. I will take you to X-ray. You will need to lie on the table.
[patient] Thank you. I am quite worried.
[nurse] It is a common injury in this context. We will get the images quickly.
[patient] My husband, Jean, is coming to pick me up. He is 57.
[nurse] That is good to have support. I will send the images to the doctor.
[doctor] I have reviewed the X-rays. Yes, this confirms a dislocation of the second and third metatarsal bases at the tarsometatarsal joint. It is a Lisfranc dislocation.
[patient] What does that mean?
[doctor] The bones that connect your toes to the midfoot have shifted out of alignment. This is a serious injury that requires specialized care.
[patient] Do I need surgery?
[doctor] Very likely. However, we need to reduce the dislocation first. I am going to apply a long leg splint to stabilize the foot and reduce the swelling.
[patient] Will you put it back in place?
[doctor] We need to perform a closed reduction. This means I will manipulate the bones back into position. It is painful, so I will give you some pain relief first.
[patient] Please, doctor. I want the pain to stop.
[doctor] I am administering an intravenous analgesic. This should help. It may take a few minutes to kick in.
[patient] My hands are shaking.
[doctor] That is normal. Take deep breaths. When the medication takes effect, I will gently pull on your foot and apply pressure to the midfoot to realign the joints.
[patient] It is starting to work. I feel a bit floaty.
[doctor] Good. Now, I am going to perform the reduction. I will count to three. One, two, three.
[patient] Ah! That hurt, but the pressure changed.
[doctor] I can feel the joints lock back into place. The alignment looks much better clinically. I will now immobilize the foot in a posterior splint, extending up to the knee.
[patient] It feels strange, but the pain is slightly less.
[doctor] I am checking the circulation in your toes. Your pulses are strong, and your toes are warm and pink. Sensation is intact.
[patient] Thank God.
[doctor] I am going to take another X-ray to confirm the reduction.
[nurse] The X-ray is being taken now.
[doctor] The post-reduction X-ray shows good alignment. There is a small fracture of the base of the second metatarsal, but the dislocation is reduced.
[patient] Is that good news?
[doctor] It is a good start. However, because of the ligamentous injury, you will need to see an orthopedic surgeon for further management, likely surgical fixation.
[patient] Where do I go?
[doctor] I am referring you to <ORGANization>Hopital de la Pitié in Lyon. I have written a referral letter. You need to go to their emergency department or contact their orthopedic service.
[patient] How soon?
[doctor] As soon as possible. Ideally within 24 hours.
[patient] I will call them now. Do I have your contact information?
[doctor] You can reach our clinic at 04 78 12 34 56. For the hospital, you should call their main line.
[patient] I will email my husband the details. My email is mc.durand54 at gmail dot com.
[doctor] That works. In the meantime, keep your foot elevated and iced. Avoid putting weight on it.
[patient] What about medication for pain?
[doctor] I am prescribing you ibuprofen and acetaminophen. Take them as directed on the label.
[patient] And for the swelling?
[doctor] Elevation is key. Keep it above heart level when possible.
[patient] Do I need to come back here?
[doctor] I would like to see you in 48 hours to check the splint and your progress.
[patient] When exactly?
[doctor] Let's say Thursday at 10:00.
[patient] Thursday at 10:00. I will make a note.
[doctor] Please bring your ID and this referral letter.
[patient] I have my ID with me.
[doctor] Good. Do you have any other questions?
[patient] Will I be able to walk again?
[doctor] Yes, but it will take time. Recovery from a Lisfranc injury is lengthy. You may be non-weight bearing for several weeks, and rehabilitation will be crucial.
[patient] That is a long time.
[doctor] It is a significant injury, but with proper treatment, most people regain good function.
[patient] I am worried about work.
[doctor] I will write a certificate of absence for the next few days. Your employer will need to be informed.
[patient] I will send them a copy.
[doctor] Make sure you follow up with the orthopedic surgeon. Do not delay.
[patient] I understand. Thank you, doctor.
[doctor] You are welcome. The nurse will give you the prescriptions and the discharge instructions.
[nurse] Here are your prescriptions. Take the ibuprofen with food. Keep the splint dry. If you notice increased pain, numbness, or coldness in your toes, go to the emergency room immediately.
[patient] I will be careful.
[nurse] Also, if you have a fever or signs of infection, contact us.
[patient] Thank you, nurse.
[nurse] You are welcome. Good luck.
[patient] Thank you.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Pain in the right shoulder and neck, and rib tenderness, following a motor vehicle accident yesterday.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Carlos Mendes, a 54-year-old male, presents for a telehealth follow-up regarding injuries sustained in a motor vehicle collision. He reports right shoulder pain rated 7/10 on a numeric scale, described as sharp, and neck stiffness with pain rated 5/10, described as a dull ache. He has been taking paracetamol, approximately 2 grams in the last 24 hours. He reports mild chest tightness with deep inspiration but denies shortness of breath. He had a mild headache and some nausea at the hospital, which have resolved. He denies weakness, vision changes, or urinary issues. He is currently resting at home and has stopped his regular exercise routine at Fitness Club Milano for the past two weeks.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Denies fever, chills. Reports fatigue.
Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain, palpitations.
Respiratory: Denies cough, shortness of breath. Reports mild tightness with deep breaths.
Gastrointestinal: Denies nausea, vomiting currently. Had mild nausea at the hospital.
Neurological: Denies weakness, numbness, dizziness (other than orthostatic), vision changes, speech difficulty.
Musculoskeletal: Reports pain in right shoulder, neck, and ribs.
Psychiatric: Reports anxiety related to the accident and work. Denies depression.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Heart Rate: 78 bpm
Temperature: Afebrile (per patient report)
Respiratory Rate: 16 bpm
Oxygen Saturation: 98% on room air (per patient report)

RESULTS
