[doctor] good morning . please , have a seat . my name is dr . keller . i see you are here about an injury from skiing ?
[patient] yes , good morning . it is my left knee .
[doctor] could you tell me a bit more about what happened ?
[patient] i was skiing in zermatt last weekend . i was going downhill , maybe a bit fast , and i hit a patch of ice . my leg twisted and i fell .
[doctor] did you hear or feel a pop ?
[patient] yes , a loud pop . it hurt immediately .
[doctor] where exactly does it hurt ?
[patient] inside the knee , near the joint line .
[doctor] on a scale of 0 to 10 , with 10 being the worst pain imaginable , how bad is it right now ?
[patient] maybe a six or seven .
[doctor] and when did you last take pain medication ?
[patient] this morning , around 08:30 . i took some ibuprofen .
[doctor] how is that helping ?
[patient] it helps a little , but the swelling is getting worse .
[doctor] can you walk on it ?
[patient] yes , but i have to use a crutch . it feels unstable , like it might give way .
[doctor] i see . let's look at your history . you are 19 years old , correct ?
[patient] yes , i am .
[doctor] do you have any other medical conditions ?
[patient] no , i am healthy . my mother has switzerland residency , but we are from eritrea .
[doctor] understood . any allergies ?
[patient] no drug allergies .
[doctor] do you have any family history of autoimmune conditions , like hashimoto's or graves' disease ?
[patient] i don't think so . my sister has a skin condition , maybe psoriasis , but i don't know for sure .
[doctor] what about inflammatory bowel diseases like crohn's ?
[patient] no , my brother is very healthy .
[doctor] do you have a history of parkinson's or bell's palsy in your family ?
[patient] no , nothing like that .
[doctor] let's talk about your current lifestyle . what do you do for work or study ?
[patient] i am a student . i study engineering at eth zurich .
[doctor] and do you participate in any sports regularly ?
[patient] yes , i play football . i am in a team at fc basel youth academy .
[doctor] how often do you train ?
[patient] three times a week .
[doctor] do you have any hobbies outside of sports ?
[patient] i like hiking . i go with my friend david .
[doctor] where do you live ?
[patient] i live at 22 main street, 8004 zurich .
[doctor] is that your permanent address ?
[patient] yes . i moved from asmara three years ago .
[doctor] did you travel anywhere recently before the injury ?
[patient] yes , i went to london for a conference last month .
[doctor] and you are currently in zermatt for the weekend ?
[patient] yes , i came with my friend david and another guy , michael .
[doctor] okay . let's do a physical exam . please , remove your pants and socks on the left leg .
[patient] okay .
[doctor] i see significant swelling around the joint . there is tenderness along the medial joint line .
[patient] ouch , that is the spot .
[doctor] i am going to do a mcmurray's test . this might cause some pain .
[patient] got it .
[doctor] (performing exam)
[patient] that was uncomfortable .
[doctor] i felt a click . now , let's do a lachman's test .
[patient] okay .
[doctor] there is some laxity , but it has a firm endpoint .
[patient] does that mean i broke something ?
[doctor] not necessarily . we need imaging . i will order an mri .
[patient] will i need surgery ?
[doctor] not yet . we need to see the extent of the damage . if it is a simple tear , we might try conservative treatment .
[patient] what about blood tests ?
[doctor] i will order some basic labs to check for infection or inflammation .
[patient] do i need to see a specialist ?
[doctor] i am a sports medicine specialist , so i will manage this . but if surgery is needed , i will refer you to an orthopedic surgeon .
[patient] what should i do in the meantime ?
[doctor] rest , ice , compression , and elevation . keep the leg raised .
[patient] can i ski again ?
[doctor] absolutely not . you need to protect the knee .
[patient] how long will it take to heal ?
[doctor] it depends on the injury . it could be weeks or months .
[patient] i have a match in two weeks .
[doctor] you will likely miss that . we will reassess after the mri .
[patient] i have a friend named michael who is a physiotherapist . can he help ?
[doctor] that sounds good . he can start some gentle range-of-motion exercises once the acute swelling goes down .
[patient] where can i get the mri ?
[doctor] i will send the order to university hospital zurich . you should go there tomorrow .
[patient] i have my insurance card .
[doctor] please bring that . what is your ahv number ?
[patient] it is 756 1234 567 89 01 .
[doctor] and your phone number ?
[patient] it is +41 79 123 45 67 .
[doctor] i will send you a summary of our visit .
[patient] thank you , dr . keller .
[doctor] you are welcome . take care of the knee .

1. Pharmacology: Naproxen 250 mg PO BID x 7 days with food. Stop if GI distress occurs.

3. Imaging: X-ray right elbow AP/Lat views. Review results at follow-up.
4. Conservative Management: Ice application 15 minutes QID for 5 days. Activity modification: Avoid heavy lifting and repetitive wrist extension. Use ergonomic tools if possible.
5. Follow-up: Return to clinic in 6 weeks to assess response to therapy. If no improvement, consider corticosteroid injection or further imaging (MRI).

[nurse] Good morning, Mr. Rossi. I see you’re here for your follow-up. Can I confirm your date of birth, 14 March 1956?
[patient] Yes, that is correct.
[nurse] And your medical record number is ENT-2024-88910, correct?
[patient] Yes, that is my number.
[doctor] Good morning, Mr. Rossi. I am Dr. Silva. I see you were referred to us by your primary care physician, Dr. Bianchi. What brings you to the ENT clinic today?
[patient] Good morning, Doctor. I have been experiencing some issues with my ears.
[doctor] Could you describe the symptoms in more detail? When did they start?
[patient] It started about two weeks ago. I noticed a ringing sound in my left ear.
[doctor] Is the ringing constant or does it come and go?
[patient] It is mostly constant, but it gets louder when I am in a quiet room.
[doctor] Do you have any pain, pressure, or fullness in the ear?
[patient] There is some mild pressure, but no sharp pain.
[doctor] Have you noticed any hearing loss or difficulty understanding speech?
[patient] Yes, sounds seem a bit muffled in that ear.
[doctor] Did you have any recent illnesses, such as a cold or sinus infection?
[patient] I had a mild cold about a month ago, but I felt better.
[doctor] Have you been exposed to loud noises recently?
[patient] I work in a factory, but I always wear my hearing protection.
[doctor] I see. Let’s look at your history. You are 68 years old, is that correct?
[patient] Yes, I am.
[doctor] You mentioned you are from Brazil. Where are you currently living?
[patient] I live in Milan, in the City of Milan region.
[doctor] Thank you. Do you have any other medical conditions?
[patient] I have high cholesterol. My doctor calls it hyperlipidemia.
[doctor] Are you currently taking any medication for that?
[patient] Yes, I take Atorvastatin daily.
[doctor] Do you have any allergies?
[patient] No, I have no known drug allergies.
[doctor] Let’s talk about your family history. Do your parents or siblings have any hearing issues?
[patient] My mother had hearing loss when she got older, but I don’t think it was sudden.
[doctor] Did your mother have any other conditions?
[patient] She had diabetes.
[doctor] What about your brothers or sisters?
[patient] My brother, Joao, is healthy. He is 65.
[doctor] Do you smoke or drink alcohol?
[patient] I do not smoke. I drink a glass of wine in the evening, sometimes.
[doctor] Let’s move on to the physical examination. I am going to look into your ear. This may be slightly uncomfortable.
[patient] Okay, ready when you are.
[doctor] This is your left ear. I can see the eardrum. It appears intact.
[patient] Does it look normal?
[doctor] It looks a bit retracted, but there is no fluid or infection.
[doctor] Now, let’s do some hearing tests. I will place this device in your right ear and play some beeps.
[patient] I hear that.
[doctor] Good. Now the left ear.
[patient] I hear that one too, but it seems quieter.
[doctor] Thank you. Let’s check your blood pressure.
[nurse] Your blood pressure is 135/85. That is slightly elevated.
[doctor] Did you take your medication this morning?
[patient] Yes, I took my cholesterol pill.
[doctor] Do you take blood pressure medication?
[patient] No, my doctor said my pressure is borderline, so I am just monitoring it.
[doctor] I see. Let’s discuss your cholesterol. What are your last lab results?
[patient] I don’t have the numbers with me, but my doctor said they were a bit high.
[doctor] I will order new blood work to check your lipid profile.
[patient] Is that necessary?
[doctor] Yes, because high cholesterol can affect blood flow to the inner ear.
[patient] I see. So my hearing loss is because of my cholesterol?
[doctor] It is possible. We need to rule out other causes, such as Meniere’s disease or acoustic neuroma.
[patient] What is an acoustic neuroma?
[doctor] It is a benign tumor on the nerve that carries sound from the ear to the brain.
[patient] That sounds scary.
[doctor] It is usually slow-growing, but we need to check for it.
[patient] Do I need a scan?
[doctor] Yes, I will order an MRI of your brain and inner ears.
[patient] When can I do that?
[doctor] I will give you a referral. You should do it within a week.
[patient] Okay. What should I do in the meantime?
[doctor] Try to avoid loud noises and stress. Sleep on your right side if the left ear is affected.
[patient] Does sleeping on that side help?
[doctor] It can help with fluid drainage if there is any.
[patient] I will try that.
[doctor] Also, continue taking your Atorvastatin.
[patient] Will you increase the dose?
[doctor] Not yet. Let’s see the new lab results first.
[patient] When will I have those?
[doctor] You can draw blood at the clinic lab tomorrow morning.
[patient] What time does it open?
[doctor] It opens at 7:00.
[patient] I can be there at 8:00.
[doctor] Perfect. I will write the orders for you.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor.
[doctor] Do you have any other questions?
[patient] No, that is all.
[doctor] Okay. The nurse will print your instructions.
[nurse] Here are your instructions for the MRI and blood test.
[patient] Thank you.
[nurse] Do you understand the instructions?
[patient] Yes, I do.
[nurse] If you have any severe headache or double vision, go to the emergency room.
[patient] Understood.
[nurse] Anything else I can help with?
[patient] No, that is fine.
[nurse] Goodbye, Mr. Rossi.
[patient] Goodbye.

note:
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Fatma, an 85-year-old female, presents for follow-up after a fall sustained yesterday. The patient reports slipping on wet leaves in her garden and falling backwards, striking her head. She lost consciousness for approximately two minutes. The initial encounter was at the emergency department, where a CT head was negative. The police classified the event as "undetermined intent," but the patient denies suicidal ideation, attributing the fall to syncope and ataxia. She has experienced dizziness and tremor for three months.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Hypothyroidism (Hashimoto's thyroiditis).
Crohn's disease (quiescent).
Hypertension.
Recent wrist fracture.

MEDICATIONS
Levothyroxine 75 mcg daily.
Losartan 50 mg daily.
Omeprazole 20 mg daily.
Paracetamol PRN.

ALLERGIES
NKDA.

FAMILY HISTORY
Daughter Aylin (55) and granddaughter Elif (29) are healthy. Neighbor Mein provides social support.

PHYSICAL EXAM
Vital Signs: BP 150/90, HR 82, RR 16, Temp 36.8 C, SpO2 98%.
General: Alert, oriented, in no acute distress.
HEENT: Pupils equal and reactive. No facial asymmetry (rules out Bell's palsy).
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. No murmurs.
Respiratory: Clear to auscultation.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender.
Neurological: Resting tremor noted in bilateral hands. Gait is unsteady.
Musculoskeletal: Right wrist in cast. Right knee swelling, possible Baker's cyst.

LABORATORY RESULTS
TSH: 15.4 mIU/L (High).
Glucose: 110 mg/dL.
CBC: Within normal limits.

ASSESSMENT
1. Hypothyroidism, uncontrolled. Likely contributing to syncope and fatigue.
2. Fall with head trauma, undetermined intent per police, but medical cause (syncope) suspected.
3. Suspected Parkinson's disease given resting tremor and gait instability.
4. Wrist fracture, healing.
5. Crohn's disease, stable.

PLAN
1. Increase Levothyroxine to 100 mcg daily.
2. Refer to Neurology for evaluation of tremor and gait.
3. Order Ultrasound of right knee to evaluate for Baker's cyst.
4. Order blood tests for TSI and TRAb to rule out Graves' disease.
5. Referral to Ophthalmology for vision check.
6. Fall risk assessment to be completed by home health.
7. Follow-up in clinic on October 15th at 10:30 AM.
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, Fatma. Please have a seat. I see you were brought in from the emergency department yesterday after your fall. How are you feeling today?
[patient] I am okay, doctor. Just... um, tired. The bones hurt, but I think it is mostly the head.
[doctor] Let’s start with the basics. What happened?
[patient] I was in my garden. It was Friday. I slipped on some wet leaves. I fell backwards. My head hit the stone path.
[doctor] Did you lose consciousness?
[patient] Yes. For a moment. Maybe two minutes? My granddaughter Elif found me. She was 28 then, now she is 29. She called the ambulance.
[doctor] Thank you for clarifying. Elif is your granddaughter?
[patient] Yes, her mother Aylin is my daughter. Aylin is 55.
[doctor] I see. Did you hit your head before the fall, or just during?
[patient] Just during. I felt dizzy before. Like the world was spinning. This has been happening for three months.
[doctor] Dizziness for three months? That is important. Do you have a tremor?
[patient] Yes. In my hands. The doctor in Frankfurt said it might be Parkinson's. But he was not sure.
[doctor] I see. We will need to review that. Let’s check your vitals. Nurse, please take her blood pressure and oxygen levels.
[nurse] Right away, Dr. Hoffman.
[nurse] Fatma, I’m going to put this on your finger now. Breathe normally.
[patient] Okay.
[nurse] Your oxygen is 98%. Blood pressure is 150/90. Heart rate is 82.
[doctor] Thank you. Fatma, you are hypertensive. Are you on medication for that?
[patient] Yes. Losartan. I take it every morning.
[doctor] Good. Now, about the fall. The police came to the hospital, didn't they?
[patient] Yes. They asked questions. They were very polite. But I told them it was an accident.
[doctor] Did they determine the intent?
[patient] They said "undetermined intent." I don't know what that means. I am an old woman. I don't jump from high places.
[doctor] I understand. It is a standard protocol when an elderly patient falls and hits their head. We need to rule out other causes.
[patient] Like what?
[doctor] Like a medical event causing the fall. You mentioned the dizziness. Do you have any vision changes?
[patient] Yes. Sometimes things blur. I see double.
[doctor] That could be related to your thyroid. You have Hashimoto's thyroiditis, correct?
[patient] Yes. My TSH is high. I take Levothyroxine.
[doctor] When was your last lab work?
[patient] Two weeks ago. The results were... bad.
[doctor] Can you show me the paper?
[patient] Here. It says my TSH is 15.4. That is very high.
[doctor] Yes, that is significantly elevated. It could explain the fatigue and the dizziness. We need to adjust your dose.
[patient] Will it help?
[doctor] It might. But we also need to check for other conditions. Do you have any joint pain?
[patient] Yes. My knee. It swells up.
[doctor] Do you have a lump behind your knee?
[patient] No. But the doctor in Istanbul said it might be a Baker's cyst.
[doctor] I see. We will order an ultrasound of your knee to check for that.
[patient] And the dizziness?
[doctor] We need to rule out Graves' disease, even though your history suggests Hashimoto's. Sometimes the antibodies switch. We will order blood tests for TSI and TRAb.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] You also mentioned a tremor. Is it resting or action?
[patient] It is when I rest. When I hold a cup, it is okay. But when I sit, my hand shakes.
[doctor] That is classic for Parkinson's disease. We will refer you to neurology.
[patient] Will I have to go back to Istanbul?
[patient] No, you can see a specialist here in Berlin. I will write a referral.
[patient] Thank you.
[doctor] Now, let’s talk about the fall itself. You said you slipped on wet leaves.
[patient] Yes.
[doctor] Did you try to catch yourself?
[patient] Yes. I put my hand out. I broke my wrist.
[doctor] I see the cast. How is the pain?
[patient] It hurts. 6/10 maybe.
[doctor] Okay. Are you taking pain medication?
[patient] Yes. Paracetamol and sometimes Ibuprofen.
[doctor] Be careful with Ibuprofen. It can raise your blood pressure.
[patient] I will stop it.
[doctor] Good. Let’s look at your other medications. You have Omeprazole for stomach acid.
[patient] Yes. I have Crohn's disease.
[doctor] Is it active right now?
[patient] No. It is quiet. I just have it.
[doctor] I see. Do you have any facial weakness?
[patient] No.
[doctor] Just checking. Sometimes after a fall, we see Bell's palsy, but you don't have that.
[patient] Good.
[doctor] Now, Fatma, I want to discuss the police report. "Undetermined intent" can be problematic for insurance.
[patient] My insurance is AOK.
[doctor] I see. If they suspect self-harm, they might deny coverage.
[patient] I am not suicidal. I am just... tired.
[doctor] I believe you. But we need documentation. I will write a detailed note stating that the fall was due to syncope from hypothyroidism and ataxia, not intent.
[patient] Thank you.
[doctor] You should see Elif more often. She is your granddaughter, right?
[patient] Yes. She lives in Stuttgart.
[doctor] You are in Berlin?
[patient] Yes. I live alone in Charlottenburg.
[doctor] Living alone at 85 is risky. Did you have a fall risk assessment?
[patient] No.
[doctor] I will order one. Also, we need to check your vision.
[patient] My eyes are bad.
[doctor] We will refer you to ophthalmology.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] What about your diet? Do you eat enough?
[patient] Yes. My neighbor Mein brings me soup sometimes.
[doctor] Mein? Is that a person?
[patient] Yes. His name is Mein. He is nice.
[doctor] I see. Mein is a good name.
[patient] Yes.
[doctor] Back to the medical side. Your blood glucose is 110 mg/dL. That is acceptable.
[patient] I don't have diabetes.
[doctor] Correct. But we monitor it because of the steroids you might need for the Crohn's if it flares.
[patient] I don't take steroids now.
[doctor] Good.
[doctor] Let’s summarize. You fell due to syncope. You have hypothyroidism. You have a wrist fracture. You have a possible Parkinson's disease.
[patient] Yes.
[doctor] I am increasing your Levothyroxine dose. I am referring you to neurology for the tremor. I am ordering an ultrasound for the knee.
[patient] What about the head?
[doctor] The CT scan from yesterday was negative for bleeding. But you need rest.
[patient] How long?
[patient] Two weeks.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] When do you want to come back?
[patient] As soon as possible.
[doctor] Let’s schedule for October 15th at 10:30 AM.
[patient] Is that good?
[doctor] Yes.
[patient] I will be there.
[doctor] Please have Elif or Aylin drive you.
[patient] Elif will come.
[doctor] Good. If you fall again, call emergency services.
[patient] I will.
[doctor] Do you have any questions?
[patient] No. Thank you.
[doctor] You are welcome. Goodbye, Fatma.
[patient] Goodbye, doctor.

REFERRAL LETTER

Dear Dr. Schneider,

I am writing to refer my patient, Julian Baumann, 30-year-old male, for your evaluation and management of chronic left arm pain.

Mr. Baumann is a software engineer employed by TechNova Solutions in Zurich. He resides at Bahnhofstrasse 45, 8001 Zurich. He moved from Bern to Zurich approximately five years ago.

**History of Present Illness:**
Mr. Baumann presents with a 3-week history of left shoulder and upper arm pain, radiating to the elbow. The pain began around mid-October 2023, coinciding with increased work hours. He reports tingling sensations and stiffness in the neck. The pain is exacerbated by lifting the arm and looking over the shoulder. He recently traveled to Paris for a business trip, which did not involve injury but involved prolonged sitting.

**Previous Medical History:**
He has no significant past medical history other than a remote appendectomy. He previously visited Dr. Keller at Keller Medical Practice on October 15, 2023. Laboratory results from that visit showed a CRP of 8 mg/L and Vitamin D level of 12 ng/mL. He is currently self-medicating with <PROFESSSION>Nurofen</PROFESSSION> (ibuprofen) as needed.

**Physical Examination:**
- **Vitals:** BP 135/85 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, Temp 36.8°C.
- **Shoulder Exam:** Tenderness noted at the 3 o’clock position on the left shoulder. Limited range of motion behind the back.
- **Cervical Spine Exam:** Positive Spurling’s test on the left side, reproducing radicular pain down the left arm.

**Assessment:**
Suspected cervical radiculopathy or shoulder impingement syndrome. Given the positive neurological signs and persistence of symptoms despite conservative measures, I believe a specialist evaluation is warranted.

**Request:**
I would appreciate your assessment and further diagnostic workup (e.g., MRI, EMG) as deemed necessary. Please contact me or the patient’s employer, TechNova Solutions, if any workplace accommodations are required.

Patient’s AHV number: 756.12.345.678.90.

Sincerely,

Dr. Hans Meier
Meier General Practice
Zurich

note:
SUBJECTIVE
Patient is an 82-year-old male presenting with right elbow pain for three months. Pain described as deep, aching, 6/10 in severity, worse in the morning and with lifting activities. Onset occurred after lifting a heavy bucket of sand at a playground. Patient reports no numbness or tingling. Previous visit to Dr. Keller at Clinique de la Paix two weeks ago, prescribed painkillers with limited relief. Patient takes Lisinopril 10 mg daily for hypertension. Recently took a trip to London.

OBJECTIVE
Vital Signs: BP 140/90 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, Temp 36.8°C.
Physical Exam:
- Right elbow: Tenderness over the lateral epicondyle. Pain with resisted wrist extension. Range of motion slightly limited by pain. No swelling, no warmth, no skin changes.
- Neurological: Intact sensation in fingers, normal grip strength (limited by pain).

ASSESSMENT
1. Lateral epicondylitis (Tennis Elbow), Right.
2. Essential Hypertension, stable but elevated on today's check.

PLAN
1. Referral to Physiotherapy: Twice weekly for 6 weeks for strengthening and stretching exercises. Referral sent to Physio Center Neuchâtel.
2. Medication:
   - Discontinue Ibuprofen.
   - Start topical diclofenac gel, apply 4 times daily to the elbow.
   - Acetaminophen 500 mg as needed for pain, max 3g/day.
3. Home Care: Ice the elbow for 15 minutes after activity if pain flares up. Avoid heavy lifting.
4. Follow-up: Monitor blood pressure at home. Log readings.
5. Appointment: Follow-up in clinic on October 15 at 10:30 am to reassess progress.
6. Labs: None indicated at this time.
dialogue:
[doctor] Bonjour, Monsieur Dubois. I see you’re here for an elbow issue. How are you feeling today?
[patient] Bonjour, Doctor. To be honest, not great. The pain in my right elbow has been getting worse for three months.
[doctor] Three months is a long time to be in pain. Can you describe the onset? When did it first start?
[patient] It started gradually. I was helping my grandson at the playground in the park near his school. I lifted a heavy bucket of sand, and the next day, the arm felt stiff and sore.
[doctor] So, a specific movement triggered it. What kind of pain is it? Sharp, dull, burning?
[patient] It’s a deep, aching pain. Like a bruise that won’t heal. It’s about a 6 out of 10 on a scale of 1 to 10 when I lift things.
[doctor] And when is it most severe?
[patient] In the morning, right after I wake up. It takes an hour or two to loosen up. By 2 pm, it’s better, but it flares up if I use the arm too much.
[doctor] I see. Let’s take a look. Please extend your arm on the table. I’m going to palpate the area. Does this hurt?
[patient] Yes, right there. Just above the bone on the outside.
[doctor] That’s the lateral epicondyle. This is a classic sign. Let’s check your range of motion. Try to clench your fist against my hand.
[patient] Ugh. That’s painful.
[doctor] I understand. You have tenderness over the lateral epicondyle and pain with resisted wrist extension. This is consistent with lateral epicondylitis, commonly known as tennis elbow.
[patient] Tennis elbow? I haven’t played tennis in years. I’m an accountant, not an athlete.
[doctor] The name is a bit misleading. It’s often caused by repetitive strain or a sudden strain, like lifting that bucket of sand. At 82, the tendons are less elastic, so they’re more prone to injury.
[patient] I see. I’m worried it’s something worse. Arthritis, maybe?
[doctor] Arthritis is possible, but the location of the pain and the specific trigger points point more toward tendinitis. Let’s rule out other issues. Do you have any numbness or tingling in your fingers?
[patient] No, not really. Just the pain.
[doctor] Good. That makes nerve compression less likely. When was your last visit to a doctor for this?
[patient] I saw Dr. Keller at Clinique de la Paix in Fribourg two weeks ago. He gave me some painkillers.
[doctor] And did those help?
[patient] A little, but not enough. I’m still struggling to hold a coffee cup in the morning.
[doctor] I see. Let’s look at your history. You mentioned you moved from Geneva?
[patient] Yes, I lived in Geneva for forty years before moving to Neuchâtel last year to be closer to my daughter.
[doctor] I understand. And your record number here is CH-7742019. I have your previous records. I see you had a hip replacement in March 2021.
[patient] Yes, that was a while ago. I’m doing well with that now.
[doctor] Good. Any other medical conditions? Diabetes, hypertension?
[patient] Just high blood pressure. I take medication for it.
[doctor] What medication are you currently taking?
[patient] Lisinopril 10 mg daily. And I take ibuprofen for the elbow pain, maybe twice a day.
[doctor] Okay. I’m concerned about the ibuprofen, especially with your blood pressure and age. Let’s discuss a different plan. I’ll refer you to a physiotherapist for specific exercises.
[patient] Physiotherapy? Is that necessary?
[doctor] Yes, it’s crucial. Exercises will strengthen the forearm muscles and reduce strain on the tendon. I’ll also prescribe a topical anti-inflammatory cream. It has fewer side effects than oral painkillers.
[patient] That sounds better. How often should I see the physiotherapist?
[doctor] Twice a week for six weeks. I’ll send the referral to Physio Center Neuchâtel. You can contact them at info@physiocenter-ne.ch to book an appointment.
[patient] I will. Do I need an X-ray?
[doctor] Not at this stage. The clinical diagnosis is clear. If the pain doesn’t improve after six weeks of physiotherapy and medication, we might consider an MRI to rule out other issues like a tear or bone spur.
[patient] Okay. I had a trip to London last month. I did a lot of walking and sightseeing. Did that make it worse?
[doctor] It’s possible. Increased activity can aggravate the condition. It’s important to rest and ice the area when the pain flares up.
[patient] I’ll be careful. My blood pressure was 140/90 yesterday. Is that okay?
[doctor] It’s a bit high. Please monitor it at home and keep a log. Bring the log to your next appointment. If it stays above 140/90, we may need to adjust your medication.
[patient] I will. So, no more ibuprofen?
[doctor] I recommend stopping it. Use the cream instead. If you need pain relief, you can use acetaminophen, but avoid the NSAIDs like ibuprofen for now.
[patient] Understood. I’ll use the cream and the acetaminophen if needed.
[doctor] Perfect. Let’s schedule a follow-up in six weeks to see how you’re progressing.
[patient] That works. I’ll come in on October 15?
[doctor] Yes, October 15 at 10:30 am is free. I’ll book that now.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor. I feel a bit more confident now.
[doctor] You’re welcome. Remember, consistency with the exercises is key. Rest when it hurts, but keep moving gently.
[patient] I will. Thanks.
[doctor] Goodbye, Monsieur Dubois.
[patient] Goodbye.

note:
SUBJECTIVE
Werner Braun, an 84-year-old male, presents for an occupational health visit regarding a non-pressure chronic ulcer on the right foot. He reports the onset of symptoms approximately three weeks ago during a trip to Switzerland. He describes the pain as throbbing, rated 7/10, which worsens with weight-bearing. He is a retired accountant who moved from Stuttgart to Munich ten years ago. He resides with his son in Munich. He was referred by Dr. Heinrich Müller from University Hospital Cologne for wound management. Past medical history is significant for Parkinson’s disease (diagnosed 5 years ago), Hashimoto’s thyroiditis (diagnosed 2 years ago), and hypertension. Current medications include Levodopa/Carbidopa 250/25 mg TID, Euthyrox 75 mcg daily, and Aspirin 100 mg daily. He denies fever, chills, or systemic symptoms. He mentions enjoying watching Bayern Munich football but has reduced mobility due to pain.

OBJECTIVE
Vitals: BP 145/85 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, Temp 36.8°C, SpO2 98% on room air.
General: Alert, oriented x3. No acute distress.
Neurological: Mild rigidity in upper and lower extremities. Resting tremor in hands. Bradykinesia noted. Reflexes 2+ bilaterally.
Musculoskeletal: Right foot: 2 cm x 1.5 cm ulcer on the lateral aspect of the midfoot. Wound bed is 50% granulation tissue, 30% slough, 20% necrotic tissue. No purulent discharge. Surrounding skin is slightly erythematous but not warm. Capillary refill < 3 seconds in toes. Pulses: Dorsalis pedis 1+, Posterior tibial 1+ bilaterally.
Labs (pending): CBC, BMP, HbA1c ordered.

ASSESSMENT
1. Non-pressure chronic ulcer of other part of right foot, unspecified severity (ICD-10: L97.519). Likely secondary to neuropathy from Parkinson’s disease and poor circulation.
2. Parkinson’s disease, moderate stage.
3. Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, controlled.
4. Hypertension, stage 1.

PLAN
1. Wound Care:
- Debridement of necrotic tissue performed in clinic.
- Apply non-adherent moist dressing (e.g., Adaptic) followed by Flexifix tape.
- Instruct patient to clean wound with normal saline twice daily.
- Elevate right leg 30 minutes twice daily to reduce edema.

2. Medications:
- Start Duloxetin 30 mg daily for neuropathic pain. Increase to 60 mg after one week if tolerated.
- Continue Levodopa/Carbidopa and Euthyrox as prescribed.
- Continue Aspirin 100 mg daily.

3. Referrals:
- Vascular Surgery consult at St. Josef Hospital for assessment of peripheral arterial disease.
- Physical Therapy for balance and gait training, focusing on safe ambulation.

4. Follow-up:
- Return to clinic in one week for wound re-evaluation.
- If signs of infection (increased redness, warmth, purulence, fever) develop, return immediately or contact office at 089-1234567.

5. Labs:
- Review CBC, BMP, and HbA1c results before next visit.

I am writing to refer my patient, Mr. Vance, aged 80, for evaluation and management of unspecified atrial fibrillation. He presented to our clinic today for a follow-up visit.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Vance reports recurrent episodes of palpitations and fatigue. He recently traveled to Portland to visit his daughter, Sarah (48), during which he experienced dizziness. He is currently compliant with his prescribed Eliquis. He also reports a recent injury to his right knee, sustained in the kitchen, with a pain score of 4/10.

RELEVANT HISTORY
Family history is significant for his father suffering a stroke at 75. He has no known history of cardiac conditions other than the current arrhythmia. He is otherwise independent.

EXAMINATION AND VITALS
- Blood Pressure: 110/70 mmHg
- Heart Rate: 112 bpm, irregularly irregular
- Oxygen Saturation: 94% on room air
- Pain: 4/10 at the right knee

LABORATORY DATA
Blood work has been ordered to assess renal function (Creatinine) and electrolytes, given his age and anticoagulation status.

PLAN
1. Continue current anticoagulation therapy with Eliquis.
2. Monitor renal function.
3. Referral to cardiology for potential rhythm control or ablation evaluation.
4. Home care for knee injury with ice and elevation.

Sincerely,

Dr. Sarah Jenkins
Springfield General Clinic
123 Maple Avenue, Apt 4B, Springfield, IL 62704
555-019-8822

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
Patient presents with acute onset of pain, swelling, and erythema in the left ankle and first metatarsophalangeal joint. Symptoms began two weeks ago after walking in a park. Pain is exacerbated by weight-bearing and physical activity, including a recent session at the gym. Morning stiffness is present. Patient reports no fever or systemic symptoms. Patient recently traveled to Kandy, Sri Lanka for a family wedding.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
No prior history of gout, kidney stones, or autoimmune diseases. Patient mentions family history of arthritis in her mother and kidney issues in her brother. Patient denies history of Bell’s palsy or other neurological conditions.

SOCIAL HISTORY:
Patient is a secondary school teacher at Lyceum Zurich. She reports standing for long periods during work hours. She recently returned from a trip to Sri Lanka. She takes blood pressure medication manufactured by Novartis.

EXAMINATION:
Vitals: BP 130/85, HR 72, Temp 36.8°C.
Left ankle: Mild edema, warmth, and tenderness. Range of motion limited by pain.
Left foot: Erythema and swelling over the first MTP joint. No open wounds or skin lesions.

ASSESSMENT:
1. Acute monoarthritis, left ankle and foot. Differential diagnosis includes acute gout, septic arthritis, or reactive arthritis. Gout is the most likely diagnosis given the presentation and demographics.
2. Hypertension (stable).

PLAN:
1. Blood tests ordered: Uric acid, CRP, ESR, CBC, and renal panel to rule out infection and confirm gout.
2. Prescription: Ibuprofen 400 mg PO TID for pain and inflammation.
3. Advice: Rest, elevation of the affected limb, hydration, and dietary modifications (reduce red meat and alcohol).
4. Follow-up: Patient scheduled for 18 October 2024 at 10:30 to review lab results.
5. Patient advised to contact clinic at 044 123 45 67 or email e.vane@derm-zurich.ch for any urgent concerns.
6. Patient educated on non-contagious nature of the condition and safe return to work.

[doctor] Good morning, Ms. Ellis. I see you’re here for a follow-up regarding the transient tics you’ve been experiencing. Before we begin, can you confirm your date of birth and current address for our records?

[patient] Good morning, Dr. Thorne. My date of birth is March 14, 1981. I currently live at 452 Oakwood Lane, Apt 3B, Seattle, WA 98101.

[doctor] Thank you. And who referred you to my clinic initially?

[patient] It was Dr. Halloway from Cascade Neuroscience Center. She thought the tics might be neurological, but after some tests, she suggested seeing a urologist because the episodes seemed to start during bladder retention.

[doctor] I see. You mentioned in the intake form that you moved here recently. Where did you come from?

[patient] I moved from Portland, Oregon about two years ago. I found the weather here a bit milder, though the humidity has been tricky.

[doctor] How have the tics been since our last visit? You’re 43 years old, and at this age, we want to ensure there isn’t an underlying structural issue.

[patient] It’s been better, but not gone. I still get the facial twitching, especially around the eyes. It usually happens in the afternoon. I’ve been trying to manage it with the Seattle Central Gym workouts, but stress seems to make it worse.

[doctor] What kind of workouts do you do there?

[patient] Mostly yoga and some strength training. My friend Jessica goes there too; she’s actually a trainer. She’s been very supportive.

[doctor] That’s good to have support. Let’s review your vitals. Your blood pressure is 128/82, heart rate is 76, and your pain score for any associated discomfort is a 3 out of 10. Do you have any pain with urination?

[patient] Only a mild stinging sometimes, especially if I hold it for a long time. I work as a graphic designer, so I often forget to take breaks to use the bathroom.

[doctor] That retention could be aggravating the autonomic response leading to the tics. Let’s do a quick physical exam. I’m going to check your abdomen and pelvic floor. Do you have any allergies?

[patient] No, I don’t think so. I’m not allergic to anything specific. I do take Zoloft for anxiety, which Dr. Halloway prescribed.

[doctor] Noted. During the exam, I noticed a slight tenderness at the 3 o’clock position on your bladder dome, which correlates with the area where you feel the urge to move. This is consistent with a neurogenic bladder component.

[patient] Does that mean I have a serious bladder problem?

[doctor] Not necessarily. It suggests that your bladder nerve signals are a bit hypersensitive. We’ve started you on Oxybutynin to relax the bladder muscle. How is that working for you?

[patient] It helps with the urgency, but I feel a bit dry in the mouth. I’ve been drinking more water, which helps, but I’m worried about the side effects.

[doctor] Dry mouth is a common side effect. Try sugar-free gum. Also, we ordered a urinalysis last week. The results showed a white blood cell count of 15 per high-power field, which suggests a mild infection. That could be contributing to the irritation.

[patient] An infection? I didn’t have any other symptoms.

[doctor] Sometimes infections are asymptomatic, especially in women. We’ve started you on Bactrim for seven days. Make sure to finish the entire course.

[patient] I will. I’ve been taking it since Monday. I started feeling a bit better yesterday, but the tics are still there.

[doctor] The tics may take longer to resolve once the infection is cleared and the bladder is less irritated. Let’s also review your lab work. Your creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL, which is normal. Your blood sugar is 92 mg/dL, also normal.

[patient] That’s a relief. I was worried about diabetes since my mother had it.

[doctor] It’s good that your levels are normal. Keep up with your hydration and try to schedule bathroom breaks every two hours during work.

[patient] I’ll try to set a timer on my phone. I’ve been working from home since last spring, so it’s easier to forget.

[doctor] Working from home can be tricky for routine. Have you been able to see Jessica at the gym recently?

[patient] Yes, we went to the Seattle Central Gym on Saturday. It was nice to get out of the house. I’ve been feeling isolated since moving to Seattle.

[doctor] It’s important to maintain social connections. Stress management is key for tic disorders. Have you considered cognitive behavioral therapy?

[patient] I’ve looked into it, but I’m not sure my insurance covers it. My provider is Blue Cross Blue Shield.

[doctor] Let me check with our billing department. In the meantime, continue the Bactrim and Oxybutynin. If the tics worsen or you develop fever, go to the emergency room.

[patient] I will. I’m glad to hear that it’s not something more serious. I just want to get back to normal.

[doctor] That’s a reasonable goal. We’ll re-evaluate in four weeks. If the tics persist, we might consider a referral back to Dr. Halloway for a neuropsychological evaluation.

[patient] That sounds like a good plan. Thank you, Dr. Thorne.

[doctor] You’re welcome. Please make sure to drink plenty of water and avoid caffeine, which can irritate the bladder.

[patient] I drink a lot of coffee, so that will be hard, but I’ll try to cut back.

[doctor] Even reducing by half a cup a day can help. Do you have any questions before we wrap up?

[patient] No, I think I’m clear. I’ll call if I have any issues.

[doctor] Great. The nurse will be with you to discuss the next steps and provide the prescription information.

[patient] Thank you.

[doctor] Take care, Ms. Ellis.

[patient] Goodbye.

I would appreciate your assessment and recommendation for a repeat renal biopsy.

[doctor] Good morning, Mr. Perera. Please, have a seat. You’re here with your daughter, Amaya, correct?

[patient] Uh, it was... maybe two weeks ago. I was walking home from the train station in Basel and I felt it getting heavy. Just the left side.

[doctor] I see. And has it changed since then?

[patient] It got a bit worse. Now it is puffy. Like, you know, the skin is tight. I have some pain too, not sharp, but a dull ache. Maybe 4 out of 10?

[doctor] Understood. 4 out of 10 on a pain scale. Let’s take a look. Please remove your trousers and socks. I will check your pulses and look for any signs of clots.

[nurse] Here is the blood pressure cuff. Mr. Perera, can you roll up your right sleeve?

[patient] Yes, yes.

[nurse] Blood pressure is 135 over 85. Heart rate is 78 beats per minute. Temperature is normal.

[doctor] Thank you. Now, looking at the leg. There is some pitting edema around the ankle. Let me check the groin area. Hmm. I feel a small, firm lump here, at the 3 o'clock position relative to the inguinal ligament. It is slightly tender.

[patient] Ah, that is the spot. It hurts a little when I press it.

[doctor] I suspect this might be an inguinal hernia that has become incarcerated, causing the swelling and pain in the leg. We need to do an ultrasound to be sure. But first, I need to update your file. Your health insurance is with Swisscare, correct?

[patient] Yes. The policy number is SC-774-992-10.

[doctor] And your AHV number?

[patient] It is 756.921.445.678.12.

[doctor] Thank you. I will send the referral to the radiology department here at University Hospital Zurich.

[patient_guest] Doctor, is it serious? Is it cancer?

[doctor] I do not think it is cancer, Amaya. The presentation is more consistent with a mechanical issue like a hernia or perhaps a deep vein thrombosis. We will rule out the clot first with the ultrasound and a D-dimer blood test.

[patient] My brother, Kumar, had a hernia when he was forty-five. So I was worried.

[doctor] That is good to know for family history. Your mother, what about her health?

[patient] My mother passed away, unfortunately. But my brother Kumar is 52 now. He is very healthy.

[doctor] Okay. Let’s order the blood work. We will check your D-dimer, complete blood count, and kidney function.

[patient] Do I need to stop eating?

[patient] Yes, I play at the Basel Lawn Tennis Club. I go there every Tuesday and Thursday evening.

[patient] Okay, okay. No tennis.

REASON FOR VISIT
Patient presented with complaints of visual field defects, specifically missing the right side of her visual field while walking and during exercise at Studio Zenith in Lausanne. Symptoms began approximately two weeks ago.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient reports a gradual onset of visual disturbances. She noticed a gap in her vision on the right side, which led to a near-collision with a lamppost yesterday. She denies any history of trauma, though she mentions a family history of vascular issues; her mother’s brother, Jean, had a brain aneurysm. She reports mild headache, rated 4/10, on the right side. She has been taking lisinopril for hypertension.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Hypertension. No known allergies. No previous strokes or seizures.

Patient is active in pilates at Studio Zenith. She commutes between Lausanne, Fribourg, and Neuchâtel for work. She resides in Lausanne.

Vital Signs:
Blood Pressure: 140/85 mmHg
Pulse: 92 bpm
Temperature: 36.8 °C
Pain Score: 4/10 (right-sided headache)

Neurological Examination:
Visual Acuity: 20/20 bilaterally.
Pupils: Equal and reactive to light.
Fundoscopy: No papilledema.
Visual Field Testing:
Goldmann perimetry revealed heteronymous bilateral field defects. Specifically, there is an upper quadrantanopia in the right eye and a lower quadrantanopia in the left eye. This pattern suggests a lesion affecting the optic chiasm or adjacent structures, possibly involving the optic nerves.

DIAGNOSIS
Heteronymous bilateral field defects. Differential diagnosis includes optic chiasm compression (e.g., craniopharyngioma, meningioma), optic neuritis (multiple sclerosis), or vascular events.

1. MRI of the brain and orbits with contrast, ordered for Hôpital de Lausanne.

Sports Medicine Clinic

Right elbow pain, acute on chronic.

Jan Kowalski, a 19-year-old male, presents with right elbow pain. The pain began two weeks ago as a dull ache and worsened yesterday following a basketball game with his friend Piotr (21). The patient reports sharp pain with gripping and extension. He is a student and works part-time as a delivery driver for Swift Logistics. He trains frequently at Iron Grit Gym, performing heavy bench presses. He was seen by Dr. Weber at City Clinic Berlin three days ago, who suspected tendinitis and prescribed anti-inflammatories, which provided minimal relief.

No significant past medical history.

Mother, Ewa (55), has rheumatoid arthritis. Brother, Marek (24), had lateral epicondylitis two years ago.

Ibuprofen (started 3 days ago).

NKDA (No Known Drug Allergies).

BP 118/76 mmHg
HR 72 bpm

Lateral epicondylitis (Tennis Elbow), right elbow.

SUBJECTIVE
Patient Ivana, 82 years old, female, presents with daughter Milica, 38, for geriatric consultation. Chief complaint: fatigue and abdominal discomfort. History of unspecified viral hepatitis C diagnosed in 2018. History of Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Recent injury in the kitchen (slip and fall) resulting in elbow contusion. Patient reports decreased appetite and mild pruritus. No signs of hepatic coma. Patient is from Serbia, residing in Austria.

OBJECTIVE
Vitals stable. General appearance: tired, alert. Abdominal exam: mild tenderness in the right upper quadrant. Skin: mild pruritus, no jaundice. Mole noted on right shoulder at the 3 o'clock position, appears stable. Neurological exam: mild tremor, no focal deficits. No asterixis.

ASSESSMENT
1. Unspecified viral hepatitis C, chronic. No evidence of decompensation or hepatic coma.
2. Hashimoto's thyroiditis.
3. Contusion of right elbow, post-traumatic (kitchen injury).
4. Mole, right shoulder, 3 o'clock position, likely benign.

PLAN
1. Refer to hepatology clinic at Klinische Abteilung für Innere Medizin am AKH for further management of hepatitis C. Appointment scheduled for 12 October 2023 at 10:00.
2. Blood work: Liver function tests, complete blood count, thyroid function tests.
3. Monitor for signs of liver failure (jaundice, confusion, dark urine).
4. Continue current medications for Hashimoto's.
5. Avoid alcohol.
6. Follow-up in 4 weeks.
7. Insurance: SVS, ID SVS-1941-0514-8823.

[doctor] Good morning. I am Dr. Thaler. Please, have a seat. I see you are here for a geriatric consultation, but you look quite young. Can you tell me who you are and why we are meeting today?

[patient] Yes. My mother lives with me. We are in Austria now, but we are from Serbia. She has been feeling very tired for months. Um, and her stomach hurts sometimes.
[doctor] I see. Let's look at her records. Ivana, born 14 May 1941. I see she is registered with SVS. Do you have her insurance number with you?
[patient] Yes, here. It is SVS-1941-0514-8823. I checked it last week when I called the office.
[doctor] Thank you. So, the main concern is that she has a diagnosis of unspecified viral hepatitis C. Do you know when she was diagnosed?
[patient] Oh, um, it was a long time ago. Maybe 2018? I think she had blood tests because she felt weak. The doctor said it was hepatitis, but not the kind that makes people die quickly, you know? Just... it is there.

[patient] Not really coma, no. But she is very sleepy during the day. And last week, she got a little hurt. It was in the kitchen. She slipped on a wet floor.
[doctor] In the kitchen at home? Did she hit her head?
[patient] No, no head. She hit her elbow. I thought maybe she had a Baker's cyst or something, but the doctor said it was just a bruise. She is also on medication for Hashimoto's thyroiditis. That has been there for years.
[doctor] Hashimoto's is an autoimmune thyroid condition. That can cause fatigue, which might overlap with the liver issues. Let's examine her. Nurse, could you please bring in Ivana?
[nurse] Of course, Dr. Thaler. Ivana, please come in.
[patient] Mom, it is okay. The doctor is nice.
[patient_guest] Hello. I am Ivana.
[doctor] Hello, Ivana. I am Dr. Thaler. Milica is your daughter. I would like to ask you a few questions and check your health. Can you hear me clearly?
[patient_guest] Yes... yes, doctor. I am a little tired.
[doctor] How is your appetite? Are you eating well?
[patient_guest] Um, not much. I don't like food much lately. Maybe some soup.
[doctor] Okay. Do you feel any itching in your skin?
[patient_guest] Yes, a little. On my arms.
[doctor] Understood. Let's take a look at your abdomen. I will press gently. Tell me if it hurts.
[patient_guest] Okay.
[doctor] Does this hurt here? Near the right side?
[patient_guest] A little bit. Yes.
[doctor] And here?
[patient_guest] No, that is okay.
[doctor] Thank you. Now, I need to check your reflexes and coordination. Please, extend your arm.
[patient_guest] Like this?
[doctor] Yes. I see a slight tremor. This can happen with liver issues, but also with medication. Let's check your eyes. Look at this finger.
[patient_guest] I am looking.
[doctor] Good. I notice a small lesion on your right shoulder. It looks like a mole. It is located at the 3 o'clock position relative to your spine. It looks stable, but I will note it.
[patient] Oh, I didn't see that. Is it bad?
[doctor] It looks benign, but we will monitor it. It is not related to the hepatitis.
[patient] Okay. I am just worried because she had that injury in the kitchen. I was thinking maybe it was the floor. It was slippery.
[doctor] The injury in the kitchen was a soft tissue bruise, correct?
[patient] Yes. The nurse said to put ice on it. She did that.
[doctor] Good. Now, Milica, let's discuss the plan. Ivana has chronic hepatitis C. The goal is to prevent liver damage from progressing to cirrhosis or failure.
[patient] What do we do?
[doctor] We need to monitor her liver function tests regularly. We will do a blood test today. We also need to check her thyroid levels because of the Hashimoto's.
[patient] Okay. Does she need a doctor who specializes in liver?

Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR): 40 mm/hr (Elevated)
Complete Blood Count: Within normal limits
Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH): 2.1 mIU/L (Normal)

ASSESSMENT
Right hand synovitis and tenosynovitis, likely inflammatory in nature. Differential diagnosis includes early seronegative rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, or reactive arthritis. Given the elevated inflammatory markers, autoimmune etiology is suspected. No evidence of acute infection.

PLAN
1. Medication Adjustment:
   - Increase celecoxib to 200 mg orally twice daily.
   - Initiate prednisone 10 mg orally daily for 14 days, with taper as tolerated.
2. Laboratory Workup:
   - Order comprehensive autoimmune panel including ANA, anti-CCP, RF, HLA-B27, and Thyroid Antibodies.
3. Non-Pharmacologic Management:
   - Apply ice packs to the right hand for 15 minutes, three times daily.
   - Elevate the right hand when resting.
   - Avoid heavy lifting and repetitive stress on the right hand.
4. Follow-up:
   - Return to clinic in 2 weeks to review lab results and assess response to therapy.
   - If symptoms persist or worsen, refer to Rheumatology.
5. Contact Information:
   - Patient should contact the office at 555-019-2834 or via email at contact@nephrocareclinic.com for any acute changes or concerns.
   - Prescription sent to Walgreens at 5th and Main.

note:
SUBJECTIVE
Patient is an 86-year-old male, Harry G. Thorne, presenting with right elbow pain and increased urinary frequency. Elbow pain started approximately two weeks ago after a fall while gardening. He reports sharp pain with lifting, rated 6-7/10. No numbness or tingling. Urinary symptoms include nocturia (3-4 times/night) and a single episode of pink-tinged urine. Patient recently traveled to San Diego in October. He is insured by Blue Cross Blue Shield with ID BCBS-8921-447-90. He is currently taking Lisinopril for hypertension, managed by his PCP, Dr. Evans.

OBJECTIVE
Vitals: BP 135/85 mmHg, HR 78 bpm.
Right elbow exam: Tenderness to palpation at the 3 o'clock position relative to the lateral epicondyle. Pain with resisted wrist extension (positive Cozen's test). Range of motion limited in flexion.
Urinalysis: Ordered.
PSA: Ordered.

ASSESSMENT
1. Right lateral epicondylitis (Tennis Elbow) secondary to trauma/overuse.
2. Nocturia, likely secondary to benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), rule out hematuria.
3. Hypertension, stable.

PLAN
1. Elbow:
   - Ibuprofen 400 mg PO TID with food x 1 week.
   - Referral to Physical Therapy for stretching and strengthening exercises.
   - Rest and activity modification.
2. Urology:
   - Urinalysis and PSA sent to lab.
   - Follow up with results in 1 week.
   - Lifestyle modifications: limit caffeine/alcohol in evening.
3. Hypertension:
   - Continue Lisinopril.
   - Monitor BP at home.
   - Note sent to Dr. Evans.
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning. I see you’re here for an elbow issue, but the referral was from urology?
[patient] Uh, yeah. That’s the thing. I’m Harry G. Thorne, and I’m 86 years old. I live in Phoenix.
[doctor] Nice to meet you, Mr. Thorne. Let’s start with the elbow. When did the pain start?
[patient] Oh, about two weeks ago. I was gardening, you know, and I slipped.
[doctor] Slipped on what?
[patient] Just the ground. I fell on my right side. My neighbor, Betty, actually helped me up. She’s very kind.
[doctor] And the pain has been constant since then?
[patient] Mostly. It’s worse when I lift things. Like, I can’t even hold a coffee mug properly anymore.
[doctor] How would you rate the pain on a scale of 0 to 10, with 10 being the worst?
[patient] Uh, maybe a 6? Maybe 7 when it’s really bothering me.
[doctor] Okay. Any numbness or tingling in your fingers?
[patient] No, I don’t think so. Just the ache.
[doctor] Let’s take a look. Can you roll up your sleeve?
[patient] Sure.
[doctor] I’m going to palpate the lateral aspect of your elbow. Does this hurt?
[patient] Oh! Yes. Right there. It’s sharp.
[doctor] I’m feeling some tenderness at the 3 o'clock position relative to the elbow joint.
[patient] That’s the spot.
[doctor] And here?
[patient] No, that’s fine.
[doctor] Let’s check your range of motion. Try to bend your arm.
[patient] It’s stiff. I can’t get it all the way down.
[doctor] How far can you go?
[patient] Maybe halfway?
[doctor] And extending it?
[patient] That’s okay. It’s the bending that hurts.
[doctor] I’m going to do a quick test. I’ll apply pressure to the back of your hand while you extend your elbow.
[patient] Oh, that hurts.
[doctor] That’s a positive Cozen’s test. It suggests lateral epicondylitis, or "tennis elbow," even though you might not play tennis.
[patient] I don’t play tennis. I’m too old for that.
[doctor] Exactly. It’s often from repetitive strain or a minor injury. Now, since you’re in a urology clinic, I assume you have some other concerns?
[patient] Yes. I’ve been having some trouble with my urine. Frequent trips, especially at night.
[doctor] How often are you getting up at night?
[patient] Three, maybe four times.
[doctor] Any pain or burning when you urinate?
[patient] No, not really. Just the frequency.
[doctor] Have you had any blood in your urine?
[patient] I think I saw a little pink once. Maybe it was the light.
[doctor] I’m going to order a urinalysis to check for that. Also, given your age, we should check your prostate-specific antigen level.
[patient] Is that dangerous?
[doctor] No, it’s just a blood test. It helps us rule out prostate issues.
[patient] Okay. I was just in San Diego for my son’s birthday last month.
[doctor] Last month?
[patient] Yes, in October.
[doctor] Did you travel far?
[patient] Just a drive. We stayed at a hotel near the beach.
[doctor] And did you notice any changes in your urinary symptoms while you were there?
[patient] I think it was a bit worse. I was drinking more water, so maybe that’s why.
[doctor] Staying hydrated is good, but it can increase frequency. Now, let’s talk about your insurance. Do you have your card with you?
[patient] Yes, here. It’s Blue Cross Blue Shield.
[doctor] And your insurance ID number?
[patient] It’s BCBS-8921-447-90.
[doctor] Thank you. I’ll note that down. Now, for the elbow, I’m going to prescribe some anti-inflammatory medication. Have you taken anything for the pain?
[patient] Just Advil sometimes.
[doctor] I’d like you to take Ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day with food for one week.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] And I’ll refer you to a physical therapist for some stretching exercises. They can help with the stiffness.
[patient] Will that hurt?
[doctor] No, it’s gentle. It’s about regaining flexibility.
[patient] What about the urine?
[doctor] We’ll wait for the lab results. In the meantime, try to limit caffeine and alcohol, especially in the evening.
[patient] I don’t drink much alcohol. Just a little wine with dinner.
[doctor] That’s fine, but try to stop it a few hours before bed.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] Let’s check your vitals while we’re here. Your blood pressure is 135 over 85. Pulse is 78.
[patient] Is that high?
[doctor] It’s slightly elevated, but not alarming. We’ll monitor it.
[patient] I take Lisinopril for that.
[doctor] Good. Keep taking it as prescribed.
[patient] I do. My doctor, Dr. Evans, checks it every month.
[doctor] Who is Dr. Evans?
[patient] My primary care physician.
[doctor] I’ll send a note to them with our findings.
[patient] That’s good. I want to make sure everyone is on the same page.
[doctor] Absolutely. Now, do you have any questions?
[patient] Just... will the elbow get better?
[doctor] With rest, medication, and physical therapy, yes. It should improve over a few weeks.
[patient] And the urine?
[doctor] We’ll see the lab results in a few days. If it’s benign prostatic hyperplasia, which is common at your age, we can manage it.
[patient] Okay. I’m just glad to be here.
[doctor] You’re in good hands. We’ll take care of it.
[patient] Thank you.
[doctor] My nurse will get you started on the medication and the referral.
[patient] She’s nice.
[doctor] Yes, she is. She’s very helpful.
[patient] I’ll see her in a bit.
[doctor] Take your time.
[patient] Thanks.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

PATIENT IDENTIFICATION
Name: Ayse Kaya
Date of Birth: 12 March 1961
Age: 62
Record Number: HR-2023-8842
Address: Gartenstrasse 14, 60316 Frankfurt
Employer: Bosch Logistics
Occupation: Warehouse Manager

Telehealth consultation for worsening symptoms of hypertensive heart disease with heart failure.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient presents with progressive dyspnea on exertion and orthopnea over the past three weeks. Reports significant peripheral edema and a weight gain of 4 kg in two weeks. Patient recently returned from a vacation in Bodrum, where she reports increased dietary sodium intake. Missed some doses of Entresto during travel. PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
- Hypertensive Heart Disease
- Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF)
- History of hypertension since 1990
- Moved from Adana to Germany in 1990

- Cardiovascular: Orthopnea (2 pillows), paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, bilateral lower extremity edema.
- Respiratory: No wheezing, no hemoptysis.
- Neurological: No dizziness or syncope.
- General: Fatigue, weight gain.

- Heart Rate: 88 bpm
- Pain Score: 3/10 (subjective discomfort)

- Echocardiogram: 20 January 2024 (EF 35%)
- Previous physician: Dr. Werner (General Practice)

Dr. Julia Meyer
St. Hedwig's Cardiology Clinic
dialogue:
[doctor] Good afternoon, this is Dr. Meyer from St. Hedwig's Cardiology Clinic. I am looking at your record for Ayse Kaya. Do you have a moment to talk?

[doctor] No problem at all. I see your last visit was on 15 October 2023. How have you been feeling since then?
[patient] Honestly, not great. I feel very tired. For the last three weeks, I have been short of breath when I climb the stairs in my apartment.
[doctor] That is concerning. Do you have to stop and rest?
[patient] Yes, I have to sit down for a few minutes. Also, my legs are very swollen. I can't put on my old shoes anymore.
[doctor] I see. And have you weighed yourself recently?
[patient] Yes, I bought a new scale. Yesterday morning, I weighed 82.4 kilograms. That is four kilograms more than two weeks ago.
[doctor] Okay, that is a significant weight gain. It suggests fluid retention. Let's check your blood pressure. Can you bring your cuff to the camera?
[patient] One moment. Yes, here it is.
[doctor] Please wait... Okay, it reads 165/95. That is quite high. Have you been taking your medication as prescribed?
[patient] I take my Carvedilol and Entresto every morning. But I missed some doses last week because I was on vacation.
[doctor] Where were you?
[patient] I went to Bodrum for a week. I was visiting my sister. I think the salt in the food was too much.
[doctor] Dietary salt is a major trigger for heart failure exacerbations. Do you remember any other symptoms? Chest pain?
[patient] No sharp pain. Just a heaviness in my chest. And I cough at night. I have to sleep with two pillows instead of one.
[doctor] That is called orthopnea. It happens when fluid builds up in the lungs. Did you see your general practitioner, Dr. Werner, before this visit?
[patient] No, I was in Bodrum. But my neighbor, Mrs. Elif, told me to call you. She is a retired nurse, so she knows what to look for.
[doctor] Mrs. Elif is right to be concerned. We need to get your fluid levels down. I am going to increase your Furosemide dose.
[patient] How much?
[doctor] We will go from 20 mg to 40 mg twice a day. You must weigh yourself every morning and call us if you gain more than 1 kg in two days.
[patient] Okay. And what about the other pills?
[doctor] Keep taking Carvedilol and Entresto. Do not stop them. How is your job affecting this? You work at Bosch Logistics, correct?
[patient] Yes, I am a warehouse manager. It is hard to stand for eight hours. My feet hurt.
[doctor] We need to discuss activity restrictions. For now, please ask for a lighter schedule if possible. Your heart is under stress.
[patient] I will try to talk to my supervisor, Marcus. He is understanding.
[doctor] Good. I also need to order some blood tests. We need to check your kidney function and electrolytes because of the higher diuretic dose.
[patient] Do I need to go to the hospital?
[doctor] Not today. I will send the order to your local lab, City Lab Center in Frankfurt-Westend. You can go there tomorrow morning.
[patient] Is that safe?
[doctor] Yes, but if you feel dizzy or your heart rate drops below 50, do not drive. Take a taxi.
[patient] My home is at Gartenstrasse 14, 60316 Frankfurt. It is close to the lab.
[doctor] That works. Let's review your history. You were born on 12 March 1961, so you are 62 years old. You moved from Adana to Germany in 1990.
[patient] Yes, that is correct. I have lived here for a long time.
[doctor] Your medical record number is HR-2023-8842. I see you had an echocardiogram on 20 January 2024 which showed an ejection fraction of 35%.
[patient] Is that getting worse?
[doctor] It has been stable. The goal is to keep it stable and manage symptoms. Your pain score right now, if you had to rate the discomfort from 0 to 10, what would it be?
[patient] Maybe a 3? It is not pain, just tiredness.
[doctor] Okay. We need to see you again soon. I am booking an appointment for 10 June 2024 at 14:30.
[patient] Will I see you in person?
[doctor] Yes, in the clinic. We need to listen to your lungs and check your legs.
[patient] Okay. Thank you, Dr. Meyer.
[doctor] Thank you, Ayse. Please make sure to drink enough water, but limit salt. And call us immediately if you cannot breathe while lying down.
[patient] I will. Goodbye.
[doctor] Goodbye.

note:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
PATIENT: Almaz Bekele
DOB: May 12, 1935
RECORD NO: 77889900
DATE OF VISIT: April 20, 2024
REFERRING DOCTOR: Dr. Haddad from Practice Haddad
HOSPITAL: Geneva University Hospital

REASON FOR VISIT:
Follow-up for pure hypercholesterolemia, unspecified. Patient is an 89-year-old woman residing in Switzerland. She is a baker working at Keller's Bakery in Geneva.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
Patient reports feeling generally well but notes stiffness in legs and occasional palpitations when climbing stairs. No chest pain. She admits to a diet high in saturated fats, including beef, lamb, and butter, consistent with traditional Eritrean cuisine. She has been compliant with Atorvastatin 40 mg daily.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
Pure hypercholesterolemia, unspecified. Hypertension.
Previous visit: January 10, 2024.
Last lipid panel: January 10, 2024.

FAMILY HISTORY:
Mother: Myocardial infarction at 70 years.
Brother Tesfay: Type 2 Diabetes.
Sister Marta: Hypercholesterolemia.

SOCIAL HISTORY:
Lives with husband Yohannes in Geneva. Works 6 days a week as a baker. Employer: Keller's Bakery. Owner: Jonas Keller.

EXAMINATION:
Vital Signs:
BP: 145/90 mmHg
HR: 82 bpm
Pain Score: 2/10

Physical Exam:
General: Alert, oriented x3.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. Soft systolic murmur heard at the 3 o'clock position. No S3 or S4.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Extremities: No edema. Mild stiffness reported in legs.

LABORATORY RESULTS:
Total Cholesterol: 310 mg/dL
LDL: 210 mg/dL
HDL: 50 mg/dL
Triglycerides: 150 mg/dL
HbA1c: 5.4%

ASSESSMENT:
1. Pure hypercholesterolemia, unspecified.
2. Hypertension, well-controlled.
3. Cardiovascular risk factors: Family history, diet, age.

PLAN:
1. Increase Atorvastatin to 80 mg daily.
2. Dietary counseling: Reduce saturated fat (butter, red meat), increase fish and vegetables.
3. Repeat lipid panel in 3 months.
4. Follow-up appointment: October 15, 2024 at 10:30.
5. Refer to Dr. Haddad for ongoing primary care coordination.
6. Monitor blood pressure at home.

PHYSICIAN SIGNATURE:
Dr. Keller
Endocrinology Department
Geneva University Hospital
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, Almaz Bekele. It is nice to see you again. Please, have a seat. How have you been feeling since our last visit?
[patient] Oh, hello Dr. Keller. I am... um, I am okay, I guess. My legs feel a bit stiff, but that is all. I take my pills, yes?
[doctor] That is good to hear. We are here to discuss your cholesterol levels. Do you remember what your last blood test showed?
[patient] Uh, no, I do not remember the numbers. But my daughter said they were high. Very high.
[doctor] Yes, they were. Your total cholesterol was 310 mg/dL. That is quite elevated. We need to be careful with that. Have you noticed any pain in your chest or arms?
[patient] No, no pain. Just... you know, sometimes my heart feels like it is beating a little fast when I climb the stairs. But no pain.
[doctor] Okay. Let us check your vitals just to be sure. Nurse, could you come in for a moment?
[nurse] Good morning, Almaz. Let us check your blood pressure. One moment.
[patient] Yes, please.
[nurse] Your blood pressure is 145 over 90. Your heart rate is 82 beats per minute.
[doctor] Thank you. That blood pressure is a little high, but not alarming. Now, let us look at your history. You mentioned earlier that your mother had heart problems. Was that correct?
[patient] Yes, my mother. She had a heart attack when she was seventy. And my brother, Tesfay, he has diabetes.
[doctor] I see. Family history is important. Do you have any other relatives with high cholesterol?
[patient] My sister, Marta, she takes medicine for it too. But I am the only one who is... um, very high.
[doctor] I understand. Now, let us talk about your diet. I know you are from Eritrea, and I know the food there is very delicious. But do you eat a lot of fatty meats?
[patient] Oh, we eat a lot of meat, yes. Beef, lamb. And we use a lot of butter in our stews. It is very tasty.
[doctor] That is why your cholesterol is high. Butter and red meat have a lot of saturated fat. We need to reduce that. Can you try to eat more vegetables and fish?
[patient] Fish? I do not eat much fish. It is not common in Eritrea. We eat more meat.
[doctor] I understand. But for your health, it is better to try. Even just twice a week. And less butter. Use olive oil instead.
[patient] Olive oil... okay. I will try. But it is hard. My husband, Yohannes, he cooks. He likes butter.
[doctor] You can talk to him. Maybe he can try new recipes. Also, are you still working?
[patient] Yes, I work at Keller's Bakery. I am a baker. I work six days a week.
[doctor] Oh, that is a lot of work for someone your age. Do you feel tired?
[patient] Sometimes, yes. But I love my work. I have been there for ten years. My boss, Dr. Keller's husband, is very nice.
[doctor] Wait, my husband works at the bakery?
[patient] Yes! Jonas is the owner. He is very kind. He lets me sit when I am tired.
[doctor] Ah, I see. That is a coincidence. My name is Dr. Keller. My husband is Jonas.
[patient] Oh! Sorry, I did not know. I am confused. There are many Kellers in Geneva.
[doctor] Yes, it is a common name. But I am glad to know you work there. It is a nice place. Now, let us look at your physical exam. I will check your heart.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] I am listening to your heart. I hear a soft murmur at the 3 o'clock position. It is probably harmless, but I will monitor it.
[patient] Murmur? Is that bad?
[doctor] Not necessarily. Many people have mild murmurs. But we will keep an eye on it. Do you have any pain anywhere?
[patient] No pain. Maybe a little stiffness in my neck.
[doctor] Okay. Your pain score is 2 out of 10. That is manageable. Now, let us talk about your medication. You are on Atorvastatin 40 mg. Have you been taking it every day?
[patient] Yes, every day. In the morning.
[doctor] Good. But we need to increase it to 80 mg. It might help lower your cholesterol more.
[patient] 80 mg? That is a lot. Will I have side effects?
[doctor] Some people have muscle pain. If you feel pain in your muscles, tell me. But for now, we will try 80 mg.
[patient] Okay. I will try.
[doctor] Also, I want to repeat your blood test in three months. We need to see if the new dose works.
[patient] Three months? That is a long time.
[doctor] It is standard. We need to give the medicine time to work. Do you have any questions?
[patient] No, I think I understand. Thank you, doctor.
[doctor] You are welcome. I will write a summary and send it to your general practitioner, Dr. Haddad, at Practice Haddad.
[patient] Yes, I go to him every month.
[doctor] Good. He will coordinate with us. Now, when would you like to come back?
[patient] In three months, you said.
[doctor] Yes. Let us book you for October 15 at 10:30.
[patient] Okay. I will remember.
[doctor] I will send a reminder. Please, take care of your diet. Less butter, more fish.
[patient] I will try. Thank you.
[doctor] Goodbye, Almaz.
[patient] Goodbye, Dr. Keller.

note:
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Left-sided facial droop for three weeks.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is an 80-year-old woman, born on 14 March 1944, residing at Route du Lac 45, 1260 Nyon. She presents with a three-week history of left facial nerve palsy. The onset was sudden, noted in the kitchen approximately three weeks ago. Preceding this, she experienced fatigue and an expanding erythematous rash on the left leg, described as a "bullseye," following a trip to Geneva last summer. She was treated with a 10-day course of Doxycycline by her referring physician, Dr. Elise Dubois at Hôpital de Lausanne. Despite antibiotic treatment, the facial palsy has persisted, though slightly improved. She reports associated tinnitus in the left ear and mild knee pain. She denies fever, neck stiffness, or visual changes.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Fatigue present initially, resolved.
Neurological: Left facial weakness, tinnitus.
Musculoskeletal: Bilateral knee pain, resolved.
Cardiovascular: No palpitations.
Respiratory: No issues.
Gastrointestinal: No issues.
Skin: Rash resolved.
Psychiatric: Anxiety regarding diagnosis.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Alert, oriented x3.
Head and Neck: No lymphadenopathy.
Face: Left lower facial weakness. Incomplete left eye closure. Asymmetrical smile.
Eyes: No conjunctival injection.
Ears: No discharge.
Neck: No stiffness.
Extremities: No joint swelling. Range of motion intact.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation.

RESULTS
Lyme serology (from Dr. Dubois): Positive.
Blood pressure: 130/80.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Lyme disease, unspecified.
   - Patient has positive serology and compatible clinical history (erythema migrans, facial palsy, arthralgia).
   - Facial palsy persists despite antibiotic course.
   - Plan: Refer to Neurology for further evaluation and management of facial nerve palsy.
   - Referral sent to Dr. Jean-Pierre Martin at Geneva University Hospital.
   - Patient advised to call neurology on Monday at +41 22 305 5500.
2. Hypertension.
   - Continue Lisinopril.
   - Monitor blood pressure at home.
3. Prophylaxis.
   - Continue sun protection.
   - No new medications started today.
4. Follow-up.
   - Return to ENT if symptoms worsen or new symptoms develop.
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning. I see you have a referral from Dr. Elise Dubois at Hôpital de Lausanne. Can you tell me what brings you in today?
[patient] Hello. Well, um, it’s mostly the face. You know, it looks... odd. My left side just sort of drooped. It started, uh, maybe three weeks ago?
[doctor] Three weeks ago. Did it happen suddenly or gradually?
[patient] Sudden. I was in the kitchen making coffee, and I just... felt a twitch. Then it was there. I thought it was a Bell's palsy or something like that.
[doctor] Did you have any other symptoms around that time? Fever, rash, fatigue?
[patient] Oh, yes. Before the face, I was so tired. And I had a rash. It was on my... let’s see... my left leg. It looked like a big red circle.
[doctor] How big was this rash?
[patient] Um, it was spreading. Like a target. My neighbor, Marcel, he said it looked like a bullseye. I’m eighty years old, born on 14 March 1944. I live in 1260 Nyon. My address is Route du Lac 45.
[doctor] And the contact number on your file, is it still +41 22 555 0198?
[patient] Yes, that’s correct. The phone number. I was actually hiking. I went to Geneva last summer to visit my sister, Claire. She is seventy-eight.
[doctor] Did you use insect repellent during that trip?
[patient] No, I didn’t think much of it. I’m a retired librarian. I used to work at the Public Library in Nyon. I don’t usually get bites. But I think I was in the woods near the lake.
[doctor] I see. Did you notice any joint pain?
[patient] Oh, yes. My knees. They hurt a lot. Like they were swollen. It’s not my usual Baker's cyst issue, but it was both knees this time.
[doctor] And any neck stiffness?
[patient] A little bit. And I had trouble sleeping. I was so anxious. I thought I was having a stroke. My son, Luc, he is forty-five, he wanted to take me to the emergency room.
[doctor] Did you go?
[patient] No, he took me to Dr. Dubois first. She did some blood tests. I think they were positive for Lyme.
[doctor] Do you have those results with you?
[patient] No, but Dr. Dubois sent them to you. I am insured by Swisscare Insurance. My policy number is SC-8842-119.
[doctor] Let’s take a look at your face now. Can you smile for me?
[patient] Like this?
[doctor] Yes.
[patient] (Smiles)
[doctor] I can see some weakness on the left side. Can you raise your eyebrows?
[patient] (Raises right eyebrow only)
[doctor] And can you close your left eye tightly?
[patient] (Struggles to close eye)
[doctor] There is some lag. Okay. Did you have any hearing changes?
[patient] A little ringing in my left ear. Like a tinnitus.
[doctor] And any vision problems?
[patient] No, my vision is fine. I don’t have Glaucoma or anything like that.
[doctor] Let’s check your joints. Can you remove your jacket?
[patient] (Removes jacket)
[doctor] Do your knees hurt if I press here?
[patient] Oh, that’s the spot. Yes, that hurts.
[doctor] Any swelling?
[patient] I don’t see much swelling now, but it was worse two weeks ago.
[doctor] Did you have any headaches?
[patient] Mild ones. Not severe.
[doctor] Any memory issues?
[patient] I’m a bit foggy. But I think it’s just the stress. My mother had Alzheimer's, so I’m always worried.
[doctor] I understand. Let’s review your other systems. Any heart palpitations?
[patient] No. My heart is fine. I do yoga at the Nyon Yoga Studio.
[doctor] That’s good. Any respiratory issues?
[patient] No. I don’t smoke.
[doctor] Any gastrointestinal issues?
[patient] No. I don’t have Crohn's or anything like that.
[doctor] Any skin changes besides the rash?
[patient] No, the rash went away after the antibiotics.
[doctor] Did you take antibiotics?
[patient] Yes, Dr. Dubois prescribed Doxycycline. I took it for ten days.
[doctor] Did that help the face?
[patient] A little. It’s not as bad as it was. But it’s still there.
[doctor] Okay. Let’s do some quick tests. Can you say "la, la, la"?
[patient] La, la, la.
[doctor] Your speech is clear. No slurring.
[patient] I’m glad to hear that.
[doctor] Do you have any family history of autoimmune diseases?
[patient] My brother had Hashimoto's thyroiditis. And his brother had Graves' disease.
[doctor] I see. So there is a familial predisposition to thyroid issues.
[patient] Yes. I get my thyroid checked every year.
[doctor] Do you have any other chronic conditions?
[patient] Just high blood pressure. I take Lisinopril.
[doctor] Are you on any other medications?
[patient] No. Just the blood pressure pill.
[doctor] Any allergies?
[patient] No known allergies.
[doctor] Okay. I’m going to refer you to a neurologist for further evaluation of the facial nerve palsy.
[patient] Really? I was hoping you could fix it.
[doctor] It’s important to rule out other causes, especially given the duration. The Lyme serology is positive, but the facial palsy persists.
[patient] That sounds complicated.
[doctor] It is a common complication. We need to monitor it.
[patient] Will I lose my sense of taste?
[doctor] You might have some temporary changes. We’ll monitor that.
[patient] I’m a bit scared.
[doctor] It’s natural to be. But the prognosis is generally good.
[patient] Thank you. That’s a relief.
[doctor] I’ll send the referral to Dr. Jean-Pierre Martin at the Geneva University Hospital.
[patient] That’s a good doctor. I’ve heard of him.
[doctor] He is an expert in neurology.
[patient] Okay. When should I call them?
[doctor] You can call them on Monday. Their phone number is +41 22 305 5500.
[patient] I’ll write that down.
[doctor] Also, continue with your current medication for blood pressure.
[patient] Yes.
[doctor] And avoid sun exposure if you take any photosensitizing medications, though you are off the Doxycycline now.
[patient] I’m not taking it anymore. I finished the course.
[doctor] Good.
[patient] I should go. I have a appointment with my dentist.
[doctor] Take care.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor.
