[doctor] Good morning, Mrs. García. Please, have a seat. How are you feeling today?
[patient] Thank you, Doctor. I am still quite tired, but the dizziness has improved since yesterday.
[doctor] That is good to hear. I see you were admitted to the emergency department two weeks ago. Can you tell me what happened after you left the hospital?
[patient] Yes. I went straight home. I have been resting mostly. I work as a senior accountant at SwissRe, but my boss allowed me to stay home for the first few days.
[doctor] And how are things going at work now? Are you able to handle your responsibilities?
[patient] I am trying, yes. I am still here in Zürich, working from home. It is difficult to focus when I feel so out of breath.
[doctor] I understand. Let’s look at your current medications. You are taking Eliquis for your heart rhythm, correct?
[patient] Yes, twice a day. I never miss a dose.
[doctor] Excellent. Adherence is very important. Do you have any side effects, like bleeding or stomach pain?
[patient] No, nothing like that. I just feel weak. My daughter, Elena, came to see me last Sunday and she was worried.
[doctor] That is normal to feel weak after an episode of atrial fibrillation. How is your thyroid functioning? You have a history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis.
[patient] I take Levothyroxine every morning. I haven't had my blood test done in a while.
[doctor] We will check that today. Sometimes thyroid issues can trigger heart rhythm problems. Do you have any other symptoms? Shortness of breath, chest pain?
[patient] A little shortness of breath when I climb the stairs. But no chest pain.
[doctor] Okay. Let’s listen to your heart.
[patient] Does it sound bad?
[doctor] Your heart rate is 88 beats per minute. It is irregular, but not dangerously fast right now. I want to keep a close eye on this.
[patient] I am afraid of having another episode. It was scary when I was in the emergency room.
[doctor] I know it was frightening. But you are stable now. We will adjust your medication if needed. Do you still use your old beta-blocker?
[patient] I stopped taking it because I felt too cold. I read about Bell's palsy and I was just confused about all the side effects.
[doctor] That is a different condition, don't worry. But stopping medication abruptly can be risky. Let’s restart it at a lower dose.
[patient] Okay. I will listen to you.
[doctor] Also, are you sleeping well?
[patient] Not really. I wake up around 3 am and I can't go back to sleep.
[doctor] Poor sleep can increase stress on the heart. Try to keep a regular schedule. Avoid caffeine after 2 pm.
[patient] I only drink herbal tea now.
[doctor] That is perfect. One more thing. You mentioned you are living in Zürich. Is your primary care doctor here?
[patient] Yes, Dr. Müller. He is very nice.
[doctor] Good. I will send a summary to him. He needs to know about your current status and the new beta-blocker dose.
[patient] Thank you. I appreciate your help.
[doctor] Of course. We will see you again in four weeks for a follow-up. If you feel dizzy or your heart races again, go to the emergency room immediately.
[patient] I will. I have my record number, CH-2024-99821, just in case.
[doctor] Good. That will help us find your files quickly. Do you have any other questions?
[patient] No, I think that is all. I just want to feel normal again.
[doctor] We will work on that. Take care, Mrs. García.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor.

TO: Dr. Dubois

Dear Dr. Dubois,

I am writing to refer Élisabeth Vacheron, an 88-year-old female, to your care for further evaluation and management of her right hand condition.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Ms. Vacheron presents with a three-month history of progressive swelling and pain in her right hand. The symptoms began two weeks ago with morning stiffness, which improves with movement but worsens in the evening. She reports decreased grip strength, affecting her daily activities, including her hobby of playing tennis with the Club de Tennis de Genève. She has no history of trauma to the hand.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Ms. Vacheron has a history of Hashimoto's disease. She is retired and was previously a librarian at the Bibliothèque publique et universitaire de Genève. She has no history of rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, or other autoimmune conditions. Her family history is notable for Parkinson's disease in her daughter.

EXAMINATION
On examination, Ms. Vacheron is alert and oriented. Vital signs are within normal limits. Inspection of the right hand reveals mild diffuse swelling of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints. Palpation reveals tenderness over the MCP joints. Range of motion is limited in the right wrist and fingers due to pain. I noted a small, firm, non-tender nodule at the 3 o'clock position of the right wrist, which is consistent with a ganglion cyst or tenosynovitis. No erythema or warmth was noted. Neurological exam of the right hand is intact.

DIAGNOSIS
Other synovitis and tenosynovitis, right hand (ICD-10: M65.971).

INVESTIGATIONS
I have ordered the following:
1. X-ray of the right hand and wrist.
2. Blood tests: CBC, ESR, CRP, RF, Anti-CCP, Thyroid function tests.

PLAN
I have started Ms. Vacheron on Ibuprofen for pain and inflammation management. Given her age and potential gastrointestinal sensitivity, I have advised her to take it with food. I am referring her to you for a comprehensive rheumatological evaluation to determine the underlying etiology of her synovitis and to discuss long-term management options.

Her current appointment with you is scheduled for Monday, October 14, 2023 at 14:30. I would appreciate your assessment and any recommendations for further treatment or diagnostic testing.

Thank you for seeing her.

Sincerely,

Dr. Meyer
Urgent Care Clinic
Geneva

[doctor] I’m also checking the wrist. I notice some crepitus, a cracking sound, when I move it.
[patient] I hear that too sometimes.
[doctor] I’m going to order an X-ray to see if there are any bony changes. I also want to check for inflammation markers in your blood.
[patient] Is it serious?
[doctor] It’s not an emergency, but we need to investigate further. The swelling and pain suggest synovitis, which is inflammation of the lining of the joint.
[patient] I do a lot of gardening. Could that be the cause?
[doctor] Overuse can contribute, but usually, synovitis like this has an underlying cause, such as an autoimmune condition or infection.
[patient] I am a member of the Club de Tennis de Genève. I play twice a week.
[doctor] Tennis involves a lot of wrist and hand movement. Have you noticed any change in your grip or strength?
[patient] Yes, my grip is weaker. I drop my racket more often.
[doctor] I see. Do you work?
[patient] I am retired. I was a librarian at the Bibliothèque publique et universitaire de Genève for thirty years.
[doctor] That’s a long career. Thank you for your service.
[patient] It was a pleasure.
[doctor] I’m going to prescribe some anti-inflammatory medication to help with the pain and swelling in the meantime.
[patient] What is the name of the medication?
[doctor] It’s Ibuprofen. You should take it with food.
[patient] I have a mild stomach problem. Is that okay?
[doctor] Given your age and potential stomach sensitivity, I’ll prescribe a lower dose and recommend taking it with a meal. If you have any history of ulcers, let me know.
[patient] No ulcers, just some indigestion.
[doctor] Okay. I’ll also refer you to Dr. Dubois to expedite your appointment, as your current one is in two weeks.
[patient] That would be very kind.
[doctor] I’ll send the referral letter today. Make sure to bring this letter to your appointment.
[patient] I will.
[doctor] Do you have any questions for me?
[patient] No, thank you, doctor.
[doctor] If the pain gets worse or you develop a fever, come back to us immediately.
[patient] I will. Thank you.

note:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY

PATIENT NAME: Petrovic, Jelena
DATE OF BIRTH: 15.03.1937
RECORD NUMBER: RN-99821
DATE OF ENCOUNTER: 12.10.2024

REASON FOR VISIT:
Left hip pain after fall. Referral from Dr. Miller at University Hospital Vienna.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
87-year-old female presented with left hip pain following a fall. Patient reports falling while walking in Central Park in Vienna. She tripped over a tree root and fell directly on her left hip. She did not lose consciousness and did not hit her head. Pain is rated 7/10. She has been using a cane for mobility. No previous fractures.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
- Hypertension
- Hashimoto’s thyroiditis
- Osteoporosis (family history)
- Retired teacher at School 14

MEDICATIONS:
- Amlodipine 5 mg daily
- Levothyroxine 75 mcg daily
- Paracetamol 500 mg as needed (pre-fall)

SOCIAL HISTORY:
Lives in Austria. Originally from Serbia. Lives alone. Daughter Ana (48) and son Petar (52) live nearby and provide support.

EXAMINATION:
Vital signs: BP 135/85 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, Temp 36.8°C.
Left hip: Mild swelling and tenderness. Pain with internal rotation and abduction. Range of motion limited by pain. No deformity. Neurovascular status intact distally. No signs of infection.

IMAGING:
X-ray of left hip: No fracture. Soft tissue swelling noted.

DIAGNOSIS:
Left hip contusion.

PLAN:
1. Rest and activity modification. Use cane for ambulation.
2. Pain management: Paracetamol 500 mg up to 4 times daily. Topical Diclofenac gel 3 times daily to left hip.
3. Continue current medications: Amlodipine, Levothyroxine.
4. Follow-up in two weeks or sooner if symptoms worsen.
5. Results sent to Dr. Miller at University Hospital Vienna.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
- Avoid heavy lifting.
- Monitor for signs of infection (fever, redness).
- Contact clinic if pain increases or mobility decreases.

PHYSICIAN SIGNATURE:
Dr. Hans Weber
Orthopedic Clinic Vienna
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning. Please have a seat. I see you were referred to us by Dr. Miller at University Hospital Vienna. Can you tell me what brings you in today?
[patient] Hello. Dr. Miller said I need to come here because of my hip. I fell a few days ago.
[doctor] I am sorry to hear that. How old are you today?
[patient] I am 87.
[doctor] And where are you from originally?
[patient] I am from Serbia, but I live here in Austria now.
[doctor] Thank you. Let’s talk about the fall. What were you doing when it happened?
[patient] I was walking in the park. My son Petar, who is 52, usually walks with me, but he was at work that day.
[doctor] I see. So you were alone?
[patient] Yes. I was walking near the fountain. I tripped over a root and fell.
[doctor] Did you hit your head?
[patient] No, I protected my head with my hands. But I hit my left hip hard against the ground.
[doctor] That sounds painful. How is the pain now? On a scale of zero to ten, with ten being the worst?
[patient] It is about a seven. It hurts when I try to stand up.
[doctor] Can you walk?
[patient] I can walk, but very slowly. I use a cane.
[doctor] Did you see a doctor right after the fall?
[patient] No, I went home. My daughter Ana, who is 48, lives nearby. She came over and helped me.
[doctor] Did you take any pain medication?
[patient] I took some Paracetamol.
[doctor] How many tablets?
[patient] Two.
[doctor] How often?
[patient] Twice a day.
[doctor] Do you have any other medical conditions? I see you have teacher in your file, but I know you retired.
[patient] Yes, I was a teacher at School 14 in Vienna for many years. Now I am retired.
[doctor] Besides the hip, do you have any heart or lung problems?
[patient] I have high blood pressure. I take Amlodipine.
[doctor] Do you have any other conditions? Maybe diabetes or thyroid issues?
[patient] I have Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. I take Levothyroxine.
[doctor] Okay. And do you have any family history of bone problems?
[patient] My sister had osteoporosis.
[doctor] Have you ever had a fracture before?
[patient] No, this is the first time.
[doctor] Let’s take a look at your left hip. Please lie down on the table.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] This might hurt a little. I am going to move your leg.
[patient] Yes, I can handle it.
[doctor] How does that feel?
[patient] It hurts a lot when you move it outward.
[doctor] I see. Let me check your range of motion.
[patient] Please be gentle.
[doctor] I am. Your leg is a bit stiff. Do you have any swelling?
[patient] My leg looks a bit bigger than the other one.
[doctor] I can see some mild swelling. Let me check your circulation. I will press here on your foot.
[patient] I feel it.
[doctor] Good. You have a pulse. Now, I need to order some X-rays to see if there is a fracture.
[patient] Can I go home?
[doctor] Yes, after the X-ray. But you need to be careful. No heavy lifting.
[patient] I will be careful.
[doctor] Your daughter Ana can pick you up?
[patient] Yes, she is coming.
[doctor] Good. We will send the X-ray results to Dr. Miller as well.
[patient] Thank you.

[nurse] Good morning, Mrs. Petrovic. I am going to take your vital signs now.
[patient] Hello.
[nurse] Your blood pressure is 135 over 85. Your heart rate is 78.
[patient] Is that normal?
[nurse] It is slightly elevated, probably due to pain. I will let the doctor know.
[patient] Thank you.
[nurse] Do you need anything else before we do the X-ray?
[patient] No, thank you.
[nurse] The X-ray room is right next door. I will walk you there.
[patient] Thank you.

[doctor] The X-ray results are back.
[patient] Is there a fracture?
[doctor] No, there is no fracture. But I see some soft tissue swelling. It looks like a contusion.
[patient] A bruise?
[doctor] Yes, a deep bruise in the muscle.
[patient] How long will it hurt?
[doctor] It should improve in one to two weeks.
[patient] Can I walk?
[doctor] Yes, but use your cane. Do not run or jump.
[patient] I will.
[doctor] I am going to prescribe Ibuprofen for the pain.
[patient] I have stomach problems. Can I take it?
[doctor] Do you have Crohn’s disease?
[patient] No, I don’t. But I have gastritis.
[doctor] Okay, I will prescribe Paracetamol instead. And maybe Topical Diclofenac gel.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] How often should you take the Paracetamol?
[patient] Every six hours?
[doctor] Yes, up to four times a day.
[patient] And the gel?
[doctor] Three times a day, rubbing it into the hip area.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] Do you have any other medications?
[patient] I take Amlodipine and Levothyroxine.
[doctor] Continue those. Do not stop them.
[patient] Yes.
[doctor] When should you come back?
[patient] If it gets worse?
[doctor] Yes, if the pain increases, if you have fever, or if you cannot walk. Otherwise, in two weeks for a follow-up.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] Do you have any questions?
[patient] No, I think I understand.
[doctor] Good. Dr. Miller will be notified.
[patient] Thank you.

note:
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Pre-operative assessment for planned craniotomy to resect a suprasellar mass causing heteronymous bilateral field defects.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a 21-year-old female, Sarah Tesfay, residing in Zürich. She presents for pre-anesthetic evaluation prior to scheduled neurosurgical intervention at Klinik für Augenheilkunde Zürich.
The patient reports a progressive decline in visual acuity and field of view over the past three months. She initially noticed peripheral vision loss while playing soccer. The condition worsened, culminating in an incident in the kitchen last week where she dropped a knife due to impaired right-sided vision, resulting in a minor laceration to her hand which was managed conservatively at home.
She was evaluated by Dr. Meier at Klinik für Augenheilkunde Zürich on October 12, 2023. A subsequent MRI of the brain performed on October 20, 2023 revealed a mass in the suprasellar region compressing the optic chiasm. The pattern of visual field loss is described as heteronymous bilateral field defects (left temporal hemianopia and right nasal hemianopia), consistent with chiasmal compression.
The patient is currently asymptomatic regarding systemic complaints. She denies nausea, vomiting, headache, or dizziness.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever, chills, or weight change.
Eyes: Bilateral visual field defects as described. No pain, redness, or discharge.
Cardiovascular: No chest pain, palpitations, or dyspnea.
Respiratory: No cough, wheeze, or shortness of breath.
Gastrointestinal: No nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain.
Neurologic: No weakness, numbness, or seizures.
Musculoskeletal: No joint pain or muscle weakness.
Psychiatric: Mild anxiety related to upcoming surgery.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Well-appearing, alert, and oriented.
Vital Signs: Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, Heart rate 82 bpm, Respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, Oxygen saturation 98% on room air, Temperature 36.5°C.
HEENT: Pupils equal and reactive. Extraocular movements intact. Visual fields consistent with history (heteronymous bilateral defects).
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Respiratory: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender, no organomegaly.
Neurologic: Cranial nerves II-XII intact except for visual field defects. Motor strength 5/5 in all extremities. Sensation intact. Reflexes 2+ and symmetric.

RESULTS
MRI Brain (October 20, 2023): Suprasellar mass, approximately 3 cm in diameter, compressing the optic chiasm. No evidence of hydrocephalus.
Blood Work (Routine Pre-op): CBC, BMP, Coagulation profile within normal limits.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Suprasellar mass (likely craniopharyngioma) with secondary heteronymous bilateral visual field defects.
   - Patient is medically fit for general anesthesia and neurosurgery.
   - Plan: Proceed with scheduled craniotomy tomorrow at Klinik für Augenheilkunde Zürich.
   - Anesthesia Plan: General endotracheal anesthesia. Induction with standard agents. Maintain hemodynamic stability.
   - Pre-op Instructions: NPO after midnight. Arrive at hospital at 7:00 for final check.
   - Post-op: Monitor for neurological changes, endocrine dysfunction, and visual improvement.

2. History of family brain tumor (Uncle).
   - Unlikely to be directly related given age and presentation, but noted for context.

3. Anxiety.
   - Patient is anxious about surgery and visual prognosis.
   - Plan: Provide reassurance and information about the procedure. Consider pre-medication with anxiolytic if indicated.

4. Minor hand laceration (History).
   - Healed. No active infection.

Contact:
Klinik für Augenheilkunde Zürich
+41 44 123 45 67
dr.weber@klinik-zuerich.ch
Patient ID: 79204-8812
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning. I see you are here for your pre-operative assessment. My name is Dr. Weber. I am the anesthesiologist. Can you tell me your full name and date of birth, please?
[patient] Yes, good morning. My name is Sarah Tesfay. And I am twenty-one years old.
[doctor] Thank you, Sarah. I have your record here. Your medical record number is 79204-8812. Is that correct?
[patient] Yes, that is me.
[doctor] Great. We are preparing you for your surgery tomorrow at Klinik für Augenheilkunde Zürich. The main concern we are discussing is your vision. You have bilateral field defects, specifically heteronymous. Can you describe what you are seeing? Or rather, not seeing?
[patient] Um, it is... it is hard to explain. Like, when I look straight ahead, the center is okay. But on the sides, it is blurry. Or just black? I don't know. It is like a curtain is falling on the sides.
[doctor] And this is different on each side?
[patient] Yes. On my left side, I lose the outer part. And on my right side, I lose the inner part. So it is not symmetrical. That is why they call it heteronymous, I think?
[doctor] Correct. This is a specific pattern. Usually, this suggests a problem in the optic chiasm or the optic nerves. We have seen you before, have we not?
[patient] Yes. I was here October 12, 2023 for the initial consultation. Dr. Meier saw me then.
[doctor] Yes, Dr. Meier referred you to us for the surgical planning. Do you remember what he suspected at that time?
[patient] He said it might be a tumor pressing on the nerves. A craniopharyngioma? Or something like that. He did some scans.
[doctor] Yes. We have the MRI results from October 20, 2023. They showed a lesion in the suprasellar region. It is benign, but it is pressing on the optic chiasm. That is why you have these specific field defects.
[patient] I am just scared, doctor. Because I am young. I am only 21. I just want to see normally again.
[doctor] I understand. That is a very normal fear. The surgery is planned to relieve that pressure. But before we can give you anesthesia, I need to check your general health. Do you have any allergies?
[patient] No, no allergies. Not to food, not to medicine.
[doctor] Any chronic illnesses? Diabetes, asthma, heart problems?
[patient] No. I am healthy. I run a lot. I am a runner.
[doctor] That is good. Do you take any regular medications?
[patient] Only... um, iron tablets. Because I sometimes feel tired. But that is all.
[doctor] Okay. Any recent illnesses? Colds, flu, infections?
[patient] No. I have been well.
[doctor] How about your family history? Any eye problems in your family?
[patient] Um, my mother has glaucoma. She had to get drops every day. But I don't think that is related to this.
[doctor] Glaucoma is different. It affects the optic nerve head, not usually the chiasm like this. What about other family members?
[patient] My father is healthy. And my brother, his brother... wait, my brother is healthy too. But my uncle, he had a brain tumor.
[doctor] A brain tumor? What kind?
[patient] I don't know. He died when I was young. Maybe ten or twelve years ago. I don't remember the details.
[doctor] I see. We will keep that in mind, though it is likely coincidental. Now, let's look at your recent history. When did these vision problems start?
[patient] It was slow. I noticed it three months ago. I was playing soccer, and I couldn't see the ball coming from the side. I thought I was just tired.
[doctor] Did you see a doctor then?
[patient] No, I ignored it. I thought it would go away. But it got worse. Then, last week, I was in the kitchen, preparing dinner. I dropped a knife because I couldn't see it properly on my right side. It cut my hand.
[doctor] That is a significant event. Did you go to the emergency room for the cut?
[patient] No, I just put a bandage on it. It was a small cut. But that was when I realized it was serious. So I called my ophthalmologist, Dr. Meier, in Zürich.
[doctor] And he booked you for the appointment on October 12, 2023?
[patient] Yes. That was a Tuesday. I remember because it was raining.
[doctor] And the MRI was done on October 20, 2023.
[patient] Yes. I was very nervous. The machine was loud.
[doctor] How are you feeling today? Any nausea or vomiting?
[patient] No. I feel okay. A bit anxious, but okay.
[doctor] Have you eaten or drunk anything since midnight?
[patient] No. I drank some water 8:00 this morning. But no food.
[doctor] Good. We need to have an empty stomach for the anesthesia. How much water did you drink?
[patient] Maybe two glasses.
[doctor] That is acceptable. Now, let's check your vital signs. The nurse will take your blood pressure and pulse.
[nurse] Good morning, Sarah. I am Anna, the nurse. Let's get your blood pressure.
[patient] Hi Anna.
[nurse] Your blood pressure is 110 over 70. Your heart rate is 82 beats per minute. Your oxygen saturation is 98%.
[patient] Is that good?
[nurse] Yes, that is very good. You are breathing well.
[doctor] Thank you, Anna. Sarah, do you have any problems with your neck or back?
[patient] No. I am flexible. I do yoga.
[doctor] Good. Any history of difficult intubation? Did you have surgery before?
[patient] No, this is my first surgery. I have never been under anesthesia before.
[doctor] That is common. I will explain the process. We will put you to sleep, and you will not feel pain. You will wake up in the recovery room.
[patient] Will I be able to see better immediately?
[doctor] It may take some time for your vision to improve. The brain needs to adapt. But the pressure will be off the nerves, which is the main goal.
[patient] I hope so. I am an artist, you know. I paint. I need my eyes.
[doctor] That is a very important reason. We will do our best. Do you have any questions for me?
[patient] Just... will I be blind?
[doctor] No, Sarah. The damage is reversible to a large extent if we relieve the pressure now. You will not be blind.
[patient] Thank you. That is a relief.
[doctor] One more thing. Do you use any recreational drugs or alcohol?
[patient] No. I do not drink alcohol. And no drugs.
[doctor] Good. Do you smoke?
[patient] No.
[doctor] Perfect. I am satisfied with your assessment. You are fit for surgery. We will see you tomorrow at 7:00 for the final check.
[patient] Okay. I will come at 7:00.
[doctor] Please do not eat or drink anything after midnight.
[patient] I will not. Thank you, Dr. Weber.
[doctor] You are welcome. Good luck.

note:
SUBJECTIVE
Lucas Oliveira, a 32-year-old male, presents for a nephrology and allergy follow-up after a severe anaphylactic reaction to peanuts. The patient reports the incident occurred last Tuesday while dining with a friend, Marcus, at a restaurant near Palazzo della Ragione. He consumed a pasta dish containing nuts and experienced throat tightness, hives, and dyspnea approximately 15 minutes later. He was transported to the St. Jude’s General Hospital emergency department, where he was treated and admitted to the ICU for two days. He was discharged on Thursday. The patient reports a recent trip to Lisbon in June for two weeks. He has a history of mild asthma and has been taking Cetirizine daily. Family history is notable for asthma in his mother, Sofia, and eczema in his brother, Paulo (28). He currently reports a headache with a pain score of 4/10. He is a software engineer.

OBJECTIVE
Vital signs: BP 130/85 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, Temp 36.8°C.
Physical Exam: General appearance is alert and oriented. Skin shows no active hives. Respiratory effort is unlabored, no wheezing or stridor. Cardiovascular exam is regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs. Abdomen is soft and non-tender. No edema in extremities.
Labs (Pending): Blood draw performed for Creatinine, BUN, and Total IgE. Previous hospital labs showed Creatinine at 1.2 mg/dL.

ASSESSMENT
1. Food Allergy (Peanut): Confirmed anaphylaxis. High risk for recurrence.
2. Acute Kidney Injury (Resolved/Monitoring): Creatinine slightly elevated post-anaphylaxis, likely due to transient hypotension.
3. Mild Asthma: Well-controlled, but relevant for airway reactivity.

PLAN
1. Prescribe Epinephrine Auto-Injector (EpiPen) x2. Patient to carry at all times.
2. Nurse to train patient on proper administration of the auto-injector.
3. Dietary counseling: Strict avoidance of peanuts and tree nuts. Referral to dietitian for label reading support.
4. Lab work: Monitor Creatinine and BUN to ensure renal function returns to baseline.
5. Follow-up: Referral to Immunology at St. Jude’s General Hospital for skin prick testing to confirm allergen profile.
6. Patient Education: Discussed emergency protocol. If symptoms recur, use epinephrine immediately and call emergency services.
7. Contact info updated: Phone +39 333 123 4567, Email lucas.oliveira@gmail.com.
8. Address on file: 14 Via Roma, 24100 Bergamo.
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning. Please, take a seat. I see you were referred to us for a follow-up regarding a severe allergic reaction. My name is Dr. Rossi. Who is your primary care physician?
[patient] Um, yes. Hello, Dr. Rossi. My GP is Dr. Elena Vance at the Greenwood Medical Practice. She sent me here because... well, because I was in the hospital last week.
[doctor] And where was that, if I may ask?
[patient] At the St. Jude’s General Hospital in the city center. It was quite chaotic, to be honest.
[doctor] I understand. Let's go through your details to make sure our records are correct. Can I have your full name, please?
[patient] Sure. My name is Lucas Oliveira.
[doctor] And your date of birth?
[patient] I was born on March 12, 1992. So, I am 32 years old.
[doctor] Thank you, Lucas. Where do you currently reside?
[patient] I live in Bergamo, Italy. My address is 14 Via Roma, 24100.
[doctor> Got it. Now, let's talk about what happened. You mentioned a reaction to peanuts. Can you walk me through the timeline? When did this occur?
[patient] It happened last Tuesday. I was having lunch with a friend, Marcus, who is 35. We were at a small restaurant near Palazzo della Ragione.
[doctor] And what did you eat?
[patient] I ordered a pasta dish. It was, um, creamy with nuts, I think. I didn't read the ingredients carefully. I am from Brazil, so sometimes the menus... you know, they are not always clear.
[doctor] Yes, that is common. So, how soon after eating did you feel unwell?
[patient] Maybe 15 minutes later. I started feeling itchy. My throat felt tight, like something was swelling. And I got hives on my arms.
[doctor] Did you have any difficulty breathing?
[patient] Yes. It was hard to breathe. My chest felt very tight. I felt dizzy. I thought I was going to pass out. Marcus called an ambulance immediately.
[doctor] That was the right thing to do. Did you carry an epinephrine auto-injector with you?
[patient] No. I didn't know I needed one. I have been sensitive to nuts for a while, but I never had a reaction this bad before.
[doctor] I see. The ER team at St. Jude’s General Hospital treated you. What did they do?
[patient] They gave me shots. I don't know the names. They put me on oxygen. I was in the ICU for two days.
[doctor] I see. You were discharged on Thursday. How are you feeling today?
[patient] Much better, but I am still a bit shaky. I have a headache. I scored a 4 out of 10 on the pain scale when I left the hospital.
[doctor] Let's check your vitals now. Nurse, could you please take his blood pressure and heart rate?
[nurse] Of course. Lucas, I’m just going to put the cuff on your arm.
[patient] Okay.
[nurse] Your blood pressure is 130 over 85. Heart rate is 88. Temperature is 36.8 degrees Celsius.
[doctor] Thank you. Those are stable. Lucas, did you do any travel recently that might have exposed you to different allergens?
[patient] Yes. I went to Lisbon in June for two weeks. I worked remotely there. But I didn't eat peanuts there, I think. I mostly ate seafood.
[doctor] Seafood can also trigger reactions, but you identified peanuts this time. Did the allergist in the ER run any specific tests?
[patient] Yes. They took a blood sample. They said my IgE levels were high. I need to follow up with a specialist. That is why Dr. Vance sent me here.
[doctor] Correct. I am a nephrologist, but I also manage complex allergy cases in conjunction with our immunology team. I will review your labs from the hospital.
[patient] Please. I am scared this will happen again. I don't want to die.
[doctor] I understand your fear. We are going to make sure you are protected. Let's look at your medical history. Do you have any other allergies?
[patient] No, just this one. My mother, Sofia, has asthma. And my brother, Paulo, who is 28, has eczema.
[doctor] So, there is a family history of atopic conditions. That makes sense. Do you take any regular medications?
[patient] I take an antihistamine, Cetirizine, once a day. And I have a prescription for an inhaler for mild asthma, but I rarely use it.
[doctor] Good. Now, let's discuss the plan. First, you must carry an epinephrine auto-injector with you at all times. Do you know how to use it?
[patient] No. Can you teach me?
[doctor] I will have the nurse show you on a trainer. Second, we need to avoid peanuts and tree nuts. You will need to read labels carefully. In Italy, the labeling is strict, but you must still check.
[patient] I will. I am a software engineer, so I am used to reading details, but food labels... it is different.
[doctor] I understand. We will refer you to a dietitian who specializes in food allergies. Third, we need to monitor your kidney function, as severe allergic reactions can sometimes affect the kidneys due to hypotension.
[patient] My kidneys?
[doctor] Yes. Your creatinine level was slightly elevated in the hospital. It was 1.2 mg/dL. We need to make sure it returns to normal.
[patient] Okay. When will I have more blood tests?
[doctor] We will draw blood today. I want to check your creatinine, BUN, and total IgE again.
[patient] Will it hurt?
[doctor] Just a small pinch. The nurse will do it now.
[nurse] Okay, Lucas. I’m going to start the blood draw.
[patient] Okay.
[nurse] Done. I’ll send the results to Dr. Rossi.
[doctor] Thank you. Now, Lucas, do you have a phone number where we can reach you if your results are abnormal?

She reports the onset occurred during gardening activities in Mendrisio. She denies radiation of pain to the forearm or hand, and no numbness or tingling is reported.

The patient is a retired accountant. Her past medical history is significant for Type 2 diabetes mellitus, for which she is managed with Lantus. She also has a history of hypertension. Range of motion is full but painful at end range. No swelling or effusion is noted. Neurological examination of the upper extremity is intact.

Lateral epicondylitis, right elbow.

PLAN
1. Referral for physical therapy and orthopedic evaluation.
2. Patient advised on activity modification and use of a counterforce strap.
3. Ice application recommended for pain management.

Dr. Keller
Medica Ticino

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

PATIENT NAME: Marcus Thorne
DATE OF BIRTH: March 15, 1979
AGE: 45

CONTACT: (312) 555-0199
LOCATION: Chicago, IL
ORGANIZATION: Northwestern Memorial Hospital Sports Medicine Clinic

REASON FOR VISIT:
The patient presented to the clinic for a follow-up on chronic insomnia, unspecified. He reported difficulty falling asleep and maintaining sleep for the past three weeks.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
The patient, a 45-year-old male, is a shift manager at Detroit Free Press. He reports insomnia characterized by sleep onset latency and early morning awakenings, leading to daytime fatigue and impaired concentration at work. Symptoms began approximately three weeks ago, coinciding with a trip to Denver for a family reunion. He denies use of sleep aids other than over-the-counter melatonin. He reports increased anxiety, particularly concerning potential neurological conditions.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
- Routine check-up on October 12, 2023 at Chicago: Normal vital signs, no significant findings.
- Known Baker's cyst in the left knee, stable since 2021.

FAMILY HISTORY:
- Mother, Elena: History of Parkinson's disease.
- Brother, Steve: History of Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

SOCIAL HISTORY:
Works as a shift manager with erratic hours. Caffeine intake is moderate but often consumed in the late afternoon.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:
- General: Alert and oriented. No acute distress.
- Neurological: Mild tremor observed at the 3 o'clock position when holding the hand flat. No rigidity or bradykinesia noted. Reflexes 2+ and symmetric.
- Musculoskeletal: Mild tenderness over the left popliteal fossa, consistent with known Baker's cyst. No significant swelling or redness.

ASSESSMENT:
1. Insomnia, unspecified: Likely exacerbated by recent travel and stress.
2. Essential tremor vs. early Parkinson's: Tremor is noted, but clinical picture is more consistent with essential tremor or anxiety-related tremor. Family history is noted.
3. Known Baker's cyst: Stable.

PLAN:
1. Refer for polysomnography to evaluate for sleep architecture disturbances.
2. Order lab work including TSH, free T4, and complete metabolic panel to rule out thyroid dysfunction (e.g., Graves' disease).
3. Initiate Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) referral.
4. Lifestyle modifications: Limit caffeine after 2 pm, establish a consistent sleep schedule, and reduce screen time before bed.
5. Follow-up appointment scheduled for November 10, 2023 at 10:30 am.
6. If tremor worsens or new neurological symptoms develop, refer to neurology for further evaluation.

PATIENT EDUCATION:
Discussed the nature of insomnia and the role of stress and sleep hygiene. Explained the difference between essential tremor and Parkinson's disease, reassuring the patient that the current findings are not diagnostic of Parkinson's. Advised to monitor symptoms and report any changes.

DISCHARGE STATUS:
Patient is stable and has been discharged home with follow-up instructions.

[patient] Mostly, yeah. I’m a shift manager at Detroit Free Press, so my schedule is a bit erratic, but usually I manage. But lately, it’s just not happening.
[doctor] I see. You mentioned a trip recently in your intake form. Did that affect your sleep?
[patient] Oh, yeah. I went to Denver last month for a family reunion. My cousin lives out there. It was great, but the altitude and the jet lag... well, I’m from Chicago, so the time zone shift was tough.
[doctor] That can certainly disrupt your circadian rhythm. Did you notice any other symptoms while you were there?
[patient] Just some headaches, maybe a bit of fatigue. I had a routine check-up in Chicago on October 12, 2023, and everything was normal then.
[doctor] Okay, I have that record here. Your blood pressure and heart rate were within normal limits. Let’s check your file. Your date of birth is March 15, 1979, correct?
[patient] Yes, that’s right. I’m 45 years old.

[patient] That’s correct. Look, I’m worried because my brother, Steve, has Hashimoto's thyroiditis, and I’ve been feeling a bit anxious. Could this be related?

[patient] CBT-I? What’s that?
[doctor] It’s a structured program to help you change the thoughts and behaviors that are keeping you awake. It’s more effective than medication in the long run.
[patient] Okay, I’m open to trying it.

[patient] Thanks, Doctor.
[doctor] You’re welcome. I’ll schedule your next appointment for November 10, 2023 at 10:30 am.
[patient] That works for me.

[patient] No, I think I’m good.
[doctor] Great. See you then.

[patient] Oh, yes, Elsbeth Müller. That is me. Uh, good morning to you too. I am ninety years old, you know.
[doctor] Thank you, Elsbeth. Could you please give me your date of birth?
[patient] March 14, 1935. I am still celebrating it, though my knees don't really cooperate anymore.
[doctor] Understood. And what is your current home address?
[patient] I live at Bahnhofstrasse 45, 8001 Zurich. It is quite close to the station, which is convenient for my walks.
[doctor] Thank you. And who is your primary health insurer?
[patient] Zurich Insurance. The number is ZU-998877665. I have had them for a very long time.
[doctor] Perfect. Now, what brings you to the clinic today?
[patient] Well, um, my hands. Or rather, my wrists. They have been hurting for a while. And I keep dropping things. It is embarrassing.
[doctor] I see. Can you tell me more about the pain? Which hand is it?
[patient] Mostly the right one. But sometimes the left one joins in, you know? It feels like burning. And tingling. Like ants crawling.
[doctor] How long has this been going on?
[patient] Oh, maybe... three months? It started slowly. I thought it was just the cold. But now it is worse at night.
[doctor] Does anything wake you up at night?
[patient] Yes. I have to shake my hands. Like this. <patient mimics shaking hands>. It helps for a bit, but then it comes back.
[doctor] And does the pain travel down into your fingers?
[patient] Yes, to the thumb, index, and middle finger. The ring and little finger are okay, I think.
[doctor] That sounds consistent with carpal tunnel syndrome. Have you been to see anyone else about this recently?
[patient] My daughter, Anna, took me to the GP first. He said I should see a specialist. He is very nice, but he didn't have the time for a long check-up.
[doctor] That is a common path. Do you have any other medical conditions?
[patient] Well, I have high blood pressure. I take medication for that. And I had a hip replacement five years ago.
[doctor] Any history of diabetes or thyroid issues?
[patient] No, I don't believe so. My last check-up was last year, and everything was fine except for the blood pressure.
[doctor] Okay. Did you suffer any recent injuries to your hands or wrists?
[patient] Oh, yes. It was in the kitchen. I was trying to open a jar of pickles. I slipped, and I hit my wrist on the counter. It was quite hard.
[doctor] When did that happen?
[patient] Two weeks ago. I put ice on it, but the swelling went down, the numbness didn't.
[doctor] I see. Let's take a look. Please extend your right arm.
[patient] Is this it?
[doctor] Yes. I am going to press on the inside of your wrist. Does that hurt?
[patient] Oh! Yes. Right there. It stings.
[doctor] That is a positive Tinel's sign. Now, let's check your reflexes. I will tap your knee.
[patient] Is that for the legs?
[doctor] Yes, just to check your overall nerve function. Relax.
[patient] Like that?
[doctor] Yes. Your reflexes are normal. Now, let's look at your wrist again. I noticed a small, hard lump near the wrist joint.
[patient] Oh, that? I found that yesterday. I thought it was just a bone.
[doctor] It looks like a ganglion cyst. It is benign, but it can put pressure on the nerves. Let's check its position relative to the wrist crease. It appears to be at the 3 o'clock position on the dorsal side.
[patient] Is that dangerous?
[doctor] Not usually. But given your symptoms, it might be contributing to the compression. We need to see if the nerve is being squeezed.
[patient] So, what do we do now?
[doctor] We should do an ultrasound to see the size of the cyst and the state of the median nerve. And perhaps an MRI if the ultrasound isn't clear.
[patient] An MRI? I hate those machines. I feel claustrophobic.
[doctor] We can try the ultrasound first. It is less invasive. If you need the MRI, we can discuss options for anxiety management.
[patient] My son, Thomas, is a doctor. He works at the university hospital. He said I should just be patient. But I am dropping my teacup now.
[doctor] That is a valid concern. Dropping objects indicates motor involvement. We need to address this.
[patient] I also have a friend, Lupus. He has a disease with the same name as his surname. It is a strange coincidence.
[doctor] I am sorry to hear about your friend's health. How is he doing?
[patient] He is managing. He takes many pills. It is a lot for him.
[doctor] Back to you. Your blood pressure was taken when you arrived. Can you recall the numbers?
[patient] No, I didn't look. The nurse was kind, but I was nervous.
[doctor] That is fine. We have them recorded. Your pain level right now? On a scale of 0 to 10?
[patient] Um... maybe a 6? When I shake it, it goes down to a 4. But at night, it is an 8.
[doctor] Okay. So, the plan is: ultrasound today, and we will schedule a follow-up for next week.
[patient] Next week? That is far away.
[doctor] We will try to find an earlier slot. If the pain becomes unbearable before then, call the clinic.
[patient] And the medication? Will I get something for the pain?
[doctor] We might prescribe a wrist splint to keep your hand straight at night. And perhaps a short course of anti-inflammatories, if your stomach allows it.
[patient] I have a sensitive stomach.
[doctor] We will be careful. Do you have any allergies?
[patient] No, I don't think so. Maybe peanuts? I am not sure.
[doctor] We will note that. The nurse will prepare the referral for the ultrasound.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor. I feel a bit better.
[doctor] You are welcome. Please see the nurse at the front desk.
[patient] Yes, thank you. Goodbye.
[doctor] Goodbye, Elsbeth. Take care.

Denies hemoptysis, night sweats, or weight loss. Reports mild muscle soreness from recent heavy lifting. No significant chest pain.

FAMILY HISTORY:

Non-smoker. No alcohol or drug use. Travels occasionally for work.

EXAMINATION:
VITALS:

Heart Rate: 72 bpm

Respiratory Rate: 16/min
SpO2: 98% on room air

GENERAL:
Alert and oriented, in no acute distress.

CARDIOVASCULAR:
Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.

RESPIRATORY:

dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning. I'm Dr. Thorne. You're here because your GP sent you over for a follow-up on that lung nodule?
[patient] Yeah, hi. Yeah, that’s right. It’s... um, it’s been a bit on my mind, to be honest.
[doctor] Can I check your details? I see you are 29 years old. My name is Arthur. Can you confirm your full name for the record?
[patient] Sure. It’s James Miller.
[doctor] Thanks, James. And your NHS number?
[patient] Um, I think it’s 998 776 5544. I had to look it up in my mail.
[doctor] Okay, got it. So, what’s been happening since we last spoke? You mentioned some coughing?
[patient] Yeah. It started about two weeks ago. It’s not super bad, but it’s there. Mostly in the evenings. And I’ve had a bit of a fever, just low-grade.
[doctor] How high did the thermometer read?
[patient] About 38.2 degrees, I think. Nothing crazy.
[doctor] Okay. Any pain?
[patient] Not really chest pain. Maybe a bit of muscle ache from training. I’ve been lifting heavy lately.
[doctor] That makes sense. So, the nodule. It was found on a CT scan a few months ago, right?
[patient] Yeah, it was. The radiologist said it was small, like... um, 8 millimeters? Something like that.
[doctor] It was 8mm. And we decided to monitor it. But given the new symptoms, I want to take a closer look. Let’s have a nurse check your vitals first.
[nurse] Hi, James. I’m Sarah. I’ll just take your blood pressure and temperature.
[patient] Cheers.
[nurse] Your blood pressure is 120 over 80. Heart rate is 72 beats per minute. Temperature is 37.1 degrees now, so you’re afebrile.
[doctor] Good. James, let’s listen to your lungs. Take a deep breath in... and out.
[patient] Like that?
[doctor] Perfect. I’m listening here, at the 3 o’clock position on your right chest.
[patient] Is that where the nodule is?
[doctor] Not exactly. The nodule is deep in the lung tissue. I’m just listening for any crackles or wheezes that might suggest an infection or inflammation. Your breath sounds are clear.
[patient] Phew. Okay. So, do you think it’s infected?
[doctor] It’s possible. The fever and cough suggest an infectious process, maybe pneumonia or a viral infection, rather than something sinister related to the nodule itself. But we need to be sure.
[doctor] I’m going to order a new CT scan. And blood tests.
[patient] Blood tests? Like what?
[doctor] Full blood count, C-reactive protein to check for inflammation, and maybe some liver and kidney function tests. Just to make sure your body is handling things well.
[patient] Right. And the CT?
[doctor] We’ll do a contrast-enhanced CT to get a better view of the nodule and see if there’s any surrounding inflammation.
[patient] Will I need to fast?
[doctor] For the blood tests, yes. 8 hours without food. For the CT, it depends on the contrast, but usually, you can eat normally unless you’re diabetic or have kidney issues.
[patient] I’m fine with that. I’m a fitness trainer, so I’m used to watching what I eat.
[doctor] Good. So, I’ll refer you to the radiology department at St. Jude’s Hospital. They have the best scanners.
[patient] Is that far?
[doctor] It’s in Manchester, about 20 minutes from here.
[patient] I live in Bristol, actually.
[doctor] Oh, that’s quite a drive. Did you travel here specifically for this?
[patient] Yeah, I flew up last week. I’ve been staying with my brother.
[doctor] Your brother?
[patient] Yeah, Tom lives here.
[doctor] Nice of him. And your family history? Any history of lung cancer or tuberculosis?
[patient] My mother had breast cancer, but that was cured. No lung issues.
[doctor] Good to know. So, the plan is: blood tests, CT scan, and then we review the results.
[patient] When will I hear back?
[doctor] I’ll see you in two weeks. I have an appointment for you on 15th of October at 10:30.
[patient] Okay. October 15th. 10:30.
[doctor] I’ll send the details to your GP, and you can book the appointment with our clinic secretary.
[patient] Great. Thanks, Dr. Thorne.
[doctor] You’re welcome. Take care.

Dear Dr. Klaus Miller,

I am referring my patient, Maria Weber, for further management of a chronic ulcer.

Maria Weber
23-year-old female
Date of Birth: March 12, 2001
Address: 42 Lindwurmstrasse, 80337 Munich
Phone: 089-555-0192
Insurance: Barmer GEK
ID: A123456789

REASON FOR REFERRAL
Non-pressure chronic ulcer of the right heel and midfoot, unspecified severity.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient presents with a chronic ulcer on the right foot that has been present for approximately three months. The wound is located on the heel and midfoot. She reports intermittent drainage and mild pain upon walking. The ulcer is not pressure-related but may be exacerbated by prolonged standing due to her occupation as a librarian at the Central Library of Munich.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
The patient has a history of Hashimoto’s thyroiditis and mild Parkinson’s disease. There is no history of recent surgery. A routine check-up was performed last Tuesday, with normal blood work results.

SOCIAL HISTORY
The patient resides in Munich but originally moved from Freiburg five years ago. She is an active member of the Tennis Club Bavaria in Stuttgart.

1. Wound care with saline solution and appropriate bandaging.
2. Referral to Dr. Miller for specialized wound assessment and potential debridement.

Dr. Elias Thorne

Munich

note:
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Worsening lower extremity edema and elevated blood pressure in a 90-year-old male with a history of kidney transplant.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Weber is a 90-year-old male with a history of kidney transplant, presenting for follow-up. He reports increasing swelling in his lower legs over the past few weeks, describing it as uncomfortable but not painful. He was referred by Dr. Müller from his practice in Stuttgart due to elevated home blood pressure readings. Mr. Weber reports taking his immunosuppressive medications (Tacrolimus, Mycophenolate Mofetil, Prednisolone) and antihypertensive (Amlodipine) as prescribed. He denies fever, chills, dysuria, or hematuria. He reports chronic back pain, rated 3/10 in intensity, likely related to long-term steroid use. He mentions a nurse named Sclerosis who previously advised him on bone health.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: No fever, no weight loss.
Cardiovascular: Hypertension, no chest pain, no palpitations.
Respiratory: No cough, no shortness of breath.
Gastrointestinal: No nausea, no abdominal pain.
Renal: Decreased urine output not reported, but edema present.
Musculoskeletal: Chronic back pain, bilateral lower extremity edema.
Neurological: No weakness, no numbness.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs:
Blood Pressure: 152/94 mmHg
Heart Rate: 72 bpm
Temperature: 36.8°C
Respiratory Rate: 16/min
Oxygen Saturation: 97% on room air

General: Alert, oriented x3. No acute distress.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. No murmurs.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender. Transplant site in the right lower quadrant is non-tender to palpation.
Extremities: 2+ pitting edema in bilateral lower extremities, extending to mid-shin. Capillary refill < 3 seconds.
Skin: No rashes, no signs of infection.

RESULTS
Laboratory:
Serum Creatinine: 1.4 mg/dL (Previous: 1.2 mg/dL)
eGFR: 45 mL/min/1.73m²
Potassium: 4.8 mmol/L
Sodium: 138 mmol/L
Hemoglobin: 11.5 g/dL
White Blood Cell Count: 7.2 x 10^9/L
Urine Analysis: 2+ Protein, no bacteria.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Kidney Transplant Function:
- Stable but with slight rise in creatinine and elevated blood pressure.
- Plan:
  - Increase Furosemide to 60 mg daily in the morning to manage edema.
  - Continue current immunosuppressive regimen.
  - Repeat basic metabolic panel and creatinine in one week at the university hospital lab.
  - Monitor blood pressure at home; target < 130/80 mmHg.

2. Hypertension:
- Currently uncontrolled (152/94 mmHg).
- Plan:
  - Continue Amlodipine.
  - Reassess in two weeks; consider adding ACE inhibitor if BP remains elevated, monitoring for hyperkalemia.

3. Osteoporosis Risk:
- Chronic steroid use, age, and back pain suggest high risk.
- Plan:
  - Order DEXA scan.
  - Ensure adequate Vitamin D and Calcium intake.
  - Consider bisphosphonate therapy if DEXA confirms osteoporosis.

4. Follow-up:
- Next appointment with Dr. [Doctor's Name] on Thursday, the 14th of November at 10:30 AM.
- Patient has insurance with Barmer, ID number 44-82-19-00.
- Return precautions: If fever, significant increase in swelling, or decreased urine output, contact clinic immediately.

[doctor] that is good adherence . did you take your blood pressure medication ?
[patient] yes , i take amlodipine . but my home monitor shows readings around 150 over 90 in the morning .

[patient] please do .
[doctor] i am palpating your lower right quadrant . do you feel any pain when i press here ?
[patient] no , it is soft . no pain .

[patient] yes , my socks leave deep marks .

[patient] where should i go for the blood test ?
[doctor] you can go to the lab at the university hospital . they are familiar with transplant protocols .
[patient] is it the one in the north of the city ?
[doctor] yes , the clinic associated with the university . you will need to bring your insurance card .
[patient] i have it here . my insurance is with barmer . the number is 44-82-19-00 .

[patient] my back has been aching for months . it is a dull pain , maybe a 3 out of 10 on the pain scale .
[doctor] that could be related to osteoporosis from the steroids . i am going to order a dexa scan .
[patient] i know a woman named sclerosis . she is a nurse at my previous clinic . she always told me to be careful with my bones .
[doctor] i see . it is a common name , though perhaps a bit ironic given your condition . we will definitely monitor your bone density .
[patient] i am also worried about the infection risk . i am 90 years old , after all .
[doctor] age is a factor , but your immune system is stable as long as you avoid crowds and sick contacts . have you had any recent illnesses ?
[patient] no , i have been staying home mostly . i watch the news and read the newspaper .
[doctor] that is wise . let’s discuss your upcoming appointments . you need to see me again in two weeks to check the new creatinine levels .
[patient] when exactly ?
[doctor] i have an opening on thursday, the 14th of november , at 10:30 am .
[patient] thursday morning . i will mark it in my diary .
[doctor] perfect . and if your swelling gets worse , or if you have any fever , call the clinic immediately .
[patient] understood . thank you , doctor .
[doctor] you are welcome , herr weber . take care .

note:
SUBJECTIVE
Patient is a 19-year-old male with a history of acquired absence of bilateral breasts and nipples. He reports that the changes began approximately three months ago, characterized by a gradual reduction in breast volume and disappearance of nipples and areolas. The process has been bilateral and symmetrical. He denies pain, pruritus, discharge, or skin changes other than the loss of tissue. He reports recent deepening of voice and increased muscle mass, consistent with pubertal development. He had a mild febrile illness yesterday, which has resolved. He denies recent changes in medications, supplements, or topical treatments. He lives in Basel and moved from Asmara two years ago. He works as a barista and is a member of the Basel Volley Club. [doctor] It’s possible, but let’s focus on the current labs. Your protein levels are elevated, and your kidney function is reduced.
[patient] Is this serious?
[doctor] It is serious, but manageable. We need to control your blood pressure and reduce the protein in your urine.
[patient] What about my brother? He has high blood pressure too.
[doctor] Family history is important. Does your mother have any kidney problems?
[patient] No, my mother had heart issues, but not kidneys.

[patient] That sounds invasive.
[doctor] It is necessary for a precise diagnosis. I’m sending the referral to Dr. Miller at the specialist clinic.

[patient] Where is his office located?

[patient] Yes, I do.

[patient] I trust him?

[patient] That’s good to hear.
[doctor] Let’s get you out of here. The nurse will help you with the paperwork.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor.

note:
SUBJECTIVE
63-year-old female presents with pain in the left elbow for approximately one week. Symptoms started after returning from a trip to Lyon on 14th of October. Patient describes sharp pain on the lateral aspect of the elbow, exacerbated by lifting, gripping, and sleeping. Pain is localized and does not radiate. Patient reports difficulty opening jars and performing daily activities. Past medical history includes Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, managed with Levothyroxine. No other chronic conditions. No drug allergies. Patient is a librarian and reports significant repetitive hand use from computer work and knitting. Patient is a member of Leeds Yoga Collective.

OBJECTIVE
Vital Signs: BP 128/82, HR 76, Temp 36.8.
Physical Exam: Left elbow shows tenderness to palpation over the lateral epicondyle. Pain reproduced with resisted extension of the wrist and thumb (Cozen’s test positive). Pain also present with resisted supination. Range of motion is slightly limited in flexion due to pain, but full extension is intact. No swelling, redness, or deformity. Neurological exam of the arm is normal. Cervical spine is mobile without tenderness.

ASSESSMENT
1. Lateral Epicondylitis (Tennis Elbow) of the left elbow. Likely etiology: repetitive strain from occupational computer use and hobbies (knitting).
2. Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, stable.

PLAN
1. Rest: Advise patient to avoid repetitive gripping and heavy lifting for 2-4 weeks.
2. Medication: Ibuprofen 400mg TID with food for 7 days. Discontinue if gastrointestinal upset occurs.
3. Referral: Referred to physiotherapy for eccentric stretching exercises and manual therapy. Referral sent to margaret.evans1961 at hotmail dot com.
4. Support: Prescription for an elbow counterforce strap to reduce tendon load during activity.
5. Follow-up: Return to clinic if symptoms do not improve within 14 days or if they worsen.
6. Labs: CBC, ESR, CRP ordered to rule out systemic inflammation, given history. Results to be reviewed in 3 days.
7. Insurance: Verified with NHS, ID 485 772 1996.

[patient] Yeah, that’s right. It’s the left one. It’s been driving me mad for the last few days, you know?

[patient] Mostly pain. Sharp pain when I try to lift anything. Like, I couldn’t even open a jar yesterday.
[doctor] Where exactly is the pain? Can you point to it for me?
[patient] Right here. On the outer side of the elbow. Like, if I put my hand on my head, it hurts right here.
[doctor] Okay. And does it radiate anywhere? Down the arm or up towards the shoulder?
[patient] No, just stays in the elbow. But it’s annoying when I sleep. I have to keep my arm straight, otherwise it twinges.

[patient] Well, my mum had Arthritis... no, wait, she had Rheumatoid Arthritis. I don’t think I have that. My Dr. Smith checked my bloods last year and they were fine.
[doctor] I see. Do you have any other medical conditions? I see a note about thyroid issues in your file.
[patient] Oh, yes. I have Hashimoto’s. I take Levothyroxine for that. It’s been stable for years, though.
[doctor] And are you currently on any other medications?
[patient] Just the Levothyroxine. And I take some ibuprofen if I get a headache, but not regularly.
[doctor] Any allergies?
[patient] No, none that I know of.
[doctor] Okay. Let’s take a look. Please turn your palm up. Good. Now, make a fist. Squeeze it. Does that hurt?
[patient] Ouch! Yes, right there.
[doctor] Okay. Now, extend your arm straight out in front of you. Turn your palm down. Now, try to lift your thumb up against resistance.
[patient] Aaah! That’s the worst one. It’s like a stab.

[patient] I can do it, but it’s stiff. Maybe not all the way.
[doctor] Okay. Now extend it fully.
[patient] That’s okay.
[doctor] I’m going to palpate the area now. This might be tender. I’m pressing on the lateral epicondyle here.
[patient] Yes, that’s the spot. It’s very sore to the touch.
[doctor] And here, at the origin of the extensor muscles.
[patient] Still sore, but less than the bone part.
[doctor] I’m going to do a quick check on the rest of your arm to make sure it’s not referred pain. I’m checking your cervical spine. Any neck pain?

[patient] Of course.
[nurse] Your blood pressure is 128/82. Heart rate is 76. Temperature is 36.8.
[doctor] Thank you. Mrs. Evans, can I ask about your insurance? I need to verify your coverage for the potential referral to physiotherapy.

[patient] Is it serious?
[doctor] Not at all. This looks like a very common condition. It’s called Lateral Epicondylitis, commonly known as tennis elbow. It’s an overuse injury of the tendons on the outside of the elbow.

[doctor] It’s a misnomer. It can happen from any repetitive activity. Do you do any gardening? Or use a computer mouse a lot?

[doctor] Just go to Boots on the high street and show them this prescription.

[doctor] If it doesn’t improve in two weeks, please contact us. But I expect you’ll feel better in a few days with the rest and medication.
[patient] Thank you, doctor. I appreciate it.
[doctor] You’re welcome. Take care.

dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning. Please, have a seat. I am Dr. Rossi. I understand you have been feeling quite unwell lately.
[patient] Yes, good morning. It’s, um, it’s been really difficult. I don’t know how to explain it. I just feel... empty.
[doctor] Take your time. You are in a safe space here. Can you tell me when this started?
[patient] Maybe two months ago? I was on a trip to Paris with my friend Lucia, and I was having so much fun. But when I came back to Milan, the switch flipped.
[doctor] That is a very common reaction. The contrast between a holiday and daily routine can be jarring. What has changed in your daily life since you returned?
[patient] Well, work. I work as a project manager at TechNova Solutions. The stress is... it’s just too much. I can’t sleep. I lie in bed at 3 am staring at the ceiling.
[doctor] Sleep is crucial for mood regulation. Have you tried any over-the-counter remedies?
[patient] I took some Zoloft that my cousin Marco recommended, but I didn’t finish the box. I didn’t want to get dependent.
[doctor] I see. It is important not to self-medicate without supervision. Let’s talk about your family history. Does anyone else in your family struggle with similar issues?
[patient] My mother has had anxiety her whole life. And my uncle, Schizophrenia, well, actually his name is Schizo, which is funny because he doesn’t have the disease, but he is a chef.
[doctor] I understand the humor, but let’s focus on the clinical aspect. Does your mother have a formal diagnosis?
[patient] Yes, she has generalized anxiety. My father is fine. He is 55 years old. My brother Luca is 24. He is very supportive.
[doctor] Support systems are vital. How is your relationship with Luca right now?
[patient] It’s okay. He tries to cheer me up, but sometimes I just want to be alone. I feel like I’m failing at everything.
[doctor] Feeling like a failure is a common symptom of low mood. It is not a fact, but a symptom. We need to treat it. I would like to prescribe an antidepressant to help stabilize your sleep and mood.
[patient] Is it safe? I’m 29 years old. I’m still young.
[doctor> You are at an age where your brain is resilient. We will start with a low dose of Escitalopram. 10 mg once daily in the morning.
[patient] Okay. And what about the sleep?
[doctor] We can add a short-term aid for the first two weeks. Tramadol is sometimes used, but I prefer Esopiclone for a very short period to help you sleep.
[patient] I can do that. Do I need to go to the pharmacy?
[doctor] Yes. I will send the prescription electronically to your local pharmacy. Do you have your insurance card with you?
[patient] Yes, here it is. My record number is HR-88231-MI.
[doctor] Thank you. I have noted that. Now, let’s discuss lifestyle factors. Have you been exercising?
[patient] Not really. I used to go to the gym, but I just don’t have the energy.
[doctor] Gentle movement can help. Even a walk in Parco Sempione in the afternoon can improve your endorphin levels.
[patient] I might try that. I also eat a lot of sugar when I’m stressed.
[doctor] That is understandable. Try to keep meals regular. Blood sugar crashes can worsen mood swings.
[patient] I will try. By the way, my neighbor Giulia is a nurse. She told me to meditate.
[doctor] Meditation is an excellent tool. Apps like Headspace can be very helpful.
[patient] I don’t have a subscription.
[doctor] There are many free resources. We can focus on the medication first. How do you feel about seeing a psychologist?
[patient] I’m a bit nervous about that. I don’t want to talk to a stranger about my problems.
[doctor> It is normal to feel that way. We can start with just the medication and see how you respond. If you are open to it, we can refer you to a colleague for cognitive behavioral therapy.
[patient] Maybe. Let’s see how the pills work first.
[doctor] Agreed. I want to check your physical health as well to rule out any underlying causes. Can I check your blood pressure?
[patient] Sure.
[doctor] Your blood pressure is 120 over 80. That is normal. I am going to perform a quick neurological exam. Can you stick out your tongue?
[patient] Like this?
[doctor] Perfect. Now, I am going to check your reflexes. I noticed a slight asymmetry in your facial muscles. There is a minor weakness at the 3 o'clock position of your left eyelid.
[patient] Oh? Is that serious?

dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning. I see you’re here for a follow-up on that chest X-ray we ordered last week?

[patient] Yes, good morning. I’m Margaret Thorne. I’m fifty-eight.

[doctor] Hello, Mrs. Thorne. I’m Dr. Aris. Please, take a seat. How have you been feeling since we saw you two weeks ago?

[patient] Honestly, not great. I’ve had this tightness in my chest for three months now. It’s mostly when I climb the stairs at work.

[doctor] And where exactly do you feel this tightness? Is it sharp or dull?

[patient] It’s dull, you know? Like a band is squeezing me. Mostly in the center, but sometimes it radiates to my left arm.

[doctor] I see. And how would you rate that discomfort on a scale of zero to ten, with zero being no pain and ten being the worst possible pain?

[patient] Uh, maybe a four or five when it’s bad. A two at rest.

[doctor] Okay. Now, let’s look at the imaging results. I can see the report from the radiology department. It noted an "other nonspecific abnormal finding of lung field."

[patient] What does that mean? Is it cancer? Please say it’s not cancer.

[doctor] Please don’t panic. "Nonspecific" means the radiologist saw something that looked unusual, but it didn’t have the clear characteristics of a tumor. It looked more like a small patch of scarring or perhaps mild inflammation.

[patient] Inflammation? I don’t have asthma. I don’t smoke. I’ve never smoked.

[doctor] Correct, your history is negative for smoking. Given that, we need to rule out a few things. I’ve ordered a CT scan of your chest for tomorrow morning at 08:30.

[patient] Tomorrow? That’s quite quick.

[doctor] Yes, it’s better to get clarity sooner. In the meantime, I’d like you to continue the <DRUG>Naproxen</DRUG> you’re currently taking for the pain, but take it with food.

[patient] I am taking that. I bought it from the pharmacy on Broad Street yesterday.

[doctor] Good. Now, let’s check your vitals while we wait. Nurse, could you come in please?

[nurse] Right, Mrs. Thorne. Just some quick checks. Your blood pressure is 138 over 86. Your heart rate is 78 beats per minute. Your temperature is 36.8 degrees Celsius. Oxygen saturation is 98% on room air.

[patient] Is that blood pressure okay?

[nurse] It’s a little on the high side, but not alarming. We’ll monitor it.

[doctor] Thank you, Nurse. Mrs. Thorne, did you mention what you do for a living?

[patient] I work as a financial analyst at Northbridge Capital in Manchester.

[doctor] That’s a high-stress job. Do you have a colleague or friend who knows about these symptoms?

[patient] I told David. He’s my neighbor and a good friend. He’s a plumber by the way. He said I should just rest more.

[doctor] Rest is good, but we need to investigate the lung finding. Have you had any fever, night sweats, or unexplained weight loss?

[patient] No, I haven’t. I actually put on a bit of weight. I haven’t been eating much because of the anxiety.

[doctor] Okay. Let’s discuss the next steps. After the CT scan, we may need a pulmonology referral. I’ll send the referral today.

[patient] Will I be able to go back to work?

[doctor] I think it’s wise to take a few days off if you can, until we have the CT results. Stress can exacerbate chest tightness, even if it’s not cardiac.

[patient] I’ll speak to my manager. Her name is Sarah. She’s quite understanding.

[doctor] Good. Do you have any allergies to medications?

[patient] No, not that I know of. I’m allergic to <DRUG>Penicillin</DRUG> though. It causes hives.

[doctor] Noted. I’ll make sure that’s flagged in your chart. Your record number is MTC-994201.

[patient] Is there anything else I should watch out for?

[doctor] If you experience severe chest pain, shortness of breath at rest, or cough up blood, go to the emergency department immediately. Do not wait.

[patient] I understand. I’ll be careful.

[doctor] Also, keep a diary of when the pain occurs. Note what you were doing, your activity level, and the pain score.

[patient] I’ll do that. I usually get it after I’ve been sitting at my desk for four hours.

[doctor] That makes sense. Prolonged sitting can cause musculoskeletal issues that mimic chest pain. But we must rule out the lung issue first.

[patient] Yes. I’ll try to walk around the office more.

[doctor] That’s a good idea. Let’s set up the CT scan appointment. The scanner is at St. Jude’s Medical Center.

[patient] Is that far from my home?

[doctor] It’s about a twenty-minute drive from Edinburgh, where I believe you used to live?

[patient] No, I moved to Bristol last year. I used to live in Edinburgh when I was younger.

[doctor] My apologies for the confusion. Bristol is closer then.

[patient] Yes, much closer.

[doctor] The appointment is for October 14 at 08:30. Please bring this letter.

[patient] I have it.

[doctor] Do you have any questions about the diagnosis so far?

[patient] Just... what are the odds it’s serious?

[doctor] The odds are low. Most nonspecific findings turn out to be benign scarring from old infections or minor inflammation. But we must be thorough.

[patient] That’s a relief. I was worried.

[doctor] It’s understandable to be worried. Let’s get the scan done and then we can discuss the results in detail.

[patient] Thank you, Dr. Aris.

[doctor] You’re welcome, Mrs. Thorne. Nurse, can you print the CT referral and the medication instructions?

[nurse] Yes, Doctor.

[doctor] Mrs. Thorne, please follow these instructions for the Naproxen. Take 500 mg twice a day with food.

[patient] I’ll take notes.

[doctor] Also, stay hydrated. Dehydration can sometimes worsen respiratory symptoms.

[patient] I drink plenty of water.

[doctor] Good. Is there anything else?

[patient] No, I think that’s everything.

[doctor] Okay. We’ll see you after the scan. If you can’t get to the scan, please call the clinic at 0117 456 7890.

[patient] I’ll call if there’s a problem.

[doctor] Thank you.

REFERRAL LETTER

Dear Dr. Thompson,

Re: Sarah Ellis, 46
Address: 12 Oak Street, Manchester M4 5AB
Contact: 07911 123456

Thank you for referring Sarah for evaluation of bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome. She is a graphic designer residing in Manchester, having moved from Leeds in January of this year.

**History of Present Illness**
Sarah presents with a six-month history of bilateral numbness and tingling in the median nerve distribution of both hands, worse at night and upon waking. She reports shaking her hands to relieve symptoms. Symptoms have exacerbated since her move to Manchester and increased work demands at Pixelate Studio. She traveled to Lisbon in May recently, where she noted increased symptoms after prolonged computer use.

**Relevant History**
Family history is notable for Parkinson's disease in her father, David (deceased, 75), and Graves' disease in her aunt, Maria. Her mother, Patricia (68), and maternal uncle, Gerald (72), have osteoarthritis. Sarah has a known Baker's cyst in the right knee, which is stable and unrelated to the current complaint.

**Examination**
Bilateral positive Phalen’s and Tinel’s signs. Sensory loss noted in the median nerve distribution of the thumbs and index fingers. No thenar wasting. A mild soft tissue swelling was noted at the wrist, but no discrete mass at the 3 o'clock position upon palpation of the carpal tunnel.

**Investigations**
Recent blood work shows normal TSH and Free T4, excluding Hashimoto's thyroiditis as a contributing factor. Fasting glucose is 5.4 mmol/L, excluding diabetes.

**Plan**
1. Discuss corticosteroid injection for symptomatic relief.
2. Referral to hand surgery for potential decompression if conservative management fails.
3. Continue night splinting with adjusted fit.
4. Ergonomic review at work.

Please advise if any further information is required.

Yours sincerely,

Dr. Aris
Nephrologist
City General Hospital
Manchester

[patient] I think so, a little. It’s been quite damp here. I moved in January of this year. I’m finding the cold a bit harder to manage than I did back in Leeds.

[patient] No, she’s fine. But her brother, Gerald, who is 72, has severe arthritis. I worry I might have inherited something similar.

[doctor] Good morning, Mr. Perera. I see you’re here for your follow-up regarding your recent skiing incident. How have you been feeling since we last spoke?
[patient] Ah, good morning, Doctor. Um, honestly? It’s... it’s okay. I’m managing. But my knee still feels a bit stiff when I wake up in the morning.

[patient] Yes. It was last Tuesday. I was skiing at St. Moritz. I went too fast on the blue run, you know, just a small bump, and I fell. I hit my knee hard on the ice.

[patient] They did an X-ray. The doctor there said there was no fracture, but there was swelling. He gave me some physiotherapy advice and sent me home with painkillers.
[doctor] What medication were you given?
[patient] Ibuprofen, 400 milligrams. I took it as directed, three times a day. But yesterday, I felt a sharp pain when I tried to bend my knee to put on my socks.

[patient] Please be gentle.

[patient] Okay. How soon can I get that?
[doctor] I can refer you to the radiology department at University Hospital Zurich. I will send the referral today.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

PATIENT INFORMATION
Name: Jan Kowalski
Date of Birth: 1938
Age: 86
Record Number: MRN-992814
Date of Visit: February 12, 2024

REFERRAL
Referring Physician: Dr. Hoffman
Practice: St. Mary's Hospital
Reason for Referral: Evaluation of chronic joint pain and suspected rheumatoid arthritis.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is an 86-year-old male presenting with a 6-month history of progressive bilateral hand and wrist pain, stiffness, and swelling. He reports morning stiffness lasting up to two hours. Pain is rated 6/10 on a numeric rating scale, increasing to 7/10 with activity. He denies fever, night sweats, or significant weight loss. He recently traveled to Prague for a family visit. He is an active member of the Old Town Chess Club and reports no difficulty with fine motor tasks such as moving chess pieces, though he avoids strong gripping.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
- Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
- Hypertension
- Osteoarthritis (knees)

CURRENT MEDICATIONS
- Metformin 500 mg twice daily
- Arcoxia 60 mg as needed for pain

ALLERGIES
- None known

SOCIAL HISTORY
- Lives in Germany, originally from Wrocław, Poland.
- Retired.
- Non-smoker.
- Social contact via Old Town Chess Club.

VITAL SIGNS
- Blood Pressure: 145/90 mmHg
- Heart Rate: 78 bpm
- Temperature: 36.8 °C
- Respiratory Rate: 16/min

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
- General: Alert, oriented, no acute distress.
- Musculoskeletal:
  - Hands: Bilateral synovitis of the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints. Tenderness present.
  - Wrists: Bilateral wrist tenderness. A small, firm nodule palpable at the 3 o'clock position on the dorsal aspect of the right wrist.
  - Elbows: Mild tenderness over the olecranon bursae bilaterally.
  - Range of Motion: Mildly restricted in the wrists and hands due to pain.

DIAGNOSIS
1. Rheumatoid Arthritis, unspecified (Primary)
2. Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (Secondary)
3. Hypertension (Secondary)

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
The clinical presentation is consistent with rheumatoid arthritis. We will initiate treatment with a disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD) to slow disease progression and prevent joint damage.

1. Medications:
   - Start Methotrexate 7.5 mg once weekly (Sunday).
   - Start Prednisone 5 mg daily for 14 days as a bridge therapy.
   - Continue Arcoxia 60 mg as needed for pain (max 1/day).
   - Continue Metformin for diabetes management.

2. Diagnostics:
   - Blood work: CBC, ESR, CRP, RF, Anti-CCP, Liver Function Tests, Renal Function.
   - Imaging: X-ray of hands and wrists (bilateral).

3. Referrals:
   - Physical Therapy: Referral to Riverside Physical Therapy for joint preservation exercises.

4. Follow-up:
   - Next appointment: March 15, 2024 at 10:30 am.
   - Contact: j.kowalski86 at outlook dot com

PATIENT EDUCATION
- Discussed the nature of rheumatoid arthritis and the importance of early DMARD therapy.
- Instructed on proper administration of Methotrexate and side effects to watch for (e.g., mouth ulcers, fatigue, infection signs).
- Advised to maintain activity within pain limits, including participation in Old Town Chess Club.
- Encouraged to report any severe pain, swelling, or side effects.
