Patient stable, educated on new regimen, follow-up scheduled.
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning. I am Dr. Miller. Please, have a seat.
[patient] Good morning, Doctor. Thank you.
[doctor] I see you were referred to us by Dr. Hoffman at St. Mary's Hospital. He mentioned you have been dealing with some joint pain for a while.
[patient] Yes. Dr. Hoffman thought I should come to the orthopedics department because the pain in my hands is getting worse.
[doctor] I see. And where are you from originally?
[patient] I am from Wrocław in Poland. I moved here to Germany about twenty years ago.
[doctor] I see. And how old are you?
[patient] I am eighty-six.
[doctor] Thank you. Let’s talk about the pain. On a scale from zero to ten, where zero is no pain and ten is the worst pain imaginable, how would you rate your pain right now?
[patient] It is probably a six. Maybe a seven when I try to open jars.
[doctor] Okay. And where exactly is the pain located?
[patient] Mostly in my fingers. The knuckles, and the wrists. Sometimes the elbows.
[doctor] Do you have swelling?
[patient] Yes, especially in the mornings. They feel stiff.
[doctor] How long does the stiffness last?
[patient] Maybe an hour. Or two hours if it has been a cold night.
[doctor] I see. Have you had any other symptoms? Fever, fatigue, or weight loss?
[patient] No fever. But I am tired. I do not sleep as well as before.
[doctor] Did you travel recently? Sometimes travel can affect inflammation.
[patient] I went to Prague last month. I visited my daughter.
[doctor] I see. And do you have any hobbies or physical activities you are still doing?
[patient] I play chess. I am a member of the Old Town Chess Club. I go there every Tuesday.
[doctor] That sounds good for the mind. Do you still play with your hands?
[patient] Yes, I move the pieces. But I try not to grip them too hard.
[doctor] I see. Let’s take a look at your hands. Please extend your right hand.
[patient] Here.
[doctor] I see some swelling in the metacarpophalangeal joints. Let me check the wrist. I notice some tenderness here. Specifically, at the 3 o'clock position on the dorsal side of the wrist, there is a small, firm nodule.
[patient] Yes, that one hurts.
[doctor] And the left hand?
[patient] It is similar, but maybe a bit less swollen.
[doctor] I will order some blood tests to check for inflammatory markers. I will also request an X-ray of your hands and wrists.
[patient] Is it serious?
[doctor] It looks like rheumatoid arthritis. It is a chronic condition, but we can manage it well with the right treatment.
[patient] I am on some medication already.
[doctor] What are you taking?
[patient] I take Arcoxia for the pain. And my general practitioner gave me Metformin for diabetes.
[doctor] I see. Arcoxia is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug. It helps with pain, but it does not stop the disease from progressing. We need to start a disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug, or DMARD.
[patient] What is that?
[doctor] It is a medication that slows down the immune system to prevent joint damage. We usually start with Methotrexate.
[patient] I have heard that name. Is it safe for my age?
[doctor] We will monitor your blood work closely. Your liver and kidney function need to be stable.
[patient] My blood pressure is usually high.
[doctor] Let’s check it now. A nurse will be in to measure it.
[nurse] Good morning. I am going to take your blood pressure and heart rate.
[patient] Okay.
[nurse] Your blood pressure is 145 over 90. Your heart rate is 78 beats per minute.
[doctor] Thank you. We will discuss adjusting your blood pressure medication if needed.
[patient] What about the pain? Can I take more Arcoxia?
[doctor] No, you should not increase the dose without talking to me. We will start the Methotrexate, and it may take six to eight weeks to work. In the meantime, we can use a short course of corticosteroids to help with the inflammation.
[patient] Pills? Or injections?
[doctor] We can start with oral Prednisone, a low dose, for a few weeks.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] I will write a prescription for Methotrexate 7.5 mg, taken once a week. And Prednisone 5 mg, taken in the morning for two weeks.
[patient] And the Arcoxia?
[doctor] You can continue taking Arcoxia 60 mg as needed for pain, but no more than once a day.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] I will also refer you to a physical therapist. They can teach you exercises to keep your joints flexible.
[patient] Is there a therapist nearby?
[doctor] Yes, I will refer you to Riverside Physical Therapy.
[patient] I live near the park.
[doctor] That is good. They are not far from there.
[patient] What about the chess club? Can I still go?
[doctor] Yes, absolutely. Keeping active is important. Just be mindful of your grip strength.
[patient] I will try to be careful.
[doctor] Do you have any questions about the new medication?
[patient] What if I forget to take the Methotrexate?
[doctor] Try to take it on the same day every week. I suggest Sunday morning. If you forget, take it as soon as you remember that day. Do not double up the next day.
[patient] Okay. Sunday morning.
[doctor] How can we contact you if you have any side effects?
[patient] You can write to me. My e-mail is j.kowalski86 at outlook dot com.
[doctor] I will note that down. Or you can call the clinic.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] Let’s schedule your next appointment. We need to check your blood work in six weeks.
[patient] When is a good time?
[doctor] How about March 15, 2024?
[patient] That works.
[doctor] At what time?
[patient] Morning is better.
[doctor] I have an opening at 10:30 am.
[patient] Perfect.
[doctor] I will book that for you.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor.
[doctor] You are welcome. The nurse will show you out. She will also give you some information sheets about rheumatoid arthritis.
[patient] Thank you.
[doctor] Take care.
[patient] Goodbye.

[patient] It was Dr. Keller. He works at Klinikum Winterthur.

[patient] No, I was in Zurich for a business trip. I had chest pain yesterday around 08:00.
[doctor] And you went to the emergency room?
[patient] Yes, my colleague José took me. José is 48. He lives in Bern.

[patient] Laura. She is 48. She is a teacher.

[patient] I was very nervous.
[doctor] That is normal. The ECG showed ST elevation in the inferior leads. We identified a blockage in the right coronary artery.
[patient] Yes, the angioplasty.
[doctor] How was the procedure?
[patient] They put a stent in. It was two weeks ago that I had the initial check-up, but this is my first follow-up here.
[doctor] You mean the procedure was last Tuesday?
[patient] Yes, Tuesday morning.

[patient] Aspirin, Clopidogrel, Atorvastatin, and Beta-blocker.
[doctor] Can you tell me the dosages?
[patient] Aspirin 100 mg daily. Clopidogrel 75 mg daily. Atorvastatin 40 mg at night. Metoprolol 50 mg twice a day.
[doctor] Good. Are you taking them consistently?
[patient] Yes.
[doctor] Any side effects?

[doctor] That could be the blood pressure lowering. Let’s check your current vitals.

[patient] And who will supervise it?
[doctor] Ms. Weber. She is the head of rehab.

[patient] I understand.
[doctor] Do you have a pharmacy nearby?
[patient] Yes, in Bern.

[patient] Thank you.

[patient] I will be careful.

[patient] One hour.

[patient] Two hours.

[doctor] That is good. You should keep doing that.
[patient] I will.
[doctor] Do you have any hobbies?

[doctor] You can start with short hikes. No mountains for now.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] Do you have a pet?

[patient] He is 5 years old.
[doctor] That is nice.
[doctor] Let’s review the plan. You will start rehab Monday. You will continue your medications. You will see me in three weeks.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] Do you have a phone number where we can reach you?
[patient] Yes, +41 78 123 45 67.

[patient] Bern, Switzerland.
[doctor] Do you have insurance?
[patient] Yes, Swiss Health.
[doctor] Your policy number?
[patient] 12345678.
[doctor] Thank you. Do you have any other questions?
[patient] No.

SUBJECTIVE
Patient is a 35-year-old male presenting with chronic musculoskeletal complaints, primarily shoulder stiffness and back pain. He works as a project manager for Renault in Strasbourg, having recently relocated from Annecy. He reports morning stiffness and a clicking sensation in the right shoulder. Family history is notable for orthopedic issues in his mother (hip replacement) and his brother (knee surgery). He reports using Ibuprofen and Volten patches with limited relief. Referred by Dr. Vincent Lacroix from Hôpital de la Pitié-Salpêtrière.

OBJECTIVE
Physical exam reveals tenderness in the right shoulder region. Palpation identifies a slight nodularity at the 3 o’clock position on the deltoid insertion. Range of motion is limited by pain in the right shoulder. No acute swelling or erythema noted.

ASSESSMENT
Chronic musculoskeletal pain, likely related to occupational posture and possible degenerative changes given family history. The nodularity suggests a localized soft tissue issue or early bursitis.

PLAN
1. Referral to physical therapy for shoulder stabilization and posture correction.
2. Continue current analgesic regimen as needed.
3. Follow-up appointment scheduled for October 12th at 14:30 to reassess progress.
4. Insurance verified under FR-8821-4490.

note:
SUBJECTIVE
Patient is an 88-year-old male presenting with a three-week history of erythematous papules and scaling around the mouth, chin, and nose. Symptoms include burning and mild itching, exacerbated by hot foods and coffee. Patient reports using hydrocortisone cream initially, which provided temporary relief before worsening symptoms. He denies any new cosmetic products or soaps. Patient is a retired structural engineer previously employed by ÖBB Infrastruktur. He resides in Innsbruck but was referred by Dr. Hans Weber at Klinikum Salzburg due to persistent symptoms. Patient has a history of Graves' disease, managed by Dr. Maria Stein, with last lab work on September 5, 2023. He is active in FC Tirol masters league. Family history is notable for eczema in his brother, Thomas (85). Patient moved from Graz to Innsbruck ten years ago.

OBJECTIVE
Vital signs stable. Physical examination of the face reveals well-demarcated erythematous papules and vesicles clustered around the perioral area, chin, and nasolabial folds. Central face is spared. Mild scaling present. No signs of active infection or secondary bacterial colonization. Skin appears slightly dry. No lymphadenopathy in the cervical region.

ASSESSMENT
1. Perioral dermatitis. Likely exacerbated by initial use of topical corticosteroids.
2. History of Graves' disease, stable.
3. Post-operative status of right knee meniscus repair (previous visit October 12, 2023).

PLAN
1. Discontinue all topical steroids and heavy moisturizers.
2. Prescribe topical metronidazole 0.75% gel, apply twice daily to affected areas for 14 days.
3. Advise patient to use only gentle, fragrance-free cleansers and avoid spicy/acidic foods.
4. Follow up via email at dr.huber at sportklinik dot at in two weeks if no improvement.
5. Continue physical therapy for knee as scheduled on November 1, 2023 at 14:00.
6. No further immediate diagnostic testing required.
dialogue:
[doctor] good morning . i see you were referred to our sports medicine clinic by dr . hans weber at klinikum salzburg . he mentioned you had some persistent skin issues that weren't responding to standard treatments . is that correct ?

[patient] yes , that is correct . i was seen by dr . weber about three weeks ago because i thought i might have a contact allergy from new gloves i bought for gardening .

[doctor] and when did these symptoms first start ?

[patient] it started quite suddenly , maybe two weeks ago . i noticed small red bumps around my mouth and chin . i thought it was just irritation from shaving , but it got worse .

[doctor] i see . you have an appointment record from october 12, 2023 with my colleague dr . elena fischer regarding your knee . is that the same knee that was operated on ?

[patient] yes , exactly . that was for the meniscus repair . i am doing well with the recovery , but this skin problem is very annoying . i live in innsbruck , so traveling to vienna for my main doctor is difficult .

[doctor] understood . can you tell me more about the rash ? does it itch or burn ?

[patient] it burns , mostly . and it itches a bit , but the burning is worse when i eat hot food or drink coffee . i try to avoid spicy things now .

[doctor] have you applied any creams or ointments ?

[patient] i used a hydrocortisone cream my pharmacist suggested . it seemed to help for a day or two , but then it came back stronger . i stopped using it yesterday .

[doctor] that is a common pattern . steroids can sometimes worsen this specific condition . do you have any other medical conditions ? i see in your chart that you have a history of graves' disease management , but it is stable .

[patient] yes , the thyroid is fine . my endocrinologist , dr . maria stein , checks it every six months . my last blood test was on september 5, 2023 .

[doctor] good . and you mentioned you were gardening . do you use any new soaps or facial cleansers ?

[patient] no , i have used the same mild soap for years . i am an retired structural engineer for öbb infrastruktur . i have been retired for four years , so i spend a lot of time on hobbies .

[doctor] what are your hobbies ?

[patient] i am very involved in fc tirol . i play in the masters league on saturdays . we train at the stadium near amras . i also hike in the dolomites when the weather is nice .

[doctor] that is excellent for your health . does the rash appear after you train or sweat ?

[patient] not really . it seems to be there all the time . my neighbor , georg , has a similar issue . he said he was diagnosed with perioral dermatitis . i didn't know it had a name .

[doctor] yes , it is a specific inflammatory condition . it is often mistaken for eczema or rosacea . do you have any family history of skin conditions ?

[patient] my brother , thomas , who is 85 years old , has severe eczema . he lives in vienna . my sister , anna , is 82 and lives here in innsbruck . she has no skin problems .

[doctor] i see . did you move here recently ?

[patient] no , i was born in graz . i moved to innsbruck ten years ago when i retired . i prefer the mountains .

[doctor] let me take a look at your face . please lean in slightly . [examining the face] i can see small , red , papules clustered around your mouth , chin , and nose . there is some scaling . the central part of your face looks relatively spared . this presentation is very typical for perioral dermatitis .

[patient] it looks terrible in the mirror . i feel self-conscious .

[doctor] it is a common condition , though unpleasant . it is not contagious . we need to stop any potential irritants . have you been using any heavy moisturizers or makeup ?

[patient] i use a thick cream at night . i bought it at a pharmacy in old town .

[doctor] we will need to stop that . i will prescribe a topical antibiotic cream . it is not a steroid . you will apply it twice a day for two weeks .

[patient] okay . do i need to see dr . weber again ?

[doctor] no , you can contact me directly . my email is dr.huber at sportklinik dot at . if it does not improve in two weeks , please send me a message . also , avoid spicy foods , acidic fruits , and heavy creams for now .

[patient] and the sweating from football ?

[doctor] sweat can sometimes irritate it , but it is not the main cause . just wash your face gently with cool water after training . do not scrub .

[patient] i will do that . my wife , helene , is 86 and very strict about hygiene . she will make sure i wash my face .

[doctor] that is good . you have an appointment with physical therapy on november 1, 2023 . is that still scheduled ?

[patient] yes , at 14:00 . the therapist is stefan . he is very good .

[doctor] good . i will put a note in your chart . do you have any questions about the medication ?

[patient] no , it seems simple enough . i just hope it goes away . i have a tournament next month .

[doctor] we will do our best . i will send the prescription to your pharmacy in hötting . you can pick it up tomorrow morning .

[patient] thank you , doctor . i appreciate the help .

[doctor] you are welcome . please rest and keep the area clean and dry .

[doctor] Good morning, Emin. Please, have a seat. How have you been since our last visit?

[patient] Yes, my mother has Hashimoto’s, and my brother had Graves' disease. So I was worried I might have something similar.
[doctor] Your thyroid levels were normal last time. But let’s keep an eye on it. Are you on any new medications?
[patient] Um, I started taking Benadryl for allergies last month. And maybe some... uh, muscle relaxants?
[doctor] Which ones specifically?
[patient] I think it was Cyclobenzaprine. I picked it up from the pharmacy.

[doctor] Thank you. I’ll update your file. Now, regarding your history, do you have any family history of prostate issues? You’re young, so it’s unlikely, but we check.
[patient] No, my dad is healthy. My uncle had Parkinson's, but that’s different.
[doctor] Correct. Different systems. Let’s focus on the bladder. I want to order an ultrasound to check for any residual urine.
[patient] Is that painful?
[doctor] No, it’s non-invasive. Just a gel and a probe. We’ll do it here in the clinic.
[patient] Okay. And what about the stress? I feel like my anxiety is making it worse.
[doctor] It’s a common cycle. Stress tightens the pelvic floor, which makes urination harder. We might try some behavioral therapy techniques.
[patient] I’m a software engineer, so I sit for ten hours a day. I should move more.
[doctor] That’s a good insight. Try to stand up every hour. Also, limit caffeine, especially after 2 pm.

dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning. Please have a seat. I see you are here for a follow-up on your anxiety, but you look quite unwell. What’s going on?
[patient] Oh, hi Dr. Weber. Um, yes, the anxiety is... it’s okay, I guess. But I’ve been feeling terrible since, like, three days ago. I have this awful cough and my head hurts.
[doctor] When did you first notice the symptoms?
[patient] It started on Monday. I had a slight scratch in my throat, and then by Tuesday it was much worse. I’ve been running a fever.
[doctor] Do you have any other symptoms? Congestion, sore throat, body aches?
[patient] Yes, everything hurts. My body aches are really bad. And I have a headache, right behind my eyes. It’s throbbing.
[doctor] Let’s check your vital signs. A nurse will be in shortly. In the meantime, are you taking any new medications?
[patient] No, just my usual. I take Sertraline for the anxiety, and I started taking some Ibuprofen for the pain.
[doctor] How much Ibuprofen are you taking?
[patient] Uh, two tablets, maybe three times a day? It’s not helping much, though.
[doctor] Let’s wait for the nurse to get your vitals. Then we can examine your throat and lungs.
[nurse] Hello, Mrs. Nowak. I’m here to check your temperature and blood pressure.
[patient] Hi. I feel so tired.
[nurse] Your temperature is 38.5 degrees Celsius. Your blood pressure is 130 over 85. Your pulse is 92 beats per minute.
[doctor] Thank you, Nurse. Let’s take a look. Please turn your head to the left.
[patient] Like this?
[doctor] Yes. Open your mouth wide and say "ah".
[patient] Ah.
[doctor] Your tonsils look a bit red, and there is some swelling. Let’s listen to your lungs. Breathe in deeply.
[patient] (Deep breath)
[doctor] Breathe out slowly. Again, deep breath in.
[patient] (Deep breath)
[doctor] Your lungs sound clear, though there is some mild bronchial breathing. You do have a viral upper respiratory infection. It’s common in this season.
[patient] So it’s not the flu?
[doctor] It could be, but it looks more like a common cold virus. It will likely resolve on its own in about a week.
[patient] That’s good to hear. I just need to get through this week. I have a big meeting at work.
[doctor] What do you do for a living?
[patient] I work as an administrative assistant at Siemens AG. My employer is quite strict about attendance.
[doctor] I understand. Do you think you can manage to work from home for a few days?
[patient] Maybe. I’ll have to ask my boss, Mr. Schmidt. He is usually understanding if I am sick.
[doctor] That might be a good idea. Rest is important. I will write a note for you.
[patient] Thank you. I am a bit worried about my insurance, though.
[doctor] Is there a specific concern?
[patient] My insurance is with AOK Rheinland/Hamburg. I just want to make sure this visit is covered.
[doctor] It is a standard medical visit, so it will be covered. Do you have your insurance card with you?
[patient] Yes, here it is. My number is 1234567890.
[doctor] Thank you. I will note that down. Now, regarding the treatment. I recommend plenty of fluids and rest. For the pain and fever, you can continue with Ibuprofen, but do not exceed the recommended dose.
[patient] Okay. Should I take anything else?
[doctor] You could try a decongestant if your nose is blocked. And a lozenge for the sore throat. I will prescribe you some paracetamol as well, just in case the Ibuprofen isn’t enough.
[patient] Okay. And the cough?
[doctor] The cough is likely post-nasal drip. It should improve as the infection clears up. If it persists for more than two weeks, or if you develop a high fever, shortness of breath, or chest pain, you should come back immediately.
[patient] Got it. No shortness of breath, just the cough.
[doctor] Good. How is your anxiety medication working?
[patient] It’s okay. I still have some anxious thoughts, but it’s manageable. I try to do my yoga in the morning, at Studio Asana in Hamburg.
[doctor] That’s great. Exercise can help with both physical recovery and mental health.
[patient] Yes, but I haven’t been able to go in the last few days. I’m too tired.
[doctor] Take it one day at a time. When you feel better, you can resume your routine.
[patient] I think I will. I really miss it. It’s my only escape sometimes.
[doctor] I understand. Let’s schedule your next follow-up for two weeks from now, to check on your mental health status.
[patient] Okay. That works.
[doctor] Do you have any questions for me today?
[patient] No, I think that’s everything. Thank you, Dr. Weber.
[doctor] You’re welcome, Mrs. Nowak. Please rest well.

SUBJECTIVE
Luciana Ferreira, a 49-year-old female, presents to the rheumatology clinic for evaluation of a right elbow contusion sustained yesterday. She states she has been taking <DRUG>Brufen</DRUG> twice daily since yesterday evening and has applied ice for 20-minute intervals. The patient notes significant swelling and stiffness. She is a graphic designer and plays volleyball for Verona Volley Club. She moved from São Paulo to Verona three years ago. She reports a history of hysterectomy five years ago and no other significant medical history. No known drug allergies. Her primary care physician, Dr. Bianchi, performed an X-ray two days ago which was negative for fracture.

OBJECTIVE
Vitals: BP 118/76, HR 72, Temp 36.8, RR 14, SpO2 99%.

General: Alert and oriented, in mild distress due to pain.

1. Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation (RICE) protocol.

note:
SUBJECTIVE
Patient is a 25-year-old male, Julien Moreau, born on May 15, 1998. He presents with a 3-week history of left ankle and midfoot pain. He reports twisting his left ankle during a basketball game at Club de Basket Fribourg three weeks ago. He was evaluated at the emergency department in Fribourg on October 12, 2023, where X-rays were reportedly negative for fracture. He had a blood test at the lab in Fribourg on October 15, 2023. He has been taking Ibuprofen and using Voltaren gel. Pain is currently 6/10 at rest and 8/10 with weight-bearing, localized to the lateral ankle and plantar forefoot. He moved from Geneva to Rue de la Gare 15, 1700 Fribourg two years ago. He is a software engineer. No drug allergies. No smoking. Social history includes occasional alcohol use. Recent travel to Paris prior to injury. Past surgical history includes appendectomy in 2018 at CHUV.

OBJECTIVE
Vital signs: BP 120/80 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, Temp 36.8°C, RR 14/min, SpO2 99%.
Physical Exam:
- General: Alert, oriented, in no acute distress.
- Left Ankle/Foot: Mild edema around the lateral malleolus. Tenderness to palpation over the lateral malleolus and the plantar aspect of the forefoot (metatarsal heads). Pain with active and passive dorsiflexion. Talar Tilt test negative. Thompson test negative. Gait is antalgic, favoring the right foot.

ASSESSMENT
1. Left ankle sprain, likely high ankle (syndesmotic) injury vs. subtle fracture.
2. Plantar fasciitis or metatarsal stress reaction, secondary to altered gait.
3. No signs of infection or systemic inflammatory disease based on history and vitals.

PLAN
1. Imaging: MRI of the left ankle and foot ordered via referral to Hôpital de Fribourg.
2. Labs: Repeat CBC and CRP ordered to monitor inflammation.
3. Medications: Continue Ibuprofen 400 mg TID with food for pain and inflammation. Continue Voltaren gel BID to the affected area.
4. Activity: Rest, ice, compression, and elevation (RICE) for 48 hours post-activity. Avoid high-impact activities including basketball until cleared.
5. Follow-up: Return to clinic on November 10, 2023 at 10:30 to review MRI results and adjust treatment plan.
6. Referral: Physical therapy referral to be considered if no improvement after 2 weeks of conservative management.
7. Insurance: Referral sent to SwissCare, policy 123456789.
8. Contact: Patient to contact clinic if pain worsens, fever develops, or if he experiences numbness/tingling.

[doctor] Did you seek medical attention right away?
[patient] I went to the emergency room in Fribourg that same evening. They took some X-rays. I think my last visit there was on October 12, 2023.

[doctor] Did you take any medication?
[patient] Yes, I took Ibuprofen as prescribed, and my friend suggested I try Voltaren gel for the swelling.

[patient] Right now, it’s a 6. It’s manageable, but it aches constantly. When I walk, it spikes to an 8.

[doctor] I’m going to press here, on the plantar aspect of the forefoot.

[patient] Okay.
[doctor] That’s negative. Now, a Thompson test.
[patient] That doesn’t hurt.
[doctor] Good. Your vitals are stable. Blood pressure is 120/80, heart rate 72, temperature 36.8 degrees. Let’s discuss the next steps. Given the mechanism and the persistent pain in the midfoot and ankle, I’m concerned about a high ankle sprain or a subtle fracture that wasn't visible on the initial X-ray.

[patient] I’m 25 years old, and my date of birth is May 15, 1998.
[doctor] Thank you, Julien. I’ll send the referrals to your email, julien.moreau@example.com. Is there anything else?

[doctor] You’re welcome. Take care.

note:
PATIENT NAME: Carmen Garcia
DATE OF BIRTH: 14/05/1954
RECORD NUMBER: 8842-9921
DATE OF ENCOUNTER: 10/11/2024

REASON FOR VISIT
Preprocedural cardiovascular evaluation prior to scheduled knee arthroplasty.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Carmen is a 70-year-old woman presenting for preoperative clearance. She reports a recent episode of chest tightness during exertion last March, which resolved with rest. She denies current chest pain, palpitations, or syncope. She reports mild shortness of breath on stairs, attributed to knee pain. She has a history of Parkinson’s disease, diagnosed three years ago, managed by Dr. Weber at Klinik Zentralspital. Her last visit with Dr. Weber was on 12/10/2024, where her condition was deemed stable. She also has a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia. She recently traveled to Barcelona with her sister, Lucia (75), and tolerated the activity well aside from mild exertional symptoms.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
1. Parkinson’s disease
2. Hypertension
3. Hyperlipidemia
4. Osteoarthritis of the right knee

MEDICATIONS
- Levodopa/Carbidopa 250/25 mg TID
- Bisoprolol 5 mg daily
- Atorvastatin 20 mg daily (increased to 40 mg today)
- Paracetamol PRN

ALLERGIES
None known.

FAMILY HISTORY
- Mother: Died of myocardial infarction at age 82.
- Brother, Pedro: Graves’ disease.
- Husband, Miguel (73): Type 2 Diabetes.
- Daughter, Elena (42): No significant history.
- Sister, Lucia (75): History of stroke.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Lives in Zürich. Smoker: No. Alcohol: Occasional. Occupation: Retired teacher.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
- General: Well-appearing, no acute distress.
- Vitals: BP 130/80 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, RR 14/min, Temp 36.8°C.
- Cardiac: Regular rate and rhythm. Mild systolic murmur heard at the apex, radiating to the axilla. No gallops or rubs.
- Lungs: Clear to auscultation bilaterally.
- Extremities: Mild tremor in hands (consistent with Parkinson’s). No edema.

INVESTIGATIONS
- ECG: Normal sinus rhythm, no ST changes.
- Recent Labs (from Praxis HerzGesundheit): Cholesterol elevated, HbA1c normal.

PLAN
1. Preprocedural clearance for knee surgery is granted with the following conditions:
   - Increase Atorvastatin to 40 mg daily.
   - Continue Bisoprolol 5 mg daily.
   - Monitor blood pressure at home.
2. Patient instructed to report any chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or syncope to Klinik Zentralspital or call 112.
3. Follow-up appointment scheduled for 15/11/2024 at 10:00.
4. Contact information on file: carmen.garcia at example dot com.
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, Carmen. Please, come in and sit down. I see you’re here for your pre-procedural check-up before your knee surgery. How are you feeling today?
[patient] Hello, Doctor. Um, honestly, I’m a bit nervous. You know, the knee hurts, but the idea of being under anesthesia... it’s scary.
[doctor] That’s completely normal. We just need to make sure your heart is ready for it. Let’s review your history. You are seventy years old, correct?
[patient] Yes, I am. And I have this... um, you know, the shaking in my hands? Parkinson’s disease. It’s been stable, I think.
[doctor] Yes, I see that in your records. You’ve been seeing Dr. Weber at Klinik Zentralspital for that. How has the medication been working?
[patient] Well, I take my Levodopa and Carbidopa every day. But sometimes in the morning, I feel a bit stiff. Like my whole body is frozen.
[doctor] And any episodes of confusion or hallucinations?
[patient] No, no. Just the stiffness. My daughter, Elena, who is forty-two, helps me with my pills. She is very strict.
[doctor] That’s good. Now, let’s talk about your heart. You mentioned you had a chest pain episode recently?
[patient] Yes, last March. I was walking to the bakery and I felt this tightness. It went away after I sat down.
[doctor] Did you go to the emergency room?
[patient] No, I was afraid. But then I saw Dr. Rossi at Praxis HerzGesundheit in Zürich. He did some tests.
[doctor] And what were the results?
[patient] He said my arteries are a bit blocked. He prescribed Atorvastatin and Bisoprolol. I also have high blood pressure.
[doctor] Let’s check your blood pressure now. <Nurse> can you bring the cuff?
[nurse] Of course, Doctor.
[patient] I had a nice trip to Barcelona last spring. My sister, Lucia, who is seventy-five, went with me. We walked a lot.
[doctor] That sounds lovely. But did the walking make your chest tight?
[patient] A little bit. But we took it slow. Lucia is very careful. She had a stroke five years ago, so she knows about health.
[doctor] I understand. Now, regarding your family history. Does anyone in your family have heart problems?
[patient] Yes. My mother had a heart attack. She died at eighty-two. And my brother, Pedro, he has Graves’ disease. It’s in the thyroid.
[doctor] And any history of diabetes or kidney disease?
[patient] No. But my husband, Miguel, who is seventy-three, has diabetes. He takes Metformin.
[doctor] Good. Let’s look at your recent blood work. I see your cholesterol is still a bit high.
[patient] Is that bad?
[doctor] We want to keep it lower before surgery. I’m going to adjust your Atorvastatin dose. Do you have any allergies to medications?
[patient] No, no allergies. I just get a little dizzy sometimes when I stand up quickly.
[doctor] That could be the Bisoprolol. Let’s monitor your heart rate.
[patient] My heart rate?
[doctor] Yes. Let’s listen to your heart. Breathe in deeply.
[patient] (Breathing)
[doctor] I hear a slight murmur. It’s likely benign, given your age, but we will monitor it. Do you have any shortness of breath?
[patient] Only when I climb stairs. But that’s because my knee is bad, not my lungs.
[doctor] Probably. Let’s do an ECG to check your rhythm.
[nurse] I’ll prepare the electrodes now.
[patient] I had a visit with Dr. Weber on October 12th. He said my Parkinson’s was stable.
[doctor] Yes, I saw that note. It’s good to have that clearance. Now, about the surgery. It’s scheduled for November 20th.
[patient] Oh, that’s soon. I need to tell my neighbor, Anna. She is sixty and she helps me with my groceries.
[doctor] You should definitely inform her. And make sure you have someone to take you home after the surgery.
[patient] My daughter, Elena, will be there. She lives in Bern. She will drive me.
[doctor] Good. Do you have your medical record number?
[patient] It is 8842-9921.
[doctor] Thank you. Let’s review your current medications. You are taking Levodopa 250 mg three times a day, Bisoprolol 5 mg once a day, Atorvastatin 20 mg once a day, and Paracetamol as needed for pain.
[patient] Yes, that’s right.
[doctor] I’m going to increase the Atorvastatin to 40 mg. And we will continue the Bisoprolol. Do you understand?
[patient] Yes, Doctor. I will tell Elena about the new dose.
[doctor] Please write down any questions you have. And if you have any chest pain or severe shortness of breath before the surgery, call 0800 112 112 immediately.
[patient] Okay. I will be careful.
[doctor] You seem to have good cardiovascular health overall for your age. The murmur is not concerning.
[patient] That is a relief. I was worried about my heart.
[doctor] We will do a final check-up on November 15th at 10:00.
[patient] Is that in the morning?
[doctor] Yes, 10:00 in the morning. I’ll send a reminder to your email.
[patient] My email is carmen.garcia at example dot com.
[doctor] Thank you. Do you have any other questions?
[patient] No, I think that’s everything. I just want to get my knee fixed so I can walk without pain.
[doctor] We’ll do our best. Take care.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor.

note:
PATIENT NAME: Jovanović, Marko
DATE OF BIRTH: 12/04/1975
RECORD NUMBER: 88231-NS
DATE OF ENCOUNTER: 25/05/2024

REASON FOR VISIT
Follow-up for persistent fatigue and headache following a recent viral infection. Referred by Dr. Miller from General Practice of St. Stephan.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a 49-year-old male from Belgrade, Serbia who resides in Vienna, Austria. He reports a history of viral symptoms starting three weeks ago, characterized by fever, malaise, and headache. The fever resolved, but fatigue and a tight band-like headache at the occiput persist. He reports mild visual blurriness that has resolved. He denies focal neurological deficits, balance issues, or speech disturbances. He took Paracetamol and Ibuprofen for symptom management. Ibuprofen was discontinued two days ago due to gastric discomfort.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Hypertension (well-controlled). Family history of diabetes (negative personal history) and Hashimoto's thyroiditis in sister.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Civil engineer. Moved to Austria five years ago. Non-smoker. Minimal alcohol use.

EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 130/85 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, Temp 36.8°C.
General: Alert, oriented, no acute distress.
Neurological: Cranial nerves II-XII intact. No facial asymmetry (rules out Bell's palsy). Motor strength 5/5 in all extremities. Reflexes 2+ and symmetric. Sensory exam normal. Gait steady. No ataxia.

ASSESSMENT
Post-viral syndrome. The clinical picture is consistent with lingering fatigue and tension-type headache secondary to a recent viral illness. No evidence of acute neurological pathology such as stroke, encephalitis, or multiple sclerosis.

PLAN
1. Rest and hydration.
2. Avoid strenuous exercise for one week.
3. Pain management: Paracetamol PRN. Avoid NSAIDs for now.
4. Repeat blood work (CBC, CRP, ESR) in two weeks to monitor inflammatory markers.
5. Follow-up appointment scheduled for 15/06/2024 at 10:30.
6. Return precautions: Immediate emergency care if new neurological symptoms (slurred speech, weakness, visual loss) occur.

NEXT APPOINTMENT
15/06/2024 at 10:30
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, Mr. Jovanović. I see you are here for a follow-up regarding your recent viral symptoms. Please, sit down. How have you been feeling since we last spoke?
[patient] Good morning, Doctor. To be honest, it has been a tough week. I was feeling much better after that visit two weeks ago, but yesterday I started feeling the fatigue return. It’s not as bad as the first week, but it is there.
[doctor] I understand. Fatigue is a common lingering effect. Let’s review your history again to ensure we have the full picture. You mentioned you moved to Austria a few years ago. Can you tell me where you are originally from?
[patient] Yes, I am from Belgrade, Serbia. I moved here to Vienna about five years ago to work.
[doctor] Thank you. And what is your current occupation?
[patient] I am a civil engineer. I work for a construction firm.
[doctor] I see. Now, who referred you to our clinic?
[patient] It was Dr. Miller from the General Practice of St. Stephan. He sent me over because he wasn’t sure if my headache was neurological or just a post-viral issue.
[doctor] Dr. Miller is a careful physician. Did he perform any specific tests before referring you?
[patient] Yes, he did a blood test to rule out inflammation. The results came back normal, but my white blood cell count was slightly elevated, which he said is typical after a virus.
[doctor] That makes sense. Let’s look at your symptoms. You described a headache. Can you describe its location and character?
[patient] It is mostly at the back of my head and neck. It feels like a tight band. It gets worse when I look at screens for long periods.
[doctor] And have you experienced any visual disturbances?
[patient] Just mild blurriness for a few days, but it has cleared up. I had a similar issue when I was a child, my uncle had a condition where his eyes crossed, but I never had that.
[doctor] Understood. Any issues with your balance or coordination?
[patient] No, I feel steady. I walked to work yesterday, which is a good sign.
[doctor] That is positive. Did you have a fever?
[patient] Yes, for three days last week. It peaked at 38.5 degrees. I took Paracetamol to bring it down.
[doctor] Did you take any other medications?
[patient] I was taking Ibuprofen for the muscle pain in my neck. I stopped two days ago because my stomach felt a bit upset.
[doctor] Good decision. We need to be careful with NSAIDs if there is any gastric irritation. Did you have any previous medical conditions that might be relevant?
[patient] I have mild hypertension, but it is well-controlled. My doctor in Serbia used to monitor it, but now I see Dr. Miller here. I also have a family history of diabetes, but I have been tested and I am fine.
[doctor] Thank you. Let’s check your vitals. Your blood pressure is 130 over 85 today. That is within a reasonable range. Let’s perform a quick neurological exam. First, I want to check your cranial nerves. Can you follow my finger with your eyes only?
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] Good. Now, show me your teeth.
[patient] Like this?
[doctor] Yes. Your facial symmetry looks intact. No signs of Bell's palsy or other facial nerve issues. Now, let’s check your reflexes. I will tap your knee.
[patient] That tickles a bit.
[doctor] Normal response. How is your strength in your arms and legs?
[patient] I feel strong. I lifted my toolbox this morning without issue.
[doctor] Excellent. Let’s discuss the diagnosis. Based on your history, the timeline of symptoms, and the normal neurological exam, this appears to be a post-viral syndrome. It is not an acute neurological event like a stroke or multiple sclerosis.
[patient] I was worried about that, to be honest. My friend, a man named Graves, told me he had a bad virus last year that left him with brain fog for months.
[doctor] That is a difficult experience. However, in your case, the inflammation markers are resolving. The "brain fog" you might feel is often due to the body's energy being directed toward healing.
[patient] So, what do you recommend?
[doctor] Rest is key. Avoid strenuous exercise for another week. Stay hydrated. I want to repeat a blood test in two weeks to ensure the inflammation markers have normalized.
[patient] Okay. Should I continue with any medication?
[doctor] You can use Paracetamol for pain if needed, but avoid Ibuprofen for now to protect your stomach. If the headache persists or worsens, or if you develop any new symptoms like slurred speech or weakness, go to the emergency room immediately.
[patient] Understood. When should I come back?
[doctor] I will see you on the 15th of next month at 10:30 am for the follow-up and to review the blood results.
[patient] That works for me. Is there anything else I should do?
[doctor] Yes, try to get adequate sleep. Stress can exacerbate the symptoms. Also, if you notice any sensitivity to light or sound, use sunglasses and stay in a quiet environment.
[patient] I will. One last question, do I need to inform my employer?
[doctor] If you feel unwell, yes. But since you are functioning well, you can likely continue with light duties. However, if you feel dizzy, take a break.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor. I feel a bit better knowing it is not something serious.
[doctor] That is good news. We will keep a close eye on it. The nurse will give you the results of the new blood test when they are ready.
[nurse] Good morning. I have drawn your blood this morning. The sample is ready for processing. You will receive the results via your patient portal or by mail.
[patient] Thank you.
[nurse] Also, here is a summary of our discussion. If you have any questions, you can call our clinic at 01-2345678.
[patient] I have the number. Thanks.
[doctor] One more thing. Did you mention any other family health issues?
[patient] My sister has Hashimoto's thyroiditis, but I don't think that is related.
[doctor] Correct, that is an autoimmune condition and unlikely to be related to this viral episode. Just good to know for your long-term health record.
[patient] Yes, she was diagnosed in her thirties.
[doctor] Understood. I will note that in your file. Now, let’s wrap up. Do you have any other questions?
[patient] No, I think I am clear.
[doctor] Then, I will see you on the 15th. Take care.
[patient] Goodbye, Doctor.
[doctor] Goodbye, Mr. Jovanović.

note:
SUBJECTIVE
Patient Jan Kowalski, 43-year-old male, presents with complaints of palpitations described as "skipped beats" or "flutters." Symptoms began two weeks ago and occur approximately five to six times daily, predominantly in the afternoon. The patient reports no associated dizziness, syncope, or dyspnea. He notes that the symptoms are more frequent when sedentary at work. He has a history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis, diagnosed three years ago, managed with levothyroxine. He is a logistics manager at GlobalFreight Solutions and reports high stress levels and high caffeine consumption (4-5 cups daily). He resides in Hamburg and moved from Warsaw five years ago. He is married to Ewa and has a son, Tomasz. He is an active member of FC Alster United football club. Previous ECG performed on 15 October 2023 showed isolated ventricular ectopic beats. No family history of sudden cardiac death or structural heart disease. Insurance: Techniker Krankenkasse, ID TK123456789. Medical Record DR-998210.

OBJECTIVE
Vitals: BP 130/85 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, RR 14, Temp 36.8°C.
General: Well-appearing male, no acute distress.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm with occasional premature beats. S1 and S2 normal. No murmurs, rubs, or gallops. No jugular venous distension.
Respiratory: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender.
Extremities: No edema, pulses intact.
Neurological: No focal deficits.

ASSESSMENT
1. Ventricular Premature Depolarization (VPD): Likely benign given the absence of structural heart disease symptoms, but requires monitoring to quantify burden.
2. Hashimoto's thyroiditis: Stable, currently managed.
3. Lifestyle factors: High caffeine intake and sleep deprivation may be contributing triggers.

PLAN
1. Order 24-hour Holter monitor to be fitted at 9:00 tomorrow.
2. Patient to reduce caffeine intake to < 200 mg/day (approx. 2 cups of coffee).
3. Recommend improved sleep hygiene, aiming for 7-8 hours per night.
4. Continue current levothyroxine therapy for thyroid condition.
5. Follow-up appointment scheduled for 24 May 2024 to review Holter results.
6. Return precautions: Immediate ED visit for syncope, severe chest pain, or sustained tachycardia.

[doctor] Good. My nurse, Anna, will give you the details for the Holter monitor.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor Werner.

EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT NOTE

PATIENT

ARRIVAL
Time: 14:30
Date: 16 May 2024
Reason: Right hand pain and swelling following a fall.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient presents with right hand swelling and pain. Reports slipping in the kitchen on 14 May 2024 and landing on the right hand. Initial symptoms included mild pain and tenderness. Swelling progressively increased over 48 hours. No loss of consciousness. No other injuries reported.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
No significant past medical history. Family history of Hashimoto's disease in sister Kavitha (54). No personal history of autoimmune disorders.

MEDICATIONS
None prior to visit.

ALLERGIES
NKDA (No Known Drug Allergies).

EXAMINATION
Right wrist and hand: Mild to moderate swelling over the dorsal aspect of the wrist and along the extensor tendon sheaths. Tenderness to palpation over the extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis tendons. Range of motion of the wrist is limited due to pain. No deformity. Neurovascular status intact distally.

ASSESSMENT
1. Acute tenosynovitis, right hand (post-traumatic).
2. Rule out occult fracture (low suspicion given X-ray results).

PLAN
1. X-ray of right wrist: No fracture identified. Soft tissue swelling noted.
2. Pain management: Ibuprofen 400 mg orally, three times daily for 7 days.
3. Splinting: Soft wrist splint applied to immobilize the wrist in neutral position.
4. Follow-up: Referral to Gastroenterology and Rheumatology Clinic for further evaluation of persistent symptoms.
5. Instructions: Ice application, elevation, and activity modification. Return if symptoms worsen or fever develops.

DISCHARGE
Time: 16:15
Condition: Stable
Discharge Instructions: Patient educated on splint care and medication. Agreed to follow-up appointment.

[doctor] Good afternoon. I am Dr. Meier. I see you are here for a concern regarding your right breast. Can you tell me what brought you in today?
[patient] Yes, good afternoon, Dr. Meier. I found a lump in my right breast about three weeks ago. It has been bothering me.
[doctor] When did you first notice it?
[patient] It was March 12th. I was in the kitchen preparing dinner, and I felt a small, hard spot. I thought it might just be a muscle knot, but it hasn't gone away.
[doctor] I see. Has the size or shape changed since then?
[patient] No, it feels the same. It is not painful unless I press on it hard. On a scale of zero to ten, I would say the pain is a two when I press it.
[doctor] Okay. Let's check your vital signs before I examine you. Nurse Dubois, could you please take his blood pressure and temperature?
[nurse] Of course. Mr. Keller, I am going to use the cuff on your arm now. Your blood pressure is 130 over 85. Your heart rate is 78 beats per minute. Your temperature is 36.8 degrees Celsius. Your oxygen saturation is 98 percent.
[doctor] Thank you, Nurse Dubois. Now, Mr. Keller, I am going to examine your chest. Please remove your shirt.
[patient] Yes, sir.
[doctor] I can feel a distinct mass in the right breast. It is located at the two o'clock position, about five centimeters from the nipple. It feels smooth, round, and mobile. Does it move when I push it?
[patient] Yes, it moves around a bit. It doesn't feel stuck.
[doctor] Good. Is there any redness, warmth, or skin changes over the area?
[patient] No, the skin looks normal. No redness.
[doctor] And do you have any lumps in your armpit?
[patient] No, I don't think so. I checked, but I didn't feel anything there.
[doctor] Understood. Do you have a family history of breast cancer or other breast diseases?
[patient] My mother, Elise, had breast cancer when she was 65. She passed away ten years ago.
[doctor] I am sorry for your loss. Did anyone else in your family have it?
[patient] No, not that I know of. My brother, Thomas, is healthy, 55 years old.
[doctor] Thank you. Do you have a regular physician?
[patient] Yes, Dr. Laurent in Geneva.
[doctor] Okay. I would like to perform an ultrasound to look at the structure of this mass. It is a quick, painless test. Do you consent?
[patient] Yes, please.
[doctor] Let's go to the imaging room. Nurse Dubois, please accompany him.
[nurse] Follow me, Mr. Keller.
[patient] Thank you.
[doctor] (After returning from imaging) The ultrasound results are back. The mass is a simple cyst. It is fluid-filled, round, and has no solid components. This is a benign finding.
[patient] A cyst? Is that dangerous?
[doctor] No, simple cysts are very common and benign. They are not cancer. However, since you are male, we need to be careful. I recommend a referral to a specialist for further evaluation and monitoring.
[patient] What kind of specialist?
[doctor] A breast specialist or a surgeon who specializes in breast health. I will write a referral letter for you. You can take it to the Clinique de la Paix in Lausanne. They have a good breast clinic.
[patient] That is fine. Do I need to do anything else?
[doctor] No, not right now. But if the lump grows, becomes painful, or if you notice any skin changes, come back to the emergency department immediately.
[patient] Understood. How long should I wait for an appointment?
[doctor] I will call the clinic directly and try to get you an appointment within two weeks. I will also order a basic blood test to check your hormone levels, as high levels of certain hormones can sometimes be associated with breast lumps in men.
[patient] Okay. Is the test painful?
[doctor] No, it is just a simple blood draw from your arm.
[doctor] Nurse Dubois, could you please draw a blood sample from Mr. Keller?
[nurse] Yes, Dr. Meier. Mr. Keller, I am going to put a needle in your arm now.
[patient] Okay.
[nurse] That should be it. Your hemoglobin is 14.5 grams per deciliter. Your white blood cell count is 6.2 thousand per microliter. Your testosterone level is 4.5 nanomoles per liter, which is within the normal range.
[doctor] Thank you. Mr. Keller, your blood results are normal. There is nothing concerning there.
[patient] Good. I feel a bit better knowing it is just a cyst.
[doctor] I understand. It is important to follow up with the specialist, though. Please keep the appointment.
[patient] I will. My neighbor, Paul, had a similar issue a few years ago and it was nothing serious.
[doctor] That is reassuring to hear. Just make sure you follow through with the care. Do you have any questions for me?
[patient] No, I think that covers everything. Thank you, Dr. Meier.
[doctor] You are welcome. Please go to the discharge desk to get your referral letter and instructions.
[patient] Okay. I will.
[doctor] Take care.
[patient] You too.

note:
SUBJECTIVE
Patient is a 65-year-old male, João Pereira da Silva, DOB 14 March 1959, residing in Italy (originally from São Paulo). Symptoms are worse at night and relieved by shaking the hand. He works as a warehouse supervisor. Past medical history includes Hashimoto's thyroiditis and hypertension. He denies symptoms of Parkinson's disease, Crohn's disease, Graves' disease, Bell's palsy, or Baker's cyst. He mentions a friend, Marco Crohn, who has Crohn's disease, but clarifies he does not. Insurance is with ASL Nord, ID NSS-8821-4492.

OBJECTIVE
Vitals: BP 130/85 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, Temp 36.8°C.
Physical Exam:
- Left wrist: No swelling or erythema.
- Tinel's sign: Positive at the carpal tunnel, radiating to the median nerve distribution.
- Phalen's test: Positive after 45 seconds, reproducing numbness.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Lumbosacral pain radiating to the left leg, onset last Tuesday.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Signora Alves, a 72-year-old woman, presents with acute lumbosacral pain. The pain began last Tuesday after twisting her back while reaching for a pot in the kitchen. She describes the pain as sharp, located in the lower lumbar region, radiating down the left leg with a tingling sensation. The pain is exacerbated by forward bending. She has had a similar episode two years ago, evaluated at Spital Zollikon, where an MRI showed degenerative changes but no significant herniation at that time. She took Naproxen for two days with minimal relief. She recently traveled to Lisbon to visit family. She denies bowel or bladder incontinence, saddle anesthesia, or significant motor weakness.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever, chills, or weight loss.
Neurological: Paresthesia in the left lower extremity. No weakness noted.
Musculoskeletal: Pain on movement. No history of trauma other than the incident in the kitchen.
Cardiopulmonary: No chest pain or shortness of breath.
Gastrointestinal: No nausea or vomiting.
Genitourinary: No dysuria or incontinence.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: BP 130/85, HR 78, Temp 36.8.
General: Alert, oriented, in mild distress due to pain.
Back: Tenderness to palpation in the paraspinal muscles at L4-L5 level.
Neurological:
- Straight leg raise: Positive at 30 degrees on the left side, reproducing pain in the leg. Negative on the right.
- Reflexes: Diminished patellar reflex on the left side. Achilles reflexes intact bilaterally.
- Motor strength: 5/5 in all major muscle groups of the lower extremities.
- Sensation: Mildly decreased sensation in the L5 dermatome on the left side.

RESULTS
MRI Lumbosacral spine (ordered): Pending.
Laboratory: CBC, CRP, ESR ordered to rule out infection or inflammation.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Acute Lumbosacral Disc Herniation (Left L5-S1 suspected):
   - MRI Lumbosacral spine scheduled for next Friday at 9:30 AM.
   - Prescribed Celecoxib 200 mg once daily for pain management.
   - Prescribed Paracetamol 1000 mg up to three times daily as needed.
   - Advised to avoid heavy lifting and prolonged sitting.
   - Refer to physical therapy if pain persists after two weeks.
   - Educated on red flags: immediate ER visit if bowel/bladder incontinence or progressive weakness occurs.
2. Follow-up:
   - Return visit in two weeks to review MRI results and adjust treatment plan.
   - Patient resides in Chur; advised to drive safely.
   - Family history: Her brother Marco has a history of similar issues, but no genetic conditions noted.

[doctor] Good morning, Signora Alves. Please, take a seat. How are you feeling today?
[patient] Oh, hello Dr. Keller. Um, honestly? Not very well, you know? My back is... it's really hurting.

[patient] It started last Tuesday, I think. I was in the kitchen, just trying to reach a heavy pot from the top shelf. I twisted a bit, and *pop*... no, not a pop, just a sharp pain.
[doctor] And where exactly is the pain located? Can you point to it?
[patient] Right here, Dr. Keller. Low down, just above my tailbone. It radiates a bit down my left leg, but mostly it's here.
[doctor] Does the pain go down to your foot?
[patient] Sometimes, yes. Like a tingling sensation. Um, is it serious?
[doctor] We will need to investigate. Have you had any back problems before?
[patient] Yes, I did. I had a visit at Spital Zollikon about two years ago. They did an MRI and said I had some wear and tear.
[doctor] And did you have any surgery?
[patient] No, no surgery. Just some physiotherapy. My brother, Marco, has an engineer job, and he always says I should be careful with my posture.
[doctor] I see. Did you take any medication for this episode?
[patient] I took Naproxen for the first two days. But it didn't help much.
[doctor] Did you have any other symptoms? Numbness, weakness, or bladder issues?
[patient] No, no bladder issues. Just the pain and the tingling. I tried to walk, but after 10 minutes, I had to stop.
[doctor] Understood. Let's do a physical examination. Please, lie down on the table.
[patient] Okay. Dr. Keller, I was in Lisbon just last month, visiting my sister. I thought the change of climate would help, but it didn't.
[doctor] I am sorry to hear that. Let's check your reflexes. Tap here.
[patient] That's the worst part! When I bend forward, the pain shoots down my leg.
[doctor] I see. Your straight leg raise is positive on the left side. This suggests disc involvement.
[patient] Disc? Like the one I had before?
[doctor] It seems so. We will order a new MRI to confirm the displacement.
[patient] Will I need an injection? I heard my neighbor, Signora Rossi, had one. She said it helped her retired teacher life a lot.
[doctor] We might consider that if the pain persists. For now, I will prescribe Celecoxib and Paracetamol.
[patient] Thank you. And when will I see the MRI results?
[doctor] The appointment is scheduled for next Friday at 9:30 AM.
[patient] Okay. I will come. I live in Chur, so I have to drive about an hour.
[doctor] Please, drive carefully. And if you experience any loss of bladder control or severe weakness, go to the emergency room immediately.
[patient] I will. Thank you, Dr. Keller.
[doctor] You are welcome. My nurse, Ms. Weber, will give you the prescription.
[nurse] Good morning, Signora Alves. Here is your prescription. Do you have any questions?
[patient] No, I think I am clear. Ms. Weber, thank you.
[nurse] You are welcome. Take care of yourself.

dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, Mr. Petrović. I’m Dr. Müller. Thanks for letting me come by. I see you’re feeling a bit rough today. How are you managing?
[patient] Uh, hey Doctor. Yeah, not great. You know, it’s been... um, really bad these last few weeks. My stomach is just... it’s a mess.
[doctor] Can you describe what’s going on? Is it pain, bloating, or changes in your bowel habits?
[patient] Mostly pain, I guess. And the bloating. It’s been going on for three months now. I don’t know what to do anymore. I’m always worried about it.
[doctor] Okay. When did this start exactly?
[patient] Uh, well, it started about two weeks ago, really bad. But before that, I just felt a bit off. I think it started after I went to Vienna for a business trip.
[doctor] Vienna, right? Did you eat anything unusual there?
[patient] Maybe. We had a lot of... um, spicy food, I think. And coffee. I drink a lot of coffee. But I don’t think that’s it. It’s worse now.
[doctor] And where is the pain located?
[patient] Here, in the lower abdomen. It hurts when I sit down. And sometimes it feels like there’s pressure in my chest, which is weird.
[doctor] Chest pressure? That’s not typical for the stomach. Did you have any shortness of breath or sweating?
[patient] No, no breathing problems. Just a bit of tightness. Like something is squeezing. I thought maybe it was my heart, but then I remembered I had a checkup with Dr. Saric at University Hospital Graz last year. He said my heart was fine.
[doctor] I see. University Hospital Graz is a good hospital. Did you get the results from that visit?
[patient] Yes, yes. They were fine. But now this pain... I’m scared. I work long hours. I’m a software engineer at TechnoSoft GmbH. I sit all day.
[doctor] That stress can definitely affect your digestion. Do you have any history of other stomach issues?
[patient] Um, my father had Crohn’s disease. But I don’t think I have it. I don’t lose weight. I’m just... bloated.
[doctor] Okay. Let’s take a look. Can I examine your abdomen?
[patient] Sure. Go ahead.
[doctor] Please lie down. I’m going to press gently. Tell me if it hurts.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] Does this hurt?
[patient] Uh, a little. It’s tender there.
[doctor] And here?
[patient] No, that’s fine.
[doctor] Okay. I’m going to listen to your heart and lungs next. Just breathe normally.
[patient] Like this?
[doctor] Yes, that’s good. I don’t hear any abnormal sounds. Your heart rate is normal.
[patient] Thank God.
[doctor] Now, I want to check your right side. Do you have any pain in your right upper quadrant?
[patient] No, not really. Just the middle and left.
[doctor] I’m going to check for any masses. I feel a slight tenderness at the 3 o’clock position, near your liver, but no mass. That’s reassuring.
[patient] Is that normal?
[doctor] Yes, mild tenderness can happen with bloating. But we need to rule out other things. Have you had any recent injuries?
[patient] Oh, yes. Two weeks ago, I was at the gym. I was lifting weights, and I slipped. I hit my side against the bar.
[doctor] A gym injury? Did you see anyone about it?
[patient] No, I thought it was just a bruise. It hurt for a few days, but then it went away.
[doctor] That could have caused some internal bruising, but it’s unlikely to cause this chronic pain. However, it’s good to know.
[patient] I’m just worried it’s something serious. Like cancer or something.
[doctor] I understand the worry. But given your age and symptoms, it’s more likely to be functional, like Irritable Bowel Syndrome. But we need to be sure.
[patient] What do you mean by functional?
[doctor] It means the gut works normally, but it’s sensitive. Stress and diet can trigger it. Do you eat a lot of dairy or gluten?
[patient] I love cheese. And bread. A lot of bread.
[doctor] Maybe we should try reducing those for a while. Also, I want to do some blood tests and a stool test to check for inflammation or infection.
[patient] Okay. And the colonoscopy?

Patient is an 85-year-old male presenting with complaints of polyuria, polydipsia, and blurred vision for the past two weeks. He reports significant weight loss and decreased appetite. Family history is positive for Type 2 diabetes in his brother, Mario. He lives in Bergamo and is accompanied by his daughter, Luciana. He was referred by his general practitioner, Doctor Giulio Bianchi, from Ospedale San Raffaele. He denies chest pain, shortness of breath, or neurological symptoms. He is currently taking Atenolol for hypertension. He reports a hobby of playing cards and light exercise at Polisportiva Aurora in Como, attending every Tuesday and Thursday.

OBJECTIVE
Vital Signs:
Blood Pressure: 145/90 mmHg
Heart Rate: 88 bpm
Temperature: 37.1 °C
Respiratory Rate: 16 breaths/min
Oxygen Saturation: 96% on room air

Physical Exam:
General: Alert, oriented x3. No acute distress.
Eyes: Conjunctival injection noted at the 3 o'clock position of the right eye. Pupils equal and reactive to light.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. No murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation bilaterally.

[doctor] Good morning, Signor Rossi. I am Doctor Elena Moretti. Thank you for coming in today. I see you are here with your daughter, Signora Luciana?
[patient_guest] Yes, Doctor. My father is here to see you about his blood sugar. He is 85 years old.
[patient] Um, hello. Yes, it is me. I am a bit tired, you know. The car ride was long.
[doctor] It is good to meet you, Signor Rossi. I have reviewed your records from Ospedale San Raffaele. Your general practitioner, Doctor Giulio Bianchi, referred you because of high glucose levels. Can you tell me a bit about what has been happening?
[patient] Well, um, it started, uh, maybe two weeks ago. I was feeling very thirsty. All the time. And I was going to the bathroom... uh, every hour, maybe more. At night, too.
[doctor] That sounds quite disruptive. Did you measure your blood sugar at home?
[patient] Yes, my daughter bought me a meter. Luciana helped me with it. The numbers were... high. Like, above 200. Sometimes 250.
[doctor] I see. And have you noticed any changes in your weight or your vision?
[patient] Oh, yes. My eyes are a bit blurry. And I think I have lost some weight, but I am not sure. I do not eat as much as before.
[doctor] Let us take a look at you first. Please sit on the exam table. I will check your vital signs. Your blood pressure is 145 over 90. Your heart rate is 88 beats per minute. Your temperature is 37.1 degrees Celsius.
[patient] Is that bad?
[doctor] It is a little elevated, but not dangerously so. Let us look at your eyes. Please look at this light.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] I am checking for any signs of eye strain or damage. I notice a small red spot on the conjunctiva at the 3 o'clock position of your right eye. It is likely just a burst blood vessel, but we will monitor it.
[patient] A burst vessel?
[doctor] Yes, it is common. Now, let us check your feet. Please remove your shoes and socks.
[patient] Um, my feet are always cold.
[doctor] Let me feel for pulses. I can feel the pulse here and here. Your skin looks dry, but there are no open sores. Good.
[patient] I am careful with my feet. I check them every day.
[doctor] That is excellent. Now, do you have any other medical conditions? I see a history of hypertension. Are you on any medications for that?
[patient] Yes. I take an aspirin every day. And for my blood, um, I take something blue.
[doctor] What is the name of the blue pill?
[patient] Ah, yes. Atenolol. I think it is Atenolol.
[doctor] Yes, that is a beta-blocker. It is good you are taking it. Do you have any other conditions? For example, have you ever been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease or anything like that?
[patient] No, no Parkinson's. But my uncle, Franco, he had it. He passed away in Milan last 2023.
[doctor] I am sorry to hear that. And what about other family history? Does anyone have diabetes?
[patient] My brother, Mario, he has Type 2. He lives in Bergamo.
[doctor] I see. So there is a family history. Do you have any hobbies or activities that help you stay active?
[patient] Ah, yes. I go to the Polisportiva Aurora in Como. I play cards, but also I do some light exercise.
[doctor] That is wonderful. Do you still go there?
[patient] Yes, every Tuesday and Thursday. It is good for the mind.
[doctor] Great. Now, let us talk about your diet. What do you typically eat?
[patient] Um, I like pasta. And bread. And olive oil. I try not to eat too much sugar, but I like coffee with a little sugar.
[doctor] How many sugars do you put in your coffee?
[patient] Maybe two spoons. In the morning.
[doctor] Okay. And do you drink any alcohol?
[patient] A glass of wine with dinner. Red wine.
[doctor] That is fine in moderation. Now, let us look at your blood work. I see your HbA1c is 8.5 percent. This indicates that your average blood sugar has been high over the last three months.
[patient] Is that bad?
[doctor] It is higher than we would like. We need to bring it down to prevent complications. I would like to start you on a medication called metformin. It helps your body use insulin better.
[patient] Metformin. Okay.
[doctor] We will start with a low dose, 500 milligrams, once a day with dinner. You may experience some stomach upset at first, so it is important to take it with food.
[patient] I see. And do I need to stop taking the blue pill?
[doctor] No, please continue taking your Atenolol as prescribed. We will monitor your blood pressure closely.
[patient] Okay. And what about my diet? Should I stop eating pasta?
[doctor] You do not need to stop, but we should reduce the amount. Try to choose whole grain pasta and have smaller portions. Increase your vegetables and lean proteins.
[patient] Vegetables... I like tomatoes.
[doctor] Tomatoes are excellent. And try to avoid sugary drinks and snacks.
[patient] I will try. My daughter, Luciana, she will help me. She is a nurse, actually.
[doctor] That is very helpful. Having a nurse in the family is a great advantage.
[patient] Yes, she works at Ospedale Niguarda in Milan.
[doctor] I see. So she can help you monitor your blood sugar and manage your medications.
[patient] Yes. She is very careful.
[doctor] Good. Now, I would like to order some additional blood tests. We will check your kidney function and electrolytes. I will also refer you to a dietician for a personalized meal plan.
[patient] A dietician?
[doctor] Yes, someone who can help you with specific food choices. I will send a referral to Doctor Chiara Rossi at the Clinica di Nutrizione in Turin.
[patient] In Turin? That is far.
[doctor] I know. But she is a specialist in diabetes management. If that is too far, I can refer you to a local dietician in Bergamo.
[patient] Maybe local is better. I do not like long car rides.
[doctor] Agreed. I will call a local dietician. Now, let us talk about your blood sugar monitoring. You should check your blood sugar twice a day, once in the morning and once before dinner.
[patient] Twice a day. Okay.
[doctor] Yes. And keep a log of your readings. Bring the log with you to our next appointment in one month.
[patient] One month. Okay.
[doctor] If you experience any symptoms like severe dizziness, confusion, or persistent vomiting, you should go to the emergency room immediately.
[patient] I understand.
[doctor] Do you have any questions for me?
[patient] No, I think not. Thank you, Doctor.
[doctor] You are welcome, Signor Rossi. I am confident that with your cooperation and the help of your daughter, we can manage this well.
[patient] Thank you.

[nurse] Good morning, I’m Chloé, the triage nurse. Let’s get you set up. What is your full name?

[nurse] Got it. Do you have your medical record number handy? It helps us pull up your history faster.
[patient] Oh, right, I think it’s 8842-9910-33.
[nurse] Perfect. What seems to be the problem today?
[patient] Well, it started about three days ago. I’ve had a sore throat, and now my head feels really stuffy. I can barely breathe through my nose.
[nurse] Do you have a fever?
[patient] I checked this morning, it was around 38.2 degrees.
[nurse] Okay. Have you been anywhere recently? Like on a trip?
[patient] Yes, actually. I went to Zurich for a conference last week. Maybe I caught something there? The air was so dry.
[nurse] That’s possible. Did you have any contact with sick people?
[patient] My colleague, Thomas, had a bad cold. He’s the one who usually sits next to me. I think I got it from him.

[patient] Yes, thank you. It’s been getting worse. I feel really congested.
[doctor] I understand. Let’s start from the beginning. When did the symptoms start?
[patient] Um, three days ago, I think. First the sore throat, then the runny nose.
[doctor] And have you had any fever?
[patient] Yes, 38.2 this morning.
[doctor] Did you travel recently?
[patient] I was in Zurich for work.
[doctor] I see. And did you have any close contact with anyone who was sick?
[patient] My colleague Thomas had a cold. I’m sure I caught it from him.
[doctor] Got it. Let’s check your ears. Open wide, say "ahh".
[patient] Ahh.
[doctor] Thank you. I’m looking at your tympanic membrane. I see some redness at the 3 o'clock position on the right side. It looks a bit inflamed, but not purulent.
[patient] Oh, does that mean I have an ear infection?
[doctor] Not necessarily. It can just be irritation from the congestion. Let’s look at your throat.
[patient] Ahh.
[doctor] Your pharynx is erythematous, but there’s no exudate. Your neck lymph nodes are slightly tender but not significantly enlarged.
[patient] I’ve been having a dry cough too.
[doctor] Is it productive?
[patient] No, just dry. It’s worse at night.
[doctor] Do you have any shortness of breath or chest pain?
[patient] No, I’m fine there. Just the nose and throat.

[patient] I’m taking a deep breath.
[doctor] Good. Lungs are clear to auscultation. No rales or wheezes.
[patient] So, what do you think it is?
[doctor] Based on your symptoms and the exam, this appears to be an acute upper respiratory infection. It’s likely viral, given the recent travel and exposure.
[patient] So, antibiotics?
[doctor] No, not for a viral infection. Antibiotics won’t help and can cause resistance. We’ll focus on symptomatic relief.
[patient] Okay. What can I do?

[patient] Will I need to come back?
[doctor] If your symptoms worsen, if you develop high fever, or if you have trouble breathing, come back. But usually, these resolve in a week or two.
[patient] And the ear?
[doctor] I’ll monitor it. If it becomes painful or you develop discharge, we might need to re-evaluate. But for now, it’s likely just irritation.
[patient] I’m also worried about my job. I have a big presentation next week.
[doctor] I hope you’ll be feeling better by then. Make sure to stay hydrated and rest as much as possible.
[patient] I used to live in Sion, so I’m used to the mountains, but this humidity is killing me.
[doctor] Lausanne can be quite humid in this season. Stay indoors if the air is dry, or use a humidifier.
[patient] I have a friend, Marie, who told me to try steam inhalation.
[doctor] That’s a good idea. It can help loosen mucus.
[patient] I also read about Hashimoto's disease online and got worried because I have a family history.
[doctor] I understand your concern. However, your current symptoms are consistent with a common cold, not an autoimmune thyroid condition. We can check thyroid function if you have persistent symptoms, but for now, let’s treat the infection.
[patient] Okay. So, no blood tests?
[doctor] Not today. Your vitals are stable.
[patient] My blood pressure was 120/80 at home.
[doctor] That’s normal.
[patient] I work as a graphic designer, so I sit a lot.

[patient] I hurt my back last week in the kitchen while reaching for something.

[doctor] Good. Just be careful not to strain it while you’re sick.
[patient] I have a neighbour, Paul, who is a doctor. He said it’s probably just a cold.
[doctor] Your neighbour is likely correct.
[patient] I’m just anxious because I don’t feel like myself.
[doctor] It’s normal to feel this way with a URI. Your body is fighting off the virus.
[patient] Will I be contagious?
[doctor] Yes, for the first few days. Try to avoid close contact with others, especially if they are immunocompromised.
[patient] I have a sister who has Parkinson's disease. I don’t want to infect her.
[doctor] Good thinking. Wear a mask if you must see her, and wash your hands frequently.
[patient] I will.
[doctor] I’ll write up the prescription for the nasal spray. The nurse will give you the details.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor.
[doctor] You’re welcome. Take care.

[nurse] Here is your prescription for the nasal spray. Use it twice a day.

The patient completed radiation therapy three weeks ago. He reports a dry cough starting two weeks ago, which has worsened. He experiences shortness of breath, rated 6/10 on exertion and 8/10 when supine. He had a minor fall in the kitchen last week, landing on his arm, which may have exacerbated chest discomfort, but the primary symptoms are respiratory.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Laryngeal cancer, treated with radiation. No prior history of pulmonary disease. Family history: mother with rheumatoid arthritis; brother is a smoker.

MEDICATIONS
Prednisone (dose to be increased per instructions given in clinic), Omeprazole.

ALLERGIES
NKDA (No Known Drug Allergies).

Works as a logistics manager at SwissLogistics AG. Lives in Zurich. Hobbies: football with FC Winterthur, gym workouts. Advised to cease strenuous activity.

Suspected acute radiation pneumonitis. Differential includes pulmonary infection, though no fever is present.

Dr. Elias Vandermeer
ENT Clinic Zurich Head and Neck Center
