note:
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right knee pain and swelling after twisting injury yesterday.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Milan Petrović, a 21-year-old male, presents to the endocrinology clinic for an urgent evaluation of a right knee injury sustained yesterday. The patient reports twisting the knee while playing basketball. He heard a "pop" and experienced immediate pain and swelling. He has been unable to bear full weight on the right leg since the incident. He took Ibuprofen twice since the injury for pain relief. He denies loss of consciousness, numbness, or tingling. He has no prior history of knee surgery or chronic knee conditions.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever, no chills.
Musculoskeletal: Right knee pain, swelling, limited range of motion. No other joint pain.
Neurological: No numbness or weakness in the lower extremities.
Cardiopulmonary: No chest pain, no shortness of breath.
Gastrointestinal: No nausea, no vomiting.
Renal/Urinary: No change in urine output.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Alert, oriented, in mild distress due to pain.
Vitals: Blood pressure 120/80, Heart rate 72 bpm, Temperature 36.8°C, Respiratory rate 16.
Right Knee:
- Inspection: Moderate swelling, no obvious deformity.
- Palpation: Tenderness along the medial joint line and medial collateral ligament.
- Range of Motion: Flexion limited to 90 degrees due to pain; extension is full.
- Stability: Lachman test positive for increased laxity, but with a firm endpoint. McMurray test negative. Valgus stress test positive at 30 degrees.
- Neurovascular: Dorsalis pedis pulse intact, sensation intact.

RESULTS
Physical examination suggests a grade II sprain of the medial collateral ligament. MRI of the right knee is ordered to rule out meniscal or ligamentous tears.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right Knee Sprain (Grade II MCL):
- Order MRI of the right knee for further evaluation.
- Prescribe a hinged knee brace for support.
- Continue Ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily with food for pain and inflammation.
- Recommend RICE (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation) for the next 48 hours.
- Avoid weight-bearing if painful; use crutches if necessary.
2. Follow-up:
- Review MRI results in two weeks.
- Refer to PhysioFit Clinic for physical therapy if no significant ligament tear is found.
3. Patient Education:
- Discussed the diagnosis and treatment plan.
- Advised to return to the emergency room if swelling worsens significantly or if there is loss of function.
- Patient understands the plan and agrees to follow-up.

Contact Information:
Address: Wien 14, Heiligenstädter Straße 12, 1190 Wien
Phone: +43 660 123 4567
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, please come in and sit down. I see you are here for a follow-up, but your chart indicates a new injury?
[patient] Yes, good morning, Dr. Hauer. I’m Milan Petrović. I’m sorry, I know this isn’t really an endocrine issue, but I twisted my knee yesterday and I can’t walk on it properly.
[doctor] Of course. Let’s have a look. First, let’s update your details. You are currently 21 years old, correct?
[patient] Yes, that is right. I live at Wien 14, Heiligenstädter Straße 12, 1190 Wien.
[doctor] Thank you. And your contact number is still +43 660 123 4567?
[patient] Yes, that is the best number to reach me.
[doctor] Alright. So, tell me about the injury. What were you doing when it happened?
[patient] I was playing basketball at the park near my apartment. It was Friday evening. I was going for a layup, and a defender landed on my foot.
[doctor] And what did you feel at that moment?
[patient] I heard a pop, and then the pain started immediately. It swelled up very quickly.
[doctor] Did you lose consciousness or feel dizzy?
[patient] No, just the pain. It has been throbbing ever since.
[doctor] When did you last see a doctor for this specific issue?
[patient] This is my first time seeing someone for this knee. I have a history of other visits, though. I was at Klinikum Favoriten on 15 March 2023 for blood tests because of fatigue.
[doctor] I see that in the system. Did you have any operations?
[patient] No major operations. Just a dental procedure in 2021. But my mother, Ivana, has diabetes, and my brother Stefan had a knee surgery in 2019.
[doctor] Family history is important. You mentioned your mother. Does she take any specific medications?
[patient] Yes, she takes Glucofort and Metformin. I take nothing regularly, maybe just Ibuprofen when I have a headache.
[doctor] Have you taken anything for this knee pain since yesterday?
[patient] I took Ibuprofen twice. It helped a little, but the swelling is still there.
[doctor] Let’s examine the knee. Please remove your shoes and socks.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] I’m going to palpate the joint. Does this hurt?
[patient] Yes, that is quite tender.
[doctor] I’m going to perform a Lachman test. This checks the stability of the anterior cruciate ligament.
[patient] Ouch, that was a bit sharp.
[doctor] I see some laxity, but it’s not a complete tear. The McMurray test is negative. There is some effusion in the joint.
[patient] So, is it a sprain?
[doctor] Based on the physical exam, it looks like a grade II sprain of the medial collateral ligament. We will order an MRI to confirm there is no meniscus tear.
[patient] When will I get the results?
[doctor] The MRI is scheduled for Monday at 10:00 at MedCenter West. The radiologist will send the report to me.
[patient] And what do I do in the meantime?
[doctor] Rest, Ice, Compression, and Elevation. RICE. Avoid weight-bearing if it hurts. You can use crutches if needed.
[patient] I can get those. Do I need a cast?
[doctor] No, a hinged knee brace is better for this type of injury. I will write a prescription for a brace and continue with Ibuprofen for pain and inflammation.
[patient] How long should I take the painkillers?
[doctor] For three to five days, with food. If the pain is severe, you can take Paracetamol as well.
[patient] Will I be able to play basketball again?
[doctor] Not immediately. You need physical therapy after the healing phase. It will take several weeks.
[patient] I was hoping to play in a tournament next month.
[doctor] That is likely too soon. Let’s focus on healing first. I will refer you to PhysioFit Clinic once the MRI results are in.
[patient] Okay. I will go there.
[doctor] Do you have any questions about the medication?
[patient] No, that’s clear.
[doctor] Make sure you stay off the knee as much as possible. If the swelling gets worse or you cannot move the leg at all, come back to the emergency room.
[patient] Understood. Thank you, Dr. Hauer.
[doctor] You are welcome. The nurse will help you with the paperwork and the brace prescription.
[nurse] Hello, Milan. I’m Sarah, the nurse. I’ll print your prescription and the referral for the MRI.
[patient] Thank you, Sarah.
[nurse] Here is the receipt. The MRI is at MedCenter West, which is near Praterstern.
[patient] I know that area, it’s close to my job at TechStart GmbH.
[nurse] Good. You work as a software developer?
[patient] Yes, I do.
[nurse] Please make sure to bring your insurance card. Your insurance provider is ÖGK.
[patient] I have it with me.
[nurse] Perfect. If you have any questions, call us at +43 1 987 6543.
[patient] Thanks. I will rest tonight.
[nurse] Take care.

dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, please have a seat. I see you were referred by Dr. Hartmann at Klinikum rechts der Isar. What brings you in today?
[patient] Hello. Yes, Dr. Hartmann mentioned you are the specialist for... well, for this issue. I’m Thomas Weber, I’m 39.
[doctor] Thank you, Thomas. I see you are a structural engineer living in Munich. Please tell me about the symptoms that prompted the referral.
[patient] It’s mainly... well, the chest area has been getting larger for about six months. It started as a small lump, but now it’s noticeable under clothes. It’s not painful, just uncomfortable.
[doctor] I see. Did you notice any other changes? Any skin changes, nipple discharge, or pain?
[patient] No discharge. No pain. Just the size. I’m a bit self-conscious about it. I used to go to the gym, but I stopped going to the gym because people stare.
[doctor] Understood. Let’s take a quick history. Do you have any history of liver disease, heart failure, or thyroid issues?
[patient] No, I don’t. I had a checkup last year, everything was normal. I don’t drink much alcohol, maybe one beer on weekends.
[doctor] What about medications? Are you taking anything regularly?
[patient] I take Paracetamol occasionally for headaches. And my partner, Lena, has Crohn's disease, so I’m careful about what I eat, but I’m not on specific meds for it.
[doctor] I see. So no hormonal medications, no spironolactone, or similar drugs?
[patient] No. I don’t take anything for blood pressure or heart conditions.
[doctor] Okay. Let’s look at the exam findings. I can see bilateral breast tissue enlargement. On the left side, there is a distinct area of tenderness at the 3 o'clock position, just below the areola. Is that where you feel the most discomfort?
[patient] Yes, exactly there. When I press on it, it’s a bit sore, but not sharp pain.
[doctor] And on the right side?
[patient] Similar, but maybe slightly less prominent.
[doctor] I’m going to order a few tests. We need to rule out underlying causes. I’ll order blood work to check your testosterone, estrogen, prolactin, and liver function tests. I’ll also refer you for a mammary ultrasound.
[patient] Is this serious? Could it be cancer?
[doctor] Gynecomastia is common and usually benign. However, we must rule out other causes. The fact that it’s bilateral and soft suggests hormonal imbalance rather than a tumor. But we need the labs to be sure.
[patient] Okay. What about my job? I have to travel a lot.
[doctor] The blood test can be done anytime. The ultrasound will be scheduled for next week. Please avoid alcohol and any new supplements until we see the results.
[patient] I was actually thinking of starting a new supplement for stress. It’s called StressAway.
[doctor] Please hold off on that for now. Some supplements contain herbs that can affect hormones. We want a clean baseline.
[patient] Understood. I’ll stop it.
[doctor] Also, I noticed in your file that you had a minor injury in March. Was that in the kitchen?
[patient] Yes, I cut my hand while chopping vegetables. It was a small cut, but it got infected.
[doctor] Did you seek treatment?
[patient] Yes, I went to the emergency department at UKR. They gave me Amoxicillin and it healed quickly.
[doctor] Good. That infection is resolved, correct?
[patient] Yes, completely. No issues since then.
[doctor] Okay. I’m going to write a referral for the ultrasound. In the meantime, if the pain becomes severe or if you notice any redness or swelling, contact us immediately.
[patient] Will I need to change my diet?
[patient] Not specifically for the gynecomastia, but given your partner’s Crohn's disease, we both try to eat clean. But I don’t think diet is the cause here.
[doctor] Correct. It’s likely hormonal. The labs will clarify that.
[patient] When will I get the results?
[doctor] The blood results should be in 48 hours. I’ll call you with the results. The ultrasound report will take a few days longer.
[patient] Okay. I’m a bit nervous.
[doctor] It’s natural to be concerned. But remember, this is a common condition in men of your age, often related to changes in the testosterone-to-estrogen ratio. We will manage it step by step.
[patient] Thank you. I feel a bit better knowing it’s probably not cancer.
[doctor] We will confirm that with the tests. For now, wear a supportive undershirt if it helps with comfort.
[patient] I will. Do I need to stop the Paracetamol?
[patient] No, that’s fine. Just avoid the new supplement.
[patient] Okay. I’ll make an appointment for the blood draw.
[doctor] You can go to the lab at Labor Dr. Müller on Schwanthalerstraße. They are open until 4:00 PM.
[patient] I’ll go tomorrow morning.
[doctor] Good. And please bring your insurance card and ID.
[patient] I have them in my wallet.
[doctor] Is there anything else you’d like to discuss?
[patient] No, that’s all. Thanks for your help.
[doctor] You’re welcome. I’ll see you in two weeks for the follow-up.

SUBJECTIVE
Patient is a 25-year-old female presenting with acute onset right upper quadrant (RUQ) abdominal pain. Pain started approximately 19:30 this evening, described as sharp and stabbing, rated 7/10 in intensity. Pain is exacerbated by deep inspiration and palpation (positive Murphy's sign). Patient reports low-grade fever, nausea, but no vomiting, diarrhea, or constipation. No history of alcohol abuse, consuming only occasional wine or beer. No regular medication use. Patient works as a customer service representative at Swisscom in Lugano. Referred by Dr. Luca Ferrari from Bellinzona due to concern for acute abdomen. Family history notable for brother Marco having gallstones at 30. Patient's date of birth is 14/03/1999. AHV number is 756.12.44-39021. Insurance provider is Sanitas with policy number 845-221-90. Patient reports possible past reaction to penicillin, described as rash, but not confirmed allergy.

OBJECTIVE
Vital signs: BP 118/76 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, RR 16/min, Temp 37.8°C, SpO2 98% on room air.
Physical Exam: Alert and oriented. Abdomen is soft, but tender in the right upper quadrant. Positive Murphy's sign. No rebound tenderness or guarding. No jaundice. No hepatosplenomegaly.
Labs: Pending.
Imaging: Abdominal ultrasound performed. Findings: Gallbladder wall thickening (4 mm). Presence of a 10 mm gallstone in the gallbladder neck. No common bile duct dilation. No free fluid.

ASSESSMENT
1. Acute cholecystitis, likely secondary to cholelithiasis.
2. Low-grade fever.

PLAN
1. Admit to observation unit overnight.
2. NPO initially, then advance diet as tolerated.
3. IV access established. Administer IV fluids (0.9% Normal Saline).
4. Administer IV antibiotics: Augmentin 1.2g every 8 hours.
5. Pain management: Tylenol 1g orally every 6 hours as needed. If pain persists, consider IV Morphine 2-4mg as needed.
6. Repeat labs in the morning: CBC, CMP, LFTs, Lipase, CRP.
7. Consult General Surgery for potential cholecystectomy if conservative management fails or if patient is a candidate for early intervention.
8. Medical certificate provided for employment at Swisscom.
9. Patient educated on warning signs (worsening pain, vomiting, high fever) and instructed to notify nursing staff immediately.
10. Follow-up with Dr. Luca Ferrari in Bellinzona after discharge.

note:
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Shortness of breath on exertion and chest tightness.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Ramesh Kumar, a 60-year-old male, presents to the pulmonology clinic for evaluation of exertional dyspnea and chest tightness. The patient reports that symptoms began two weeks ago, initially mild, but worsened significantly during a weight-lifting session at the gym. During the episode, he experienced severe dyspnea and central chest tightness, which required a 10-minute rest period. He used his rescue inhaler (Albuterol) twice with partial relief. Since then, he has avoided strenuous activity. Yesterday, he experienced mild dyspnea after a 20-minute walk. He reports a mild dry cough, worse at night. He also reports waking up once last night gasping for air and needing to sit up. He has a history of mild childhood asthma, managed with a rescue inhaler as needed. He is a former smoker, having quit in 2015 after a 20-year pack history. He drinks alcohol occasionally. He is currently taking Lisinopril 10 mg daily for hypertension. He reports mild bilateral ankle edema in the evenings. He denies fever, weight loss, hemoptysis, or leg pain. He was referred by Dr. Anja Weber from Zürich West after a routine checkup in November 2023 where no significant abnormalities were noted.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever, no weight loss.
Respiratory: Dry cough, exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.
Cardiovascular: Chest tightness, no palpitations, no chest pain radiating to arm/jaw.
GI: No nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain.
Neurologic: No dizziness, headache, or weakness.
Musculoskeletal: No joint pain or swelling, except for mild ankle edema.
Hematologic: No bruising or bleeding.
Allergic: Penicillin allergy (rash).

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 135/85, HR 78, RR 18, Temp 36.8°C, SpO2 96% on room air.
General: Well-appearing male, in no acute distress.
HEENT: Normocephalic, atraumatic.
Neck: Jugular venous distension present.
Chest: Lungs reveal wheezing in bilateral lower lobes. No rales or rhonchi.
Cardiac: Regular rate and rhythm. No murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender, non-distended.
Extremities: 1+ pitting edema in bilateral ankles.

RESULTS
Chest X-ray: Pending.
CT Chest: Pending.
Pulmonary Function Test: Pending.
Echocardiogram: Referred to Dr. Thomas Bieri at University Hospital Zurich.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Exertional Dyspnea: Differential includes asthma exacerbation, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), or early heart failure.
2. Plan:
- Order chest X-ray and CT chest to evaluate for structural lung disease or masses.
- Order pulmonary function tests (spirometry with bronchodilator response) to assess for obstructive or restrictive lung disease.
- Refer to cardiology for echocardiogram to evaluate for cardiac function, given orthopnea, PND, and ankle edema.
- Continue current medications: Lisinopril 10 mg daily.
- Advise patient to avoid strenuous exercise, including heavy weight lifting, until further evaluation is complete.
- Follow up in clinic in two weeks to review results and discuss next steps.
- Contact: r.kumar.example.com for results.
- Insurance: Swiss Life, ID 789-456-123.

[doctor] Good morning. I see you are here for a new patient intake. Please, have a seat. My name is Dr. Meier. Can you tell me your full name and date of birth?
[patient] Good morning, Doctor. My name is Ramesh Kumar. I was born on 14/03/1964.
[doctor] Thank you, Ramesh Kumar. You are 60 years old. Who referred you to our pulmonology clinic?
[patient] It was my general practitioner, Dr. Anja Weber, from the practice in Zürich West. She sent me over because of some breathing issues.
[doctor] Understood. What brings you in today? What is your main concern?
[patient] I have been feeling very short of breath when I exert myself. Specifically, I was at the gym last week, trying to lift weights, and I felt like I couldn't get enough air. It was very frightening.
[doctor] I see. So this happened at the gym?
[patient] Yes. I have been going to the gym for years, but this time was different. I was lifting a barbell, and suddenly my chest felt tight, and my breathing became labored. I had to stop and rest for almost ten minutes.
[doctor] And when did you first notice these symptoms?
[patient] It started about two weeks ago. At first, I thought it was just fatigue. I had been working overtime at the office. But it got worse with exercise.
[doctor] Do you have any other symptoms? Cough, fever, weight loss?
[patient] I have a mild dry cough, mostly at night. No fever. I haven't lost weight. I feel fine when I am resting.
[doctor] Do you have any history of asthma, COPD, or heart disease?
[patient] I have had mild asthma since I was a child. My father, Suresh, also had asthma. He is 85.
[doctor] And your mother?
[patient] Her name is Lakshmi. She passed away a few years ago, but she had high blood pressure. I have two children. My son, Arjun, is 28, and my daughter, Priya, is 24. They are both healthy.
[doctor] Do you smoke?
[patient] I quit smoking 2015. I smoked for about 20 years before that. One pack a day.
[doctor] How long did you smoke?
[patient] From age 20 to 40. So, 20 years.
[doctor] Do you drink alcohol?
[patient] Occasionally. A glass of wine with dinner, maybe twice a week.
[doctor] Any allergies?
[patient] No known drug allergies. I am allergic to penicillin. It gives me a rash.
[doctor] What medications are you currently taking?
[patient] I take a blood pressure pill, Lisinopril, 10 mg, once a day. And I have an inhaler for my asthma, Albuterol. I only use it when I feel tight, which is rare now.
[doctor] Do you have any other medical conditions?
[patient] I had a minor knee surgery in 2018. It was a meniscus repair. Nothing else major. I had a checkup with Dr. Weber in November 2023, and my lungs sounded clear then.
[doctor] What about your family history? Any cancer, heart attacks, or genetic conditions?
[patient] My brother, Karthik, has Type 2 Diabetes. He is 58. No one in my family has had lung cancer.
[doctor] Let’s talk about the incident at the gym. How bad was the pain?
[patient] It wasn't really pain. It was more like a tightness in my chest. A squeezing feeling. And the shortness of breath was severe. I felt dizzy.
[doctor] Did you have any chest pain that radiated to your arm or jaw?
[patient] No, not really. Just the tightness in the center of my chest.
[doctor] Did you use your inhaler at the gym?
[patient] Yes, I used it twice. It helped a little, but I still felt breathless.
[doctor] Have you had any similar episodes since then?
[patient] I avoided the gym for a week. I went for a walk yesterday, and I felt a bit breathless after 20 minutes. But not as bad as at the gym.
[doctor] How is your sleep?
[patient] I sleep well, usually. But last night, I woke up once, gasping for air. I had to sit up in bed for a few minutes.
[doctor] Do you use more than one pillow to sleep?
[patient] Yes, I use two pillows. It feels more comfortable.
[doctor] Do you have any swelling in your legs?
[patient] A little bit, I think. My ankles look a bit puffy in the evening. But it goes away in the morning.
[doctor] Do you have any pain in your legs when you walk?
[patient] No, no leg pain.
[doctor] Let’s do a physical examination. Please, unbutton your shirt.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] I am going to listen to your lungs. Take a deep breath in... and out.
[patient] (Inhales and exhales)
[doctor] Again.
[patient] (Inhales and exhales)
[doctor] I hear some wheezing in the lower lobes. Your heart sounds are regular. I am checking your neck veins. They are slightly distended. I am checking your legs. There is mild edema in both ankles.
[patient] Is it serious?
[doctor] We need to do some tests to find out. I am going to order a chest X-ray and a CT scan of your chest. I also want to do a pulmonary function test to see how well your lungs are working.
[patient] Do I need to see a cardiologist?
[doctor] Possibly. The symptoms you describe could be related to your heart as well as your lungs. I will refer you to a cardiologist for an echocardiogram.
[patient] Who should I call?
[doctor] I will send a referral to Dr. Thomas Bieri at the University Hospital Zurich. You can call them directly to schedule the appointment. Their phone number is 044 255 11 11.
[patient] Okay. And what about the insurance?
[doctor] Your insurance is Swiss Life. Your insurance number is 789-456-123. I will bill them directly.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor.
[doctor] I will send the results to your email once they are ready. Can you confirm your email address?
[patient] It is r.kumar.example.com.
[doctor] And your home address?
[patient] I live in Winterthur.
[doctor] Okay. Do you have any questions for me?
[patient] Just... could it be cancer?
[doctor] It is possible, but we do not think that is the most likely cause given your history. The most likely causes are asthma exacerbation or early heart failure. We need the tests to confirm.
[patient] I am worried about my kids. I want to be healthy for them.
[doctor] I understand. We will do everything we can to help you. Please, do not overexert yourself until we have the results. Avoid heavy lifting for now.
[patient] I will. Thank you.
[doctor] You are welcome. The nurse will show you to the X-ray room.
[patient] Okay.

Entyvio (for IBD), Levothyroxine 50 mcg daily, Nimodipine 30 mg daily.

dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, Mr. Harrison. I’m Dr. Evans from St. Jude’s Medical Group. Thanks for letting me in.
[patient] Please, come in, doctor. It’s good to see you.
[doctor] How have you been feeling since we last spoke?
[patient] Honestly, not great. I’ve been feeling very tired for three months. Just exhausted, even after a good night’s sleep.
[doctor] I’m sorry to hear that. When did this tiredness really start to become a problem?
[patient] It started gradually. I noticed it more last month, but I thought it was just getting on in years.
[doctor] I understand. Have you noticed any other changes? Like shortness of breath or dizziness?
[patient] Yes. I get out of breath climbing the stairs to my bedroom. And yesterday, I felt a bit lightheaded when I stood up too quickly.
[doctor] That’s helpful to know. Have you seen any blood in your stools or urine?
[patient] No, I don’t think so. But I have had some stomach issues. I was diagnosed with Crohn’s disease ten years ago in Leeds.
[doctor] Ah, yes. I see that in your records. How has that been behaving recently?
[patient] It’s been a bit up and down. I’ve had some flare-ups the last few weeks. I’ve been taking my Entyvio as prescribed, though.
[doctor] Good. Are you taking any other medications?
[patient] Just my usual ones. Levothyroxine for my thyroid, and Nimodipine for my blood pressure.
[doctor] And the Levothyroxine—do you take it on an empty stomach?
[patient] Yes, with a glass of water, first thing in the morning.
[doctor] That’s important. Since you have a history of Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, we need to make sure that’s stable, but I suspect your anemia might be related to your gut.
[patient] Anemia? Is that why I’m so tired?
[doctor] It’s a strong possibility. Low red blood cells can cause exactly those symptoms. We’ll need to do some blood tests to confirm the type of anemia and check for iron deficiency.
[patient] I suppose that’s a good idea. I’ve been living in Bristol for the last five years, but I’m still used to the doctors back in Leeds doing more thorough checks.
[doctor] We’ll be thorough, I promise. I’m going to listen to your heart and lungs now. Could you lie down for a moment?
[patient] Of course.
[doctor] Thank you. Your heart sounds a bit rapid, which fits with the anemia. No obvious murmurs. Your lungs are clear.
[patient] Good to hear.
[doctor] I’m going to order a full blood count, iron studies, and a vitamin B12 level. We’ll also check your kidney function.
[patient] Will I need to go to the hospital for these?
[doctor] No, I can arrange for a phlebotomist to visit you tomorrow morning at 9:00.
[patient] That would be a relief. I don’t like traveling around.
[doctor] I understand. I’ll send the results to my practice. I’ll review them on Thursday and call you.
[patient] Thank you, doctor. I’m just worried. My brother Arthur had similar symptoms and it turned out to be something more serious.
[doctor] I know that’s frightening. But given your history of Crohn’s, iron deficiency from malabsorption or slow bleeding is the most common cause. We’ll rule out other things, of course.
[patient] I hope you’re right.
[doctor] We will. In the meantime, try to rest. Don’t overdo it. If you feel faint or have chest pain, call NHS 111 or your local emergency service.
[patient] Understood.
[doctor] Do you have any questions for me right now?
[patient] No, I think I’ve said everything.
[doctor] Okay. I’ll leave you to rest. The bloods will be drawn tomorrow.
[patient] Thank you, Dr. Evans.

[doctor] Good morning, I’m Dr. Moreau. Please come in and have a seat. I see you’re here for an occupational health check-up?
[patient] Yes, good morning. I’m Elise Fontaine. I was told to come in because I’ve been having some stomach trouble lately.
[doctor] Thank you, Elise. Could you tell me a little more about what’s been bothering you?
[patient] Well, it’s mostly this burning sensation in my stomach. It’s been going on for three months now, um, but it got really bad yesterday.
[doctor] I see. Where exactly does the pain feel like it is?
[patient] Right here, um, just below the ribs. It feels like something is eating into me. And I’m always hungry, but eating makes it worse. Or sometimes better, I don’t know.
[doctor] Does it wake you up at night?
[patient] Yes, usually around 2 am. I have to get up and eat some crackers or something to make it stop.
[doctor] Okay. Do you have any history of this kind of issue?
[patient] Not really. I moved from Strasbourg to Lyon about six months ago. I think the stress of the move and the new job might be a factor.
[doctor] What do you do for work?
[patient] I work as a graphic designer at a small agency in Lyon. It’s very fast-paced.
[doctor] And do you have any hobbies?
[patient] Yes, I’m actually quite into climbing. I go to a gym called Vertical World almost every week.
[doctor] That sounds good for stress relief. Do you have any other family members with similar stomach issues?
[patient] My older brother, Lucas, who is 26, has had some indigestion issues, but nothing like this. My mother, Marie, is 52, and she has been very healthy, as far as I know.
[doctor] Understood. Let’s check your details. What is your date of birth?
[patient] I was born on 14 March 2004.
[doctor] And you are currently 20 years old. What is your insurance provider?
[patient] I’m with Mutuelle Générale de Santé.
[doctor] And your policy number?
[patient] It’s MG-889201-LY.
[doctor] Thank you. Now, let’s examine your abdomen. Can you lie back for me?
[patient] Sure.
[doctor] I’m going to press gently here. Tell me if it hurts.
[patient] That’s a little tender.
[doctor] Okay. I’m feeling for any masses or tenderness. I notice some tenderness at the 3 o'clock position relative to your navel, but no obvious mass.
[patient] Does that mean I have an ulcer?
[doctor] It’s possible. The symptoms you’re describing are classic for a peptic ulcer. I’d like to order some blood work and maybe an endoscopy to be sure.
[patient] An endoscopy? That sounds scary.
[doctor] It’s a routine procedure. We’ll sedate you, and it’s very quick. It will help us see exactly what’s going on in your stomach.
[patient] Okay, I guess I can do that. I just want to get this fixed so I can get back to climbing.
[doctor] We’ll do our best. Let’s start with some blood tests to check for any signs of infection or blood loss.
[patient] Will I need to stop taking any medications?
[doctor] You mentioned you take ibuprofen for headaches sometimes?
[patient] Yes, I do. Maybe once or twice a week.
[doctor] That might be contributing to the problem. I’d recommend avoiding NSAIDs like ibuprofen and acetaminophen if possible, and using acetaminophen only if necessary, but I’d prefer you avoid it for now.
[patient] Okay, I’ll stop the ibuprofen.
[doctor] Good. Also, try to reduce stress as much as possible. Maybe take a break from climbing for a few days to let your body heal.
[patient] I can manage that. I really want to get back to the gym though.
[doctor] We’ll get you back there as soon as possible. For now, let’s focus on treating the ulcer. I’ll prescribe some medication to reduce the acid in your stomach.
[patient] What is it?
[doctor] It’s called omeprazole. You’ll take it once a day before breakfast.
[patient] Okay. How long will I need to take it?
[doctor] Usually for four to eight weeks, depending on how you feel. We’ll follow up in two weeks to see how you’re doing.
[patient] That sounds reasonable. Thank you, doctor.
[doctor] You’re welcome. If the pain gets worse, or if you start vomiting blood or having black stools, come in immediately.
[patient] I will. I’ll be careful.
[doctor] Good. The nurse will be out to take your vitals and draw your blood.
[patient] Okay, thank you.

[nurse] Hi, Elise. I’m going to take your blood pressure and heart rate now.
[patient] Okay.
[nurse] Your blood pressure is 118/76, and your heart rate is 82 beats per minute. You look a bit pale. Are you feeling dizzy?
[patient] A little, but I think it’s just from the pain.
[nurse] I see. I’m going to draw some blood now. This will help us check for any anemia or infection.
[patient] Okay, I’m ready.
[nurse] All done. The results should be back in a few days.
[patient] Thank you.
[nurse] You’re welcome. Rest well.

[doctor] Can you describe those sensations?

note:
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Resistant hypertension and fatigue.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Maria Silva, an 85-year-old woman, presents for follow-up of resistant hypertension. She reports fatigue and morning headaches. She admits to occasional non-adherence to her evening medication, textile engineer by training, retired from Swiss Textile Corp. She lives at 12 Rue de la Paix, 3000 Bern. She reports a recent fall in the kitchen resulting in a minor elbow laceration, which has healed. She has a history of a Baker's cyst in the right knee, which causes pain with ambulation.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Fatigue present.
Cardiovascular: No chest pain, no palpitations.
Neurological: Lightheadedness upon standing.
Musculoskeletal: Right knee pain, recent minor trauma to left elbow.
Endocrine: Family history of Graves' disease in mother. Patient previously screened negative.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Alert, oriented x3.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. Blood pressure 165/95 mmHg in the clinic.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender.
Extremities: Mild edema in bilateral lower extremities. Right knee shows signs of effusion consistent with known Baker's cyst. Left elbow has a healed scab.

RESULTS
Blood pressure: 165/95 mmHg (clinic), 150/85 mmHg (home average reported).
ECG: Normal sinus rhythm, no acute ST changes.
Laboratory (previous month): Potassium 3.2 mmol/L (low), Creatinine 1.1 mg/dL.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Resistant Hypertension
- Non-adherence suspected due to evening dose forgetting.
- Plan:
  - Switch to once-daily combination antihypertensive to simplify regimen.
  - Add low-dose thiazide diuretic (Chlorthalidone 12.5 mg daily).
  - Monitor electrolytes, especially potassium, given history of hypokalemia.
  - Prescribe potassium supplementation as needed.

2. Fatigue and Dizziness
- Likely related to blood pressure fluctuations and possible orthostatic hypotension.
- Plan:
  - Orthostatic vitals check at next visit.
  - Review thyroid function (TSH) to rule out recurrence of thyroid issues, given family history of Graves' disease.

3. Right Knee Pain
- Consistent with Baker's cyst.
- Plan:
  - Conservative management: Rest, ice, and compression.
  - Referral to physical therapy if pain persists.
  - Fall prevention counseling due to recent kitchen fall and dizziness.

4. Diet and Lifestyle
- High sodium intake reported.
- Plan:
  - Referral to dietitian for low-sodium Portuguese diet plan.
  - Discuss medication adherence strategies with daughter, Lucia (45), who lives nearby.

5. Follow-up
- Return in 4 weeks for blood pressure re-check and lab results.
- Contact Swiss Textile Corp alumni network? No, not applicable.
- General Practitioner notified: Dr. Keller.
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, Madame. Please, come in and sit down. I see you are here for your regular check-up, but I also noticed your blood pressure was quite high at the clinic this morning. How are you feeling today?
[patient] Oh, hello, Dr. Weber. Yes, um, I am feeling... okay, I suppose. A bit tired, you know? It has been a difficult few weeks. I am Maria Silva, by the way. I live at 12 Rue de la Paix, 3000 Bern.
[doctor] Thank you, Maria. I have your file here. You are 85 years old, correct?
[patient] Yes, exactly. Eighty-five. It seems to fly by when you are busy.
[doctor] You were a textile engineer for Swiss Textile Corp for many years, right? Did you retire long ago?
[patient] Yes, I retired twenty years ago. I worked there for almost forty years. It was a good job, but very demanding. My husband, João, is gone now, but he always supported me.
[doctor] I’m sorry to hear that. Let’s get back to the blood pressure. You mentioned feeling tired. Do you have any other symptoms? Dizziness, perhaps? Or headaches?
[patient] Uh, yes. Headaches, mostly in the morning. And sometimes I feel a bit lightheaded when I stand up too quickly. It’s annoying.
[doctor] I see. We need to be careful with that. Your blood pressure is resistant, which means it is hard to control with the usual medications. Are you taking your pills exactly as prescribed?
[patient] I try, but sometimes I forget. I am old, you know. My mind is not what it was. My daughter, Lucia, who is 45, tries to help me, but she is busy with her own family.
[doctor] That is very common. Forgetting pills is not a moral failing; it’s a human one. We can look at setting up a reminder system. But first, let’s rule out other causes. Do you have a history of thyroid problems?
[patient] My mother had Graves' disease. She suffered from it for a long time. I was tested years ago, and mine was fine, but maybe it came back?
[doctor] That is a good point to consider. Thyroid issues can affect blood pressure. We will check your thyroid function again. Do you have any other family history?
[patient] My brother, Paulo, had Crohn's disease. It was very painful for him. He passed away five years ago. I feel a connection to him sometimes.
[doctor] I’m sorry for your loss. Family history is important. What about heart conditions?
[patient] My father had a heart attack. He died at 70. It was very sudden.
[doctor] Okay. And do you have any joint problems? I recall you mentioned some knee pain last time.
[patient] Yes, the right knee. The doctor said I have a Baker's cyst. It hurts when I walk. I fell in the kitchen last week, on a wet tile. I scraped my elbow.
[doctor] Did you see anyone about the scrape?
[patient] No, it was just a small cut. It healed fine. But the knee is worse now.
[doctor] We should be careful with falls, especially with high blood pressure. Dizziness can lead to falls. Let’s check your vitals now. Nurse, could you please take her blood pressure again and do a simple ECG?
[nurse] Of course, Dr. Weber. Mrs. Silva, let’s get that cuff on your arm. Take a deep breath for me.
[patient] Okay. Breathe in... breathe out.
[nurse] Thank you. The cuff is tight, but it will be over soon.
[doctor] Thank you, nurse. I’ll review the numbers in a moment. Maria, let’s talk about your diet. Are you eating a lot of salt?
[patient] Um, I like my food to have flavor. My recipes from Lisbon are quite salty. I use a lot of salt in the stews.
[doctor] That can definitely raise blood pressure. We might need to adjust your diet. I will refer you to a dietitian who specializes in Portuguese cuisine, so it doesn’t feel like a punishment.
[patient] Oh, that would be lovely. I don’t want to give up my food. It’s part of my life.
[doctor] Absolutely. We will work with you. Now, about the medications. You are on Amlodipine and Lisinopril. Are you taking them every day?
[patient] Usually. But some days I skip the evening one. I take it at 9 pm, but sometimes I go to bed earlier.
[doctor] That is a common issue. We can switch to a once-daily combination pill if it helps. But we also need to consider adding a third medication, perhaps a diuretic, to help lower the pressure further.
[patient] A diuretic? That means I will have to go to the bathroom more often?
[doctor] It can be like that, yes. But we will start with a low dose. And we will monitor your kidney function, especially since you are 85.
[patient] Okay. I trust you, Doctor. I just want to feel better. I don’t want to be a burden to Lucia.
[doctor] You are not a burden. You are a patient, and we are here to help you. Let’s look at the lab results from last month. Your potassium levels were slightly low. That can happen with diuretics.
[patient] Low potassium? What does that mean?
[doctor] It means your heart muscles need it to work properly. We might need to supplement it. I will write a prescription for potassium tablets.
[patient] Thank you. And what about the thyroid?
[doctor] I will order a TSH test. If it is abnormal, we will treat the thyroid, which might help the blood pressure.
[patient] Okay. I will go to the pharmacy after this. The pharmacy is on Main Street.
[doctor] That is close to your home. Good. Do you have any other questions for me?
[patient] No, I think that is all. I feel a bit less worried now.
[doctor] Good. I’ll send a summary to your general practitioner, Dr. Keller. She will coordinate the care.
[patient] Thank you, Dr. Weber. Goodbye.
[doctor] Goodbye, Maria. Take care.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Right hand pain and swelling for three months.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Santos, a 62-year-old male, presents with right hand pain and swelling. He reports the onset was three months ago, following a trip to Geneva where he was lifting heavy boxes. He describes the pain as worsening with gripping, particularly affecting the ring and middle fingers. He notes warmth and stiffness in the knuckles. He has a hobby of playing golf at the Zurich Country Club, which he has discontinued due to pain. He took Ibuprofen with partial relief. He mentions a friend named Paulo who has Gout, prompting concern about crystal arthropathy.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever, chills, or weight loss.
Musculoskeletal: Right hand pain, swelling, stiffness. No other joint involvement reported.
Family History: Mother had arthritis; maternal uncle had joint pain.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Well-appearing, no acute distress.
Right Hand: Swelling and warmth noted in the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint of the ring finger and the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint of the middle finger. Tenderness to palpation in these areas. Range of motion is limited due to pain. No erythema or skin changes. No deformities.

RESULTS
Pending: Blood tests (CRP, uric acid, ESR, ANA) and hand ultrasound.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Right hand synovitis/tenosynovitis, likely inflammatory.
2. Rule out rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, or crystal arthropathy.

Plan:
- Blood work: CRP, ESR, Uric Acid, ANA, RF.
- Imaging: Ultrasound of the right hand to evaluate for tenosynovitis and effusions.
- Medications: Paracetamol 1g TID PRN for pain. Avoid NSAIDs until renal function is confirmed, given age and potential for interaction.
- Referral: Rheumatology consult if inflammatory markers are elevated.
- Activity: Rest the right hand, avoid gripping. Gentle range-of-motion exercises as tolerated.
- Follow-up: Return in 2 weeks on 14 days from now to review results.
- Insurance: Sanitas, ID 778899123.
- Patient: Santos, DOB 14/03/1963, logistics manager at TransAlpina AG, living in Zurich.

Patient is a 75-year-old male presenting with right wrist pain and paresthesias in the median nerve distribution (thumb, index, and middle fingers) for three months. Symptoms were noted to be worsening over the last two weeks. He reports nocturnal awakening with hand numbness, relieved by shaking out the hand. Physical Exam:
- Right wrist: Mild swelling observed at the 3 o'clock position. Tenderness to palpation over the carpal tunnel.
- Phalen's test: Positive (reproduces numbness in median nerve distribution after 30 seconds).
- Tinel's sign: Positive (tingling elicited by tapping over the carpal tunnel).

Dear Dr. Stein,

I am referring this patient to your care for further evaluation and management of a suspected left knee Baker's cyst and possible meniscal pathology.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
The patient is an 18-year-old female who presented to the Emergency Department on May 20, 2024 at approximately 14:30 with acute onset of left knee pain and swelling. The injury occurred yesterday during a soccer match while she was running and changing direction. She reported an audible "pop" followed by immediate swelling behind the knee. She describes the pain as sharp, rated 9/10 initially, and now 7/10 at rest.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
No significant past medical history. Denies history of Crohn's disease, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Graves' disease, or Bell's palsy. No prior knee injuries or surgeries.

FAMILY HISTORY:
Mother has Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Father has Parkinson's disease.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS:
Constitutional: No fever, chills, or night sweats.
Musculoskeletal: Pain and swelling in left knee. No joint pain in other extremities.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:
Vital Signs:
BP: 118/76 mmHg
HR: 92 bpm
Temp: 37.1°C
RR: 16/min
SpO2: 99%

Left Knee Examination:
- Inspection: Visible swelling in the popliteal fossa. No erythema or warmth.
- Palpation: Tender, fluctuant mass posterior to the knee joint. No joint line tenderness on palpation.
- Range of Motion: Limited due to pain. Flexion 90 degrees, Extension 0 degrees.
- Special Tests:
  - McMurray's test: Negative.
  - Lachman's test: Negative.
  - Varus/Valgus stress: Stable.
  - Posterior drawer: Negative.

DIAGNOSTIC RESULTS:
Ultrasound (Left Knee):
- Demonstrates a 3.5 cm fluid-filled cystic structure in the popliteal fossa, consistent with a Baker's cyst.
- No free fluid in the joint space.
- Meniscal cartilage appears intact on ultrasound, but MRI is recommended for definitive evaluation.

Laboratory Results:
- CBC: Within normal limits.
- CRP: 15 mg/L (Mildly elevated).
- ESR: 12 mm/hr.

ASSESSMENT:
1. Suspected left knee Baker's cyst.
2. Rule out meniscal tear.

PLAN:
1. Referred to Orthopedics for MRI of the left knee without contrast.
2. Conservative management initiated:
   - RICE (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation).
   - Ibuprofen 600 mg PO TID with food for 10 days.
   - Activity restriction: No sports or high-impact activities for 2 weeks.
3. Follow-up with Orthopedics for MRI review and management plan.
4. Return precautions: Immediate return to ED if fever >38.5°C, increased redness, warmth, or inability to bear weight.

Thank you for your care of this patient.

Sincerely,

Dr. Hans Keller
University Hospital Zurich

[patient] It's, uh, really sharp. Like, a 9 out of 10 when I try to move it.

[doctor] Okay. Can you show me where it hurts?
[patient] Right here, behind the knee. It feels like there's a lump there.
[doctor] Mm-hmm. Let me have a look. You don't have any history of knee issues before this, do you?
[patient] No, not really. I'm pretty active. I play for FC Winterthur Ladies. My coach was worried, so he sent me straight to the ER.
[doctor] I see. Your coach is probably Mr. Weber, right?
[patient] Yeah, that's him.
[doctor] Alright. Let's do a quick exam. I'm going to press on this area behind your knee. Does that hurt?
[patient] Ouch! Yes!
[doctor] Okay. This presentation is very classic for a Baker's cyst. It's a fluid-filled sac that can form behind the knee, often due to irritation from an underlying issue like a meniscus tear or arthritis, though in your age group, it's usually mechanical.
[patient] Is it serious? I have a tournament next weekend.
[doctor] I can't say for sure yet. We need to rule out other causes. Do you have any other medical conditions? Anything like Crohn's disease, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, or Graves' disease?

[patient] Does that mean it's infected?

[patient] Okay. Can I go back to playing soon?
[doctor] We need to wait for the imaging results. If it is a Baker's cyst, it might resolve on its own with rest and anti-inflammatories. But if there's a meniscus tear, we might need Dr. Sarah Stein from the orthopedics department to look at it.
[patient] I live in Bern, actually. I'm just visiting my friend in Zurich.
[doctor] That's fine. I can write a referral for you. Do you have your insurance card?
[patient] Yes, here. The number is 756.1234.567.89.
[doctor] Thank you. I'll note that. I'm going to prescribe you Ibuprofen 600 mg, three times a day, with food, and some ice.
[patient] Okay. And no soccer?
[doctor] No high-impact activity for at least two weeks. Rest, ice, compression, elevation. If the swelling doesn't go down or if you get a fever, come back immediately.
[patient] Will I need surgery?
[doctor] Unlikely for a first-time cyst. But we'll refer you to Dr. Stein for a follow-up MRI to be safe.
[patient] That's Dr. Stein at Zurich Ortho Clinic?
[doctor] Yes. I'm sending the referral today. You should be able to get an appointment within a week.
[patient] Okay, that sounds good. Thanks, Doctor.
[doctor] You're welcome. The nurse will show you out. Make sure to keep that leg elevated when you get home.
[patient] I will.
[nurse] Here is your prescription and the referral letter. Dr. Keller has signed it. You need to bring this to Dr. Stein when you go to the appointment.
[patient] Thanks.
[nurse] Do you have any questions about the medication?
[patient] No, I think I'm good. Just the ibuprofen, right?
[nurse] Yes, and plenty of water. And if the pain gets worse, don't hesitate to call the clinic.
[patient] Okay. Thank you.

PATIENT DEMOGRAPHICS
Name: Almeida, João
Date of Birth: 1956-03-14
Age: 69
Nationality: Brazilian

Medical Record Number: BR-99821
Referring Physician: Dr. Rossi at Clinica San Paolo

REASON FOR VISIT
Psychiatry follow-up for anxiety and sleep disturbance secondary to recent trauma. Patient has a history of unilateral renal hypoplasia (right kidney).

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient reports significant anxiety since an injury sustained two weeks ago. He was at a playground assisting his grandson, Pedro (7), when he slipped on wet pavement and fell. He was evaluated at Sant'Elena Hospital Bergamo and diagnosed with a renal contusion of the hypoplastic right kidney.

MEDICAL HISTORY
- Unilateral renal hypoplasia (right)
- Essential hypertension
- Generalized anxiety disorder

MEDICATIONS
- Amlodipine 5mg twice daily (recently increased from once daily)
- Escitalopram 10mg daily
- Trazodone 50mg at bedtime (new prescription)

EXAMINATION
- Blood Pressure: 135/85 mmHg
- Heart Rate: 78 bpm
- General: Alert, oriented, appears anxious but cooperative
- Abdomen: Soft, non-tender, no palpable masses
- Neurological: Non-focal

ASSESSMENT
1. Generalized Anxiety Disorder, exacerbated by recent medical trauma and fear of renal failure.
2. Unilateral renal hypoplasia, stable function post-contusion.
3. Hypertension, currently controlled with adjusted dosage.

PLAN
1. Continue Amlodipine 5mg twice daily.
2. Continue Escitalopram 10mg daily.
3. Start Trazodone 50mg at bedtime for sleep and anxiety.
4. Patient to maintain adequate hydration and avoid nephrotoxic agents.

[doctor] you are welcome . take care of yourself , mr . almeida .

CHIEF COMPLAINT

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Miller is an 88-year-old male who presents to the neurology clinic for evaluation of a right lower leg contusion. He was referred by Dr. Evans at St. Jude’s General Hospital. The pain is described as a dull ache, currently rated 4/10. There is no numbness or tingling. He has been taking acetaminophen for pain control. He uses a cane for ambulation due to pain with weight-bearing. He reports no other injuries. He lives in Chicago and moved from Ohio ten years ago. He is accompanied by his daughter, Sarah, who is 52. His grandson, Tom, is 8. He is a member of the Bluebirds Bowling Club and the Eastside Senior Center.

Constitutional: No fever, chills, or weight loss.
Cardiovascular: No chest pain or palpitations. History of hypertension.
Respiratory: No cough or shortness of breath.
Gastrointestinal: No nausea or vomiting.
Neurological: No numbness, tingling, or weakness in the lower extremities.
Musculoskeletal: Pain and swelling in the right lower leg.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 130/80, HR 72, Temp 98.6 F.
General: Alert and oriented x3.
Right Lower Leg: Inspection reveals ecchymosis and swelling over the anterior aspect of the shin. Palpation reveals tenderness maximal at the 3 o'clock position relative to the tibial crest. No crepitus. No deformity.

RESULTS
X-ray right lower leg: No fracture identified. Soft tissue swelling consistent with contusion.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Contusion of right lower leg, initial encounter.
   - Ice: Apply ice packs for 20 minutes on, 40 minutes off, 3-4 times daily.

[doctor] Thank you. You’re living in Lyon currently, correct?
[patient] Yes, mostly. I work in the city center.
[doctor] Great. I see a note from your GP, Dr. Claire Dubois, referring you for this evaluation. She mentioned you have Chronic Kidney Disease, stage 3. Can you tell me a bit about that? When did you first notice symptoms?

[patient] No, I took some ibuprofen, but I knew I shouldn’t, right? So I just waited it out. But I was worried.

[patient] Oh, yes. Last month, I went on a trip to Barcelona. I got some kind of stomach bug there. Diarrhea for three days. I lost a bit of weight.
[doctor] Did you drink enough water?
[patient] Well, we were out a lot. I think I was a bit dehydrated. My partner, Sophie, kept nagging me to drink water. She’s very good at that.
[doctor] And how is your kidney function now? What are your latest creatinine levels?
[patient] The lab results came back yesterday. My creatinine is 1.8 mg/dL. My eGFR is around 55.
[doctor] Okay. That confirms stage 3. We need to be careful with anesthesia and pain management. We will avoid NSAIDs. Do you have any other medications?

[patient] A bit. My legs cramp at night. I also have a hobby that’s quite intense. I play rugby for Union Sportive Lyon. We train three times a week.

[patient] I’ve had that mole for years. My father, Pierre, has a similar one. He’s 68 now.

[patient] She’s 38. She lives in Annecy.

[patient] I’m a software engineer at TechnoSoft Solutions. It’s a lot of sitting, which isn’t great for my back.

[patient] Sure. It’s antoine.girard at chu-strasbourg dot fr.
[doctor> I’ll send the records there. Do you have any allergies?

[patient] I understand. I just want to get this over with. The gallstones are annoying.

[patient] I’ll be careful. Thanks, Dr. Moreau.
[doctor] You’re welcome. The nurse will help you out.

SUBJECTIVE
Patient is a 75-year-old female presenting with a three-month history of episodic dizziness and giddiness. She describes the sensation as lightheadedness and blurriness, particularly upon standing up quickly or turning her head. The symptoms are not constant but occur in waves. She reports a near-fall incident yesterday in the kitchen, where she felt the floor tilt and had to hold onto the counter. She denies spinning vertigo, chest pain, or shortness of breath. She has a history of hypertension and is currently on medication. She moved from Jaffna, Sri Lanka to Switzerland twenty years ago. She is retired; previously, she worked as a textile quality inspector for Lakshmi Textiles Ltd. She is an active member of the Kulturhaus Zentraltanz dance club but has been skipping sessions for two weeks due to dizziness. She recently traveled to Paris last month to visit family, noting that the dizziness was worse during and after the flight. Family history is notable for her mother having heart disease and her maternal uncle passing away from a stroke.

OBJECTIVE
Vitals: Blood pressure is elevated today.
Exam: General appearance is alert and oriented. Neurological exam shows no focal deficits. Ophthalmologic exam is unremarkable. A small, slightly raised lesion is noted on the scalp near the ear, at the 3 o'clock position. The lesion appears benign with no signs of inflammation or infection.

ASSESSMENT
1. Dizziness, likely orthostatic or vestibular in origin, given the positional nature and lack of spinning vertigo.
2. Hypertension, currently poorly controlled or requiring dosage adjustment.
3. Benign scalp lesion, to be monitored.
4. Family history of cardiovascular disease, increasing risk profile.

PLAN
1. Refer for audiogram to evaluate for inner ear dysfunction.
2. Refer for tilt-table test to assess for orthostatic hypotension.
3. Review blood pressure medication dosage with primary care physician.
4. Advise patient to stand up slowly from sitting or lying positions.
5. Recommend adequate hydration to prevent dehydration-related dizziness.
6. Monitor scalp lesion for any changes in size or appearance.
7. Follow-up in four weeks with test results.

[doctor] Good morning, Herr Gruber. Please, sit down. How are we feeling today?
[patient] Morning, Doc. Well, let’s say... um, my ankle is acting up again. The left one. And my toes are all stiff.
[doctor] Okay. When did this start?
[patient] Just last night. I was walking to the bus stop, and suddenly it felt like I was walking on broken glass. You know that feeling?
[doctor] I do. Sharp pain?
[patient] Sharp. Very sharp. I took some Advil, but it only helped a little.
[doctor] Did you injure it? Did you twist it or fall?
[patient] No, no falling. But I was at the gym the day before. I was doing some lunges, and I think I overdid it. The floor was slippery, you know?
[doctor] I see. And the stiffness in the toes? Is that new?
[patient] Yes. My big toe is swollen. I can’t even put on my socks this morning.
[doctor] Let’s take a look. Please, remove your shoe and sock.
[patient] Sure. Oh, ouch.
[doctor] Can you point your toes up and down for me?
[patient] Like this?
[doctor] Yes. And now spread your toes.
[patient] Ah! That’s the bad one. The big one.
[doctor] I see some redness and swelling there. Let’s check your vitals first. Nurse, could you come in, please?
[nurse] Right away, Doctor.
[patient] Hi, Nurse.
[nurse] Hello, Herr Gruber. I’m going to check your blood pressure and temperature.
[patient] Okay.
[nurse] Your blood pressure is 145 over 90. Heart rate is 88. Temperature is 37.2 degrees.
[doctor] Thank you, Nurse. You can step out.
[nurse] Okay.
[doctor] So, Herr Gruber, given your history of kidney issues, I’m a bit concerned about the combination of NSAIDs like Advil and your current kidney function.
[patient] I know, I know. But the pain was so bad.
[doctor] I understand. But we need to be careful. Let’s do a blood test today to check your creatinine and uric acid levels.
[patient] Is it gout?
[doctor] It’s possible. Gout often affects the big toe. But it can also be related to your kidney disease or other inflammatory conditions. We need to see the numbers.
[patient] I had a trip to Salzburg last week. Maybe the stress from travel?
[doctor] Travel can be a trigger, yes. Dehydration, change in diet. Did you drink enough water?
[patient] I was busy. I didn’t drink as much as usual.
[doctor] That could be a factor. Let’s get the blood work done. In the meantime, I want you to rest the ankle. Ice it for 15 minutes, three times a day.
[patient] Ice? I don’t have ice at home.
[doctor] You can use a bag of frozen peas from the freezer. It works just as well.
[patient] Okay. And the painkillers?
[doctor] I want to switch you to Paracetamol for now. Avoid Ibuprofen or Aspirin until we see the kidney results.
[patient] Got it. Paracetamol.
[doctor] Yes. And if the pain gets worse, or if you develop a fever, come back to the emergency department.
[patient] Okay. I’ll be careful.
[doctor] Good. The blood test will take about 30 minutes. The nurse will call you when it’s ready.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor.
[doctor] You’re welcome. See you soon.
[patient] Bye.
[doctor] Nurse, please prepare the venipuncture for Herr Gruber.
[nurse] Yes, Doctor.
[nurse] Herr Gruber, the blood draw is ready. Can you roll up your sleeve?
[patient] Sure.
[nurse] This will pinch a little.
[patient] Okay.
[nurse] Done. You’re all set.
[patient] Thank you.
[nurse] The results will be ready in 30 minutes. You can wait here or take a walk.
[patient] I think I’ll wait here. My ankle hurts if I walk too much.
[nurse] Understood. I’ll check on you in 30 minutes.
[patient] Thanks.
[nurse] (30 minutes later) Herr Gruber, the results are in. The doctor will see you now.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] Thank you for waiting. The results are back. Your creatinine is slightly elevated, but within your expected range for your kidney stage. Your uric acid is high, at 8.5 mg/dL.
[patient] So it is gout?
[doctor] It’s very likely. The high uric acid, the redness, the swelling in the big toe – it all fits.
[patient] What do we do now?
[doctor] We need to control the inflammation. Since we can’t use NSAIDs, I’m going to prescribe a short course of Colchicine and Prednisone.
[patient] Steroids?
[doctor] Yes, a low dose for five days. It will help reduce the inflammation quickly.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] And I want to refer you to Dr. Miller in the rheumatology department for a long-term management plan.
[patient] Dr. Miller? I’ve heard he’s good.
[doctor] He is. I’ll send the referral today. You can book an appointment within two weeks.
[patient] That sounds good.
[doctor] Also, please increase your water intake. Aim for at least two liters a day.
[patient] I’ll try.
[doctor] And avoid alcohol and high-purine foods like red meat and shellfish for now.
[patient] Got it.
[doctor] Do you have any questions?
[patient] No, I think that’s it.
[doctor] Good. The prescription is in your patient portal. If you have any side effects from the steroids, call us.
[patient] Okay. Thank you, Doctor.
[doctor] You’re welcome. Get some rest.
[patient] Bye.
[doctor] Bye.

note:
PATIENT
Mustafa Kaya, 78 years old male, born 14 March 1946.
Medical Record: RM-89201

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Other difficulties with micturition.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient presents with complaints of urinary hesitancy, weak stream, and frequency, ongoing for three months. Symptoms worsened over the last two weeks. Reports no hematuria or significant pain, only mild dysuria at terminal voiding. Denies fever or flank pain. Patient is a member of the Bosporus Rowing Club and remains physically active. Recent travel to Istanbul reported without acute exacerbation.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, Hypertension. Family history notable for Yusuf (brother) with Parkinson's disease. No history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis or Crohn's disease.

MEDICATIONS
Metformin 500 mg BID, Lisinopril 10 mg QD, Atorvastatin 20 mg QN.

EXAMINATION
Vitals stable. Abdomen soft, non-tender. No suprapubic distension. Prostate exam deferred pending further imaging.

ASSESSMENT
1. Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) suggestive of Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH).
2. Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
3. Hypertension.

PLAN
1. Urinalysis and post-void residual volume measurement.
2. Transrectal ultrasound of the prostate and bladder.
3. Continue current medications.
4. Follow-up appointment scheduled for 20 October 2024 at 10:30.
5. Results to be sent to m.kaya at gmail dot com.
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, Mustafa. Please, take a seat. How are you feeling today?
[patient] Good morning, Doctor. I am... um, well, it is getting harder, you know? The last two weeks have been very difficult.
[doctor] I see. You mentioned in your referral that you are having issues with urination. Can you describe what has changed?
[patient] Yes, yes. It is not just one thing. It is... for three months, I feel the need to go very often. But when I sit on the toilet, it takes a long time to start.
[doctor] And once it does start, is the stream strong?
[patient] No. It is weak. Like... yesterday, I waited and waited, and then it came out in drops. Very frustrating.
[doctor] I understand. That sounds like retention or obstruction. Have you had any pain or burning?
[patient] Sometimes. A little burning at the end. But the main problem is the flow. Also, I am worried because my father had prostate issues.
[doctor] Let's check your history. You are 78 years old, born on 14 March 1946, correct?
[patient] Yes, that is me. My record number is RM-89201. I hope you have my file.
[doctor] Yes, it is here. I see you are currently taking Tamsulosin 0.4 mg?
[patient] No, I am not taking that. I am taking Metformin for sugar and Lisinopril for blood pressure.
[doctor] Okay. I see you are also on Atorvastatin. Do you have any other conditions? Like Hashimoto's or Crohn's?
[patient] No, no. I am healthy in that way. But my brother, Yusuf, he has Parkinson's. It is very sad.
[doctor] I am sorry to hear that. Does your condition affect your mobility?
[patient] Not really. I am still active. I go to the <ORGANization>Bosporus Rowing Club every Tuesday. I row on the water.
[doctor] That is excellent. Exercise is good. But with these urinary symptoms, we need to be careful. Have you traveled recently?
[patient] Yes, I went to Istanbul last month to visit my nephews. I was there for one week.
[doctor] Did you have any issues while traveling?
[patient] No, but I drank a lot of tea. Maybe that helped? Or hurt? I am not sure.
[doctor] Let's look at your labs. I see your PSA was checked last year. It was within normal limits. But given your symptoms, we need to do a urine test and perhaps an ultrasound.
[patient] Yes, yes. I want to be sure. It is scary when you cannot go.
[doctor] We will send you to radiology for an ultrasound of the prostate and bladder. It will take about 20 minutes.
[patient] When should I come back?
[doctor] Let's schedule your follow-up for 20 October 2024 at 10:30.
[patient] Okay. Can you send the results to my email?
[doctor] Sure. Could you spell your email address for me?
[patient] It is m.kaya at gmail dot com.
[doctor] Thank you. I will send the report there. Do you have any questions before we finish?
[patient] Just... is it cancer? Please tell me.
[doctor] I cannot say that yet. It could be benign prostatic hyperplasia, which is very common at your age. But we must investigate. The ultrasound will help us see the size of the prostate.
[patient] Okay. I trust you, Doctor.
[doctor] Thank you. The nurse will guide you to the lab. Please do not hold your urine before the test.
[patient] I will do that. Thank you.

note:
PATIENT INFORMATION
Name: Antonio Silva
Date of Birth: March 14, 1946
Age: 78
Record Number: 889201
Insurance Number: 756.892.104
Address: Limmatstrasse 12, 8001 Zurich, Switzerland

CLINICAL HISTORY
Chief Complaint: Displaced fracture of the lateral malleolus of the right fibula.
History of Present Illness: Patient presented to the clinic yesterday after slipping on a wet pavement. He heard an audible crack and was unable to bear weight. He was initially evaluated at the emergency room, where a closed fracture was diagnosed and a splint was applied. He was referred to this clinic for definitive management.
Past Medical History: Hypertension. History of pneumonia in 2019 with residual scarring noted on CT scan performed two weeks ago. No history of active lung disease, though he reports mild dyspnea on exertion for the past three months, which is under review by pulmonology.
Social History: Patient is a former smoker, quit in 2010. He lives in Zurich, having relocated from Porto, Portugal approximately twenty years ago. He is employed as a conductor for Swiss Railways.
Family History: Father, Jose, died of myocardial infarction. Mother, Amelia, had respiratory issues. Brother, Paulo, sustained a hip fracture at age 75.

MEDICATIONS
Current Medications:
- Losartan 50 mg once daily
- Paracetamol as needed for pain (discontinued today)
Allergies: No known drug allergies.

EXAMINATION
Physical Examination: Right ankle is swollen and tender to palpation over the lateral malleolus. Range of motion is limited due to pain. No open wounds. Neurovascular status intact distally.
Imaging: X-ray of the right ankle reveals a displaced fracture of the lateral malleolus of the right fibula. No involvement of the talar dome.

ASSESSMENT
1. Closed fracture, lateral malleolus, right ankle, displaced.
2. Hypertension.
3. History of pneumonia.

PLAN
1. Surgery: Open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) of the right lateral malleolus.
   - Scheduled for October 24 at 08:30.
   - Pre-operative instructions: NPO after midnight on October 23.
2. Pain Management: Ice application. Avoid Paracetamol for now. Post-operative pain management to be prescribed after surgery.
3. Mobility: Non-weight bearing on the right lower extremity for 6-8 weeks post-operatively. Crutches/walker prescribed.
4. Follow-up: Return to clinic for suture removal and X-ray review in two weeks.
5. Referral: Continue follow-up with Dr. Rossi for respiratory symptoms. Order DEXA scan to evaluate bone density given family history.
6. Administrative: Medical certificate issued for employer, Swiss Railways. Insurer notified.
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning. Please, have a seat. I am Dr. Weber. How are you feeling today?
[patient] Good morning, Doctor. Well, um, it hurts. You know, the ankle. It’s... it’s very painful.
[doctor] I see. Let’s start with the basics. Can you tell me your full name for the record?
[patient] Yes, Antonio Silva.
[doctor] And your date of birth?
[patient] March 14, 1946.
[doctor] Thank you. I see you are 78 years old. You are currently residing in Zurich, correct?
[patient] Yes, I live here. But I moved from Porto in Portugal about twenty years ago.
[doctor] I understand. Before we look at the X-rays, can you describe what happened? How did the injury occur?
[patient] Um, yesterday. I was walking to the bus stop. It was slippery, you know? The pavement was wet. I slipped.
[doctor] Did you fall directly on the ankle?
[patient] Yes. I landed on my right side. I heard a crack. *Crack*. It was loud.
[doctor] Did you lose consciousness?
[patient] No, no. But I couldn’t stand up immediately. My neighbor, Marcus, helped me.
[doctor] Who is Marcus?
[patient] He is my neighbor. We live in the same building. He called the ambulance.
[doctor] I see. You were taken to the emergency room at Kantonsspital Zürich?
[patient] Yes. I was there for a long time. They put a splint on it.
[doctor] And this is your first visit to our clinic for this specific injury?
[patient] Yes. The ER doctor told me to come here. He said, "Go to Pulmonology and Orthopedics Center."
[doctor] Okay. Let’s look at the X-ray. This shows a displaced fracture of the lateral malleolus of the right fibula.
[patient] Fracture? Broken?
[doctor] Yes, the bone is broken and the pieces have shifted out of alignment. This is a closed fracture, meaning the skin is not broken, which is good.
[patient] I am so worried. I don’t want to have surgery. I am old, you know.
[doctor] I understand your concern. Let’s discuss the options. Given the displacement, non-operative treatment might not heal correctly.
[patient] So, what do you suggest?
[doctor] I recommend open reduction and internal fixation. That means surgery to realign the bone and hold it with plates and screws.
[patient] Surgery? When?
[doctor] We would schedule it for next week. But first, we need to rule out any other issues. You mentioned you have been having some shortness of breath recently?
[patient] Yes. For three months, I feel a bit out of breath when I climb the stairs.
[doctor] That is important. Your primary issue is the ankle, but we must ensure your lungs are okay before anesthesia. Do you smoke?
[patient] No, I quit 2010. But I used to smoke a lot.
[doctor] Okay. Your father, Jose, did he have any lung problems?
[patient] No, my father died of a heart attack. But my mother, Amelia, she had asthma. Wait, no, that’s not a disease name like that. She had respiratory issues.
[doctor] Okay. And do you have a family history of bone diseases or fractures?
[patient] My brother, Paulo, he broke his hip when he was 75.
[doctor] I see. That is relevant for bone density. We should order a DEXA scan after the ankle heals. For now, let’s focus on the fracture.
[patient] I take some medication for my blood pressure. Losartan. And sometimes Paracetamol for the pain.
[doctor] Please stop the Paracetamol for now and use ice. We will prescribe a stronger painkiller after the surgery.
[patient] Okay. And I work for Swiss Railways. I am a conductor.
[doctor] That is a physically demanding job. You will need time off work.
[patient] Yes, I have already called my boss, Mr. Keller. He said I can stay home.
[doctor] Good. We will provide a medical certificate. Your insurance number is 756.892.104, correct?
[patient] Yes. 756.892.104.
[doctor] We will contact your insurer. Now, about the shortness of breath. Since you are a pulmonology patient in this clinic, I want to be thorough.
[patient] Yes. I am seeing Dr. Rossi for my lungs.
[doctor] I see. Did she do a CT scan recently?
[patient] Yes, two weeks ago. She said I have some scarring from when I had pneumonia in 2019.
[doctor] Okay. So, no active infection. That is good for surgery.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor. I just want to walk again. I love to walk in Zürichberg park.
[doctor] You will be able to walk again, but it will take time. Expect six to eight weeks of non-weight bearing.
[patient] Six weeks? I cannot stay in bed for six weeks.
[doctor] You will not be in bed. You will use crutches or a walker. But you cannot put weight on the right foot.
[patient] Okay. I will try.
[doctor] The surgery is scheduled for October 24 at 08:30.
[patient] October 24. That is next Tuesday.
[doctor] Yes. You must fast after midnight on Monday.
[patient] Okay. I will tell my neighbor, Marcus, to check on me.
[doctor] Good idea. If you have any chest pain or severe shortness of breath before the surgery, call us immediately.
[patient] I will. Thank you, Doctor.
[doctor] You are welcome. The nurse will guide you to the pharmacy.
