[doctor] good morning . i see you are here for hip pain . how can i help you today ?
[patient] good morning . yes , my right hip has been bothering me for quite some time now .
[doctor] how long has this been going on ?
[patient] it started about three months ago . it was just a mild ache , but it has gotten worse .
[doctor] can you describe the pain ? is it sharp or dull ?
[patient] it is mostly a deep , dull ache . sometimes , when i get out of a chair , it feels stiff .
[doctor] where exactly is the pain located ? is it in the groin , the side of the hip , or the buttock ?
[patient] mostly in the groin area , but it radiates down the front of my thigh .
[doctor] does it go below the knee ?
[patient] no , it stays above the knee .
[doctor] what makes it better or worse ?
[patient] rest helps . walking a long distance makes it worse . i live in cologne , but i used to live in berlin . the flat here has more stairs than my old place , which makes it harder .
[doctor] i see . do you have any other medical conditions ?
[patient] just high blood pressure . i take medication for that .
[doctor] what medication are you currently taking ?
[patient] i take novartis brand cozaar every morning .
[doctor] any allergies ?
[patient] no , no known allergies .
[doctor] do you have any family history of joint problems ?
[patient] yes , my father , heinrich , had hip replacements in both hips . he was 68 when he had the first one .
[doctor] i understand . let’s have a look at your hip . please lie down on the table .
[patient] okay .
[doctor] i am going to move your leg . please try to relax .
[patient] it hurts a bit when you lift it .
[doctor] i notice some tenderness here . let’s check your range of motion . can you bend your knee and bring it to your chest ?
[patient] yes , but it is tight .
[doctor] and can you lift your leg straight up while lying down ?
[patient] yes , but not very high .
[doctor] i see a limitation in internal rotation . let’s check for any specific signs . i am going to press here .
[patient] that spot is tender .
[doctor] i found a small area of tenderness at the 3 o'clock position relative to the greater trochanter . this is consistent with bursitis or osteoarthritis .
[patient] osteoarthritis ?
[doctor] given your age , 64 , and the family history , primary osteoarthritis is likely . but we need to rule out other causes .
[patient] what else could it be ?
[doctor] infection , fracture , or referred pain from the spine . but your history suggests the hip itself .
[patient] i have a son , lukas , who is 12 . he is very active in soccer . i worry about passing this on to him .
[doctor] primary osteoarthritis is not directly inherited in a simple mendelian way , but genetic factors can play a role . it is more related to wear and tear , weight , and activity levels .
[patient] i am a software engineer . i sit for long hours .
[doctor] that can contribute to stiffness . do you do any exercise ?
[patient] i used to swim , but i stopped two weeks ago because it hurt to get in and out of the pool .
[doctor] swimming is usually good for the joints . maybe the entry was the issue .
[patient] yes , i have to climb in .
[doctor] we should get an x-ray to see the state of the joint . i am going to order that now .
[patient] will i need a referral ?
[doctor] yes , i will refer you to an orthopedic specialist for further evaluation and management .
[patient] who do you recommend ?
[doctor] i know dr . vogel at rheinland clinic is very good with hip cases .
[patient] that sounds good .
[doctor] in the meantime , i am going to prescribe some pain relief . you can take ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day with food .
[patient] will that hurt my stomach ?
[doctor] it can . take it with food . if you have any stomach issues , let me know .
[patient] i also take aspirin low dose for my heart .
[doctor] combining ibuprofen and aspirin can increase bleeding risk . let’s use paracetamol instead . 1000 mg up to three times a day .
[patient] okay .
[doctor] and for the stiffness , try to move gently . avoid heavy lifting .
[patient] i will try .
[doctor] do you have any questions ?
[patient] how long will it take to get the x-ray results ?
[doctor] usually , i can see them within a few hours . i will review them and then send the referral to dr . vogel .
[patient] thank you .
[doctor] you are welcome . the nurse will help you with the x-ray .
[nurse] hi , i’m sarah . i’ll take you to radiology now .
[patient] thank you , sarah .
[nurse] no problem . let’s go .

Dear Dr. Thomas Keller,

I am writing to refer my patient, Lucas Moreau, 53 years old, born on 14/08/1971, for further evaluation of hematuria.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Lucas presents with a three-month history of intermittent gross hematuria associated with mild flank pain (3/10) during physical exertion, specifically running. The symptoms were most prominent yesterday. He reports no fever, dysuria, or weight loss. He was evaluated by Dr. Antoine Girard at Hôpital de la Croix-Rousse two weeks ago, who performed a urinalysis and culture, which were negative for infection.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
No significant past medical history. No known drug allergies.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Lucas is a software engineer residing in Lyon. He is an avid runner, training four times a week. He is a non-smoker and consumes alcohol socially.

Vital signs: BP 135/85 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, Temp 36.8°C.

Hemoglobin: 14.2 g/dL
Creatinine: 1.1 mg/dL

Sincerely,
Dr. Sophie Martin
Clinique de la Paix
Lyon

note:
SUBJECTIVE
Steinbacher, a 77-year-old male, presents to nephrology follow-up with new onset left shoulder pain. Patient reports pain started two weeks ago while lifting weights at Wiener Turnverein. Pain is sharp, rated 6/10 at rest and 7/10 with movement. He reports no trauma other than the weightlifting incident. Patient is currently on Losartan for hypertension and chronic kidney disease. He reports recent travel to Milan in October without significant renal complications. He lives in Graz at Josefsgasse 14, 8010 Graz.

OBJECTIVE
Vitals: BP 145/90 mmHg, HR 78 bpm.
Exam: Left shoulder shows tenderness to palpation over the supraspinatus tendon. Full range of motion is limited by pain. No swelling or deformity.
Labs: Most recent creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, eGFR 42 mL/min/1.73 m2. Electrolytes within normal limits.

ASSESSMENT
1. Chronic Kidney Disease (Stage 3b), stable.
2. Left shoulder pain, likely musculoskeletal etiology (rotator cuff strain vs. tendinopathy).
3. Hypertension, slightly uncontrolled.

PLAN
1. Refer to physical therapy for shoulder rehabilitation.
2. Continue Losartan 50 mg daily. Monitor blood pressure.
3. Analgesia: Acetaminophen 500 mg PRN, max 3g/day. Avoid NSAIDs due to renal history.
4. Repeat renal function labs in six weeks.
5. Patient to contact nephrology.vienna@meduniv.ac.at for any worsening symptoms.
6. Medical Record Number: NR-8842-991.
7. Referred by Dr. Huber from Klinikum Währing.

Dear Dr. Emil Weber,

I am referring Arben Hoxha, a 45-year-old male, born on 14th of March, 1979, for your evaluation and management of hallux rigidus, right foot.

He presents with progressive pain and stiffness in the right first metatarsophalangeal joint, which has been worsening over the past six months. The initial symptom onset was preceded by a twisting injury sustained in the kitchen while making pasta. He has been managing symptoms with Advil and Ibuprofen, but the pain persists, rated at 6-7/10, particularly with weight-bearing and morning stiffness.

Physical examination reveals significant limitation of active and passive dorsiflexion of the right first MTP joint, with tenderness and mild swelling over the joint. There is no evidence of deformity, but the range of motion is severely restricted. The patient denies symptoms of other systemic conditions. He has a history of hypertension, managed with Losartan. Family history is notable for father with Parkinson’s disease, but the patient has no symptoms of this condition. There is no history of autoimmune disorders such as Hashimoto’s or Graves’ disease.

I have initiated conservative management with analgesics and recommended custom insoles with a rocker sole. However, given the severity of the stiffness and impact on his occupational activities, I believe a specialist assessment is warranted to discuss potential surgical options, such as cheilectomy or arthrodesis, if conservative measures fail.

The patient’s health insurance is with Helvetia, policy number 774-892-10345. His contact number is +41 79 555 0192.

Please let me know if you require any further information. Thank you for your care of this patient.

Sincerely,

Dr. Sarah Klein
Sports Medicine Clinic
Zurich

Exertional dyspnea and fatigue for 3 months.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Magda Kowalski, a 48-year-old female, presents with progressive exertional dyspnea and fatigue over the last 3 months. She reports orthopnea, requiring two pillows to sleep. She notes bilateral ankle edema in the evenings. Chest pain is described as a heaviness, rated <SCORE>3/10</SCORE>. She was referred by Dr. Weber at Charité University Hospital in October of the previous year for evaluation of a heart murmur. Initial echocardiogram confirmed nonrheumatic mitral insufficiency. She recently traveled to Prague and tolerated the trip with mild fatigue. She is a member of Swim Club Neukölln and swims twice weekly.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Cardiovascular: Positive for dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, and edema. Negative for chest pain, palpitations, or syncope.
Respiratory: History of asthma, managed with <DRUG>Salbutamol</DRUG> PRN. No current wheezing or cough.
Constitutional: Fatigue and malaise.
GI: No nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain.
MSK: No joint pain or swelling.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP <VITAL>135/85 mmHg</VITAL>, HR <VITAL>92 bpm</VITAL>, RR <VITAL>16/min</VITAL>, SpO2 <VITAL>97%</VITAL> on room air, Temp <VITAL>36.8°C</VITAL>.
General: Alert, oriented, in no acute distress.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. Systolic murmur heard at the apex, radiating to the axilla. Additional component noted at the <POSITION>3 o'clock position</POSITION> on the chest wall.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation bilaterally. No crackles or wheezes.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender. No hepatomegaly.
Extremities: 2+ pitting edema in bilateral ankles.

RESULTS
Labs (from last week):
Creatinine: <LAB>1.2 mg/dL</LAB> (slightly elevated)
Potassium: <LAB>4.1 mmol/L</LAB>
Hemoglobin: <LAB>13.0 g/dL</LAB>
B-type Natriuretic Peptide: <LAB>180 pg/mL</LAB> (mildly elevated)

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Nonrheumatic Mitral Insufficiency
- Start <DRUG>Carvedilol</DRUG> 6.25 mg BID for rate control and afterload reduction.
- Start <DRUG>Furosemide</DRUG> 20 mg daily for fluid management.
- Monitor renal function and electrolytes, especially given elevated creatinine.
- Order Transesophageal Echocardiogram (TEE) to assess valve morphology and severity for potential surgical intervention.

2. Asthma
- Continue <DRUG>Salbutamol</DRUG> inhaler PRN.

3. Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
- Continue <DRUG>Metformin</DRUG> 500 mg BID.

Plan:
- Follow-up appointment scheduled for October 20th at 09:00 AM.
- TEE scheduled for Friday, the 14th at 10:30 AM.
- Patient to limit intense physical activity until further evaluation.
- Contact via magda.kowalski@example.com for updates.
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, Magda. Please, have a seat. And you are Piotr, her husband?
[patient] Yes, I am.
[doctor] How are you feeling today, Magda? You mentioned some concerns over the phone.
[patient] I have been feeling very tired lately. It started about three months ago. I get out of breath when I walk up the stairs to my apartment in Berlin.
[doctor] That is helpful context. And do you have any chest pain?
[patient] Not really pain, but a heaviness. Maybe a <SCORE>3 out of 10</SCORE> on the pain scale if I push myself.
[doctor] I see. When did you last see a cardiologist?
[patient] I was referred by Dr. Weber at Charité University Hospital last October. They did an echo then.
[doctor] And what did they find?
[patient] They said I have a problem with my heart valve. Mitral insufficiency, I think. Non-rheumatic.
[doctor] Correct. Let’s look at your current status. You are 48 years old, correct?
[patient] Yes, I turn 49 next month.
[doctor] Thank you. Do you have any shortness of breath at night? Do you have to sleep propped up?
[patient] Yes, I sleep with two pillows now. Before I only used one.
[doctor] That suggests some fluid retention. Have you noticed swelling in your legs?
[patient] Yes, my ankles are puffy by the evening.
[doctor] Okay. Let’s check your vitals. <Nurse>Jessica</Nurse>, can you please assist?
[nurse] Of course. Blood pressure is <VITAL>135 over 85</VITAL>. Heart rate is <VITAL>92 beats per minute</VITAL>. Oxygen saturation is <VITAL>97 percent</VITAL>.
[doctor] Thank you, Jessica. Now, Magda, can I listen to your heart?
[patient] Sure.
[doctor] Please remove your top. I am going to listen to your chest.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] I am hearing a systolic murmur. It is loudest at the apex, but I also note a component at the <POSITION>3 o'clock position</POSITION> on the chest wall.
[patient] Does that sound bad?
[doctor] It indicates the severity of the leak. We need to update your echo. I am going to order a transesophageal echocardiogram.
[patient] Will I need surgery?
[doctor] Not necessarily. We will monitor it closely. But we need to manage the fluid. I am going to start you on <DRUG>Carvedilol</DRUG> and <DRUG>Furosemide</DRUG>.
[patient] I take <DRUG>Metformin</DRUG> for my sugar. Will these interact?
[doctor] No, they are safe together. But you must monitor your potassium. I will order blood work.
[patient] I am a bit nervous.
[doctor] It is normal. Do you have any other medical conditions?
[patient] I have asthma. I use <DRUG>Salbutamol</DRUG> inhaler occasionally.
[doctor] That is fine. Now, let’s talk about your lifestyle. You mentioned you are active?
[patient] Yes, I swim at Swim Club Neukölln twice a week.
[doctor] That is great for your lungs, but we need to be careful with intensity right now.
[patient] I understand. I also travel a lot. I just got back from a trip to Prague last week.
[doctor] How did you feel during the trip?
[patient] I was tired, but I managed. I walked a lot.
[doctor] That is good to know. Let’s look at your labs from last week. Your creatinine is <LAB>1.2 mg/dL</LAB>, which is slightly elevated. We need to keep an eye on kidney function when we use diuretics.
[patient] Is that dangerous?
[doctor] Not yet, but we will recheck in two weeks.
[doctor] I am going to send you an appointment confirmation to your e-mail. Can you confirm your address?
[patient] It is magda.kowalski@example.com.
[doctor] Thank you. Piotr, are you staying for the rest of the visit?
[patient] Yes, I can help her with the medication reminders.
[doctor] That is excellent. Let’s summarize. You have nonrheumatic mitral insufficiency. We are starting beta-blockers and diuretics. We will repeat the echo in three months.
[patient] And the surgery?
[doctor] We will decide after the transesophageal echo. If the valve is repairable, we might consider it.
[patient] Okay. What is the next step?
[doctor] You will have the echo on Friday, the 14th at 10:30 AM.
[patient] I will put that in my calendar.
[doctor] Please. And if you have any questions, call our office.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor.
[doctor] You are welcome. Jessica, please schedule the follow-up.
[nurse] Already done. It is set for October 20th at 09:00 AM.
[patient] Thank you.

note:
CHIEF COMPLAINT
"Back pain for two weeks, worse with movement."

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Lucas Andrade, an 18-year-old male, presents with a two-week history of acute back pain. The pain began two weeks ago while lifting weights at the gym. He describes the pain as sharp and stinging, rated 8/10 in the clinic and 9/10 with movement. The pain is located in the lower back and radiates down the left leg to the knee. He reports mild numbness in the toes. He has been unable to sit comfortably in class for the past three weeks. He moved from Recife, Brazil, to Padova, Italy, one year ago. He lives with his mother, Carla (45), and his sister, Maria (12). He is a student.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General: No fever, chills, or weight loss.
Cardiovascular: No chest pain or palpitations.
Respiratory: No cough or shortness of breath.
Gastrointestinal: No nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain.
Genitourinary: No changes in bowel or bladder control.
Neurological: Mild paresthesia in the left foot. No weakness.
Musculoskeletal: Pain in the thoracic, thoracolumbar, and lumbosacral regions.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: BP 120/80, HR 72, Temp 36.8, RR 14.
General: Alert, oriented, in mild distress due to pain.
Back: Tenderness to palpation at the thoracolumbar junction. Limited range of motion. Positive straight leg raise test at 45 degrees on the left side.
Neurological: Sensation intact in the lower extremities, except for mild hypoesthesia in the left foot. Motor strength 5/5 in all lower extremity muscle groups. Reflexes 2+ bilaterally.

RESULTS
MRI Thoracic, Thoracolumbar, and Lumbosacral Spine: Pending.
Lab Work: CBC, ESR, CRP ordered to rule out infection or inflammatory conditions.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Unspecified thoracic, thoracolumbar, and lumbosacral intervertebral disc disorder.
   - MRI of the spine ordered.
   - Referral to physical therapy at Studio Fisioterapia Moderna.
   - Prescribed <DRUG>ibuprofen</DRUG> 600 mg TID with food and <DRUG>paracetamol</DRUG> 1000 mg BID PRN.
   - Ice application for 15 minutes TID.
   - Activity modification: Avoid heavy lifting for 4 weeks.
   - Return precautions: Immediate return if loss of bowel or bladder control, progressive weakness, or fever.
   - Follow-up in 2 weeks with MRI results.

PATIENT INFORMATION
Name: Émile Vasseur
Date of Birth: 14/03/1964

CLINICAL ENCOUNTER
Date: 12/05/2024
Time: 09:15
Clinician: Dr. Jean-Marc Moreau

REASON FOR VISIT
Patient presented with left elbow pain for 3 weeks. Referred by Dr. Lucien Perrin from Hôpital de la Tour.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient, a 60-year-old male, reports onset of left lateral elbow pain during tennis play at Club de Tennis de Lausanne. Pain radiates to the ring finger. Pain score is 6/10 with movement, 2/10 at rest. Numbness and tingling present, worse at night.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY

Plays tennis twice weekly.

Left Elbow: Tenderness at lateral epicondyle.
Cozen's test: Positive.
Grip Strength: 25 kg (Left), 32 kg (Right).
Neurological: Mild sensory deficit in ulnar distribution of left hand.

ASSESSMENT
1. Left lateral epicondylitis.
2. Possible radial tunnel syndrome or nerve irritation.

PLAN
1. Prescribed Ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for 7 days.
2. Referral to Dr. Antoine Dubois, Orthopedic Surgeon, Centre Médical du Lac, for further evaluation and potential electromyography.
3. Advice: Rest, ice application, avoid heavy lifting and repetitive wrist extensions.
4. Follow-up in 4 weeks if symptoms persist or worsen.

Referring Doctor: Dr. Lucien Perrin, Hôpital de la Tour

Colleague/Friend: Martin (Shared medical history)

note:
PATIENT: Élise Dupont
DOB: January 12, 1945
AGE: 79
MRN: NR-8920441
ADDRESS: 14 Rue des Vosges, 67000 Strasbourg
PHONE: +33 6 12 34 56 78

REASON FOR VISIT: Follow-up for heart failure and evaluation of new-onset dizziness and cognitive slowing.

HISTORY: Patient reports increased fatigue and dizziness over the past month. She notes a fall in the kitchen two weeks ago where she struck her head on a counter, resulting in brief dizziness but no loss of consciousness. She mentions a recent trip to Paris which was followed by significant exhaustion. She has stopped attending her regular swimming sessions at Club des Nageurs due to lack of energy. Family history is non-contributory to current complaint, but daughter Sophie (42 years old, residing in Annecy) reports that the patient has been speaking slowly and appearing confused. Son Jean (38 years old, software engineer in Lyon) is aware of the symptoms.

MEDICATIONS: Carvedilol, Furosemide, Lisinopril. Compliance is reported as good.

EXAM:
Vitals: BP 110/70, HR 78, RR 16, SpO2 96% on room air.
Neuro: Alert and oriented. Mild nystagmus observed on left lateral gaze, specifically noted at the 3 o'clock position. Cranial nerves II-XII intact. Motor strength 5/5 in all extremities. Sensation intact. Gait is unsteady, wide-based. No focal deficits.
Cardiovascular: S3 gallop present. No new murmurs. Lungs clear to auscultation. No peripheral edema.

ASSESSMENT:
1. Heart failure, unspecified. Current symptoms of fatigue and dizziness may be related to over-diuresis or low cardiac output, possibly exacerbated by the recent trip and fall.
2. Post-concussive syndrome vs. Vestibular dysfunction. The kitchen fall was minor, but dizziness persists.
3. Medication review needed. BP is on the lower side, which could contribute to orthostatic dizziness.

PLAN:
1. Order Echocardiogram to assess ejection fraction and ventricular function.
2. Order MRI Brain with contrast to rule out intracranial pathology or small infarct given the fall and cognitive changes.
3. Hold Furosemide for 48 hours to assess impact on volume status and dizziness.
4. Continue Carvedilol and Lisinopril.
5. Patient advised to avoid rapid position changes and to rest.
6. Follow-up appointment scheduled for March 15, 2024 at 10:30 AM to review imaging and echo results.

note:
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Persistent facial redness, itching, and papules for three weeks.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Arthur, a 46-year-old male, presents with a three-week history of worsening facial erythema and papulopustular lesions. The symptoms began around March 12th after outdoor exposure to wind. The redness is localized to the nose and cheeks, accompanied by itching and a sensation of skin thickening. The patient previously used an over-the-counter capsaicin cream, which likely exacerbated the inflammation. He denies pain, purulent discharge, or systemic symptoms such as fever.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for fever, chills, weight loss, or joint pain. No history of Parkinson's, Crohn's, or Graves' disease in the patient. Family history is notable for Bell's palsy in his brother. No history of autoimmune disorders.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: BP 128/82, HR 76.
Skin: Erythema and telangiectasia noted on the central face, particularly the nose and cheeks. Multiple erythematous papules present. No signs of infection. No lymphadenopathy. No abnormalities noted at the 3 o'clock position of the face or other body areas.

RESULTS
Pending: None requested at this time. Basic metabolic panel normal if recently checked, but not rechecked today.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Diagnosis: Rosacea (Papulopustular subtype).
2. Plan:
- Discontinue use of capsaicin cream immediately.
- Start Doxycycline 40 mg orally once daily for 8 weeks.
- Start Metronidazole 0.75% gel topically once daily in the evening.
- Sun protection: Recommend broad-spectrum SPF 50 sunscreen daily and wide-brimmed hat, especially given his outdoor work as a pipeline inspector for Manchester Water Authority.
- Lifestyle modifications: Limit alcohol and spicy foods.
- Follow-up: Appointment scheduled for June 15th in Edinburgh.
- Contact: Patient reachable at 07911 123456.
- Education: Discussed the chronic nature of the condition and the non-contagious aspect to reassure the patient and his relative.

[doctor] that’s a common worry , but rosacea is distinct . it’s an inflammatory disorder . we won’t rule out other things , but the presentation here is classic .

[doctor] oh , please stop using that immediately .

note:
PATIENT DEMOGRAPHICS
Name: Marco Bianchi
Date of Birth: 14 March 1971
Age: 53
Address: Via Roma 12, 20121 Milan
Record ID: MR-998214
Occupation: Scaffolder

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Shortness of breath and chest tightness for 24 hours.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a 53-year-old male with no significant past medical history, presenting with acute onset dyspnea and chest tightness starting yesterday at approximately 15:00. He works as a scaffolder in Como and was exposed to organic dust. He reports no prior history of asthma, though his mother has Hashimoto's thyroiditis. He denies fever, cough, or hemoptysis. He took Paracetamol with minimal relief.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for weight loss, night sweats, or joint pain.

VITAL SIGNS
HR: 110 bpm
BP: 135/85 mmHg
RR: 24 /min
Temp: 37.2°C
SpO2: 92% on room air

EXAMINATION
General: Alert, anxious, in mild respiratory distress.
Respiratory: Tachypneic, bilateral fine crackles at lung bases.
Cardiac: Tachycardic, regular rhythm, no murmurs.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender.

ASSESSMENT
1. Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis (suspected)
2. Acute respiratory distress

PLAN
1. Administer supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 > 94%.
2. Start oral Prednisone 40 mg daily for 5 days, then taper.
3. Obtain blood work: CBC, D-dimer, CRP, ESR.
4. CT chest without contrast to rule out PE and assess for interstitial changes.
5. Discharge with close follow-up with pulmonology.
6. Follow-up appointment scheduled with Dr. Ferrari at San Raffaele Hospital on 20 October 2023 at 10:00.
7. Patient advised to avoid exposure to organic dust and use N95 mask at work.
8. Discharged with wife, Elena, at 18:30.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS
Monitor symptoms. Return to ED if shortness of breath worsens, fever develops, or chest pain occurs.

[doctor] Good morning. I’m Dr. Rossi. What brings you in today?
[patient] Uh, hi. It’s, um, it’s hard to breathe. Really hard. Since... well, yesterday afternoon. I’m Marco Bianchi.
[doctor] Okay, Marco. You’re 53 years old, born on 14 March 1971, correct?
[patient] Yes. And I live at Via Roma 12, 20121 Milan.
[doctor] Noted. Your medical record number is MR-998214. What do you do for a living?
[patient] I work in construction. I’m a scaffolder. Mostly on sites near Como, though I’m from Turin originally. I moved here about ten years ago.
[doctor] I see. You moved from Turin to Como?
[patient] No, I moved to Milan for work, but I spend a lot of time on a job site in Como. The air out there... you know, the dust?
[doctor] The dust. Do you wear a mask?
[patient] Sometimes. Uh, not always. If the wind is strong, I take it off for a second to talk to my friend, Luca. He’s a foreman. He says it’s fine, but I feel like my chest is tight.
[doctor] When did the symptoms start?
[patient] Around 15:00 yesterday. I was working on the beams. I felt this burning in my throat, and then my chest got tight. I thought it was just asthma, but I don’t have asthma. Or do I?
[doctor] Let’s find out. Do you have a history of other conditions? Diabetes? High blood pressure?
[patient] No, no. My mother has Hashimoto's thyroiditis, but I’m fine. My friend Luca has Parkinson's, but that’s him. I’m healthy, usually.
[doctor] Okay. Any recent illnesses? Fevers?
[patient] A bit of a chill last night. Maybe 22:00. I took some Paracetamol. Did that help? Not really.
[doctor] Let’s check your vitals. Nurse, can you come in?
[nurse] Of course. Let’s get your blood pressure and oxygen levels.
[patient] Do I need a mask?
[nurse] Not yet. Let’s see how you are.
[doctor] Your oxygen saturation is 92% on room air. That’s a bit low. Your heart rate is 110. Blood pressure is 135/85.
[patient] 92? That’s not good, is it?
[doctor] It’s low enough that we need to investigate. I’m concerned about Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis. It’s an inflammation of the lungs caused by breathing in organic dusts, like moldy hay or bird droppings. In your case, maybe the wood dust or mold on the scaffolding.
[patient] Wood dust?
[doctor] Yes. Or fungal spores. It’s not an allergy in the traditional sense, but an immune reaction.
[patient] Can you treat it?
[doctor] We can. We’ll give you oxygen and some steroids. Prednisone. But first, we need to rule out other things. Like a pulmonary embolism or pneumonia.
[patient] Pulmonary embolism? That’s a blood clot, right?
[doctor] Yes. We’ll do a D-dimer test and a CT scan.
[patient] Okay. I’m scared.
[doctor] It’s natural. We’re here to help. Let’s start with the blood draw.
[nurse] I’ll draw your blood now.
[patient] Ouch.
[doctor] How is the pain? On a scale of 0 to 10?
[patient] Maybe a 4.
[doctor] Okay. Let’s check your lungs. Listen here.
[patient] It sounds like crackling?
[doctor] Yes, fine crackles at the bases. That’s consistent with interstitial inflammation.
[patient] What does that mean?
[doctor] It means the small air sacs in your lungs are inflamed. It’s why you’re short of breath.
[patient] Will I be okay?
[doctor] Most people recover fully if they avoid the dust. But you need to see a pulmonologist. I’ll schedule you for a follow-up.
[patient] When?
[doctor] I’m calling Dr. Ferrari at San Raffaele Hospital. She has an opening on 20 October 2023 at 10:00.
[patient] That’s good.
[doctor] In the meantime, take your Prednisone as prescribed. Avoid the dust. Wear a proper N95 mask.
[patient] I’ll do that.
[doctor] Do you have anyone to drive you home?
[patient] My wife, Elena. She’s waiting outside.
[doctor] Good. I’ll write you a discharge summary.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor.
[doctor] You’re welcome. We’ll see you at the follow-up.

[doctor] Good morning, Mrs. Gable. I see you’re here for a new problem. Please, sit down. How can I help you today?
[patient] Hi, Dr. Aris. I’m here because I keep slipping and tripping. It’s been getting worse.
[doctor] I’m sorry to hear that. Can you tell me when this started?
[patient] It started about three months ago. At first, it was just once in a while.
[doctor] And how often is it happening now?
[patient] Every day. Mostly when I’m walking to the kitchen or going up the stairs.
[doctor] Do you actually fall, or do you catch yourself?
[patient] I catch myself. I haven’t fallen, but I’m terrified I will. I bruised my knee yesterday when I stumbled.
[doctor] I see. Do you have any pain in your legs or feet when this happens?
[patient] Not really pain, just a weird feeling. Like my feet are heavy or numb.
[doctor] Okay. Let’s check your vitals first. I’ll call my nurse, Sarah, to get your blood pressure.
[nurse] Hello, Mrs. Gable. I’m Sarah. Let’s get your blood pressure and heart rate.
[patient] Hi, Sarah.
[nurse] Your blood pressure is 135 over 85. Heart rate is 72 beats per minute. Temperature is 98.6 degrees.
[doctor] Thank you, Sarah. Please go ahead and check the rest of the room.
[nurse] Okay, I’ll be right back.
[patient] Dr. Aris, I work at Harborview Logistics. I’m a logistics coordinator. I’m on my feet a lot.
[doctor] That must be difficult. Do you wear comfortable shoes?
[patient] Yes, I have good walking shoes. But the floors in the warehouse are slippery sometimes.
[doctor] I understand. Let’s look at your skin and legs. I want to check for any signs of nerve issues or skin changes.
[patient] Sure.
[doctor] I’m going to look at your feet. Please take off your socks.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] I see some dryness on your heels. I also notice a small, rough patch on the outside of your left foot.
[patient] Oh, that’s there. I didn’t notice it.
[doctor] It’s a small area of thickened skin. I want to check your reflexes too.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] I’m going to tap your knee.
[patient] That was fast.
[doctor] Good. Now I’m going to check your sensation. I’ll use this light brush. Tell me if you feel it.
[patient] Yes, I feel it.
[doctor] And here?
[patient] Yes.
[doctor] And on the bottom of your foot?
[patient] Yes, but it feels a little dull.
[doctor] I see. Let’s check your balance. Please stand up and close your eyes.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] Hold that position.
[patient] I’m swaying a little.
[doctor] Yes, I see that. It’s called a positive Romberg test. It suggests a balance issue.
[patient] Is that serious?
[doctor] Not necessarily, but it needs investigation. It could be from your inner ear, your nerves, or your medication.
[patient] I take metformin and lisinopril.
[doctor] I see. Lisinopril can sometimes cause dizziness. But we need to rule out other causes.
[patient] My friend, Mark, has Parkinson’s disease. He said I should get a neurologist.
[doctor] That’s a good idea. But first, let’s do some basic tests. I want to check your vitamin B12 levels.
[patient] Why?
[doctor] Low B12 can cause nerve damage and balance problems. I’ll order a blood test.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] I also want to check your blood sugar.
[patient] I don’t have diabetes.
[doctor] I know, but we need to make sure your levels are stable.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] I’m going to write you a referral for a neurologist. Their office is at 123 Medical Plaza, Suite 400.
[patient] That’s close to my house.
[doctor] Yes, it is. You can call them at 555-0199 to make an appointment.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] I also want to see you again in two weeks to review the blood test results.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] In the meantime, be careful when you walk. Use handrails.
[patient] I will.
[doctor] Do you have any questions?
[patient] No, that’s all.
[doctor] Great. I’ll send the referral to your primary care doctor, Dr. Miller.
[patient] Thank you.
[doctor] You’re welcome.

[doctor] Hello, I’m Dr. Meyer. I’m here for your home visit today. I see from the records that you’ve been having some unusual movements lately?
[patient] Yes, hello doctor. Um, I’m Sara Abbas. It’s... it’s weird. I can’t really control it.
[doctor] I understand. Can you describe what’s happening? When did you first notice it?
[patient] It started maybe two weeks ago. First, it was just my eyes blinking a lot. Like, I’d be reading, and suddenly I’d blink five or six times in a row.
[doctor] Blinked repeatedly. And then?
[patient] Then, um, my mouth started twitching. And sometimes I make this... uh, clicking sound with my tongue. It’s embarrassing. My sister, Hana, says I’m doing it on purpose.
[doctor] That must be frustrating. Are the movements happening throughout the day, or at specific times?
[patient] All the time. But they get worse when I’m stressed. Like, Hana was talking about her job, and I just started shrugging my shoulders.
[doctor] Shrugging. Okay. Have you seen any other doctors about this?
[patient] No, not yet. I’m a bit scared to go to the hospital. It’s expensive, and I don’t want to worry my parents.
[doctor] I see. You’re with SwissCare, right? Let me check your coverage. What’s your insurance number?
[patient] It’s SC-992104-BX. I was born on 14/03/2003.
[doctor] Thank you. Sara, these sounds like tics. They are often temporary. But I need to rule out other things. Do you have any headaches?
[patient] Sometimes. But not bad ones. Just a dull ache behind my eyes.
[doctor] Any weakness in your arms or legs? Any trouble speaking?
[patient] No. I can talk fine. Just the tics.
[doctor] Okay. Let’s look at you for a moment. Can you raise your arms?
[patient] Like this?
[doctor] Yes. Hold them there.
[patient] (Holds arms up)
[doctor] Good. Now, while you’re holding them, can you make a fist?
[patient] Yes.
[doctor] I see a slight tremor, but it’s consistent with anxiety or fatigue, not a neurological deficit. Do you take any medications?
[patient] No, not really. Maybe some painkillers if I have a headache. Ibuprofen?
[doctor] Right, Ibuprofen. Do you consume caffeine?
[patient] Yes. Lots of coffee. Maybe three cups a day.
[doctor] Caffeine can exacerbate tics. I recommend reducing that. Also, have you been sleeping well?
[patient] No. I wake up a lot. My mind is just... racing.
[doctor] Stress is a major trigger. Have you been under any particular stress lately?
[patient] Well, I started a new internship last month. At TechnoSwiss. It’s very fast-paced. And my sister... she’s been in a fight with her boyfriend, David.
[doctor] David. Is he living with you?
[patient] No, he’s just her partner. But they argue a lot. It makes the house tense.
[doctor] I understand. Tension in the home can definitely affect your condition. Are there any other symptoms? Any sounds you make?
[patient] Sometimes I grunt. Like a low, guttural sound. I hate it.
[doctor] That’s called a vocal tic. It’s part of the same spectrum. Sara, I’m not worried about a serious brain issue right now. This looks like a transient tic disorder.
[patient] Is it... is it permanent?
[doctor] Usually, no. Transient tics often go away on their own within a few months. But we need to manage the triggers.
[patient] What can I do?
[doctor] First, reduce caffeine. Second, try to relax. Maybe some breathing exercises. Third, avoid watching people with tics, as it can be contagious.
[patient] I don’t know anyone with tics.
[doctor] Good. And if the tics get very severe, or if you develop weakness or severe headaches, you must come to the emergency department.

[patient] Yes, Dr. Keller.
[doctor] I’ll fax it to Dr. Keller. In the meantime, try to rest.
[patient] I will.
[doctor] Any questions for me?
[patient] No. Thank you.
[doctor] Take care, Sara.

[doctor] Good morning, Maria. I am Dr. Rossi. Thank you for having me come to your home today. I see on my schedule that we have been seeing you quite regularly since March 2021. How are you feeling today?

[patient] Okay.
[doctor] Your blood pressure is 130 over 85. That is slightly elevated, likely due to the pain. I will check your reflexes and muscle strength in your legs. Please, keep your legs straight. I am going to tap your knees and ankles. Tell me if you feel a tingle.
[patient] Yes, it feels like a tingle.
[doctor] Good. Now, let's assess your range of motion. Can you bend forward to touch your toes?
[patient] I try, but I can only get halfway down. It hurts a lot when I stretch.
[doctor] That is expected with a disc disorder. Let's look at the thoracic region. Can you turn your head to the left and right?
[patient] I can, but it feels stiff. I have had stiffness in my upper back for about three months. I think it is related to my posture at work.
[doctor] Posture is a major factor. You mentioned that you have been taking a specific medication. Can you confirm the name and dosage?

[doctor] Ibuprofen is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug. It helps with inflammation, but it can be hard on the stomach if taken for a long time. Do you have any history of stomach ulcers or gastrointestinal issues, such as Crohn's disease?

[patient] Understood. I also have a question about my work. Can I continue working as a graphic designer?

[doctor] I have sent the referral to PhysioCare Clinic today. You can call them to book an appointment. Here is my direct line: 02 5550 1234. If you have any questions, feel free to call.

[patient] Okay, I will do that. Do I need to see you again soon?

note:
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Fatigue and bilateral ankle edema for 2 weeks.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Müller, a 57-year-old male, presents with increasing fatigue and lower extremity edema. He reports shortness of breath with exertion (climbing stairs), rated 4/10. He denies chest pain or orthopnea. He moved from Freiburg to Munich ten years ago. He works as a project manager. He is currently taking Novartis medication and AstraZeneca’s Entresto. He reports adherence to his medication but notes decreased efficacy. He experienced one episode of orthostatic dizziness last month.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Cardiovascular: Positive for edema, negative for chest pain.
Respiratory: Positive for dyspnea on exertion.
Constitutional: Positive for fatigue.
Renal: History of Stage 4 CKD.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 158/92 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, SpO2 96%.
Lungs: Diminished breath sounds at the bases. Crackles noted at the 3 o’clock position of the right mid-lung field.
Extremities: 2+ pitting edema in bilateral ankles.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, S1 and S2 normal, no murmurs.

RESULTS
Labs (recent): eGFR 35 mL/min/1.73m², Potassium 5.2 mEq/L, Creatinine 2.8 mg/dL.
Weight: Increased by 2 kg in 1 week.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Hypertensive heart disease with heart failure (HFrEF).
2. Chronic kidney disease, Stage 4.

Plan:
- Increase diuretic dose to manage fluid overload.
- Monitor potassium levels closely given hyperkalemia risk (K+ 5.2).
- Continue AstraZeneca’s Entresto.
- Patient instructed to monitor daily weights and BP.
- Next appointment: Monday, October 14th at 09:30.
- Contact 089 555 0123 for acute symptoms.
- Insurance ID: KV 998877665.
dialogue:
[doctor] good morning , herr müller . please have a seat . i see you are here for a follow-up regarding your heart and kidney issues . how have you been feeling since we last spoke ?
[patient] good morning , dr . huber . to be honest , not great . i’ve been feeling quite fatigued , and my ankles are swelling up again by the evening .
[doctor] i understand . let’s take a look at your vitals first . <nurse> please assist him .
[nurse] of course . your blood pressure is currently 158 over 92 . your heart rate is 88 beats per minute . your oxygen saturation is 96% .
[patient] that pressure feels high . i’ve been taking my novartis medication , specifically the pharmacist recommended dose , but it doesn’t seem to be working as well as it used to .
[doctor] we are aware that your chronic kidney disease has progressed . your latest lab results show an egfr of 35 . this places you in stage 4 . this is why managing your fluid balance and blood pressure is so critical right now .
[patient] stage 4 ? that sounds serious . i’ve been living in munich for ten years , but i moved from freiburg originally . the water here feels different , or maybe it’s just the stress of my job as a project manager .
[doctor] stress can certainly impact blood pressure . did you have any chest pain or shortness of breath ?
[patient] some shortness of breath when i climb the stairs . no chest pain . i rate the shortness of breath as a 4 out of 10 .
[doctor] okay . let’s check your lungs . i’m going to listen to your chest . do you feel any discomfort ?
[patient] no , it’s fine .
[doctor] i’m listening to your right lung . i notice some diminished breath sounds at the base . and here , at the 3 o’clock position of your right mid-lung field , i hear some crackles . this suggests some fluid buildup .

[doctor] it’s consistent with heart failure exacerbation . your heart is struggling to pump efficiently , likely due to the high blood pressure and kidney strain . we need to adjust your diuretics .
[patient] can we increase the lasix dose ?
[doctor> yes , but we must monitor your potassium levels closely . your recent potassium was 5.2 , which is on the higher side . we will continue with astrazeneca’s entresto to help with the heart failure , but we might need to add a potassium binder .
[patient] i see . my wife , anna , is very worried . she is 54 years old . she’s been taking me to all these appointments .
[doctor] that’s good support . who is your primary care physician ?
[patient] dr . stein . i’ve known him for years . he referred me to you for the specialist care .
[doctor] i’ve reviewed the notes from dr . stein . he mentioned you had a minor episode of dizziness last month . did that happen again ?
[patient] just once . i stood up too fast . i think i’m a bit dehydrated , but i’m afraid to drink too much because of the swelling .
[doctor] that is a common dilemma . we need to find a balance . your weight has increased by 2 kilograms in the last week . this is a clear sign of fluid retention .
[patient] i noticed . i’m 57 years old , and i don’t want to be putting extra strain on my heart .
[doctor] you are doing the right thing by coming in . let’s schedule a follow-up . i want to recheck your labs in two weeks .
[patient] when is the next appointment ?
[doctor] we have an opening on monday, october 14th at 09:30 .
[patient] that works for me . can i call your office if i feel worse ?
[doctor] yes , please call 089 555 0123 if your symptoms worsen , especially if you have chest pain or severe shortness of breath .
[patient] thank you . i’ll make sure anna knows the number .
[doctor] also , keep a log of your daily weights and blood pressure readings . bring that log to your next visit .
[patient] i will . my son , lukas , is 28 and lives in stuttgart . he’s a doctor himself , actually . he might call you if i don’t show up , just in case .
[doctor] that’s a good contingency plan . please ensure he has your insurance details . your insurance id is kv 998877665 .
[patient] he has that . thank you , dr . huber .
[doctor] you’re welcome . take care .

note:
REFERRAL LETTER

Dear Dr. Anna Keller,

I am writing to refer my patient, Carlos Mendes, 26 years old, born on March 12, 1998, for further evaluation of a nonspecific abnormal finding in the lung field.

The patient is a logistics coordinator working for Swiss Freight Solutions in Zurich. He originally emigrated from Spain three years ago. He is a non-smoker and denies exposure to occupational dust or chemicals. He is physically active, participating in futsal matches at FC Westside twice a week.

During the initial assessment, the patient reported mild chest tightness, rated 2/10 on a pain scale, primarily upon deep inspiration. He denies fever, night sweats, weight loss, or hemoptysis. He mentioned a mild upper respiratory infection approximately two weeks ago which resolved spontaneously.

Family history is notable for asthma in his mother, Elena, and a history of persistent cough in his brother, Pablo, which was attributed to allergies.

Current medications include occasional use of Paracetamol and Ibuprofen for analgesia. No known drug allergies.

Vital signs at the time of examination were: Blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, Heart rate 72 bpm, Respiratory rate 14 bpm, Temperature 36.8°C, and SpO2 98% on room air.

Recent imaging (CT Chest without contrast) revealed a small, nonspecific nodule or opacity in the right lower lobe. Given the patient's age and lack of significant symptoms, I would appreciate your expert opinion on the nature of this finding and whether further diagnostic workup, such as high-resolution CT or biopsy, is warranted.

I have already discussed the referral with the patient. He is aware of the need for prompt evaluation. I have scheduled a follow-up appointment with him on November 15th at 14:30 to review your findings.

Please send the report directly to my office or via the secure patient portal.

Sincerely,

Dr. Weber
Urology Clinic
MediZurich
Switzerland
dialogue:
[doctor] good morning , carlos mendes . please , have a seat . i see you are here for a follow-up regarding a finding on your recent chest imaging . can you tell me what brought you in today ?
[patient] hello , dr . weber . yes , i received the results of the ct scan i had last week . it mentioned a nonspecific abnormal finding in my lung field , and i was quite worried . i am 26 years old , and i have no history of smoking .
[doctor] i understand your concern . nonspecific often means it is not immediately identifiable as a specific disease like cancer or active tuberculosis , but it does require clarification . let's review your history . you mentioned you are from spain ?
[patient] yes , i was born in seville . i moved to zurich about three years ago to work .
[doctor> okay . and what is your current profession ?
[patient] i am a logistics coordinator for swiss freight solutions . i work out of the office in hallwylstrasse , but i travel frequently to warehouses .
[doctor] that can sometimes involve exposure to dust or mild irritants . do you have any hobbies or social activities that might affect your respiratory system ?
[patient] i am quite active . i play futsal every tuesday and thursday at fc westside . we play in the indoor hall at letzigrund .
[doctor> interesting . do you wear a mask or have any protective equipment during those sessions ?
[patient] no , it is an indoor court , so the air is generally good . but i do notice i get a bit short of breath if i push too hard .
[doctor] let's check your vitals first . your blood pressure is 120/80 , heart rate is 72 beats per minute , and your oxygen saturation is 98% on room air . your temperature is 36.8 degrees celsius . how would you rate any current pain or discomfort on a scale of 0 to 10 ?
[patient] i would say it is a 2/10 . just a mild tightness in my chest when i breathe deeply , but it goes away quickly .
[doctor] okay . do you currently take any medications for this ?
[patient] no . i only use paracetamol occasionally for headaches , and sometimes ibuprofen if i have muscle soreness after futsal .
[doctor] good . any allergies ?
[patient] no known drug allergies . i had a mild rash once from penicillin , but i was told it was just a coincidence .
[doctor> understood . let's look at your family history . does anyone in your family have lung conditions , such as asthma , copd , or cancer ?
[patient] my mother , elena , has asthma , but she manages it well with inhalers . my brother , pablo , had a persistent cough for a few months two years ago , but his doctors said it was just allergies .
[doctor] thank you . have you had any recent infections , fevers , or night sweats ?
[patient] no fever . i did have a mild cold about two weeks ago , but it cleared up . no night sweats .
[doctor] and any weight loss ?
[patient] i have been maintaining my weight , maybe even gaining a little bit because i am eating well in zurich .
[doctor> we will need to repeat the imaging to see if this finding changes . i am going to refer you to a pulmonologist for a more detailed evaluation . they may want to do a high-resolution ct or perhaps a bronchoscopy if the finding persists .
[patient] that sounds serious . is it likely to be something bad ?
[doctor] nonspecific is a broad term . it could be a small granuloma from a past minor infection , a small lymph node , or even an artifact . however , because you are young and asymptomatic , we need to rule out rarer conditions . the pulmonologist will take it from there .
[patient] who is the doctor i should contact ?
[doctor] i am writing a referral to dr . anna keller at the pulmonology center zurich . she is an expert in interstitial lung diseases and thoracic imaging .
[patient] how do i get an appointment ?
[doctor] i will send the referral electronically to her office . they will call you to schedule . given the urgency of clarification , they usually try to see new referrals within two to three weeks .
[patient] that is a long time to wait without knowing .
[doctor] i agree . if your symptoms worsen—such as increased shortness of breath , coughing blood , or high fever—do not wait . go to the emergency room . but for now , we are monitoring .
[patient] okay . what should i do in the meantime ?
[doctor] continue your normal activities . avoid smoking and secondhand smoke . if you play futsal , ensure the ventilation is good , but don't stop exercising unless you feel unwell . keep taking your medications only if needed for pain .
[patient] i will . do i need to stop my ibuprofen ?
[doctor] no , but avoid taking it on an empty stomach . it is safe for occasional use .
[patient] understood . my insurance number is 1234567890 . will you send the documents to them ?
[doctor] yes , the referral will include your insurance details . you will receive a letter in the mail confirming the appointment .
[patient] thank you , dr . weber . i feel a bit better knowing there is a plan .
[doctor] it is important to have a plan . let's schedule a follow-up with me in six weeks to review the results from the pulmonologist .
[patient] when would be a good time ?
[doctor] how does november 15th at 14:30 sound ?
[patient] that works for me . i will be in the office in the morning , so i can take the afternoon off .
[doctor> excellent . i will book that now . you will get a confirmation sms .
[patient] perfect . is there anything else i should watch for ?
[doctor] just be aware of any new cough , especially if it is dry and persistent . if you start coughing up any blood , even a small amount , seek medical attention immediately .
[patient> i will keep that in mind .
[doctor] do you have any questions for me before we finish ?
[patient] no , i think i have everything . thank you for being so clear .
[doctor] you are welcome . take care , carlos .

note:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
PATIENT NAME: Carmen Alvarez
DATE OF BIRTH: 15/03/2005
RECORD NUMBER: CH-2023-88912
DATE OF VISIT: 10/08/2024
REFERRING DOCTOR: Dr. Garcia
REFERRING ORGANIZATION: Hospital Clínic de Barcelona
ADDRESS: Mittlere Strasse 12, 4051 Basel

REASON FOR VISIT:
Acute left flank pain, hematuria, referred from Barcelona for evaluation of suspected kidney stone.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
19-year-old female student presenting with acute onset left flank pain radiating to the groin, starting three days ago. Pain is colicky, rated 8/10. Associated with nausea, vomiting (x2), and gross hematuria. No fever or chills. Patient reports moving from Spain to Switzerland for university.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
Unremarkable. No prior history of kidney stones.

FAMILY HISTORY:
Mother has history of recurrent nephrolithiasis. Brother has Graves' disease. Sister had Bell's palsy.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS:
Constitutional: Negative for fever.
GI: Positive for nausea/vomiting.
GU: Positive for hematuria, dysuria.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:
Vitals: BP 110/70, HR 95, Temp 36.8°C, RR 16, SpO2 99%.
General: Alert, in mild distress due to pain.
Abdomen: Soft, non-distended. Tenderness to palpation in the left flank. No rebound or guarding.
Back: Costovertebral angle tenderness present on the left side.
Skin: No rash.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. No murmur.
Respiratory: Clear to auscultation bilaterally.

INVESTIGATIONS:
Urinalysis: Positive for blood (3+), RBCs >50/hpf, WBCs negative, Nitrites negative, Leukocyte esterase negative.
Renal Ultrasound: Left hydronephrosis. 5mm echogenic focus in the left proximal ureter with posterior acoustic shadowing. No renal cortical thinning.

ASSESSMENT:
1. Acute left ureteral calculus (5mm) causing obstructive uropathy.
2. Hematuria secondary to ureteral stone.

PLAN:
1. Pain management: Ibuprofen 400mg TID with food.
2. Medical Expulsive Therapy: Tamsulosin 0.4mg PO daily to facilitate stone passage.
3. Hydration: Encourage intake of >2L water daily.
4. Follow-up: Return to clinic on 10/24 at 10:00 for repeat imaging and symptom check.
5. Return precautions: Immediate ER visit if fever >38°C, intractable vomiting, or worsening pain.
6. Labs: Urine culture pending (negative for infection currently).

DISPOSITION:
Discharged to home with follow-up.
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning. Please have a seat. I see you’ve been referred here for some abdominal pain. Can you tell me what’s going on?
[patient] Um, yes. Hello. It hurts... a lot. Like, really sharp pain on my left side. I’ve been coming here from Barcelona for my university exchange, but I’m staying in Basel now.
[doctor] Okay. I’m Dr. Weber. How old are you?
[patient] I am 19 years old.
[doctor] And your name?
[patient] Carmen Alvarez.
[doctor] Thank you, Carmen. You mentioned you were referred to us. Who sent you over?
[patient] Oh, my cousin Lucas was also here last week. He had a stomach bug. But I think my doctor in Spain sent the referral? Or maybe it was just the hospital?
[doctor] I see. Do you have a referral letter from a specific doctor?
[patient] Um, yes. I think it was Dr. Garcia at the Hospital Clínic de Barcelona. I have the email, but I didn't print it.
[doctor] That’s fine. We can look it up. Let’s focus on the pain. When did it start?
[patient] About three days ago. It was in the middle of the night. I was sleeping and then... ugh. It just started.
[doctor] Where exactly is the pain?
[patient] Here. My left flank. It goes down to my... uh, my groin area.
[doctor] Does it move?
[patient] Yes! It moves. Like, it throbs. And sometimes it’s in my back, sometimes it’s in my front. It’s very confusing.
[doctor] On a scale of one to ten, how bad is it right now?
[patient] Eight. Maybe nine when I try to walk.
[doctor] Have you had any nausea or vomiting?
[patient] Yes. I threw up twice this morning. I couldn't keep down the water.
[doctor] And any fever?
[patient] I don't think so. I felt cold, but no fever.
[doctor] Have you noticed any blood in your urine?
[patient] Oh! Yes. It was a bit pink this morning. I was scared.
[doctor] Okay. Do you have any history of kidney stones?
[patient] No. But... um... my mother, she has them. All the time. So I thought maybe it’s genetic?
[doctor] That’s possible. Family history is a risk factor. What about your other family?
[patient] My father is healthy. My brother... well, he has Graves' disease. And my sister had Bell's palsy when she was young.
[doctor] I see. Any other medical conditions for you?
[patient] No. I’m healthy. I’m a student, so I don't have time to be sick. I study engineering at the university.
[doctor] Where do you live in Basel?
[patient] I live in a dormitory. The address is Mittlere Strasse 12, 4051 Basel.
[doctor] Do you have your insurance card with you?
[patient] Yes. Here. My record number is CH-2023-88912.
[doctor] Thank you. Let me examine you. Please stand up and pull down your pants slightly. I need to listen to your heart and lungs first.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] Deep breath in... good. Now, let’s check your abdomen. It’s going to be a little tender.
[patient] Ow.
[doctor] Right lower quadrant?
[patient] No, no, left side.
[doctor] Okay. Let me check your back.
[patient] Ah!
[doctor] Tenderness there?
[patient] Yes. It’s very sensitive.
[doctor] I’m going to do a quick ultrasound to look at your kidneys. This will help us see if there are any stones or blockages.
[patient] Is it painful?
[doctor] No, just cold gel.
[nurse] Here, this is the gel. It’s a bit cold.
[patient] Ouch.
[nurse] Sorry.
[doctor] I can see your left kidney. There is some dilation of the ureter. And I see a bright spot... yes, there is a stone. It’s about five millimeters.
[patient] A stone?
[doctor] Yes. It’s causing the pain and the blood in your urine. This is called a ureteral calculus.
[patient] What do I do?
[doctor] We need to manage the pain and help the stone pass. Since it’s small, it might pass on its own. But we need to make sure you’re not infected.
[patient] How do I know if I’m infected?
[doctor] If you have a high fever, chills, or the pain gets much worse, you need to go to the emergency room immediately.
[patient] Okay. What medicine?
[doctor] We’ll prescribe painkillers and an alpha-blocker to help relax the ureter. This is called tamsulosin.
[patient] I can take that?
[doctor] Yes. And plenty of water. You need to drink at least two liters of water a day.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] We also need to check your urine for infection. I’ll send you to the lab to give a sample.
[patient] Where is the lab?
[nurse] It’s on the first floor, right next to the pharmacy.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] Once the results are back, I’ll call you. But in the meantime, if the pain is unbearable, don’t hesitate to come back.
[patient] Will I need surgery?
[doctor] Not right now. We try to avoid surgery for small stones. We call it "medical expulsive therapy."
[patient] That sounds scary.
[doctor] It’s not. It’s just medicine to help the body do its job.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] Do you have any allergies?
[patient] No.
[doctor] Any medications you’re taking?
[patient] No.
[doctor] Good. I’ll write the prescriptions. You can pick them up at the pharmacy.
[patient] Thank you, doctor.
[doctor] You’re welcome. I want to see you again in two weeks to make sure the stone has passed.
[patient] When is the appointment?
[doctor] Let’s say October 24 at 10:00. I’ll send you a confirmation email.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] Do you have a preferred contact email?
[patient] Yes, carmen.alvarez at gmail dot com.
[doctor] Got it. Is there anything else?
[patient] No. I just want to go home. My roommate is worried.
[doctor] You can tell her the plan. Drink water, take the meds, and watch for fever.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] The nurse will help you with the urine sample and the paperwork.
[nurse] Here is the cup. Just collect a mid-stream sample.
[patient] Okay.
[nurse] Please label it with your name and date of birth.
[patient] Done.
[nurse] Thank you.
[doctor] Carmen, please come back to the exam room in ten minutes so I can review the urine test results with you.
[patient] Okay.

note:
REFERRAL LETTER

TO: Dr. Jeanne Petit, Nephrologist
Clinique des Bauges
Annecy

RE: Marie Dubois
DOB: 12 March 1977
Address: 12 Rue des Lacs, 74000 Annecy

Dear Dr. Petit,

I am writing to refer Marie Dubois, a 47-year-old female, for ongoing nephrology follow-up following an acute kidney injury secondary to blunt abdominal trauma.

HISTORY
The patient presented to the emergency department after falling from a balcony in Annecy. The intent of the fall was undetermined; she reported prodromal dizziness resembling Parkinson's tremors, but no neurological deficit was found. She has a history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis (stable) and Crohn's disease (in remission). She was initially treated at Hôpital Édouard Herriot in Lyon before being referred to our center.

CURRENT STATUS
The patient is currently hemodynamically stable. Her pain is managed with oral paracetamol, rated at 6/10. We have held her home diuretic (Lasix) and initiated IV fluid resuscitation.

EXAMINATION
Vital signs: BP 135/85 mmHg, HR 92 bpm, Temp 37.1°C, SpO2 98%.
Physical exam: Mild tenderness palpated at the 3 o'clock position of the left flank. No active hematuria.

LABORATORY RESULTS
- Creatinine: 1.8 mg/dL (baseline 0.9 mg/dL)
- Potassium: 5.2 mmol/L
- Urine Output: 40 mL/hr

PLAN
1. Continue IV hydration until urine output stabilizes.
2. Monitor renal function (Creatinine, BUN, Electrolytes) daily.
3. Avoid nephrotoxic agents (NSAIDs like Mobic).
4. Dietary restriction of potassium.
5. Psychological support referral for post-traumatic stress.

I have scheduled a follow-up appointment for Marie Dubois on October 15, 2024 at 14:30 to review her progress. Please contact me directly if her creatinine rises or if she requires dialysis.

Sincerely,

Dr. Antoine Laurent
Hôpital Édouard Herriot
Lyon

SUBJECTIVE
Mr. Vance is a 68-year-old male presenting to the Massachusetts General Hospital emergency department with a chronic non-pressure ulcer of the right heel and midfoot, associated with signs of infection. He reports the wound began approximately two months ago as a small red spot, which has since progressed to a draining lesion. He describes the pain as 6/10, worsening with movement. He has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, Parkinson's disease, and Hashimoto's thyroiditis. He is currently on Metformin, Levothyroxine, and Levodopa. He denies drug allergies. He was referred by his primary care physician, Dr. Elena Rossi of Beacon Hill Medical Group, who was contacted via email at rossi.e@beaconhillmed.com. Mr. Vance resides in Boston and previously lived in Ohio. He has a family history of diabetes (mother, Margaret) and hypertension (brother, Robert, age 65). He is a former smoker, quit ten years ago, and drinks wine occasionally.

OBJECTIVE
Vital signs: Blood pressure 135/85 mmHg, Heart rate 82 bpm, Temperature 99.4°F (37.4°C), Respiratory rate 16/min, Oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Physical Exam:
General: Alert and oriented x3. In no acute distress.
Right Lower Extremity:
- Inspection: Non-healing ulcer on the plantar surface of the right heel and midfoot. The heel ulcer is approximately 2 cm in diameter with a fibrinous base and surrounding erythema extending 3 cm from the wound edge. Purulent drainage is present.
- Palpation: Tenderness to palpation over the right heel and midfoot. Warmth and induration noted in the surrounding tissue.
- Neurovascular: Dorsalis pedis pulse palpable. Capillary refill < 3 seconds. Decreased sensation in the foot, consistent with diabetic neuropathy.

- HbA1c: 7.8%.
Imaging:
- Right foot X-ray: Pending. No obvious fracture. Soft tissue swelling noted. No definitive bony destruction seen, but early osteomyelitis cannot be excluded.

ASSESSMENT
1. Chronic non-pressure ulcer of right heel and midfoot with cellulitis. Likely secondary to diabetic neuropathy and poor wound care.
2. Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
3. Parkinson's Disease.
4. Hashimoto's Thyroiditis.
5. Rule out osteomyelitis.

PLAN
1. Wound Care:
   - Debridement of necrotic tissue performed in ED.
   - Wound swab obtained for culture and sensitivity.
   - Apply sterile non-adherent dressing.
   - Offloading of the right foot is critical. Patient to use a walker and avoid weight-bearing on the affected foot.
2. Antibiotics:

3. Imaging:

5. Neurology:

6. Disposition:
   - Admit to medical floor for IV antibiotics and wound management.
   - Discharge planning to include home health nursing for wound care and podiatry follow-up.
7. Patient Education:
   - Discussed the importance of offloading and daily wound inspection.
   - Provided written instructions on foot care for diabetic patients.

REASON FOR REFERRAL
I am writing to refer my patient, Lukas Steiner, born 14 May 2004, a 20-year-old male, for a specialist evaluation regarding a recent spontaneous pneumothorax and the subsequent partial resection of lung tissue. Mr. Steiner is currently under my care for generalized anxiety disorder, which has been exacerbated by this acute medical event.

CLINICAL HISTORY
Mr. Steiner presented to the emergency department at AKH Vienna on 12 June 2024 following a sharp onset of right-sided chest pain while exercising at a gym. A CT scan confirmed a right-sided pneumothorax caused by the rupture of a subpleural bleb. He was treated with a chest tube, which was removed after 48 hours once the lung re-expanded. The surgical team performed a video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) to resect the bleb, resulting in a small, localized absence of lung parenchyma.

CURRENT STATUS
Post-operatively, Mr. Steiner reports no residual dyspnea or chest pain at rest. However, he exhibits significant hypervigilance and panic symptoms related to the fear of recurrence. His current psychiatric regimen includes Zoloft 50 mg daily, which I am increasing to 75 mg, and I have initiated Propranolol 10 mg twice daily for somatic anxiety symptoms. He is employed as a mechanic in Vienna and is eager to return to full duty but requires medical clearance and reassurance regarding his respiratory reserve.

EXAMINATION FINDINGS
On physical examination today, Mr. Steiner is a well-appearing male in no acute distress. Vital signs are stable. Respiratory examination reveals clear breath sounds bilaterally. Upon percussion, there is a slightly duller note at the right apex, consistent with the previous resection site. On auscultation, a faint, localized crepitus is noted at the 3 o'clock position of the right upper lobe, likely related to the surgical scarring. No wheezes or rales are present.

REQUEST FOR SPECIALIST INPUT
I would appreciate your assessment of his long-term pulmonary health, specifically:
1. Evaluation of the remaining lung capacity and any residual structural abnormalities.
2. Guidance on physical activity restrictions, particularly given his job as a mechanic which may involve heavy lifting.
3. Recommendations for monitoring to prevent recurrence.

I have attached his recent CT scan reports and discharge summary from AKH Vienna. Please feel free to contact me at psych.keller@med.example if you require further information.

Thank you for your time and expertise.

Sincerely,
Dr. Anna Keller
Private Practice for Psychiatry and Psychotherapy
Vienna

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Acute asthma exacerbation with wheezing and shortness of breath.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a 90-year-old woman with a history of mild intermittent asthma who presents with a three-day history of worsening wheezing, chest tightness, and dry cough. She reports that symptoms began after a trip to Strasbourg in October, where she visited her sister Claire and old friend Marie. She notes exposure to cold, dry air during the trip. She has been using her rescue inhaler (Ventolin) multiple times daily with only transient relief. She denies fever, chills, or purulent sputum. She reports a history of a mild upper respiratory infection one week prior to the exacerbation. She is currently on maintenance therapy with Seretide 250/50, one inhalation twice daily. Pain is rated 4/10, described as chest pressure.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Denies fever, chills, or fatigue.
Respiratory: Positive for wheezing, shortness of breath, and dry cough.
Cardiovascular: Denies chest pain, palpitations, or edema.
Gastrointestinal: Denies nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain.
Neurological: Denies dizziness or syncope.
Musculoskeletal: Denies joint pain or stiffness.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs:
Blood Pressure: 135/85 mmHg
Heart Rate: 102 bpm
Respiratory Rate: 24 breaths/min
Temperature: 36.8°C
Oxygen Saturation: 92% on room air

General: Alert, oriented, in mild respiratory distress.
Lungs: Widespread expiratory wheezes heard bilaterally. No rales or rhonchi.
Cardiovascular: Tachycardic, regular rhythm. No murmurs.

Extremities: No edema.

Complete Blood Count: Eosinophils 4.5% (elevated)

Basic Metabolic Panel: Within normal limits

   - Advised frequent use of Ventolin (Salbutamol) as needed, with a spacer to improve delivery.

2. Follow-up:

[patient] in.. . and out .

SUBJECTIVE
The patient is a 55-year-old male residing in Lugano, who relocated from Rome approximately five years ago. He presents for a follow-up on his diagnosis of epilepsy, unspecified, not intractable, without status epilepticus. He reports an increase in simple partial seizures (auras) characterized by olfactory hallucinations (burnt hair) and déjà vu, occurring 1-2 times weekly, predominantly in the afternoon. He admits to occasional missed doses of Levetiracetam due to his demanding schedule as a structural engineer at SwissBridge Construction. He reports a fall at the Club Lugano Tennis Academy last week, striking his head on a net post without loss of consciousness. He denies fever, headache, or recent illness. He reports recent travel to Zurich for work, which was associated with poor sleep and increased stress. He is under the care of Dr. Rossi for Hashimoto's disease, which is currently stable on Levothyroxine. His partner, Elena, reports that he has been more fatigable in the mornings. Family history is notable for Parkinson's disease in his mother.

OBJECTIVE
Vitals: BP 130/80 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, Temp 36.8°C.
General: Well-appearing male, no acute distress.
HEENT: Pupils equal and reactive. No nystagmus.
Neurological: Alert and oriented x3. Cranial nerves II-XII intact. Motor strength 5/5 in all extremities. Fine motor function slightly impaired due to resting tremor in the right hand, noted to be chronic but exacerbated by stress. Sensation intact. Reflexes 2+ and symmetric. No focal deficits.
Abdominal: Soft, non-tender. Mild fullness noted at the 3 o'clock position relative to the umbilicus, non-tender, likely related to bloating or medication side effects.
Skin: Bruising noted on the forehead, consistent with recent trauma.

ASSESSMENT
1. Epilepsy, unspecified, not intractable, without status epilepticus. Current status: Subtherapeutic control likely due to medication non-adherence and stress/sleep deprivation triggers. Increased frequency of auras suggests a need for dosage adjustment.
2. Hashimoto's disease. Stable, managed by Dr. Rossi.
3. Head injury, minor. No signs of intracranial pathology based on clinical presentation.
4. Medication side effects. Fatigue and gastrointestinal bloating likely related to Levetiracetam.

PLAN
1. Increase Levetiracetam to 750 mg twice daily. Patient and partner Elena to reinforce adherence strategies, including use of medication alarms.
2. Repeat serum electrolytes and Levetiracetam level check in 2 weeks.
3. Refer back to Dr. Rossi for thyroid function monitoring to rule out hypothyroidism contributing to fatigue.
4. Neurological exam to be re-evaluated in 3 months to monitor the hand tremor; no immediate imaging required as the last MRI in January 2023 was stable.
5. Patient advised to avoid high-risk activities such as clay court tennis until seizure control is optimized.
6. Follow-up appointment scheduled for September 15, 2023.

[doctor] I see. I’m feeling the joint here. I notice a slight crepitus, or grinding sensation, at the 3 o'clock position of the joint capsule. This is consistent with wear and tear.
[patient] Is it serious?

[patient] I’m 79 years old, so I know my body isn’t what it used to be. But I really want to keep playing tennis.

[patient] I moved here from Lisbon in 2015. I’ve been living in Zürich ever since.

[doctor] Not yet. We will try conservative management first. Physical therapy and pain management. If that doesn’t work, we can discuss other options.

[patient] Is that covered by my insurance?

[patient] Thank you. I’m a bit worried about falling again.

[doctor] Yes, walking is very good for you. Just avoid high-impact activities like running or jumping for now.
[patient] I will walk in the park.
[doctor] That sounds like a good plan.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor.
[doctor] You’re welcome, Mrs. Costa. Take care.
[nurse] I’ll help you with your clothes.
[patient] Thank you.

ASSESSMENT

2. Differential diagnosis includes early rheumatoid arthritis given family history and symmetric potential (though currently unilateral), or osteoarthritis/tenosynovitis due to overuse.

PATIENT NAME: Valdetina Krasniqi
DATE OF BIRTH: 15th April 1932
RECORD NUMBER: 8842-9910-KS

DIAGNOSIS
Unilateral primary osteoarthritis, right knee.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient is a 92-year-old female presenting with chronic pain and stiffness in the right knee, worsening over the last three months. She reports morning stiffness and pain rated 7-10/10. She currently uses a walker for ambulation. She lives in Zurich.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Pacemaker implantation in 2019. No history of cardiac events since.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient is retired. She enjoys dancing and was previously active in the Shqipëria club in Winterthur. She lives with her daughter, Elira (54), and is visited by her son, Leon (28), who is a software engineer.

FAMILY HISTORY
Sister Besnik diagnosed with Parkinson's disease.

EXAMINATION
Right knee: Mild swelling, tenderness on medial joint line, limited range of motion (flexion 80 degrees). No effusion in the left knee. Gait: Antalgic, uses walker.

ASSESSMENT
Severe osteoarthritis of the right knee. Given the patient's advanced age and history of pacemaker, surgical intervention (total knee arthroplasty) is considered high risk. Conservative management is indicated.

PLAN
1. Increase Celebrex to 200 mg twice daily for two weeks, then reassess.
2. Initiate topical Voltaren gel to the right knee TID.
3. Refer to PhysioMed in Switzerland for physical therapy.
4. Continue walker for all ambulation.
5. Follow-up in one month.

[doctor] Good morning, Valdetina. It is good to see you again. How have your legs been treating you since we last spoke?
[patient] Oh, doctor, you know, it is... it is difficult. The right knee, the right one, it is very stiff in the morning. I wake up and I cannot move it. It feels like... like it is locked.
[doctor] That sounds painful. Can you walk? Or do you need your walker?
[patient] I have the walker, yes. But I try to walk to the kitchen. My daughter, Elira, she is 54 years old, she is always worrying. She says, "Mom, sit down!" But I want to go to the garden.

[patient] Um, okay. *grunts* It hurts when I bend it. Especially when it is cold. The weather here in Zurich is so wet.
[doctor] Yes, humidity can make joint pain worse. I see some swelling on the right side. Is the left knee okay?
[patient] The left one? No, the left one is fine. It is only the right. It has been this way for three months. Maybe more.
[doctor] Three months. And how is the pain on a scale of one to ten?
[patient] Seven, eight... sometimes ten when I stand up too fast. I take the Medimo medicine, the tablets. But it is not enough.
[doctor] You are taking the Celebrex as prescribed?
[patient] Yes, twice a day. But my neighbor, Arben, he has the same problem. He says he takes something else.

[doctor] Right. I remember. That makes NSAIDs a bit risky. Let’s look at the X-rays I ordered last week.

[doctor] Yes, that was 12th March. The images show significant narrowing in the right knee joint. It is severe osteoarthritis.
[patient] Is it... is it cancer? No, I know, I am silly. My sister, Besnik, she had the Parkinson’s disease. I was afraid of bad things.

[doctor] I agree. Let’s do this. I will increase your Celebrex dose slightly, but only for two weeks. And I will add Voltaren gel. You rub it on the knee three times a day.

[doctor] Safety first. We can try again in one month. If the pain is still ten, we will discuss other options.
[patient] And the dancing?
[doctor] Maybe just sitting and clapping your hands. The Shqipëria club is nice, but be careful.
[patient] Okay. I will call Elira. She can come with me to the therapy.
[doctor] That is a good idea. She can help you remember the exercises.
[patient] She is very strict. Like a teacher.
[doctor] Good. I will send the referral to PhysioMed in Switzerland.
[patient] Thank you, doctor.
[doctor] You are welcome. Take care.

note:
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Dry cough, fever, and fatigue.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Sara Al-Tariq is an 18-year-old female, born on 14 March 2006, residing in Switzerland, originally from Eritrea. She presents to the pulmonology clinic with a three-week history of dry cough, subjective fevers, and fatigue. The patient reports that the symptoms began after a recent trip to Thailand. She also notes a malar rash on her arm four weeks ago, which was diagnosed as early Lyme disease by her referring physician, Dr. Julian Voss at Kantonsspital Aarau. She has been treated with Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily. Despite this, her respiratory symptoms have persisted and worsened. She reports chest pain upon inspiration, rated 4/10, and shortness of breath with exertion. She has experienced night sweats and mild weight loss. Her mother, Mariam (45), is concerned about her condition. The patient has no history of smoking or alcohol use.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: Fevers, chills, night sweats, fatigue, mild weight loss.
Respiratory: Dry cough, dyspnea on exertion, pleuritic chest pain.
Cardiovascular: Occasional palpitations, no chest pain at rest.
Gastrointestinal: Mild nausea, no vomiting, no diarrhea.
Musculoskeletal: No joint pain or swelling.
Neurological: Mild tingling in fingers, no weakness or numbness.
Skin: History of erythema migrans, currently resolved.
Lymphatic: Cervical lymphadenopathy.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs:
Blood Pressure: 118/76 mmHg
Heart Rate: 88 bpm
Temperature: 38.2 °C
Respiratory Rate: 18/min
Oxygen Saturation: 96% on room air

General: Well-appearing young female, in mild distress due to coughing.
HEENT: Normocephalic, atraumatic. Sclerae anicteric. Conjunctiva clear.
Neck: Supple, non-tender. Mild bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Respiratory: Decreased breath sounds in the left lower lobe. Fine crackles heard at the 3 o'clock position of the left lower lobe. No wheezes or rhonchi.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender, non-distended. Normal bowel sounds.
Extremities: No edema, cyanosis, or clubbing. Full range of motion.
Neurological: Alert and oriented x3. Cranial nerves II-XII intact. Mild paresthesia in bilateral fingers.

RESULTS
Chest X-ray: Pending.
CT Chest: Pending.
Complete Blood Count: WBC 12.5 x 10^9/L (elevated), Hb 13.5 g/dL, Plt 250 x 10^9/L.
C-Reactive Protein: 45 mg/L (elevated).

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN

- Obtain CT Chest without contrast to evaluate for consolidation, nodules, or other pathology.
