dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning. I see you’ve been referred to our clinic. Could you please state your full name and date of birth for the record?
[patient] My name is Sara Al-Tariq. My date of birth is 14 March 2006.
[doctor] Thank you, Sara. You are 18 years old today, correct?
[patient] Yes, I just turned 18.
[doctor] I see. Your medical record number here is 7842-9931. Do you have any questions about that?
[patient] No, it looks fine.
[doctor] Who referred you to us?
[patient] It was Dr. Julian Voss from the Kantonsspital Aarau. He sent me over because my cough wasn’t getting better with standard treatment.
[doctor] I see. Can you tell me why you are here today? What is your main concern?
[patient] I have had a dry cough for about three weeks. It’s getting worse at night. I also feel very tired and have had some fevers.
[doctor] When did this start?
[patient] It started about three weeks ago. I was traveling in Thailand at the time.
[doctor] Did you notice any rashes or joint pain?
[patient] Yes, I had a rash on my arm about four weeks ago. It looked like a bull’s-eye. My friend Lena, who is 19, said it looked like Lyme disease.
[doctor] Did you see a doctor about the rash?
[patient] I saw Dr. Julian Voss there. He started me on antibiotics, but the cough persisted. He suspected there might be something else going on, or perhaps the Lyme treatment wasn't enough for a specific complication.
[doctor] Have you had any chest pain?
[patient] Yes, a mild pain in my chest when I breathe in. It’s a 4 out of 10 on the pain scale.
[doctor] Any shortness of breath?
[patient] Yes, when I walk up stairs. I live in Basel, but I moved from Asmara two years ago.
[doctor] I see. Let’s check your vitals. The nurse has already taken them. Your blood pressure is 118/76, heart rate 88, temperature 38.2 degrees Celsius, and oxygen saturation is 96% on room air.
[patient] That’s high for a temperature?
[doctor] Yes, it indicates a fever. Let’s listen to your lungs. Take a deep breath in... and out.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] I hear some crackles in the lower left lung field. Specifically, there are fine crackles at the 3 o'clock position of the left lower lobe on auscultation.
[patient] Is that serious?
[doctor] It suggests inflammation or fluid, possibly related to an infection. Given your history of travel and the rash, we need to rule out a few things. Have you had any night sweats?
[patient] Yes, mostly at night.
[doctor] Any weight loss?
[patient] Maybe a little, but I’ve been eating less because of the cough.
[doctor] Let’s look at your recent lab results. Your CBC shows a white blood cell count of 12.5 x 10^9/L, which is slightly elevated. Your CRP is 45 mg/L.
[patient] What does that mean?
[doctor] It means your body is fighting an infection. We need to check for specific pathogens. Since you were in Thailand, we also need to consider tuberculosis, even though it’s less common.
[patient] I had a skin test in Asmara years ago, and it was negative.
[doctor] That’s good, but immunity can wane, or you could have been exposed recently. We will do a chest X-ray today.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] Also, regarding the Lyme disease, did Dr. Voss test for it?
[patient] Yes, he did a blood test. It was positive for IgM but negative for IgG.
[doctor] That suggests a recent or early infection. However, pulmonary involvement in Lyme is rare. Usually, it affects the heart or nerves. But we must keep it in mind.
[patient] My mother, Mariam, is 45, and she is worried sick.
[doctor] I understand. We will do our best. Have you been taking the antibiotics as prescribed?
[patient] Yes, I am taking Doxycycline 100 mg twice a day.
[doctor] Good. Did you have any side effects?
[patient] Just some stomach upset. I take it with food now.
[doctor] That’s the right way. Let’s review your other symptoms. Any heart palpitations?
[patient] Sometimes, yes.
[doctor] We may need an ECG to check your heart rhythm.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] Any neurological symptoms? Numbness or tingling?
[patient] A little tingling in my fingers.
[doctor] Noted. Let’s look at your physical exam again. Your heart sounds are normal, no murmurs. Your abdomen is soft and non-tender. Your lymph nodes in the neck are slightly enlarged.
[patient] Does that happen with Lyme?
[doctor] It can happen with any infection.
[doctor] I will order a CT scan of your chest to get a better look at the lungs.
[patient] Is that necessary?
[doctor] Yes, to see if there is any consolidation or nodules.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] We will also send a sputum sample for acid-fast bacilli and culture to rule out tuberculosis.
[patient] I hope I don’t have TB.
[doctor] It’s a possibility given your travel, but let’s see the results.
[patient] How long will it take?
[doctor] The CT results will be in a few hours. The TB cultures can take up to six weeks, but we can do a rapid PCR test that gives results in a day or two.
[patient] That’s better.
[doctor] In the meantime, continue your antibiotics. If your fever goes above 39 degrees, or if you feel significantly worse, call the clinic or go to the emergency room.
[patient] I will.
[doctor] Do you have any allergies?
[patient] No known drug allergies.
[doctor] What about food?
[patient] No.
[doctor] Are you taking any other medications?
[patient] No, just the Doxycycline.
[doctor] Are you on any supplements?
[patient] No.
[doctor] Do you smoke or use alcohol?
[patient] No, I don’t smoke or drink.
[doctor] Good. Let’s summarize. You are an 18-year-old woman with a history of recent travel to Thailand, a rash suggestive of Lyme disease, and a persistent dry cough with fever.
[patient] Yes.
[doctor] We need to differentiate between a post-infectious cough, a complication of Lyme disease, or a new infection like TB or atypical pneumonia.
[patient] That sounds complicated.
[doctor] It is, but we have a plan. We will monitor you closely.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor.
[doctor] You’re welcome. The nurse will guide you to the radiology department for the CT scan.

note:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
PATIENT NAME: Giulia Rossi
DATE OF BIRTH: 15/08/1950
RECORD NUMBER: ORD-2023-99812
INSURER: Swiss Life
INSURANCE NUMBER: SL-889-204-11
CONTACT: +41 91 456 78 90
RESIDENCE: Lugano, Paradiso District
REFERRED BY: Dr. Marco Bianchi, University Hospital Zurich

CLINICAL NOTE
PATIENT DEMOGRAPHICS
Giulia Rossi, a 73-year-old female, residing in Lugano, presented to the orthopedic clinic with a three-month history of chest pain. The patient is originally from Italy, specifically Milan, and has lived in Switzerland for twenty years. She works as a librarian.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
The patient reports non-cardiac chest pain, localized to the left upper chest near the sternum. The pain is described as sharp and exacerbated by deep inspiration and palpation. The symptoms began three months ago and worsened two weeks ago. The pain occasionally radiates to the left shoulder upon head rotation. There is no history of radiation to the jaw or arm. The patient reports significant tenderness to palpation at the third and fourth costochondral joints on the left side. She recently traveled to Paris last summer for her birthday and reports extensive walking and carrying a heavy bag.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
The patient has a history of hypertension, managed intermittently with Losartan. She has a history of gastroesophageal reflux disease, managed with Omeprazole. She denies history of cardiac disease, diabetes, or peptic ulcer disease. Family history is notable for her husband, Paolo (75), who has coronary artery disease. Her daughter, Lara (28), and sister, Elena, are healthy.

EXAMINATION
VITAL SIGNS
Blood Pressure: 135/85 mmHg
Heart Rate: 72 bpm
Respiratory Rate: 16 breaths/min
Temperature: 36.8°C
Oxygen Saturation: 98% on room air

PHYSICAL EXAM
General: Alert and oriented. No acute distress.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm. No murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Respiratory: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Musculoskeletal: Significant tenderness to palpation at the left 3rd and 4th costochondral junctions. Reproduction of pain with palpation. No swelling or erythema observed. Range of motion of the thoracic spine is normal.

INVESTIGATIONS
ECG: Normal sinus rhythm. No ST-segment changes. No Q waves.
Blood Work:
Troponin I: 0.02 ng/mL (Normal)
D-dimer: 0.45 mg/L (Normal)
C-Reactive Protein: 8 mg/L (Mildly elevated)
Complete Blood Count: Within normal limits

ASSESSMENT
1. Costochondritis (Left-sided)
2. Hypertension (Intermittent control)
3. Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease

PLAN
1. Diagnosis: Costochondritis is the most likely diagnosis given the reproducibility of pain with palpation and the absence of cardiac risk factors or ECG changes. Cardiac causes have been ruled out by normal ECG and troponin levels.
2. Medications:
   - Ibuprofen 400 mg orally three times a day with food for 10 days.
   - Voltaren 1% gel applied to the affected area four times a day.
   - Continue Omeprazole 20 mg daily.
   - Resume Losartan 50 mg daily for blood pressure control.
3. Self-Care:
   - Apply warm compresses to the chest for 15-20 minutes, three times a day.
   - Avoid heavy lifting and strenuous upper body exercises for two weeks.
   - Practice good posture.
4. Follow-up:
   - Patient will be contacted by the clinic at +41 91 456 78 90 within 48 hours to review blood results.
   - If pain persists or worsens, or if new symptoms (shortness of breath, sweating, palpitations) develop, patient should seek immediate medical attention.
5. Patient Education:
   - Discussed the nature of costochondritis and its benign prognosis.
   - Emphasized the importance of consistent blood pressure medication.
   - Advised on proper body mechanics to prevent recurrence.

SIGNATURE
Dr. Alex Thorne
Orthopedic Specialist
Lakeview Orthopedic Clinic
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, Giulia Rossi. Please have a seat. I see you were referred to us by Dr. Marco Bianchi at the University Hospital Zurich. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

[patient] Good morning. Yes, uh, it is the pain. It’s been... um, it is in my chest, but not like a heart attack. You know? It’s more... sharp. Like when I breathe in deep.

[doctor] I see. How long has this been going on?

[patient] Uh, for three months. It started maybe... two weeks ago it got worse? No, wait, it started three months ago, but it was mild. Then two weeks ago, it became very painful.

[doctor] Okay, so a three-month history, worsening two weeks ago. Does it radiate anywhere? To your back, your jaw, your arm?

[patient] No, no. It stays here, Giulia points to her upper chest, near the sternum. Sometimes it goes to the left shoulder, but only when I turn my head.

[doctor] That’s a good sign. Does it hurt more when you press on the area?

[patient] Yes! Oh my god, yes. When I touch it here... Giulia points to the costochondral junction. It’s so tender. My daughter, Lara, who is 28, tried to rub it for me yesterday, and I nearly screamed.

[doctor] Tenderness to palpation is a key feature of musculoskeletal chest pain. Do you have any history of heart disease?

[patient] No, no. My blood pressure is good. I take Losartan for it, but only sometimes. I stopped taking it for a bit because I felt fine.

[doctor] We should discuss that later. You are insured by Swiss Life, correct? I see your insurance number here: SL-889-204-11.

[patient] Yes, yes. Swiss Life. The number is correct. I live in Lugano, in the Paradiso district.

[doctor> And you were born in Italy, if I recall correctly?

[patient] Yes, I moved from Milan to Switzerland twenty years ago. I work as a librarian at the public library here in Lugano.

[doctor] Thank you. I see you recently traveled to Paris?

[patient] Yes, last summer. I went to Paris for my birthday. I was 73 then? No, wait, I turn 73 this month. Yes, I went to Paris to celebrate with my sister, Elena.

[doctor] That’s wonderful. Did you do any heavy lifting or unusual activities there?

[patient] No, we just walked. A lot of walking. Maybe I carried my bag too much? I don’t know. But when I got back, the pain started.

[doctor] Let’s do a quick physical exam. Can you take your shirt off?

[patient] Yes, of course.

[doctor] Take a deep breath for me.

[patient] (Inhales deeply) Oof. That hurts.

[doctor] I can see some swelling in the third and fourth costochondral joints on the left side. Pressing here... does that reproduce your pain?

[patient] Yes! That’s exactly it. That is the pain.

[doctor] Okay. Your heart sounds are normal. No murmurs. Your lungs are clear. I’m going to check your vital signs. Your blood pressure is 135/85. Your heart rate is 72 beats per minute.

[patient] Is that bad?

[doctor] It’s slightly elevated, but not alarming. Given your age and symptoms, I want to be thorough. I’m going to order an ECG and some blood tests.

[patient] Blood tests? For what?

[doctor] To rule out any cardiac markers. Troponin, D-dimer, just to be safe. Even though this sounds very much like costochondritis, we must exclude other causes.

[patient] Okay. I am a little scared, you know? My husband, Paolo, is 75, and he has heart problems. I don’t want to be like him.

[doctor] I understand. But the tenderness to palpation is very specific. It’s likely inflammatory. We will start you on Ibuprofen 400 mg, three times a day, after meals.

[patient] Ibuprofen? I usually take Paracetamol.

[doctor] Ibuprofen is better for inflammation. But please be careful with your stomach. Do you have a history of ulcers?

[patient] No, I don’t think so. I take Omeprazole sometimes for reflux.

[doctor] Good. We will continue that. You should also apply a warm compress to the area. I will write you a prescription for Voltaren gel as well.

[patient] Thank you. When will I see the results of the tests?

[doctor] The ECG will be done here in the clinic. The blood tests will take a day or two. I will call you at +41 91 456 78 90 to discuss the results.

[patient] Yes, please. That is my number. I am usually home in the afternoon.

[doctor] Understood. If the pain becomes severe, or if you experience shortness of breath, chest tightness, or sweating, go to the emergency room immediately.

[patient] I will. Thank you, doctor.

[doctor] You’re welcome. The nurse will help you with the ECG and blood draw.

[patient] Okay. Thank you.

[doctor] Please wait in the next room.

[patient] Yes.

[nurse] Hi, Giulia. I’m here to help you with the ECG and blood work.

[patient] Hello. Thank you.

[nurse] Let’s start with the ECG. Can you relax your muscles?

[patient] Yes.

[nurse] Okay, that’s done. Now, for the blood test. I’ll put this on your arm.

[patient] That’s fine.

[nurse] Done. You’ll need to press on the cotton for five minutes.

[patient] Okay.

[nurse] You can go to the waiting area. The doctor will contact you with the results in 48 hours.

[patient] Thank you.

note:
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a 91-year-old woman with a history of Parkinson’s disease and Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. She presents with a two-week history of urinary incontinence. Symptoms began after a fall in the kitchen two weeks ago, which resulted in a hip bruise. She reports stress incontinence, particularly with coughing and sneezing. She recently returned from a trip to Chicago last month, which she notes caused significant stress. She denies fever, dysuria, or hematuria.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
- Parkinson’s disease (diagnosed 5 years ago)
- Hashimoto’s thyroiditis
- Hypertension
- Osteoarthritis

MEDICATIONS
- Levothyroxine 100 mcg daily
- Carbidopa-Levodopa 25/100 mg three times daily
- Lisinopril 10 mg daily

ALLERGIES
- NKDA

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: BP 145/85, HR 78, Temp 98.6 F, RR 16.
General: Alert and oriented x3.
Abdomen: Soft, non-distended. Mild tenderness in the right upper quadrant, likely related to recent fall. No masses.
Neurologic: Motor strength 5/5 in upper and lower extremities. Reflexes 2+ and symmetric. No clonus. Gait is steady but slow, consistent with Parkinson’s disease.

ASSESSMENT
1. Urinary incontinence (stress type), likely multifactorial:
   - Underlying Parkinson’s disease
   - Recent fall and pain
   - Stress from recent travel
2. History of Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, currently stable.
3. Recent fall in the kitchen with hip contusion.

PLAN
1. Start Oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily for bladder overactivity.
2. Refer to pelvic floor physical therapy for biofeedback and exercises.
3. Recommend home safety modifications, including removal of loose rugs in the kitchen.
4. Continue current medications.
5. Follow-up in 4 weeks to assess response to treatment.
6. Copy of this note sent to Dr. Sarah Jenkins at St. Jude’s Medical Center.
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, Ms. Eleanor Vance. I see here that you were referred to me by Dr. Sarah Jenkins at St. Jude’s Medical Center. How are you feeling today?
[patient] Good morning, Doctor. I’m a bit tired, but I’m here.
[doctor] Thank you for coming in. I understand you’re dealing with some issues regarding urinary control. Can you tell me a little more about what’s been happening?
[patient] Yes. It started about two weeks ago. I haven’t been able to get to the bathroom fast enough.
[doctor] I see. Was there a specific event that triggered this, or did it come on gradually?
[patient] Well, I had a fall. It was in the kitchen. I slipped on a wet spot near the stove and hit my hip.
[doctor] That is a common place for injuries. Did you see anyone about the fall after it happened?
[patient] Yes, I went to the urgent care. They said my hip was bruised but not broken. They also mentioned that my blood pressure was a bit high that day.
[doctor] Understood. Have you noticed any changes in your strength or balance since the fall?
[patient] My left side feels a little weaker. My doctor, Dr. Jenkins, mentioned that I have early signs of Parkinson’s disease, so I think that might be related.
[doctor] That is a good point. Parkinson’s can affect movement and bladder control. Have you been taking your medications as prescribed?
[patient] Yes. I take my pills every morning at 8:00. I also had a trip to Chicago last month to visit my granddaughter.
[doctor] That sounds like a nice trip. Did the incontinence start before or after you returned from Chicago?
[patient] It was right after I got home. I was stressed about the flight and the long drive back to Portland.
[doctor] Stress can certainly exacerbate these symptoms. Have you experienced any fever, chills, or burning during urination?
[patient] No, no burning. I don’t think I’m sick. I just lose control when I cough or sneeze.
[doctor] That sounds like stress incontinence. It’s very common in women your age. Have you tried any pelvic floor exercises?
[patient] My daughter, Mary, told me to do some, but I don’t know how to do them right. She is a physical therapist, so I trust her.
[doctor] That is helpful. I can refer you to a specialist who can teach you the correct technique. In the meantime, have you had any recent blood tests?
[patient] Yes, Dr. Jenkins ordered some labs last week. I think I have a condition called Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, so my thyroid levels need monitoring.
[doctor] Correct. We need to ensure your thyroid is stable, as that can also impact bladder function. Did the labs show anything else concerning?
[patient] I think my kidney function was normal. I was worried because I have a family history of kidney issues.
[doctor] Good news then. Let’s do a quick physical exam to check your abdominal area and your neurological reflexes. Please lie down for me.
[patient] Okay. I feel a bit dizzy when I lie down.
[doctor] That can happen with age and blood pressure changes. Take your time. Now, I’m going to check your abdomen for any masses or tenderness.
[patient] It hurts a little when you press near my ribs.
[doctor] That might be related to the bruise from your fall in the kitchen. I’ll note that. Now, let’s check your lower back.
[patient] My back is stiff. I’ve had it like this for three months.
[doctor] Chronic stiffness is common. I’m going to check your reflexes in your legs. I’m going to tap here.
[patient] My leg kicked out.
[doctor] Good, that’s a normal reflex. Now the other side.
[patient] Same thing.
[doctor] Okay. Your reflexes appear symmetrical. This is reassuring. I don’t see any signs of a spinal cord issue, which is good.
[patient] I was worried I might have a stroke or something.
[doctor] Based on what you’ve told me, that seems unlikely. The combination of your fall, the stress, and your underlying Parkinson’s disease is the most likely cause.
[patient] So what do I do?
[doctor] We are going to start with some behavioral changes and pelvic floor therapy. I’m also going to prescribe a medication to help relax your bladder muscle.
[patient] What is the name of the medicine?
[doctor] It’s called Oxybutynin. You will take it twice a day. Please watch out for dry mouth, which is a common side effect.
[patient] I see. I drink a lot of water, so that might be an issue.
[doctor] You should still drink plenty of water, but you might need to take sips more frequently. Let’s discuss your other medications.
[patient] I take Levothyroxine for my thyroid and Carbidopa-Levodopa for my movement issues.
[doctor] Yes, those are important. We need to make sure there are no interactions. I’ll check with your pharmacist.
[patient] My pharmacist is at CVS Pharmacy on Main Street.
[doctor] I’ll send the new prescription there. You can pick it up tomorrow.
[patient] That works for me. I usually go in the morning.
[doctor] Perfect. I also want to make sure you are safe at home. Since you fell in the kitchen, are there any loose rugs or obstacles?
[patient] I have a rug by the sink. I didn’t know it was slippery.
[doctor] I recommend removing it or using a non-slip pad. Falls can worsen incontinence due to pain and fear of falling.
[patient] I will talk to Mary about that. She is very good at organizing the house.
[doctor] That’s a great idea. Also, try to keep a bladder diary for the next few days. Write down when you drink fluids and when you urinate.
[patient] I can do that. I keep a journal for my symptoms anyway.
[doctor] Excellent. That will help us understand the pattern. If you develop fever, blood in your urine, or severe pain, please call our office immediately.
[patient] And if I can’t reach you, where do I go?
[doctor] You can go to the emergency room at St. Jude’s Medical Center. Their number is 503-555-0199.
[patient] I have it written down. Thank you, Doctor.
[doctor] You’re welcome. I’ll send a copy of this note to Dr. Jenkins at St. Jude’s Medical Center to keep her in the loop.
[patient] That’s good. I don’t want my doctors to be confused.
[doctor] We’ll coordinate. Do you have any questions for me?
[patient] No, I think that covers everything.
[doctor] Great. The nurse will help you with the follow-up appointment.
[nurse] Hi, Ms. Vance. I’m going to schedule your next visit.
[patient] Yes, please.
[nurse] How about October 15th at 10:30?
[patient] That works for me.
[nurse] Perfect. I’ll email the confirmation to eleanor.vance1933 at gmail dot com.
[patient] Yes, that’s my email.
[nurse] You’re all set. Take care.
[patient] Thank you.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Chronic combined systolic and diastolic heart failure, worsening dyspnea and edema.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
70-year-old male with history of chronic heart failure presents for follow-up. Reports increased leg swelling for three months and new onset of chest heaviness and dizziness yesterday. Symptoms exacerbated by standing for long periods at work.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY

MEDICATIONS
- Lasix (Furosemide)
- Carvedilol
- Levothyroxine (for Hashimoto's)

EXAMINATION
- Blood Pressure: 150/90 mmHg
- Heart: Murmur audible at 3 o'clock position
- Lungs: Bibasilar crackles
- Extremities: 2+ pitting edema in bilateral lower extremities
- Neck: Distended jugular veins

ASSESSMENT
1. Chronic combined systolic and diastolic heart failure, decompensated.
2. Hashimoto's disease, stable.

PATIENT INFORMATION
Herr Gruber, 70-year-old male, residing in Vienna. Born in Innsbruck.

Insurance: ÖGK, Number: A8392014.
Medical Record Number: 405921.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Follow-up for solitary pulmonary nodule identified on chest X-ray three weeks ago. Also reports right knee stiffness and swelling for two months.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient presents for evaluation of a solitary pulmonary nodule found incidentally on chest X-ray ordered by primary care physician Dr. Klein three weeks ago for a persistent cough. Cough has lasted for two months without associated weight loss or hemoptysis. Patient also reports new onset of right knee stiffness and swelling, noted by wife Ingrid (68), who is a nurse. Pain is present with deep flexion. No trauma reported.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
No significant past medical history. No prior orthopedic surgeries.
Family History: Father Johann died of lung cancer at 75. Brother Peter (65) has Parkinson's disease. No family history of Crohn's disease, Hashimoto's, Graves' disease, or Bell's palsy.

Vitals: BP 135/85, HR 72, Temp 36.8°C.

Lungs: Clear to auscultation bilaterally.

ASSESSMENT
1. Solitary pulmonary nodule. Etiology unclear. Family history of lung cancer is a risk factor.
2. Right knee Baker's cyst, likely secondary to meniscal tear or early osteoarthritis.

PLAN
1. CT Chest with contrast to characterize the pulmonary nodule. Ordered for AKH Vienna.
2. MRI Right Knee to evaluate meniscal integrity and confirm Baker's cyst.

dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, Herr Gruber. Please have a seat. I see you are here for a follow-up regarding the finding on your recent chest X-ray.
[patient] Yes, doctor. I am quite worried. I am a retired structural engineer who used to work for Baumeister AG, so I know what a fracture looks like, but this... this is different.
[doctor] I understand your concern. Let’s look at the records. You are seventy years old, correct? And you live in Vienna?
[patient] Correct. I have lived in Vienna for twenty years, but I was born in Innsbruck. My insurance is with ÖGK, and my number is A8392014.
[doctor] Thank you. Your medical record number here is 405921. Let’s go back to the beginning. When did you first notice any symptoms, or was this an incidental finding?
[patient] It was incidental. Dr. Klein, my primary care physician, ordered a chest X-ray three weeks ago because I had a lingering cough.
[doctor] And what was the result?
[patient] The X-ray showed a small shadow. Dr. Klein referred me to you immediately. He said it was a solitary pulmonary nodule.
[doctor] A solitary pulmonary nodule is a common finding. It can be benign, such as a granuloma from a past infection, or it can be something else. We need more information. Did you have any pain, shortness of breath, or weight loss?
[patient] No pain. Just the cough. It has been going on for two months. I also noticed some stiffness in my right knee, which is odd because I don't usually have orthopedic issues.
[doctor] Stiffness in the knee. Is it painful?
[patient] Only when I bend it deeply. My wife, Ingrid, who is 68, says I am limping. She has nurse experience, so she is very particular.
[doctor] I see. Let’s examine the knee. Please remove your shoe and sock.
[patient] Yes.
[doctor] I am going to palpate around the joint. Do you feel this tenderness here?
[patient] Yes, that is the spot.
[doctor] And here, behind the knee?
[patient] Oh, that’s sore too.
[doctor] I can feel a fluid-filled swelling behind your knee. This is likely a Baker's cyst. It is often associated with knee arthritis or meniscal tears.
[patient] A Baker's cyst? I have heard of that. Does it have anything to do with the lung?
[doctor] Not directly. Orthopedic issues are separate from pulmonary findings. However, systemic inflammation can sometimes affect both. Let’s focus on the knee first. I will perform a McMurray's test to check the meniscus. Please bear with me.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] I hear a slight click. This suggests a possible meniscal tear. We should get an MRI of the knee to confirm.
[patient] And the lung? What do we do about that?
[doctor] We need a CT scan of the chest with contrast. This will give us the size, shape, and characteristics of the nodule. It will help us decide if it is likely benign or if we need to biopsy it.
[patient] How soon can that be done?
[doctor] I will order it today. You can go to AKH Vienna for the scan. They have a fast track for orthopedic referrals.
[patient] I see. And the insurance?
[doctor] Since you are with ÖGK, the referral should go through smoothly. Make sure to bring your insurance card, number A8392014.
[patient] I have it here.
[doctor] Good. Now, regarding your family history. Does anyone in your family have lung cancer or other serious illnesses?
[patient] My father, Johann, had lung cancer. He was 75 when he died. My brother, Peter, is 65 and he has Parkinson's disease.
[doctor] That is important information. A family history of lung cancer increases the risk, but it does not mean you have it. The CT scan will clarify things.
[patient] What about the knee? Do I need surgery for the Baker's cyst?

[patient] I see. So, next steps: CT scan of the chest, MRI of the knee, and physical therapy.
[doctor] Exactly. I will send the orders to your primary care physician, Dr. Klein. He will coordinate the appointments.
[patient] Thank you, doctor. I am relieved to have a plan.
[doctor] You are welcome, Herr Gruber. Please come back with the results of the CT scan and MRI. We will review them together and decide on the next steps.
[patient] I will.
[doctor] Is there anything else you would like to discuss?
[patient] No, that is all.
[doctor] Then we are done for today. Take care.
[patient] Thank you.

[doctor] Good morning. My name is Dr. Rossi. I see you have an appointment for a follow-up regarding your kidney stone history, but I noticed your file mentions some other issues. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

[doctor] Thank you, Maria. Let’s start with the stone. When did you first notice the pain?
[patient] It started about three days ago. Sharp pain on the left side, radiating to the groin. I took Albavir but it didn't help much.
[doctor] How would you rate the pain on a scale from zero to ten?
[patient] It’s an eight. Very sharp. I have a medical record number, 8842-109-33, if you need to look up my previous scans.
[doctor] I have it open. You were born on 14/03/1949, correct?
[patient] Yes, that is my date of birth. I was in the hospital in 2021 for a similar episode.
[doctor] Right. Do you have a fever or nausea?
[patient] No fever, but I feel nauseous. I haven't eaten much since yesterday.
[doctor] Let’s check your vitals. Your blood pressure is 150/90, heart rate 88. That’s a bit elevated. Do you have any history of heart problems?
[patient] No, but I do have Hashimoto's thyroiditis. I take Euthyrox daily.
[doctor] Understood. And do you have any other chronic conditions? I see a note about Crohn's disease in your history.
[patient] Yes, I was diagnosed with Crohn's in 1998. It’s been stable for years, but I still take Imodium if I have diarrhea.
[doctor] Good. Let’s look at the kidney stone again. Did you pass any blood in your urine?
[patient] A little bit, pinkish color. I’m worried it’s getting infected.
[doctor] We’ll do a urine test. In the meantime, let’s discuss your medication. You are on Aspirin 100mg daily?
[patient] Yes, my cardiologist, Dr. Verdi, prescribed it for my blood pressure.
[doctor] We might need to pause that temporarily if the stone is causing significant bleeding, but let’s see the labs first. How is your mobility?
[patient] I’m using a cane. I have a Baker's cyst in my right knee, so walking is difficult.
[doctor] I see. That explains the difficulty with moving. Do you have any other pain?
[patient] My left hand has been weak. I dropped my coffee cup this morning.
[doctor] Any facial drooping or difficulty speaking?
[patient] No, just the hand. I read about Bell's palsy on the internet and got scared.
[doctor] It’s unlikely to be Bell's palsy given the symptoms, but we’ll monitor it. Let’s check your reflexes. I’m going to tap your knee.

[doctor] Reflexes are normal. Now, let’s talk about your lifestyle. Do you exercise?

[doctor] That’s excellent. How much water do you drink daily?

[doctor] Good. Let’s look at your blood work from last month. Your creatinine was slightly elevated at 1.2. We need to repeat that today.
[patient] Will it be ready soon?
[doctor] Usually within two hours. I’ll have the nurse draw your blood. [nurse] Can you come in to take some blood?

[patient] No, she is at work in Bellinzona. She is a teacher.
[doctor] I hope she is doing well. Let’s get your blood results. [nurse] The blood is drawn.

[patient] Okay. Thank you, Doctor.
[doctor] You’re welcome. I’ll call your GP, Dr. Moretti, in Mendrisio, to update them.
[patient] Thank you.
[doctor] Please come back if the pain worsens or if you develop a fever.
[patient] I will. Goodbye.
[doctor] Goodbye.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Elira Hoxha, a 51-year-old woman, presents with worsening right hand numbness and pain, primarily affecting the thumb and index finger. Symptoms have been present for three months and worsened yesterday. She reports nocturnal symptoms requiring shaking of the hand to relieve discomfort. She works as a graphic designer at PixelPerfect Studio and uses a mouse extensively. She recently traveled to Rome for work. She lives in Zurich, having moved from Prishtina.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Hashimoto's thyroiditis (diagnosed 5 years ago). No history of diabetes or trauma. Family history includes a friend with Parkinson's disease, but no direct family history of neurological disorders. She has a daughter, Amina, aged 24, and a son, Ben, aged 10.

MEDICATIONS
Levothyroxine daily. No known drug allergies.

EXAMINATION
Right wrist inspection shows mild swelling. Tinel's sign is positive on the median nerve distribution. Phalen's test is positive. Grip strength is mildly reduced in the right hand compared to the left. Sensation is diminished in the median nerve distribution. No thenar atrophy noted. Vital signs are stable, with blood pressure 118/76.

ASSESSMENT
Right carpal tunnel syndrome, moderate severity. Aggravated by repetitive wrist flexion and extension at work.

PLAN
1. Nighttime wrist splinting: Patient to wear a custom-fitted splint to maintain neutral wrist position during sleep.
2. Activity modification: Avoid prolonged mouse use; take breaks every 30 minutes.
3. Pharmacology: If symptoms persist in two weeks, consider corticosteroid injection via Dr. Keller.
4. Follow-up: Return in four weeks for reassessment.
5. Insurance: Claims submitted to Swisscare under policy SC-8842-9921.
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, Elira Hoxha. Please, take a seat. How have you been since our last visit two weeks ago?
[patient] Hello, Dr. Weber. It’s been a bit difficult. The pain in my right hand is still there, especially at night.
[doctor] I see. You mentioned this started three months ago. Has it gotten worse recently?
[patient] Yes, yesterday I woke up with a lot of numbness in my thumb and index finger. I had to shake my hand to get the feeling back.
[doctor] That sounds like classic symptoms. You work as a graphic designer for PixelPerfect Studio, correct?
[patient] Yes, I do. I sit at my computer for about eight hours a day. I think the mouse usage makes it worse.
[doctor] It is common for repetitive strain to aggravate carpal tunnel syndrome. Do you have any other medical conditions we should consider?
[patient] I have had Hashimoto's thyroiditis for about five years now. My thyroid levels are stable, but I take medication for it.
[doctor] Thank you for reminding me. Are you still taking Levothyroxine?
[patient] Yes, every morning. I also have a friend, Mira, who has Parkinson's disease, so I am a bit worried about neurological issues, but I know this is different.
[doctor] Don't worry, carpal tunnel is a peripheral nerve issue, not a central one like Parkinson's. Let’s check your insurance details. Your insurer is Swisscare, is that correct?
[patient] Yes, it is. The number is SC-8842-9921.
[doctor] Noted. You mentioned you moved to Zurich from Prishtina a few years ago. How are you settling in?
[patient] I like it here. My daughter, Amina, who is 24 years old, studies here. She is very helpful.
[doctor] That is good to know. Did you travel recently?
[patient] Yes, I went to Rome last month for a work conference. It was lovely.
[doctor] And your son, Ben?
[patient] He is 10 years old. He is with my husband, Arben, in Prishtina for the summer.
[doctor] I understand. Now, let's look at your right hand. Can you make a fist and release it?
[patient] Yes, like this?
[doctor] Yes. You don't need to use your left hand to help.
[patient] Okay, that’s done.
[doctor] Now, I will press on the inside of your wrist. Does that cause any pain or tingling?
[patient] Oh, that tingles a bit. Yes.
[doctor] That is a positive Tinel's sign. Let's check the Phalen's test. Please hold your wrists together with the backs of your hands touching. Keep that for 60 seconds.
[patient] This is uncomfortable.
[doctor] Yes, that is expected. If you feel numbness in the thumb, index, or middle finger, let me know.
[patient] I feel it starting in my index finger.
[doctor] Okay, stop. That is positive. I will check the nerve conduction study results from last week. They show median nerve slowing.
[patient] Does that mean I need surgery?
[doctor] Not yet. We will try conservative management first. I want you to stop using the mouse for two hours in the afternoon. Can you do that?
[patient] That is hard, but I can try.
[doctor] Also, I am prescribing a wrist splint for night use. Do you have one?
[patient] I bought one at the pharmacy, but it feels too loose.
[doctor] We can adjust it or get a custom one. Your insurance should cover it.
[patient] Thank you.
[doctor] I will send a prescription to your doctor, Dr. Keller, for a corticosteroid injection if the splint doesn't help in two weeks.
[patient] Okay.
[doctor] Let's check your blood pressure while you are here. Nurse, please take her vitals.
[nurse] Of course, Ms. Hoxha.
[patient] My blood pressure is usually around 120/80.
[nurse] It is 118/76 today. Good.
[doctor] Thank you. Do you have any questions?
[patient] Just one. I read about Crohn's disease. Could this be related to inflammation?
[doctor] Crohn's is a gastrointestinal issue. While systemic inflammation can sometimes affect nerves, your carpal tunnel is likely due to mechanical compression and your Hashimoto's.
[patient] I see.
[doctor] Make sure to get enough rest. Your daughter, Amina, can help you with household tasks if the pain is bad.
[patient] She is very kind.
[doctor] Let's schedule a follow-up in four weeks.
[patient] Okay, I will book that.
[doctor] If the numbness spreads to your whole arm or you lose strength in your hand, come in sooner.
[patient] Understood. Thank you, Dr. Weber.
[doctor] You are welcome, Elira.

note:
SUBJECT: Signora Rossi
DOB: 1934
MRN: 882910

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
90-year-old female presents with acute exacerbation of unspecified asthma. Symptoms began yesterday evening with dyspnea and chest tightness while climbing stairs. Patient reports worsening symptoms over the last three weeks. Trigger identified as dust exposure in the kitchen. Rescue inhaler (Salbutamol) provided minimal relief. Nocturnal coughing and orthopnea reported.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
- Unspecified asthma
- Hypertension
- History of minor head trauma from fall in pool area two years ago.

MEDICATIONS:
- Budesonide inhaler 200mcg BID
- Antihypertensive (name not specified in HPI, assumed continued)

ALLERGIES:
- Dust mites
- No drug allergies reported

VITAL SIGNS:
BP: 140/85 mmHg
HR: 92 bpm
RR: 22 breaths/min
SpO2: 92% on room air

EXAMINATION:
- Lungs: Bilateral wheezing, more pronounced on the right. Decreased air entry.
- Heart: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs.
- General: Alert, oriented, mild distress due to dyspnea.

ASSESSMENT:
Acute asthma exacerbation, moderate severity. Likely triggered by environmental allergens (dust). No signs of infection (afebrile, no purulent sputum).

PLAN:
1. Initiated nebulizer treatment with Salbutamol and Ipratropium. Patient responded well to initial dosing.
2. Prescribed oral prednisone 40mg daily for 5 days to reduce inflammation.
3. Increased maintenance inhaler to Budesonide 400mcg BID plus Formoterol 12mcg BID.
4. Referral to respiratory therapist at Clinica del Respiro for breathing exercises.
5. Advised on trigger avoidance, particularly regarding pet dander (cat Felice) and dust.
6. Follow-up in 2 weeks.
7. Return precautions: Immediate ER visit if SpO2 < 90%, severe chest pain, or unrelieved dyspnea.

CONTACT INFO FOR FAMILY:
Son: Mario (60), 035 123 456
Daughter: Elena (34) lives in Milan.

REFERRING PHYSICIAN:
Dottore Bianchi, San Raffaele Hospital

TREATING PHYSICIAN:
Dr. Silva, Sports Medicine Clinic, Bergamo
dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, Signora Rossi. Please have a seat. I see Dottore Bianchi from the San Raffaele Hospital referred you to us. What seems to be the issue today?

[patient] Good morning, Doctor. I am feeling very short of breath. It started yesterday evening. I was trying to climb the stairs in my apartment in Bergamo, and I just couldn't keep going.

[doctor] That sounds distressing. How long has this breathing difficulty been happening?

[patient] It has been getting worse for about three weeks. But yesterday was the worst. I had to stop and rest on the landing.

[doctor] Do you have a history of asthma?

[patient] Yes, I have had it since I was young. But it was well controlled. I use my inhaler, but yesterday it didn't seem to help as much as usual.

[doctor] I understand. Let's listen to your lungs. Please take a deep breath in... and out.

[patient] (inhales and exhales)

[doctor] I can hear some wheezing, particularly on the right side. Do you have any chest pain?

[patient] Not really pain, just tightness. Like a band around my chest. My daughter Elena is 34 years old, and she is very worried. She lives in Milan now.

[doctor] Your concern is valid. Let's check your oxygen levels. We will place this small clip on your finger.

[patient] Okay.

[doctor] Your oxygen saturation is 92%. That is a bit low. We need to improve this. Do you have any other medical conditions?

[patient] I have hypertension. I take medication for that. Also, my sister Giovanna has Hashimoto's disease, but I don't think I have that.

[doctor] Got it. Do you have any allergies?

[patient] No known allergies. I am allergic to dust, which is why I have asthma.

[doctor] Okay. Where were you when you felt this acute worsening?

[patient] I was in the kitchen. I was cleaning up after lunch. The dust from the flour and the old rug I was vacuuming nearby seemed to trigger it.

[doctor] That makes sense. Dust mites are a common trigger. Did you use your rescue inhaler?

[patient] Yes, I used the blue one. Salbutamol. I took two puffs, but it only helped for a few minutes.

[doctor] I see. I am going to give you some nebulizer treatment now to open up your airways. A nurse will bring the equipment.

[nurse] Hello, Signora Rossi. I am Lucia. I am going to set up the nebulizer for you. Please put this mask over your nose and mouth.

[patient] Thank you, Lucia.

[nurse] Please breathe in and out normally. Do not hold your breath.

[patient] (breathing through the mask)

[doctor] How are you feeling?

[patient] It is a little bit easier. I can feel the air coming in.

[doctor] Good. Let's keep this going for another five minutes. In the meantime, can you tell me about your daily routine? Do you do any physical activity?

[patient] I used to go to the Circolo Canottieri in Como for swimming. But I stopped two years ago because my knees hurt.

[doctor] Swimming is excellent for lung capacity. Why did you stop?

[patient] I had a fall in the pool area. I hit my head on the edge of the pool. It was a minor bump, but I was scared to go back.

[doctor] I am sorry to hear that. Have you had any headaches since then?

[patient] No, just a bruise. It healed quickly.

[doctor] Okay. Do you have a partner or family here in Bergamo?

[patient] My husband passed away five years ago. I live with my son, Mario. He is 60 years old. He works as a banker.

[doctor] Is he here today?

[patient] No, he is at work. I called him. He said he would come later. His phone number is 035 123 456 if you need to reach him.

[doctor] Noted. How is your sleep?

[patient] Not very well. I wake up at 3 am coughing. I have to sit up to breathe.

[doctor] That is a sign of nocturnal asthma. We need to adjust your maintenance medication. You are currently on what?

[patient] I take a pink inhaler, Budesonide, twice a day.

[doctor] I see. I am going to increase the dose slightly and add a long-acting beta-agonist. This will help keep your airways open for longer.

[patient] Is that safe?

[doctor] Yes, it is a standard treatment. The side effects are usually mild, like a slight tremor or fast heartbeat. Do you have a history of heart problems?

[patient] No, just the high blood pressure.

[doctor] Good. We will monitor that. Do you have a cat or dog at home?

[patient] I have a cat. His name is Felice.

[doctor] Cat dander can also be a trigger. Have you noticed if he is around when your symptoms are worse?

[patient] He sleeps on my bed. Maybe I should make him sleep elsewhere?

[doctor] That might be a good idea. Let's see if the treatment helps. I am going to prescribe you a short course of oral steroids to reduce the inflammation in your lungs.

[patient] Steroids? I am a bit afraid of those.

[doctor] It is a short course, only five days. It will help bring the swelling down quickly. The long-term risks are not an issue for such a short period.

[patient] Okay. I will take them.

[doctor] Also, I am referring you to a respiratory therapist for breathing exercises. They can teach you techniques to help you breathe easier.

[patient] Where is that?

[doctor] It is at the Clinica del Respiro in Bergamo. I will write you a referral. You can call them at 035 987 654 to book an appointment.

[patient] Thank you, Doctor. I will call my son and ask him to help me make the appointment.

[doctor] That sounds like a good plan. Do you have any other questions?

[patient] No, I think that is all. I just want to be able to breathe normally again.

[doctor] We will work on that. I will see you in two weeks to check your progress. In the meantime, if you feel worse, especially if your oxygen drops or you have severe chest pain, go to the emergency room immediately.

[patient] I will do that. Thank you for your help.

[doctor] You are welcome, Signora Rossi. Take care.

[patient] Goodbye, Doctor.

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Palpitations and shortness of breath.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Carlos Javier Mendoza, a 33-year-old male, presented to the pulmonology clinic for evaluation of new-onset atrial fibrillation. He reports that approximately last week, at 2:30 pm, he experienced sudden onset of rapid, irregular heartbeats while at work as a data analyst. He described the sensation as "fluttering" in the chest, accompanied by dizziness and mild dyspnea. He denied chest pain. He sought care at the Kantonsspital Aarau emergency department, where an ECG confirmed atrial fibrillation. Blood work showed normal thyroid function (TSH, T4) and electrolytes, with mildly elevated inflammatory markers. He has no prior history of cardiac arrhythmias. He attributes the episode to possible viral illness, noting a mild cold two weeks prior. He moved from Barcelona, Spain to Zurich, Switzerland five years ago. He resides in the Zürichberg neighborhood.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Constitutional: No fever, chills, or significant weight loss.
Cardiovascular: Palpitations, dizziness. No chest pain, orthopnea, or PND.
Respiratory: Mild dyspnea during the episode. No cough or hemoptysis.
Gastrointestinal: No nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain.
Neurological: No focal deficits, slurred speech, or unilateral weakness.
Musculoskeletal: No joint pain or swelling.
Skin: No rashes or lesions.
Psychiatric: No anxiety or depression reported.
Family History: Father Roberto, 58, has hypertension. Mother Elena, 55, had a stroke ten years ago. Brother Diego, 30, is healthy.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vitals: BP 130/85, HR 110, RR 18, Temp 36.8°C, SpO2 98% on room air.
General: Well-appearing, no acute distress.
Heart: Tachycardic, irregularly irregular rhythm. No murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation bilaterally. No wheezes or crackles.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender. A small, mobile, non-tender mass is palpable at the 3 o'clock position relative to the navel.
Extremities: No edema, pulses intact.
Neurological: Cranial nerves II-XII intact. Motor strength 5/5 in all extremities.

RESULTS
ECG (ED): Atrial fibrillation, ventricular rate ~110 bpm.
Blood Work: TSH 2.5 mIU/L, T4 8.5 ug/dL (normal). Electrolytes within normal limits. CRP mildly elevated at 8 mg/L.
Imaging: No imaging performed today.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Atrial fibrillation, new onset.
- Plan: Initiate rate control with metoprolol 50 mg twice daily.
- Schedule echocardiogram to assess cardiac structure and function.
- Consider cardioversion if rhythm does not convert spontaneously within 48 hours or if symptoms persist.
- Monitor for signs of thromboembolism.
- Patient educated on warning signs (chest pain, severe dizziness, focal neuro deficits) and instructed to seek emergency care if they occur.

2. Abdominal mass (suspected lipoma).
- Plan: CT scan of abdomen/pelvis with contrast to characterize the mass at the 3 o'clock position.
- Follow up with results in one week.

3. Lifestyle modifications.
- Advise reduction in alcohol and caffeine intake.
- Continue beta-blocker as prescribed; do not discontinue without consultation.

4. Follow-up.
- Return to clinic in three months for rhythm assessment and medication adjustment.
- Results sent to Dr. Keller at Practice Zurich Central.
- Patient to use patient portal for updates.

St. Hedwig Clinic
Munich

note:
RE: Maria Silva, RM-2024-89431
Date: October 12, 2023

Dear Dr. James Thorne,

I am writing to refer my patient, Maria Silva, a 41-year-old female, to your care for further evaluation and management of bilateral breast hypertrophy.

History of Present Illness:
The patient is a logistics coordinator at LogistiCare Italia and resides in Milan. She is originally from Brazil. She presents with a six-month history of progressive bilateral breast enlargement, which she describes as significant heaviness and discomfort. The onset was gradual, without associated pain or nipple discharge. She reports difficulty sleeping on her side and physical strain during her work duties, which involve lifting. She denies recent weight gain.

Past Medical History:
- Crohn's disease (diagnosed 2020), currently in remission on Salazopyrin.
- Insulin resistance, managed with Metformin.
- Right knee injury sustained at the gym last month, diagnosed with a Baker's cyst.
- No history of Parkinson's, Bell's palsy, or other neurological conditions.

Family History:
- Sister, Ana (45), has Hashimoto's thyroiditis.
- Mother had Graves' disease.
- Son, Pedro (14) and daughter, Sofia (10), are healthy.

Social History:
- Non-smoker, occasional alcohol use.
- Lives with her partner and children.

Medications:
- Metformin 500 mg twice daily.
- Salazopyrin 500 mg twice daily.

Physical Examination:
- General: Well-appearing, no acute distress.
- Breast Exam: Significant bilateral hypertrophy. Glandular tissue is dense. Palpation reveals mild tenderness at the 3 o'clock position on the right breast, likely due to mechanical stress. No discrete masses, skin changes, or nipple discharge.
- Musculoskeletal: Mild right knee effusion consistent with her known Baker's cyst.

Assessment:
1. Bilateral breast hypertrophy, cause undetermined. Differential includes primary hypertrophy, hormonal imbalance (pituitary/thyroid), or medication side effect (less likely).
2. Crohn's disease, stable.
3. Right knee Baker's cyst.

Plan:
- Ordered comprehensive metabolic panel, including prolactin, testosterone, estradiol, TSH, and Free T4.
- Mammography and Breast Ultrasound scheduled for next Tuesday.
- Referral to University of Milan Breast Center for specialist evaluation regarding potential reduction mammaplasty if hypertrophy proves refractory to medical management or causes severe functional impairment.

Please let me know if you require any additional information.

Sincerely,

Dr. Elena Rossi
Ospedale San Raffaele
Milan

[doctor] Good morning. I see you are here with Dr. Rossi. Please, have a seat. How are you feeling today?
[patient] Good morning, doctor. I’m... um, I’m doing okay, I guess. It’s just really heavy, you know? I’ve been struggling with this for a while now.
[doctor] I understand. Let’s take a look. Can you describe when you first noticed this change?
[patient] Well, it started... um, maybe six months ago? It wasn't painful, just... heavy. I’m 41, so I thought maybe it was just weight gain, but I haven’t eaten differently.
[doctor] I see. And who referred you here, just so I have the right context?
[patient] It was my general practitioner, Dr. Elena Rossi. She works at the Ospedale San Raffaele clinic in Milan. She said I should see a rheumatologist because she was worried about inflammation or something related to my joints.
[doctor] Okay, Dr. Rossi is a fine colleague. Thank you. Let’s do a quick physical exam. Please remove your top. I’ll be in and out quickly.
[patient] Yes, of course. Here you go.
[doctor] Thank you. So, I can see significant bilateral enlargement. Let’s palpate. Does this hurt?
[patient] No, not really. Just a dull ache sometimes, especially when I lift things.
[doctor] I’m feeling the tissue here. Is there any tenderness at this specific spot?
[patient] Oh, that’s a little sore. Why there?
[doctor] Just mapping it out. I’m checking for any discrete masses or cysts. At the 3 o'clock position, I feel a slight firmness, but it seems consistent with the glandular tissue, not a distinct lump.
[patient] Okay. I’m just glad it’s not a tumor, you know? My friend Maria had a scare last year.
[doctor] We will order imaging to be sure. But let’s talk about your history. You mentioned you are from Brazil?
[patient] Yes, I’m from São Paulo. I moved to Italy about five years ago. I work as a logistics coordinator for LogistiCare Italia. It’s a stressful job, lots of lifting boxes.
[doctor] That physical demand could certainly exacerbate any discomfort in the chest wall. Do you have any other medical conditions?
[patient] Well, my sister, Ana, who is 45, has Hashimoto's thyroiditis. And my mother had Graves' disease. I’ve had some fatigue, but I don’t have the eye problems Graves causes.
[doctor] Family history of autoimmune thyroid disease is noted. Have you had any joint pain or swelling?
[patient] Um, my knees have been acting up. I fell at the gym last month. I twisted my knee and I think I have a Baker's cyst now. The physio said it was swollen.
[doctor] I see. And have you ever had any facial weakness or numbness?
[patient] No, no facial issues. I read about Bell's palsy online and got scared when I had a headache, but it was just tension.
[doctor] Understood. What about your gastrointestinal health?
[patient] I have had some stomach issues. I was diagnosed with Crohn's disease three years ago. It’s mostly in remission, but I’m sensitive to certain foods.
[doctor] Okay. And have you had any tremors or movement issues?
[patient] No, I don’t have Parkinson's or anything like that. My hands are steady.
[doctor] Good. Let’s talk about your medications.
[patient] I take Metformin for insulin resistance, and I use Salazopyrin for my Crohn's.
[doctor] Do you take any hormonal contraceptives?
[patient] No, I don’t use any hormones. I have a son, Pedro, he is 14. And a daughter, Sofia, she is 10.
[doctor] Thank you. Your medical record number is RM-2024-89431. I’ll be entering this into the system.
[patient] Yes, I have my card here.
[doctor] Do you have any allergies?
[patient] No, no drug allergies. Just penicillin for the rash, but I think I’m out of that.
[doctor] We will note that. Now, regarding the breast hypertrophy. This condition can be primary, meaning it develops during puberty, or secondary, due to medications or other conditions. Given your age and onset, it’s likely related to hormonal fluctuations or medication side effects, though you mentioned no hormones.
[patient] Could it be my Crohn's meds?
[doctor] It’s possible, but Salazopyrin is not typically associated with breast growth. However, significant weight fluctuations or other metabolic factors could play a role. We need to rule out a pituitary issue or other endocrine causes.
[patient] So what happens next?
[doctor] I’m going to order an ultrasound of the breasts and a blood panel. We need to check your prolactin, testosterone, estrogen, and thyroid function.
[patient] Okay. How long will that take?
[doctor] The blood test can be done today. The ultrasound needs an appointment. I’ll schedule it for next Tuesday.
[patient] That works. I can be there at 9:00.
[doctor] Perfect. I’ll also refer you to a breast specialist, Dr. James Thorne, at the University of Milan Breast Center, for a second opinion on the hypertrophy itself, as it may require surgical consultation if it becomes debilitating.
[patient] Oh, is surgery an option?
[doctor] Reduction mammaplasty is an option if the hypertrophy is causing significant physical or psychological distress. But first, we must understand the cause. If it’s hormonal, we might manage it medically.
[patient] That’s a relief. I just can’t sleep on my side anymore. It’s very uncomfortable.
[doctor] I understand. We will manage the pain in the meantime. I’ll prescribe some topical anti-inflammatories for the skin irritation you might be experiencing from the weight.
[patient] Thank you, doctor. I appreciate you listening.
[doctor] Of course. Please call the clinic if you have any worsening symptoms or if you notice any new lumps.

Fatigue, leg swelling, and dizziness upon standing.

Marguerite is a 92-year-old woman presenting with increased fatigue and bilateral lower extremity edema for the past two weeks. She reports difficulty walking and heavy legs, particularly in the evenings. She also experiences orthostatic dizziness, usually in the morning around 7:00. She has a history of hypertensive heart disease, chronic kidney disease stage 4, and heart failure. She is currently taking Norvasc and Cozaar daily. She mentions occasional forgetfulness with medications, for which her neighbor, Jean, helps her. She is semi-retired and works as a bookkeeper at Comptabilité Rhin. She resides in Strasbourg. She is active in the Les Crochets de la Paix knitting club, meeting on Fridays.

Constitutional: Fatigue, no fever.
Cardiovascular: Palpitations denied, dizziness present.
Respiratory: No dyspnea at rest, mild orthopnea.
Gastrointestinal: No nausea or vomiting.
Neurological: No focal deficits.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Blood pressure: 145/85 mmHg.
Heart: Regular rate and rhythm. A systolic murmur is heard at the 3 o’clock position.
Lungs: Bilateral basilar crackles noted.
Extremities: 2+ pitting edema in bilateral lower extremities.
General: Alert and oriented.

RESULTS
Laboratory results from last week show stable kidney function for stage 4 CKD. Electrolytes are within normal limits.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
1. Hypertensive heart disease with heart failure:
- Increase Lasix to manage fluid overload.
- Monitor electrolytes after adjustment.
2. Chronic kidney disease stage 4:
- Continue current management.
- Avoid nephrotoxic agents.
3. Orthostatic hypotension:
- Evaluate for medication side effects.
- Advise slow position changes.

- Next appointment on the 15th of next month at 10:00.
- Results will be sent to marguerite.dubois@orange.fr.
- Coordination with Dr. Laurent for general care.

note:
REFERRAL LETTER

Dear Dr. Samuel Weber,

I am writing to refer Arjun Nair, 72 years old, born on 14 March 1952, for the evaluation and excision of a suspicious melanocytic nevus.

The patient is a resident of Zurich. He presented to my clinic with a complaint of a changing pigmented lesion on his lower back, first noticed approximately six weeks ago. He reports that the lesion has increased in size and darkness. He also mentions a recent trip to Bali in January, during which he was exposed to significant sunlight.

Upon examination, I noted an asymmetric, irregularly bordered, and variegated nevus on the lower right back, measuring approximately 8 mm in diameter. The patient reports mild itching, with a pain score of 2/10. There is no bleeding or crusting. Several other stable nevi were noted on the trunk.

The patient’s medical history includes hypertension, managed with medication, and Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, diagnosed five years ago. He has a family history of melanoma in his father, who passed away in 2002. He has no known drug allergies. He takes Omeprazole daily for acid reflux.

Vital signs today: Blood pressure 130/80 mmHg, Heart rate 72 bpm.
Laboratory values (ordered today): Complete Blood Count, Basic Metabolic Panel.

I have ordered a full excision biopsy to be performed at your earliest convenience. Please send the pathology report to my attention at the Rossi Medical Practice.

Thank you for seeing him.

Sincerely,

Dr. Elena Rossi
Rossi Medical Practice
Zurich
dialogue:
[doctor] good morning . i’m dr . elena rossi . please , have a seat .
[patient] uh , good morning . yes , thank you .
[doctor] so , the reason for this visit is the marks on your trunk that you mentioned in your message ?
[patient] yes , exactly . you know , it’s been bothering me . i noticed them about , uh , three weeks ago .
[doctor] can you show me where they are ?
[patient] sure . they’re mostly here , on my lower back , and a few here on my chest .
[doctor] let’s take a look . please , unbutton your shirt .
[patient] okay .
[doctor] let’s look at this one here on your right side . it’s quite dark .
[patient] yes , it’s very black . and it’s a bit bigger than the others .
[doctor] it does look asymmetric . and the borders are a bit irregular .
[patient] is that bad ?
[doctor] not necessarily , but we need to be careful . do you have any pain there ?
[patient] uh , no , not really . maybe a tiny bit if i press hard , but it’s more of an itch .
[doctor] and any bleeding or crusting ?
[patient] no , no bleeding . just the itch .
[doctor] okay . how long have you had these spots ?
[patient] i think i’ve had the small ones for years . but this big one.. . it appeared , uh , recently .
[doctor] recently , like what , last month ?
[patient] yes , maybe six weeks ago . i was in the garden , you know , working on my tomatoes .
[doctor] and did you notice any change in color or size since then ?
[patient] it got darker , i think . and a bit flatter .
[doctor] let’s check your vitals just to be safe . can you roll up your sleeve ?
[patient] sure .
[doctor] blood pressure is 130 over 80 . heart rate is 72 . that’s normal .
[patient] good .
[doctor] do you have any other medical conditions ?
[patient] well , i have high blood pressure , but it’s controlled . and my brother has parkinson’s , so i’m a bit worried about that , but i don’t have it .
[doctor] understood . any history of skin cancer in your family ?
[patient] no , i don’t think so . my father had melanoma , but that was many , many years ago .
[doctor] when was that ?
[patient] oh , in 1995 . he passed away in 2002 .
[doctor] i see . and do you have any allergies ?
[patient] no , no allergies . i take some medication for my stomach , though .
[doctor] what is that ?
[patient] omeprazole . for acid reflux . i’ve had it for about ten years .
[doctor] okay . and have you been traveling recently ?
[patient] yes , i was in bali in january .
[doctor] oh , that’s a sunny place . did you spend a lot of time in the sun ?
[patient] yes , quite a lot . i went surfing .
[doctor] did you use sunscreen ?
[patient] i tried , you know . but it was hot , so maybe not enough .
[patient] i’m a member of the zurich rowing club , so i’m used to being outside , but the sun in bali was different .
[doctor] that makes sense . let’s look at the other spots .
[patient] here , on my left shoulder .
[doctor] this one looks stable . regular borders , uniform color .
[patient] yes , i’ve had that one for a long time .
[doctor] and this one on your abdomen ?
[patient] i found this one yesterday . it’s small , but it’s reddish .
[doctor] it looks like an inflamed mole , or maybe a seborrheic keratosis . but given the other spot , we need to check it .
[patient] should i be worried ?
[doctor] i’m not saying it’s cancer . but the main one on your back has some features that make me want to remove it and have it looked at under a microscope .
[patient] so , a biopsy ?
[doctor] a full excision , actually . we want to make sure we get all the edges .
[patient] that sounds serious .
[doctor] it’s a precaution . it’s better to be safe .
[patient] okay . who will do it ?
[doctor] i can refer you to a dermatologist . specifically , dr . samuel weber at the city hospital zurich .
[patient] do i need an appointment ?
[doctor] yes . i’ll write a referral letter for you .
[patient] will you remove it here , or will he do it ?
[doctor] he will do it . it’s a minor procedure , usually done under local anesthesia .
[patient] how long does it take ?
[doctor] about 30 minutes . you can go home the same day .
[patient] and the results ?
[doctor] it takes about one to two weeks for the pathology report .
[patient] okay . what if it’s bad ?
[doctor] then we will discuss further treatment . but let’s not jump to conclusions .
[patient] right . i’m just.. . nervous .
[doctor] that’s normal . but the fact that you noticed it early is a good thing .
[patient] do i need to stop taking my omeprazole ?
[doctor] no , you can continue taking it . just make sure to tell dr . weber about it .
[patient] i do . i also have a mild case of hashimoto’s thyroiditis , diagnosed five years ago .
[doctor] okay , i’ll note that down . it’s good to have a full picture .
[patient] and my blood work , is that necessary ?
[doctor] we usually check a full blood count before any procedure . i’ll order that today .
[patient] okay .
[doctor] do you have any pain right now ?
[patient] no , not really . maybe a 2 out of 10 if i rub it .
[doctor] that’s manageable .
[patient] i was actually injured a bit last week , in the kitchen . i cut my finger while cutting onions .
[doctor] does that affect anything ?
[patient] no , it’s healed . i just wanted to mention it because i was worried about infection , but it’s fine .
[doctor] good to know . so , let’s summarize . we are going to refer you to dr . weber for an excision of the nevus on your back . we will also monitor the other spots .
[patient] and the small one on my abdomen ?
[doctor] we will keep an eye on it . if it changes , we will remove that too .
[patient] okay .
[doctor] i will send the referral to his office today .
[patient] thank you .
[doctor] do you have any other questions ?
[patient] just.. . is it common for men my age to get these ?
[doctor] yes , moles can appear or change at any age , especially after sun exposure .
[patient] i see .
[doctor] remember , any new mole , or a changing mole , should be checked .
[patient] i will .
[doctor] great . i’ll see you in two weeks for a follow-up , just to check on how you’re feeling and to get the pathology results if they’re ready .
[patient] okay .
[doctor] here is your referral letter .
[patient] thank you , doctor .
[doctor] you’re welcome . take care .

[patient] Yes, a 4 seems right. It’s not sharp pain, more like a deep ache and stiffness. I was trying to walk to the Limmat river last weekend, but I had to stop after just a few minutes because of the heat.

[doctor] That sounds like Uhthoff's phenomenon, which is common with MS. Have you been taking your medications as prescribed? You are on Avonex and Betaseron as per our previous plan.

[patient] I am taking them. However, my insurance, SanaCare, recently sent a letter asking for additional documentation. My insurance number is SC-9988776655. They questioned why I need both disease-modifying therapies.

[patient] Yes, I took a short trip to Geneva in May 2024 to see my sister, Marie. The climate was very different, and I think the change in altitude and temperature triggered the current symptoms.

[doctor] Environmental factors can indeed exacerbate MS symptoms. Let’s review your recent lab results. Your Vitamin D levels were low at 15 ng/mL, so we started you on Uvedose supplements. Have you been taking those?

[patient] Yes, I take the Uvedose daily. I also had a blood test in April 2024 that showed slightly elevated liver enzymes, which worried me.

[doctor] Those were likely transient. The follow-up test in June 2024 showed normalization. Your white blood cell count is currently 5.2 x 10^9/L, which is within normal limits. Your platelet count is 250 x 10^9/L.

[patient] That’s a relief. I had a minor injury in the kitchen a few weeks ago. I slipped on a wet floor and bruised my hip. It took a while to heal, and the pain was quite significant, around a 7/10 initially.

[patient] (Reads the line) Yes, it’s clear.

[doctor] Good. Your visual acuity is 20/20. Let’s talk about your daily routine. Do you have any difficulties with daily activities?

[patient] I have some trouble with fine motor skills. Buttoning my shirt takes a long time. I used to be very independent, but now I need a button hook.

[doctor] Occupational therapy can be very helpful for that. I will refer you to the outpatient OT department at Klinik Hirslanden. They are specialists in adaptive strategies.

[patient] That sounds good. I had a previous therapy session there in January 2024, and it was very useful.

[doctor] I’m glad to hear that. Let’s review your medication list again. You are currently taking Avonex once a week, Betaseron every other day, Uvedose daily, and Omeprazole as needed. Do you have any side effects from these?

[patient] The Betaseron sometimes gives me flu-like symptoms for a day after the injection. The Avonex is generally well-tolerated.

We will monitor your Vitamin D levels in three months. I am referring you to occupational therapy at Klinik Hirslanden. You should follow up with me in August 2024.

note:
SUBJECTIVE
Giuseppe Rossi, a 79-year-old male, presents to the emergency department with a chief complaint of rapid weight gain and bilateral lower extremity edema. The patient reports a 5 kg weight increase over the past three weeks. He states the symptoms began after returning from a trip to Porto, Portugal, which concluded on October 19. He notes worsening dyspnea on exertion and orthopnea, requiring three pillows to sleep. He reports waking up 3-4 times per night to urinate. He denies chest pain, palpitations, or fever. He reports a pain score of 3/10 in the ankles due to tightness. He admits to increased salt intake following his trip. He is currently taking Lasix 20 mg daily and Levothyroxine 75 mcg daily. He has a history of hypertension and Hashimoto's thyroiditis. His family history is notable for his mother having thyroid disease and his brother Marco having similar issues. He lives in Milan, Italy.

OBJECTIVE
Vital Signs: BP 150/95 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, RR 18/min, Temp 36.8°C, SpO2 96% on room air.
Physical Exam:
General: Alert, oriented x3, in no acute distress.
HEENT: No jugular venous distension.
Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm, no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Lungs: Bilateral crackles heard at the bases, extending to the mid-lung fields.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender, no hepatomegaly.
Extremities: 3+ pitting edema in bilateral lower extremities, extending up to the shins. Skin is dry.
Neurological: No focal deficits.

Assessment
1. Acute decompensated heart failure vs. Nephrotic syndrome vs. Hypothyroidism exacerbation. The rapid weight gain and edema are concerning for fluid overload. The history of hypertension and recent high salt intake supports a cardiac or renal etiology. The history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis suggests a possible contribution from hypothyroidism, though the acute nature makes this less likely as the sole cause.
2. Chronic Kidney Disease (Stage 3), as evidenced by elevated creatinine from recent labs at Ospedale San Raffaele on October 25.
3. Hypertension, poorly controlled.

PLAN
1. Diagnostics:
   - Echocardiogram to evaluate left ventricular ejection fraction and wall motion.
   - Chest X-ray to assess for pulmonary edema and pleural effusion.
   - Repeat basic metabolic panel, including electrolytes, BUN, and creatinine.
   - Thyroid function tests (TSH, Free T4) to rule out hypothyroidism exacerbation.
   - Urinalysis and urine protein-to-creatinine ratio to evaluate for nephrotic syndrome.
2. Medications:
   - Continue home medications: Lasix 20 mg PO daily, Levothyroxine 75 mcg PO daily.
   - Consider IV diuresis if inpatient admission is required.
3. Dietary Advice:
   - Strict sodium restriction (< 2 g/day).
   - Fluid restriction to 1.5 L/day pending further evaluation.
4. Follow-up:
   - Patient to follow up with his cardiologist, Dr. Bianchi, at Ospedale San Raffaele within 48 hours.
   - Patient advised to contact Anna (dietitian) at anna.dieta at libero dot it for dietary support.
   - Return precautions: Return to ED for worsening dyspnea, chest pain, or syncope.
dialogue:
[nurse] Good morning, Mr. Rossi. I see you're here for that sudden weight gain. Can I check your vitals quickly before the doctor comes in?
[patient] Sure, sure. Just... um, I feel a bit heavy lately. Like, really heavy. Not just in the body, you know, but in the spirit.
[nurse] Okay, let's start with the blood pressure. Relax your arm.
[patient] It’s been a stressful few weeks. I just got back from Porto. Beautiful city, but the food... well, the food was incredible, but I think I overdid it.
[nurse] Blood pressure is 150 over 95. Heart rate is 88. Respiratory rate is 18. Oxygen saturation is 96 percent on room air. You look a bit puffy around the ankles.
[patient] Yes! The ankles. My shoes are tight. I used to wear a 42, now I need a 43, maybe 44. It’s been happening for about three weeks.
[nurse] I’ll let the doctor know. Do you have any pain?
[patient] Not really pain, just discomfort. Maybe a 3 out of 10 if I push on the swollen part. It’s mostly just the swelling.
[nurse] Okay. The doctor will be with you shortly.
[doctor] Hello, Mr. Rossi. I’m Dr. Silva. I see the nurse has checked your vitals. How can I help you today?
[patient] Doctor, I’m Giuseppe Rossi. I’m seventy-nine years old. I live in Milan. I’m worried because I’ve gained about five kilograms in just three weeks. Five kilos!
[doctor] That is a significant amount of weight gain in a short period. Can you tell me more about when this started?
[patient] It started right after I returned from my trip. I went to Porto for my niece’s wedding. It was October 12. I came back on October 19. I noticed the swelling in my ankles by October 22.
[doctor] Okay, and since then, has it gotten worse?
[patient] Yes, every day it’s a little worse. My neighbor, Luigi, saw me the other day and said I looked like a balloon. He’s a dear man, but he’s blunt.
[doctor] I understand. Have you noticed any shortness of breath?
[patient] A little. When I walk up the stairs in my apartment in Como—wait, I live in Milan, but I spent some time in Como with my sister. Yes, I get winded. It’s like... uh, my lungs are full of water.
[doctor] And do you have to sleep with extra pillows?
[patient] Yes, I have to sleep with three pillows now. Two is not enough. I wake up in the night needing to go to the bathroom.
[doctor] How often are you waking up?
[patient] Maybe three or four times a night. It’s disrupting my sleep.
[doctor] I see. Let’s talk about your medical history. Do you have any known heart conditions?
[patient] I had a check-up with my cardiologist, Dr. Bianchi, at Ospedale San Raffaele last year. He said my heart was fine, but I have high blood pressure. I take Lasix daily.
[doctor] Are you taking your medication regularly?
[patient] Yes, every morning at 8:00. I never miss it. I am very disciplined.
[doctor] Good. Have you changed your diet recently?
[patient] Well, as I said, the trip to Porto... and since then, I’ve been eating more salt. I miss the food. I’m an old man, I can’t resist a good piece of cheese.
[doctor] High salt intake can cause fluid retention. But five kilograms is quite a lot for just salt. Let’s look at your labs. I see you had some blood tests done at Ospedale San Raffaele on October 25.
[patient] Yes, I went there because I was feeling tired. The nurse took my blood.
[doctor] Those results show that your kidney function is slightly impaired. Your creatinine is elevated.
[patient] What does that mean?
[doctor] It means your kidneys aren’t filtering as well as they should. This can lead to fluid buildup.
[patient] But I don’t have pain in my back or anything.
[doctor] Kidney issues don’t always cause pain. Let’s check your thyroid as well. I recall you have a history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis.
[patient] Yes, my mother had it too. She passed away when I was twenty. I think it runs in the family. My brother, Marco, also has thyroid problems.
[doctor] Are you taking thyroid medication?
[patient] Yes, Levothyroxine. I take it every morning, on an empty stomach.
[doctor] Have you noticed any other symptoms? Dry skin, hair loss, constipation?
[patient] My skin is a bit dry, yes. And my hair... well, I’m seventy-nine, so it’s thinning anyway. But I do feel cold more than usual.
[doctor] That can be consistent with hypothyroidism, but your weight gain is acute, so we need to rule out heart failure or kidney issues.
[patient] Doctor, I’m scared. I don’t want to die.
[doctor] I understand. We are going to investigate this thoroughly. I’m going to order an echocardiogram to check your heart function.
[patient] Will it hurt?
[doctor] No, it’s painless. We’ll also do an X-ray of your chest to see if there is fluid in your lungs.
[patient] Okay. And the blood tests?
[doctor] We’ll repeat the blood tests to check your electrolytes and kidney function again.
[patient] Do I need to stop my medication?
[doctor] No, continue your current medications for now. But avoid high-salt foods. Try to eat fresh vegetables and lean proteins.
[patient] I’ll try. I’ll call my friend Anna, she is a dietitian, and ask her for advice. Her email is anna.dieta at libero dot it.
[doctor] That’s a good idea. In the meantime, if you notice any severe shortness of breath, chest pain, or if you cannot breathe while lying flat, come back to the emergency department immediately.
[patient] I will. I’ll be careful.
[doctor] Let’s get you started on the tests. A nurse will guide you to the radiology department.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor. You are very kind.
[doctor] It’s my job. Take care, Mr. Rossi.
