[doctor] Good morning. Please, have a seat. I see you’re here for a follow-up on your headaches. How have you been since we last spoke?
[patient] Um, honestly, it’s been a bit of a rollercoaster. I’ve had maybe three or four bad ones since then.
[doctor] I see. And what does a "bad one" look like for you now?
[patient] Well, it’s usually that throbbing pain on the left side. And the light sensitivity is still really bad. I have to stay in a dark room for hours.
[doctor] Do you get the aura with these?
[patient] Sometimes. Just those zig-zag lines. But mostly it’s just the pain and the nausea. I take my sumatriptan, and it helps, but it takes a while to kick in.
[doctor] How often are you taking that acute medication?
[patient] Uh, maybe once a week? Or every ten days? I’m trying to be careful because I don’t want to get overusing it.
[doctor] That’s a good instinct. Overuse can actually make migraines worse. Now, are there any new symptoms? Any weakness, speech issues, or vision changes that are different from the usual?
[patient] No, no. Just the standard stuff. I did notice some stiffness in my neck though. It’s tight, especially in the morning.
[doctor] Okay. I’m going to check your neck mobility just to be safe. Please turn your head to the right.
[patient] There.
[doctor] And to the left.
[patient] Ouch. That’s the tight side.
[doctor] I notice there is some tenderness at the 3 o'clock position of your right shoulder joint. Is that new?
[patient] Yeah, actually. I’ve been lifting a lot of boxes from my recent move.
[doctor] Ah, a move. Where did you move to?
[patient] We finally made it to Edinburgh. We left Manchester about two weeks ago.
[doctor] Edinburgh is a beautiful city. Did the move stress you out? Stress is a huge trigger.
[patient] Oh, definitely. It was chaotic. My sister, Sophie, came over to help us pack. She’s 42 and very energetic, but it was a lot to coordinate.
[doctor] And your husband? Is he David?
[patient] Yes, David. He’s 39. He’s been trying to keep calm, but he’s been under a lot of pressure at work lately.
[doctor] What does he do, if I may ask?
[patient] He’s a software engineer for a fintech firm called Novatek Solutions. They’re scaling up, so he’s working late.
[doctor] That sounds intense. How is your sleep?
[patient] Terrible. I’m waking up at 3 am most nights. I can’t seem to fall back asleep.
[doctor] Poor sleep definitely exacerbates migraine frequency. Have you changed any other medications?
[patient] No. I’m still on the propranolol you prescribed. I stopped the topiramate because I felt so foggy.
[doctor] That’s a reasonable decision. The cognitive side effects can be debilitating. Let’s talk about prevention. Since the acute treatment isn’t keeping you completely symptom-free, and your frequency is increasing, I think we should consider a preventive strategy.
[patient] Is there anything new? I’ve heard about those injections.
[doctor] Yes, there are several options. One class is CGRP inhibitors. They target a specific protein involved in migraine pathways. They’re given either monthly or every three months.
[patient] Do they work quickly?
[doctor] It usually takes a few months to see the full benefit. But many patients report a significant reduction in frequency and severity.
[patient] What about the side effects?
[doctor] Generally, they are well-tolerated. Some people get a sore injection site or a mild headache. It’s not like the systemic side effects of older drugs.
[patient] That sounds appealing. I just want to get my life back. I missed a work trip to Paris last month because I was in so much pain.
[doctor] I’m sorry to hear that. It’s frustrating when health limits your plans.
[patient] Yeah. My colleague, James, was going, but I had to cancel. He’s 35 and he was so nice about it, but I felt awful.
[doctor] Let’s try to prevent that from happening again. I’m going to refer you to our headache nurse specialist to discuss the specific CGRP options and insurance coverage.
[patient] Okay. Do I need to stop any other meds?
[doctor] No, you can continue the propranolol for now. We can review that later. But make sure you’re keeping a headache diary.
[patient] I have been. I log the time, the pain level, and what I ate.
[doctor] Excellent. Did you notice any food triggers?
[patient] I think aged cheese makes it worse. And red wine.
[doctor] Common triggers. Try to avoid those for the next few weeks and see if there’s a difference.
[patient] I will. Also, I’ve been seeing a physiotherapist for the neck stiffness.
[doctor] That’s good. Physical therapy can help with tension headaches which often co-exist with migraines.
[patient] The physiotherapist suggested some stretches. I do them every night.
[doctor] That’s a good habit. Now, before we finish, do you have any questions?
[patient] Um, what if I have a really severe one that the sumatriptan doesn’t touch?
[doctor] If it lasts more than 72 hours, or if it’s significantly different from your usual pattern, you should seek urgent care. But for a standard severe migraine, you can take the triptan and rest in a dark, quiet room.
[patient] Okay. And if I’m in Edinburgh, do I just go to the ER?
[doctor] Yes, the local emergency department at Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh would be appropriate if you feel you need immediate assessment.
[patient] Thanks. I’ll look up the number.
[doctor] I’ve listed the number on your discharge summary.
[patient] Great. One last thing. My mom, Clare, has Hashimoto's thyroiditis. She asks if I should get my thyroid checked.

[patient] I do feel a bit tired, but I blame the sleep.

dialogue:
[doctor] Good morning, Herr Gruber. Please, have a seat. I see you are here for a follow-up regarding your respiratory status. How have you been feeling since our last consultation?
[patient] It has been... manageable, Doctor. I am 53 years old, and my stamina is certainly not what it was when I was living in Graz. I moved to Vienna about two years ago, and the air quality feels different here.
[doctor] I understand. You mentioned moving from Graz. Did you continue with your respiratory physiotherapy here?
[patient] Yes. I am seeing a specialist at Universitätsklinik Wien. My brother, Lukas, who is 49, actually drove me there last week. He is very worried about my condition.
[doctor] It is good that you have support. Let’s look at your latest imaging. I am reviewing the CT scan from October 12, 2023. The findings show the expected changes in the left hemithorax.
[patient] Yes, the left side is gone, essentially. I had the surgery back in 2019. It was a difficult time. I was working as a structural engineer at the time, and I had to take a long leave.
[doctor] I recall that. You had a pneumonectomy. How is your compensation for the missing lung? Are you experiencing significant shortness of breath on exertion?
[patient] Only when I climb stairs. I live on the fourth floor in Wieden without an elevator. It is a struggle. But my daily activities are fine. I am trying to keep active.
[doctor] That is important. Let’s check your vitals. Your blood pressure is stable. Your oxygen saturation is 96% on room air, which is excellent for a post-pneumonectomy patient.
[patient] I am glad to hear that. I do get anxious sometimes, especially at night. I worry about waking up and not being able to breathe.
[doctor] Anxiety is common after such a major surgery. Have you discussed this with anyone? Perhaps your wife, Eva?
[patient] Eva is 50. She is very supportive, but I do not want to burden her. She works long hours as a nurse at AKH Wien.
[doctor] It is important to communicate with your partner. Stress can exacerbate respiratory symptoms. I would like to refer you to a psychologist who specializes in chronic respiratory conditions.
[patient] That sounds reasonable. By the way, my cousin, Thomas, who suffers from asthma, actually has a friend named Gruber who is a doctor. I think there is a genetic component, though I am not sure.
[doctor] Interesting. A family history of respiratory issues is worth noting. Does your mother, Anna, who is 78, have any lung problems?
[patient] No, she is very healthy. But my father passed away from heart disease in 2015. He was a smoker. I quit smoking in 2018, shortly before my diagnosis.
[doctor] That was a crucial decision. Let’s discuss your current medications. You are on a bronchodilator, correct?
[patient] Yes, I use my inhaler twice a day. I also take a daily multivitamin. I am not on any other prescription drugs.
[doctor] Good. I want to ensure you are up to date on your vaccinations. Have you had your flu shot this season?
[patient] No, I have not. I was planning to go to the pharmacy, but I have not found the time.
[doctor] I recommend you get it as soon as possible. I can administer it here, or you can go to your local pharmacy. Do you prefer that?
[patient] I would appreciate it if you could do it here. It saves me a trip.
[doctor] Certainly. We will schedule that. Also, I want to review your surgical history. The operation was performed on March 4, 2019, at LKH Graz. The surgeon was Dr. Hofmann.
[patient] Yes, Dr. Hofmann. He was very skilled. I remember the post-operative care was excellent. I stayed in the hospital for 14 days.
[doctor] That is a standard recovery period for that procedure. Did you experience any complications?
[patient] I had a small pleural effusion that drained for a few days, but otherwise, I recovered well. I started walking again within a week.
[doctor] That is positive. Let’s look at your physical exam. I am listening to your lungs. I hear clear breath sounds in the right lung. There is a slight crackle at the 3 o'clock position on the right base, which is likely due to mild atelectasis.
[patient] Is that serious?
[doctor] No, it is a minor finding. It is common in post-pneumonectomy patients due to the shift of the mediastinum. It does not require specific treatment, but we will monitor it.
[patient] Thank you. I feel a bit better knowing that. I do try to do some breathing exercises. I follow a routine I found online.
[doctor] That is good. Deep breathing exercises can help expand the remaining lung tissue. Ensure you are doing them correctly to avoid increasing intra-abdominal pressure.
[patient] I will be careful. I also do some light yoga. It helps with my posture.
[doctor] That is beneficial. Posture can affect lung capacity. Ensure you are not slouching, especially when sitting at your desk.
[patient] I work from home now, since the pandemic. I have a standing desk, which helps.
[doctor] That is an excellent setup. Ergonomics are important for respiratory health. Let’s discuss your lifestyle. Do you consume alcohol?
[patient] Occasionally, a glass of wine with dinner. Nothing excessive.
[doctor] That is acceptable. What about your diet?
[patient] I try to eat a balanced diet. I cook most of my meals myself. I enjoy baking, but I have cut down on sugar.
[doctor] Baking can be a hobby that involves flour dust, which might trigger respiratory symptoms. Do you wear a mask when baking?
[patient] I do. I learned my lesson. I once had a bad reaction to flour dust in the kitchen, and I started wheezing. So I wear a mask now.
[doctor] That is a smart precaution. The kitchen is a common place for inhalational triggers. Ensure your ventilation is good.
[patient] I have a range hood, and I open the windows. It helps a lot.
[doctor] Good. Let’s address your mental health. You mentioned anxiety. Have you tried any relaxation techniques?
[patient] I meditate for ten minutes every morning. It helps calm my mind.
[doctor] That is a valuable tool. Meditation can reduce the perception of breathlessness. I encourage you to continue.
[patient] I will. I also talk to my friend, Stefan, who is a therapist. He gives me good advice.
[doctor] It is good that you have a support network. Stefan sounds like a valuable resource.
[patient] He is. We meet twice a month for coffee.
[doctor] That is a good frequency. Let’s finalize our plan. I will order a follow-up chest X-ray in six months.
[patient] When should I come back for that?
[doctor] I have scheduled an appointment for you on April 15, 2024, at 10:30.
[patient] That works. I will add it to my calendar.
[doctor] Please confirm the appointment. You can reach us at +43 1 234 5678 or via email at contact@fam.med.vienna.at.
[patient] I will. Is there anything else I should watch out for?
[doctor] Watch for signs of infection, such as fever, increased sputum, or worsening shortness of breath. If you experience chest pain or severe dyspnea, go to the emergency room.
[patient] Understood. I will be vigilant.
[doctor] Also, ensure you stay hydrated. Dehydration can thicken mucus and make it harder to clear.
[patient] I drink plenty of water. About two liters a day.
[doctor] That is adequate. Let’s proceed with your flu vaccination. I will prepare the vaccine.
[patient] Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate your thoroughness.
[doctor] It is my duty to ensure you are as healthy as possible. Do you have any other concerns before we finish?
[patient] No, I think we have covered everything. I feel confident about my management plan.
[doctor] Good. I am glad to hear that. Take care of yourself, Herr Gruber.
[patient] Thank you. See you in April.
